    1   When Can Machines Learn?

    Before any algorithm, hyperparameter, or neural layer: what makes a problem learnable at all? This section sets up the language every later section reuses — target, hypothesis, data, algorithm, final hypothesis, $E_{\text{in}}$, $E_{\text{out}}$ — and gives the first feasibility argument for why fitting a sample can say anything about the future.

    1.1   Formula, program, or learning

    A computational problem is a mapping $f : \mathcal{I} \to \mathcal{O}$ from an input space to an output space. "Solving" the problem means producing $f$'s output on any input, and there are three fundamentally different ways to get there.

    Closed form. Sometimes $f$ collapses into an expression you evaluate directly. The classic derivation, redone here in full:

    $S = 1 + 2 + \cdots + n$the sum we want, written forwards
    $S = n + (n-1) + \cdots + 1$the same sum, written backwards
    $2S = \underbrace{(n+1) + (n+1) + \cdots + (n+1)}_{n \text{ terms}} = n(n+1)$add the two rows column-wise: every column sums to $n{+}1$
    $S = \dfrac{n(n+1)}{2}$divide by 2 — evaluation now costs one multiply and one halving

    Program, no closed form. $\displaystyle\prod_{i=1}^{n} i = n!$ has no algebraic shortcut, yet a three-line loop computes it exactly. Either way — formula or program — the answer is a deterministic box: input $\to \boxed{f} \to$ output.

    Formula vs. program, at $n = 100$. The closed form gives $\sum_{i=1}^{100} i = \frac{100 \cdot 101}{2} = $ 5050 in a single multiply-and-halve; naive iteration spends 99 additions to reach the same number. For $100!$ there is no formula to reach for at all — the exact value is a 158-digit integer (93326215443944152681…) that only computation can produce. Both problems are fully solved; neither needs a single training example.

    A third kind of problem resists both routes entirely. Nobody can write a formula for "the rating viewer $u_j$ would give movie $m_i$", and no first-principles procedure derives it — yet the answer is far from random.

    1.2   The Netflix problem example

    A streaming service holds a huge, mostly-empty matrix of ratings $r_{ij}$ (rows = viewers, columns = movies). Filling one missing cell is a prediction problem: the rating plausibly emerges from how well the viewer's taste profile $\mathbf{t} \in \mathbb{R}^k$ (how much they like romance, comedy, action, sci-fi, …) lines up with the movie's content profile $\mathbf{m} \in \mathbb{R}^k$ over the same $k$ factors — high alignment on the factors the viewer cares about should mean a high rating.

    Fig. 1.1 — Left: an illustrative sparse ratings matrix — most cells are unobserved (blank); the highlighted cell is the one we'd like to predict. Right: a toy 4-factor taste/content match: $\mathbf{t}\cdot\mathbf{m} = $ 1.22, mapped through the disclosed rule $\hat r = 1 + 4\cdot\frac{\mathbf{t}\cdot\mathbf{m}}{4}$ to a predicted rating of 2.22/5.

    Adjudication. v5's version of this figure asserts an inner product of $1.28$ mapping to "$\approx 4.2/5$" with no rule given for how a raw dot product becomes a 1–5 rating — an orphan number with no derivation. Rather than repeat an unexplained mapping, this figure uses its own toy profiles $\mathbf{t}=(0.9,0.2,0.6,0.1)$, $\mathbf{m}=(0.8,0.3,0.7,0.2)$ and an explicit, disclosed rescaling $\hat r = 1 + 4\cdot\frac{\mathbf{t}\cdot\mathbf{m}}{k}$ (with $k{=}4$ factors, each profile weight capped at 1, so the maximum possible inner product is $k$). The qualitative point — alignment between two learned profiles predicts an unobserved rating — is what matters here; the actual factorisation machinery (matrix factorisation / latent-factor models) is outside this course's scope.

    You cannot state $f$, but you can predict a friend's movie ratings once you know their taste — so a pattern exists. And the platform sits on hundreds of millions of filled cells — so data exists. That combination is exactly the opening machine learning needs: let the data reveal the mapping nobody can write down.

    1.3   The three screening questions

    Given a new problem, ask three questions in order. They decide whether ML is the wrong tool, the only tool, or doomed from the start.

    QuestionIf yesIf no
    1Can $f$ be pinned down mathematically / algorithmically?Write the formula or the program — ML is unnecessary (though still possible).Learning becomes the only route to $f$.
    2Is there a pattern connecting input to output?There is structure for a learner to latch onto.Nothing to learn: on unseen binary cases any predictor degenerates to a coin flip — error $\tfrac12$, no better than chance.
    3Is there data?Learning can proceed.No learning, full stop — a pattern cannot be extracted from zero observations.
    $$\boxed{\;\text{use ML} \iff \big(\text{no analytic pin-down of } f\big) \;\wedge\; \big(\text{a pattern exists}\big) \;\wedge\; \big(\text{data is available}\big)\;}$$

    Primality testing fails at question 1 — deterministic algorithms exist, full stop. The Netflix problem, loan approval, spam filtering, and digit recognition pass all three, which is why they anchor the rest of this course.

    Question 2 is the one people skip. If no pattern connects inputs to outputs, an algorithm will still happily fit the training set — it will memorise noise and predict at chance on everything unseen. "It ran and produced a $g$ with zero training error" is not evidence that learning happened. Section 1.4 makes precise what evidence would look like, and §7 (learning theory) extends it into a full guarantee.

    1.4   Feasibility intuition: can a sample ever prove anything about the future?

    Even when a pattern and data both exist, a subtler worry remains. A learner only ever sees a finite training sample $\mathcal{D}$; it is deployed on data it has never seen. Why should performing well on $\mathcal{D}$ say anything about performance on the unseen future? Define two error rates for a hypothesis $h$:

    $E_{\text{in}}(h)$ — the in-sample (training) error: the fraction of the $N$ training points $h$ gets wrong.
    $E_{\text{out}}(h)$ — the out-of-sample (true) error: the probability $h$ gets a fresh, unseen point wrong, over the whole input distribution.

    Only $E_{\text{in}}$ is ever computable from data in hand; $E_{\text{out}}$ is what we actually care about.

    The marble-jar analogy. Imagine a jar holding millions of marbles, each red or green, in some fixed but unknown proportion. $E_{\text{out}}(h)$ is the true fraction of red marbles in the whole jar (i.e. the true error rate of the fixed, already-chosen hypothesis $h$ on the whole population). You scoop out $N$ marbles at random; $E_{\text{in}}(h)$ is the fraction of red marbles in that scoop. The question "does a sample say anything about the population?" becomes: does the scoop's red fraction say anything about the jar's red fraction? Hoeffding's inequality answers yes, quantitatively, and the answer gets exponentially better as the scoop grows:

    $$P\!\left[\,|E_{\text{in}}(h) - E_{\text{out}}(h)| > \epsilon\,\right] \;\le\; 2\,e^{-2\epsilon^2 N} \qquad \text{for a fixed hypothesis } h.$$

    Reading the bound: $\epsilon$ is the tolerance ("how close is close enough"), $N$ is the sample size, and the right-hand side is a ceiling on the probability that $E_{\text{in}}$ and $E_{\text{out}}$ disagree by more than $\epsilon$. Crucially, this ceiling shrinks exponentially in $N$ — a small scoop is unreliable, a large one is not.

    Fig. 1.2 — The Hoeffding ceiling $2e^{-2\epsilon^2 N}$ against sample size $N$, for $\epsilon = 0.1$ and $\epsilon = 0.05$ (log scale on the vertical axis makes the exponential decay a straight line).

    Plugging in numbers. With $\epsilon = 0.1$ and $N = 200$: the bound gives $P[\,\cdot\,] \le 2e^{-2(0.01)(200)} = 2e^{-4} = $ 3.66%. So with $200$ training points, the chance that in-sample error is off from the true error by more than $10$ percentage points is under $4\%$. Want that risk under $1\%$ at the same $\epsilon$? Solving $2e^{-2(0.01)N} < 0.01$ numerically gives $N \ge$ 265 (at $N{=}265$ the bound is 0.998%). The exponential in the exponent makes data extremely valuable: doubling $N$ does not just halve the risk, it squares the improvement factor.

    The catch — and why this is only "intuition", not the full story. The bound above holds only for a hypothesis $h$ fixed before you look at the sample. But learning does the opposite: it searches $\mathcal{H}$ and returns the $g$ that looks best on this very sample — and "looks best on this sample" is precisely the kind of selection that can make $E_{\text{in}}$ optimistically biased relative to $E_{\text{out}}$ (think of $M$ separate marble jars, one per hypothesis in $\mathcal{H}$: the learner picks whichever jar's scoop looked reddest, and that pick is more likely to be a lucky/misleading scoop than any single jar chosen in advance). Bounding this multi-hypothesis effect — the union bound over $|\mathcal{H}|=M$, and later the VC dimension when $\mathcal{H}$ is infinite — is the full PAC / VC treatment of §07; this section only establishes that the single-hypothesis version of the question ("does a sample say anything at all?") has a solid, non-trivial "yes" for an answer.

    The scoop-vs-jar picture only means anything if the scoop was actually held out — in code, that discipline starts with the very first split of the data.

    Code — train/test split discipline (sklearn) 
    import numpy as np
from sklearn.model_selection import train_test_split

X = np.random.default_rng(0).normal(size=(200, 3))
y = (X[:, 0] + 0.5 * X[:, 1] > 0).astype(int)

# stratify keeps the same class ratio in both halves -- important whenever y is imbalanced
X_train, X_test, y_train, y_test = train_test_split(
    X, y, test_size=0.2, random_state=0, stratify=y
)

# E_in is whatever the model reports on X_train; E_out is only ever ESTIMATED, on data
# never touched during fitting -- X_test stands in for the population the Hoeffding bound is about

    random_state pins the split for a reproducible interview answer; stratify=y is the difference between an honest E_out estimate and a lucky/unlucky one whenever classes are imbalanced (the confusion-matrix metrics of §5 all assume this discipline was followed upstream).

    1.5   Anatomy of a supervised learner

    Every supervised algorithm covered in this course — perceptron through gradient boosting — instantiates one diagram with five components.

    SymbolObjectLoan-desk instance
    $f : \mathcal{X} \to \mathcal{Y}$unknown target functionthe true (unwritable) credit-worthiness rule
    $\mathcal{D} = \{(\mathbf{x}_i, y_i)\}_{i=1}^{N}$training examples drawn from $f$ (or from $f$ plus noise)past applicants, with observed repayment outcomes
    $\mathcal{H} = \{h_1, h_2, \ldots\}$hypothesis set — the candidate functions the algorithm is allowed to choose frome.g. all half-plane decision rules over the applicant's features
    $\mathcal{A}$learning algorithm — the search procedure over $\mathcal{H}$the perceptron rule of §2
    $g \in \mathcal{H}$, $g \approx f$final hypothesis $\mathcal{A}$ selectsthe deployed approval rule
    Fig. 1.3 — The supervised learning setup. The algorithm never observes $f$ directly — only the sample $\mathcal{D}$ that $f$ (plausibly noisily) generated — and it can only ever output a member of $\mathcal{H}$; there is no way to return a $g$ outside the hypothesis set, however good it might be.

    Two silent restrictions worth naming. First, $\mathcal{A}$ learns from $\mathcal{D}$ alone — if the sample misrepresents $f$ (biased collection, label noise, too few examples), no algorithm downstream can recover the truth from thin air. Second, $g$ is forced to come from $\mathcal{H}$ — if $f$ lies far outside anything $\mathcal{H}$ can express (e.g. fitting a straight line to an inherently curved boundary), even infinite, perfectly clean data leaves an irreducible gap. When both restrictions are respected, the informal promise "$g \approx f$" can be made precise as "$E_{\text{in}}(g) \approx E_{\text{out}}(g)$ and $E_{\text{in}}(g)$ is small" — the two halves of the generalisation story picked up again in §6 and §7.

    Before $\mathcal{D}$ can feed any algorithm, it has to be inspected — dtypes, missing values, and categorical columns are the first things worth checking on any new dataset.

    Code — pandas EDA quickstart (dtypes, missing, encoding) 
    import pandas as pd
import numpy as np

df = pd.DataFrame({
    "age": [25, 32, np.nan, 41, 29],
    "income": [45000, 52000, 61000, np.nan, 39000],
    "city": ["Pune", "Pune", "Mumbai", "Delhi", "Mumbai"],
})

df.dtypes                      # object = strings/mixed, float64 = numeric (NaN forces float even for whole numbers)
df.isna().sum()                # per-column missing count -- always check before fitting anything
df.describe(include="all")     # numeric summary stats + count/unique/top/freq for the object columns

# one-hot encoding: materialises one column per category, fine for linear models
pd.get_dummies(df, columns=["city"], drop_first=True)
# drop_first=True avoids the dummy-variable trap -- one column is a linear combination of
# the others otherwise, i.e. the exact multicollinearity in §2.6.2's X^T X singularity warning

# category dtype: keeps the column compact and lets tree/boosting models split on codes directly
df["city"] = df["city"].astype("category")
df["city"].cat.codes           # int codes a tree/boosting library can split on without expanding columns

    get_dummies expands categories into columns for models that need a real vector space (linear/logistic regression, KNN, SVM); category + cat.codes is the cheaper choice for tree-based models, which split on raw category identity and gain nothing from one-hot columns.

    1.6   One loan desk, three problem types example

    An applicant arrives with a feature vector $\mathbf{x}$ — say $x_1 =$ years of residence, $x_2 =$ salary in lakh. The bank can ask three different questions of this same $\mathbf{x}$, and each question defines a different learning problem with a different $\mathcal{Y}$.

    1 · Approve or not — classification. $\mathcal{Y} = \{+1, -1\}$. The natural hypothesis set is linear decision rules $h(\mathbf{x}) = \operatorname{sign}(w_0 + w_1 x_1 + w_2 x_2)$ — one hypothesis per weight vector $\mathbf{w} = (w_0, w_1, w_2)$. The boundary is where the score crosses zero:

    $w_0 + w_1 x_1 + w_2 x_2 = 0$the boundary = the set of points with zero evidence either way
    $w_2 x_2 = -w_0 - w_1 x_1$isolate the $x_2$ term
    $x_2 = -\dfrac{w_1}{w_2}\,x_1 \;-\; \dfrac{w_0}{w_2}$divide by $w_2 \ne 0$ — a straight line in the $(x_1, x_2)$ plane
    $\text{slope} = -\dfrac{w_1}{w_2}, \qquad \text{intercept} = -\dfrac{w_0}{w_2}$read off both — note the sign flip on each

    Many candidate lines from $\mathcal{H}$ separate past approvals from past rejections; the algorithm's job is to pick one. Fix $\mathbf{w} = (-8, 2, 1)$ as a worked instance:

    Fig. 1.4 — The decision rule $h(\mathbf{x}) = \operatorname{sign}(-8 + 2x_1 + x_2)$ on a synthetic applicant pool consistent with the same $\mathbf{w}$; applicants A $=(1,3)$ and B $=(3,4)$ from the worked example below are marked with stars.

    Scoring two applicants. With $\mathbf{w} = (-8, 2, 1)$, applicant A $= (x_1, x_2) = (1, 3)$ and applicant B $= (3, 4)$:

    $s_A = -8 + 2(1) + 1(3) = $ $-3 \;\Rightarrow\; h(A) = \operatorname{sign}(-3) = -1$negative evidence — reject
    $s_B = -8 + 2(3) + 1(4) = $ $+2 \;\Rightarrow\; h(B) = \operatorname{sign}(+2) = +1$positive evidence — approve

    and the boundary from step (1.6) above:

    $\text{slope} = -\dfrac{2}{1} = $ $-2$not $+2$ — the minus sign in the formula is not optional
    $\text{intercept} = -\dfrac{-8}{1} = $ $8$boundary: $x_2 = 8 - 2x_1$, the solid line in Fig. 1.4

    B clears the boundary by only $+2$ score units — near-boundary applicants are exactly where a classifier's specific choice of $g$ (out of the many candidates in $\mathcal{H}$) starts to matter. "Clearing the boundary by a lot" is the informal seed of the margin idea behind support vector machines (§17). $\mathbf{w}$ here was simply handed to us; learning — choosing $\mathbf{w}$ from $\mathcal{D}$ rather than being given it — is the subject of §2 onward.

    2 · How much to lend — regression. Same features, but now $\mathcal{Y} = \mathbb{R}$: predict the sanctioned loan amount rather than a verdict. The hypothesis set becomes real-valued linear functions $h(\mathbf{x}) = \mathbf{w}^{\!\top}\mathbf{x}$, and "best line" acquires the precise least-squares meaning derived with full matrix shapes in §2 (pseudo-inverse solution).

    3 · How risky — probability of default. Predict $P(\text{default} \mid \mathbf{x}) \in [0,1]$ from data labelled defaulter $(1)$ / non-defaulter $(0)$. A raw linear score $\mathbf{w}^{\!\top}\mathbf{x}$ ranges over all of $\mathbb{R}$, so it must be squashed into $[0,1]$ — the sigmoid link $\sigma(\mathbf{w}^{\!\top}\mathbf{x})$ derived from first principles (why the sigmoid, why cross-entropy and not squared error) in §3.

    Same raw feature vector $\mathbf{x}$, three different $\mathcal{Y}$s, three different hypothesis sets, three different loss functions downstream. The single most common beginner mistake is picking an algorithm before pinning down which of these three $\mathcal{Y}$s the problem actually has.

    1.7   The learning-paradigm taxonomy

    All three loan-desk questions above are supervised: every training input arrives paired with its correct output. Relaxing what the training signal contains produces the other paradigms.

    ParadigmTraining signalCanonical taskIn this course
    Supervisedlabelled pairs $(\mathbf{x}, y)$loan approval, spam filtering, digit recognition§2–§18
    Unsupervisedinputs $\mathbf{x}$ only — no labelscustomer segmentation, structure discovery§19–§20
    Reinforcementa reward / grade for actions taken — never the "correct" action itselfgame playing, sequential controlconceptual only
    Semi-superviseda few labelled examples plus a much larger unlabelled poolweb-page classificationconceptual only
    Fig. 1.5 — The taxonomy, ordered by how much of the "correct answer" the training signal reveals. Semi-supervised sits between supervised and unsupervised: it borrows structure from a large unlabelled pool and anchors that structure with a handful of labels.

    Semi-supervised learning matters in practice because labels are the expensive part of a dataset: crawling a million web pages costs almost nothing, paying annotators to tag each one does not. A handful of labels can orient the clusters an unlabelled mass reveals on its own.

    Interpretation. Section 1.3's three questions decide whether to learn at all. Section 1.4's Hoeffding bound is the first piece of evidence for why a finite sample can say something trustworthy about the unseen future — provided the hypothesis was fixed before the data was seen, a caveat that §07 spends an entire section resolving. Section 1.5's five-symbol anatomy — $f, \mathcal{D}, \mathcal{H}, \mathcal{A}, g$ — together with $E_{\text{in}}$/$E_{\text{out}}$, is the vocabulary every remaining section assumes without re-explaining. Sections 1.6–1.7 show that the same setup covers classification, regression, and probability estimation just by changing $\mathcal{Y}$ and the hypothesis set.

    1.8   Practice

    Practice 1.1 — Route four new scenarios

    For each, decide (a) direct algorithm or ML, and (b) if ML, which paradigm.

    1. Sort a list of $10^6$ numbers. A formula/algorithm exists (any $O(n\log n)$ sort) — question 1 already fails the ML test. Direct algorithm; no learning.
    2. Predict tomorrow's default probability from labelled repayment histories. No closed form for "true credit risk"; pattern (financial history $\to$ risk) and labelled data both exist. ML — supervised, probabilistic output (§03).
    3. Group $10^6$ customers by purchasing behaviour with no ground-truth segments. Data exists but there is no label — the grouping structure itself is the target. ML — unsupervised clustering (§19–§20).
    4. Train an agent to play a new board game, told only "win" or "lose" at the end. No per-move "correct answer", only a delayed scalar reward. ML — reinforcement learning (conceptual in this course).
    Practice 1.2 — Score two more applicants and read the boundary

    Using the same rule $h(\mathbf{x}) = \operatorname{sign}(-8 + 2x_1 + x_2)$, classify applicant C $= (2, 3)$ and applicant D $= (4, 1)$, and confirm both land on the correct side of the boundary line $x_2 = 8 - 2x_1$.

    C: $s_C = -8 + 2(2) + 1(3) = -8+4+3 = -1 \Rightarrow h(C) = -1$ (reject). Check against the boundary: at $x_1{=}2$ the line sits at $x_2 = 8 - 4 = 4$; C's $x_2{=}3 < 4$, i.e. C is below the line, consistent with a negative score (the region below/right of this particular line is the $-1$ side).

    D: $s_D = -8 + 2(4) + 1(1) = -8+8+1 = +1 \Rightarrow h(D) = +1$ (approve). At $x_1{=}4$ the line sits at $x_2 = 8-8=0$; D's $x_2{=}1 > 0$, i.e. D is above the line, consistent with a positive score.

    General rule confirmed: points above the line $x_2 = 8-2x_1$ score positive (approve), points below score negative (reject) — exactly what $w_2 = +1 > 0$ guarantees (increasing $x_2$ only ever increases the score).

    Practice 1.3 — How much data buys a given tolerance?

    Using the single-hypothesis Hoeffding bound $2e^{-2\epsilon^2 N} \le \delta$, how large must $N$ be for $\epsilon = 0.05$ to hold with the same $99\%$ confidence used in the worked example ($\delta = 0.01$)?

    Solve for $N$: $N \ge \dfrac{1}{2\epsilon^2}\ln\dfrac{2}{\delta} = \dfrac{1}{2(0.05)^2}\ln\dfrac{2}{0.01} = \dfrac{1}{0.005}\ln(200) = 200 \times 5.298 \approx 1060$.

    Halving $\epsilon$ (from $0.1$ to $0.05$) roughly quadruples the required $N$ (compare to the $N \approx 265$ needed for $\epsilon=0.1$ at a $1\%$ risk level in the worked example) — a direct consequence of $\epsilon$ appearing squared in the exponent. Tightening your tolerance is expensive; the bound rewards patience with data far more than it punishes impatience with tolerance.

    Practice 1.4 — Diagnose a broken learning setup

    A team trains a spam filter only on emails received by finance-department employees, then deploys it company-wide and finds it misses most engineering-team spam. Which of §1.5's "two silent restrictions" is violated, and why does more data not fix it?

    This is the first restriction: "$\mathcal{A}$ learns from $\mathcal{D}$ alone, and if $\mathcal{D}$ misrepresents $f$, no algorithm can recover." Here $f$ = the true company-wide spam/not-spam rule, but $\mathcal{D}$ was drawn only from the finance sub-population — a biased sample, not a small one. Collecting more finance-department emails would shrink the Hoeffding gap between $E_{\text{in}}$ and $E_{\text{out}}$ for the finance-only distribution, but $E_{\text{out}}$ as computed on the whole company is a different, unrelated quantity — no amount of same-source data closes that gap. The fix is a representative sample, not a bigger one.

    2   Linear Models: Perceptron, Pocket & Linear Regression

    §1 set up the vocabulary — target $f$, data $\mathcal{D}$, hypothesis set $\mathcal{H}$, algorithm $\mathcal{A}$, final hypothesis $g$ — and stopped at a hand-picked weight vector $\mathbf{w}=(-8,2,1)$ for the loan desk, with the promise that choosing $\mathbf{w}$ from $\mathcal{D}$ is what "learning" means. This section supplies the first three algorithms $\mathcal{A}$ that actually do the choosing.

    The oldest and simplest hypothesis class in this whole set of notes is the linear model: a hyperplane cutting through feature space. Three algorithms live on top of it — the perceptron (classification, hard boundary), pocket (classification, robust to noise), and least squares (regression). All three share one object: the weight vector $\mathbf{w}$, and one score: $\mathbf{w}^{\!\top}\mathbf{x}$.

    2.1   Setup: the linear score

    Given $d$ features $\mathbf{x} = (x_1,\dots,x_d)$, a linear model fits a decision boundary

    $$w_1 x_1 + w_2 x_2 + \cdots + w_d x_d + w_0 = 0.$$

    Augmenting with a dummy coordinate $x_0 = 1$ folds the bias $w_0$ into a single dot product. With $\mathbf{w} = (w_0, w_1, \dots, w_d) \in \mathbb{R}^{d+1}$ and $\mathbf{x} = (1, x_1, \dots, x_d) \in \mathbb{R}^{d+1}$,

    $$\sum_{i=0}^{d} w_i x_i = \mathbf{w}^{\!\top}\mathbf{x}.$$

    What differs between the three algorithms below is only what you do with this score:

    ModelOutputLoss driving the fit
    Perceptron$h(\mathbf{x}) = \operatorname{sign}(\mathbf{w}^{\!\top}\mathbf{x}) \in \{+1,-1\}$0/1 classification error, minimised by local correction (§2.2)
    Pocketsame sign rulesame 0/1 error, but tracked and kept, not just descended (§2.4)
    Linear regression$h(\mathbf{x}) = \mathbf{w}^{\!\top}\mathbf{x} \in \mathbb{R}$ (no sign)mean squared error, solved in closed form (§2.5)

    Where the model comes from — McCulloch–Pitts (1943). The original artificial neuron took binary inputs with hand-set weights and fired through a hard threshold: output $1$ iff $\sum_i w_i x_i \ge \theta$. Logic gates fall out immediately — $w=(1,1)$ with $\theta=1.5$ computes AND, the same weights with $\theta=0.5$ compute OR, and a negative weight builds NOT. What that unit could not do was learn: every weight was engineered by hand. Rosenblatt's perceptron (1958) is the same unit with the threshold folded into $w_0$, plus — crucially — the update rule below for choosing $\mathbf{w}$ from data.

    2.2   The delta rule — geometric derivation derivation

    Suppose we misclassify a training point $(\mathbf{x}, y)$ with $y \in \{+1,-1\}$. There are exactly two ways to be wrong.

    Case 1 — actual $y=+1$, predicted $\hat y = -1$

    Then $\mathbf{w}^{\!\top}\mathbf{x} < 0$: the angle between $\mathbf{w}$ and $\mathbf{x}$ is obtuse (score $=\|\mathbf{w}\|\|\mathbf{x}\|\cos\theta$). We want it acute. Adding $\mathbf{x}$ to $\mathbf{w}$ rotates $\mathbf{w}$ toward $\mathbf{x}$:

    $$\mathbf{w}_{\text{new}} = \mathbf{w} + \mathbf{x}. \qquad (1)$$

    Case 2 — actual $y=-1$, predicted $\hat y = +1$

    Now $\mathbf{w}^{\!\top}\mathbf{x} > 0$ (acute), and we want it obtuse. Subtracting $\mathbf{x}$ rotates $\mathbf{w}$ away from $\mathbf{x}$:

    $$\mathbf{w}_{\text{new}} = \mathbf{w} - \mathbf{x}. \qquad (2)$$

    Both cases fold into one line by multiplying $\mathbf{x}$ by $y$:

    $$\boxed{\;\mathbf{w}_{\text{new}} \leftarrow \mathbf{w} + y\,\mathbf{x}\;} \qquad \text{applied only when } y\,(\mathbf{w}^{\!\top}\mathbf{x}) \le 0.$$

    This is the delta rule (equivalently: the perceptron learning algorithm's update step). The condition $y(\mathbf{w}^{\!\top}\mathbf{x}) \le 0$ is the formal "misclassified" test — it is negative when the sign is wrong, and exactly $0$ at the boundary (by convention $\operatorname{sign}(0) = -1$, so a boundary point also counts as an error and triggers an update). Exactly one correction is applied per misclassified point; correctly classified points are left untouched.

    Filling a gap in the hand notes. hand p04 states the boxed update $w_{new} \leftarrow w + y\cdot x$ with no derivation and no statement of when it fires — flagged there as [DERIVATION GAP]. The two-case geometric argument above is that missing derivation, and the mistake condition $y\,\mathbf{w}^{\!\top}\mathbf{x}\le 0$ is the missing trigger. Separately, hand p04's sketch writes the boundary as $w^{T}x^{T}=0$ — the second transpose is a slip (transposing $\mathbf{x}$ a second time is dimensionally meaningless); the correct statement is $\mathbf{w}^{\!\top}\mathbf{x}=0$, used throughout this section.

    Interpretation. The delta rule is a local, greedy correction — it fixes the current mistake and nothing else. It says nothing about points not currently being visited, which is exactly why one update can un-fix a point that was previously correct. That is what "cycling through all points until zero errors in a full pass" is for.

    Shapes

    $\mathbf{w} \in \mathbb{R}^{(d+1)\times 1}$, $\mathbf{x} \in \mathbb{R}^{(d+1)\times 1}$, $y \in \{+1,-1\}$ a scalar, $\mathbf{w}^{\!\top}\mathbf{x}$ a $(1\times(d+1))\cdot((d+1)\times1) \to$ scalar. The update $\mathbf{w}+y\mathbf{x}$ is a $(d{+}1)$-vector plus a scaled $(d{+}1)$-vector — shapes match trivially since perceptron has no hidden layers to track.

    2.3   Numerical check example

    Start with $\mathbf{w}=(0,0,0)$ (bias included) and three augmented points in $\mathbb{R}^2$:

    $i$$\mathbf{x}$ (with $x_0=1$)$y$
    1(1, 2, 1)+1
    2(1, -1, -1)-1
    3(1, 1, -1)+1

    Pass 1. Point 1: $\mathbf{w}^{\!\top}\mathbf{x}_1 = 0$, sign convention maps $0\mapsto -1 \ne y_1$. Misclassified — update:

    $$\mathbf{w} \leftarrow (0,0,0) + 1\cdot(1,2,1) = (1,2,1).$$

    Point 2: $\mathbf{w}^{\!\top}\mathbf{x}_2 = 1-2-1=-2$, sign $-1=y_2$. Correct, no update. Point 3: $\mathbf{w}^{\!\top}\mathbf{x}_3=1+2-1=2$, sign $+1=y_3$. Correct.

    Pass 2 re-checks all three points against $\mathbf{w}=(1,2,1)$ — zero updates fire. Converged after a single update, boundary $1+2x_1+x_2=0$.

    2.4   Convergence and the pocket algorithm

    Novikoff's convergence theorem (statement only — full PAC-style proof lives outside this section's scope). If the training data is linearly separable, the perceptron learning algorithm converges to a separating $\mathbf{w}$ in a finite number of updates, bounded by $(R/\gamma)^2$ where $R = \max_i\|\mathbf{x}_i\|$ and $\gamma$ is the margin of the best separator. The intuition: every update strictly increases $\mathbf{w}^{\!\top}\mathbf{w}^\star$ (alignment with an optimal separator $\mathbf{w}^\star$) faster than it can increase $\|\mathbf{w}\|$, so the two cannot diverge forever.

    Convergence is only guaranteed when the data is linearly separable. On a non-separable set — the classic XOR configuration $\{+,-,-,+\}$ on the corners of a square being the canonical example — the perceptron oscillates forever: $E_{\text{in}}(\mathbf{w})$ never settles, because every full pass keeps finding at least one misclassified point to correct, and fixing it re-breaks a previously correct one.

    Vanilla PLA has no way to report an answer if it never stops. The fix is a small modification called the pocket algorithm:

    1. Run the perceptron update rule as usual, cycling through the training points.
    2. After each update, compute the in-sample error $E_{\text{in}}(\mathbf{w}) = \frac{1}{N}\sum_i \mathbb{1}[\operatorname{sign}(\mathbf{w}^{\!\top}\mathbf{x}_i)\ne y_i]$ for the new $\mathbf{w}$.
    3. Keep the best $\hat{\mathbf{w}}$ seen so far "in your pocket" — replace it only if the new $E_{\text{in}}$ is strictly lower than the pocketed value.
    4. Stop after a fixed update budget and report $\hat{\mathbf{w}}$, not the current (possibly still-cycling) $\mathbf{w}$.

    Vanilla perceptron treats the current $\mathbf{w}$ as the answer. Pocket decouples exploration (keep updating, even into worse territory) from exploitation (report only the best $\mathbf{w}$ ever seen). It is the simplest instance of "early stopping with a memory" — the same idea reappears with model checkpoints in gradient-based training (§4).

    Worked example — pocket on a non-separable set example

    Take the classic XOR corners plus two near-duplicates (so a plain cyclic sweep does not trivially "converge" the moment it revisits corner 1):

    $i$$(x_1,x_2)$$y$
    1(1.0, 1.0)+1
    2(-1.0, -1.0)+1
    3(1.0, -1.0)-1
    4(-1.0, 1.0)-1
    5(1.2, 1.1)+1
    6(-1.1, 1.05)-1

    Points 1–4 are literally XOR: same-sign quadrants labelled $+1$, mixed-sign quadrants labelled $-1$ — provably not linearly separable (no single line has all four correctly on their side simultaneously). Starting from $\mathbf{w}=(0,0,0)$ and cycling through the six points, the current $E_{\text{in}}(\mathbf{w}_t)$ bounces between $0.17$ and $0.83$ over 40 update steps and never settles at zero. The pocket-tracked $E_{\text{in}}(\hat{\mathbf{w}})$, in contrast, is monotone non-increasing and locks onto $\tfrac{1}{6}\approx 0.167$ (one point wrong) after step 7, holding there for the rest of the budget.

    An exhaustive grid search over $(w_0,w_1,w_2)$ certifies $\tfrac16$ as the best any linear separator can do on this set — pocket found the floor, not just a local plateau.

    Interpretation. Pocket costs one extra $O(N)$ error evaluation per update compared to vanilla PLA — cheap relative to what it buys: a well-defined stopping answer on data that isn't perfectly separable, which is the common case in practice. Its main limitation is that it has no principled early-exit criterion beyond a fixed budget (unlike, say, cross-validated early stopping in §6), and each candidate replacement still requires a full $O(N)$ pass to recompute $E_{\text{in}}$, making it markedly slower than the plain perceptron on large $N$.

    2.5   Practice: k-of-n concepts and a real convergence check

    Practice 2.1 — design a perceptron for "3-or-more of 5 inputs are +1"

    Let $x_1,\dots,x_5 \in \{+1,-1\}$ and $k$ = number of inputs equal to $+1$. Then $\sum_i x_i = k-(5-k)=2k-5$:

    $k$012345
    $\sum x_i$-5-3-1+1+3+5
    target-1-1-1+1+1+1

    The sign flips between $k=2$ and $k=3$, exactly where $\sum x_i$ crosses $0$; any $w_0\in(-1,1)$ works, take $w_0=0$:

    $$\boxed{\;h(\mathbf{x})=\operatorname{sign}\Big(\textstyle\sum_{i=1}^{5}x_i\Big),\quad w_0=0,\;w_1=\cdots=w_5=1.\;}$$

    Exhaustively checked against all $2^5=32$ possible input patterns — every one classifies correctly. General "$k$-of-$n$" rule with unit weights: $w_0 = n-2k+1$.

    Practice 2.2 — run PLA on the 7-segment even/odd problem; how many epochs does it actually take?

    A 7-segment display encodes digits 0–9 as binary strings over $[s_1,\dots,s_7]$; label even digits $+1$, odd $-1$. This is not a hand-derivable formula like Practice 2.1 — it has to be trained. Running the plain cyclic PLA (digits visited in order $0,1,\dots,9$, repeated) from $\mathbf{w}=\mathbf{0}$:

    Converges after 6 epochs (18 total updates) to

    $$\mathbf{w} = (w_0; w_{s_1},\dots,w_{s_7}) = (0;\,-1,\,1,\,-1,\,-1,\,6,\,2,\,-1).$$

    Every one of the 10 digits' scores $\mathbf{w}^{\!\top}\mathbf{x}_d$ matches its target sign — verified directly, not asserted.

    Adjudication — a v5 claim we cannot reproduce. v5 §01 asserts this problem "converges in 10 epochs" to $\mathbf{w}=(-4,1,-3,-3,8,4,1)$ with $w_0=-1$, and flags itself as unprovenanced (the epochs are asserted, not shown). Running the actual perceptron learning algorithm here gives a different separating hyperplane, in 6 epochs, not 10. Both weight vectors correctly classify all 10 digits — this is not a contradiction: the perceptron solution is not unique whenever a separable dataset admits more than one separating hyperplane (as this one clearly does, being only $10$ points in $\mathbb{R}^7$), and the converged $\mathbf{w}$ depends on the visitation order and starting point. What v5 got right qualitatively (a single-layer perceptron does separate this labelling) stands; the specific weights and epoch count in v5 have no derivation trail and are superseded here by a fully reproducible run.

    The fact that PLA converges at all is the proof this parity labelling is linearly separable in $\mathbb{R}^7$ — convergence is itself a constructive existence proof. In our run the largest-magnitude weight lands on $s_5$ (lower-left segment, weight $+6$): $s_5$ is on for most even digits and off for most odd ones, so it carries the dominant signal, with the smaller weights patching up the exceptions.

    2.6   Linear regression: model & loss

    Same linear score as the perceptron, but the output is the score itself — no sign, since the target is now continuous (e.g. predicting a loan amount from salary and tenure, rather than approve/reject):

    $$h(\mathbf{x}) = \mathbf{w}^{\!\top}\mathbf{x} \in \mathbb{R}.$$

    The per-point residual is $e_i = \mathbf{w}^{\!\top}\mathbf{x}_i - y_i$, and the in-sample error is Mean Squared Error:

    $$E_{\text{in}}(\mathbf{w}) = \frac{1}{N}\sum_{i=1}^{N}\big(\mathbf{w}^{\!\top}\mathbf{x}_i - y_i\big)^2.$$

    2.6.1   Matrix form — shapes at every step

    Stack all $N$ training points. With $d$ features (plus bias), define:

    $$\mathbf{w}=\begin{pmatrix}w_0\\w_1\\\vdots\\w_d\end{pmatrix}_{\!(d+1)\times 1},\qquad X = \begin{pmatrix}-\mathbf{x}_1^{\!\top}-\\-\mathbf{x}_2^{\!\top}-\\\vdots\\-\mathbf{x}_N^{\!\top}-\end{pmatrix}_{\!N\times(d+1)},\qquad Y = \begin{pmatrix}y_1\\\vdots\\y_N\end{pmatrix}_{\!N\times 1}.$$

    Then $X\mathbf{w}$ has shape $(N\times(d{+}1))\cdot((d{+}1)\times1) = N\times1$ — one predicted score per row — and $X\mathbf{w}-Y \in \mathbb{R}^{N\times1}$ is the residual vector. Using $\|\mathbf{v}\|_2^2 = \mathbf{v}^{\!\top}\mathbf{v}$,

    $$E_{\text{in}}(\mathbf{w}) = \tfrac{1}{N}\|X\mathbf{w}-Y\|_2^2.$$

    2.6.2   Closed-form minimiser derivation

    $E_{\text{in}} = \tfrac{1}{N}(X\mathbf{w}-Y)^{\!\top}(X\mathbf{w}-Y)$square the norm; shape check: $(1\times N)(N\times1)\to$ scalar
    $\phantom{E_{\text{in}}} = \tfrac{1}{N}\big[\mathbf{w}^{\!\top}X^{\!\top}X\mathbf{w} - 2\mathbf{w}^{\!\top}X^{\!\top}Y + Y^{\!\top}Y\big]$expand; $Y^{\!\top}X\mathbf{w}=(\mathbf{w}^{\!\top}X^{\!\top}Y)^{\!\top}=\mathbf{w}^{\!\top}X^{\!\top}Y$ since it's a scalar
    $\nabla_{\mathbf{w}}E_{\text{in}} = \tfrac{2}{N}\big[X^{\!\top}X\,\mathbf{w} - X^{\!\top}Y\big]$gradient of a quadratic form; $X^{\!\top}X$ is $(d{+}1)\times(d{+}1)$, so the gradient is $(d{+}1)\times1$ — matches $\mathbf{w}$'s shape
    Set $\nabla_{\mathbf{w}}E_{\text{in}}=\mathbf{0}$:   $X^{\!\top}X\,\mathbf{w} = X^{\!\top}Y$the normal equations
    $\boxed{\;\mathbf{w}^\star = (X^{\!\top}X)^{-1}X^{\!\top}Y = X^{+}Y\;}$$X^{+}$ is the Moore–Penrose pseudo-inverse; $(X^{\!\top}X)^{-1}$ is $(d{+}1)\times(d{+}1)$, so $\mathbf{w}^\star\in\mathbb{R}^{(d+1)\times1}$ — the shapes close correctly

    $(X^{\!\top}X)^{-1}$ exists only if $X$ has full column rank — features must be linearly independent. If two features are perfectly collinear (or $N < d{+}1$), $X^{\!\top}X$ is singular and the closed form breaks. Concretely: for the 3 points $(x_1,x_2)\in\{(1,2),(2,4),(3,6)\}$ with $x_2=2x_1$ exactly,

    $$X^{\!\top}X = \begin{pmatrix}3&6&12\\6&14&28\\12&28&56\end{pmatrix},\qquad \det(X^{\!\top}X)=0.$$

    No inverse exists — the fix is regularisation (ridge, §6) or dropping the redundant feature.

    2.7   Numerical check example

    Fit $y = w_0 + w_1 x$ to three points $(1,2),(2,2),(3,4)$:

    $$X = \begin{pmatrix}1&1\\1&2\\1&3\end{pmatrix},\quad Y=\begin{pmatrix}2\\2\\4\end{pmatrix}.$$

    $X^{\!\top}X = \begin{pmatrix}3&6\\6&14\end{pmatrix}$, $\det = 3\cdot14-6\cdot6=6$, so $(X^{\!\top}X)^{-1}=\tfrac16\begin{pmatrix}14&-6\\-6&3\end{pmatrix}$. Next $X^{\!\top}Y=\begin{pmatrix}8\\18\end{pmatrix}$, hence

    $$\mathbf{w}^\star = \tfrac16\begin{pmatrix}14&-6\\-6&3\end{pmatrix}\begin{pmatrix}8\\18\end{pmatrix} = \tfrac16\begin{pmatrix}112-108\\-48+54\end{pmatrix} = \begin{pmatrix}2/3\\1\end{pmatrix}.$$

    Best-fit line: $\hat y = \tfrac23 + x$. Residuals $(\hat y_i - y_i)$: $-\tfrac13,\ \tfrac23,\ -\tfrac13$; $\text{SSE}=\tfrac{2}{3}$, MSE $=\tfrac{2}{9}\approx0.222$, $R^2 = 0.75$.

    A second worked example — 2 features, so $X$ is genuinely $N\times(d{+}1)$ with $d>1$

    Predict an exam score $y$ from hours studied $x_1$ and hours slept $x_2$, over 5 students:

    $x_1$ (hrs studied)$x_2$ (hrs slept)$y$ (score)
    2655
    4770
    6578
    8895
    10692

    Here $X$ is $5\times3$ ($N=5$, $d{+}1=3$), so $X^{\!\top}X$ is the $3\times3$ matrix

    $$X^{\!\top}X = \begin{pmatrix}5&30&32\\30&220&194\\32&194&210\end{pmatrix},\qquad \det(X^{\!\top}X) = 1020,$$

    and solving $X^{\!\top}X\,\mathbf{w}=X^{\!\top}Y$ by cofactor inversion gives

    $$\mathbf{w}^\star \approx (29.04,\ 4.79,\ 3.16),$$

    i.e. $\widehat{\text{score}} \approx 29.04 + 4.79\,x_1 + 3.16\,x_2$: each extra hour studied is worth about $4.8$ points, each extra hour slept about $3.2$ points, on top of a $29$-point baseline. SSE $=47.07$, MSE $=9.41$, $R^2=0.956$ — the two-feature line explains 95.6% of the score variance across these five students.

    The same fit, three ways: the pseudo-inverse from §2.6.2's derivation, the normal equations directly, and the production sklearn API.

    Code — least squares: numpy pseudo-inverse vs. sklearn (numpy / sklearn) 
    import numpy as np

# --- from-scratch: pseudo-inverse solution, matches §2.6.2's normal equations exactly ---
X = np.array([[1, 2, 6], [1, 4, 7], [1, 6, 5], [1, 8, 8], [1, 10, 6]], dtype=float)  # bias column first
y = np.array([55, 70, 78, 95, 92], dtype=float)

w_star = np.linalg.pinv(X) @ y                    # Moore-Penrose pseudo-inverse -- degrades gracefully if X^T X is singular
w_normal_eq = np.linalg.solve(X.T @ X, X.T @ y)    # equivalent when X has full column rank; raises LinAlgError if not

# --- sklearn: same fit, production API ---
from sklearn.linear_model import LinearRegression

reg = LinearRegression()          # fit_intercept=True by default -- do NOT also prepend a manual bias column
reg.fit(X[:, 1:], y)              # drop the bias column here; sklearn fits its own intercept_
reg.coef_, reg.intercept_         # coef_ matches w_star[1:], intercept_ matches w_star[0]

    np.linalg.pinv never raises on a singular X^T X (it returns the minimum-norm solution instead), which is why it — not np.linalg.solve — is the safer default when you haven't first checked the rank; sklearn's LinearRegression re-centres internally, so fit_intercept and a manual bias column must never both be used or the intercept is double-counted.

    Interpretation. The pseudo-inverse solution is a single matrix computation — no iteration, no learning rate, no convergence check — which is exactly why it is the right tool whenever $d$ is small enough that inverting a $(d{+}1)\times(d{+}1)$ matrix is cheap ($O(d^3)$ for the inversion, $O(Nd^2)$ to form $X^{\!\top}X$). It stops being the right tool once $d$ is large (the inversion cost dominates) or $X^{\!\top}X$ is near-singular (collinearity) — both are exactly where gradient-based fitting (§4) and ridge regularisation (§6) take over.

    2.8   The geometry of least squares: the hat matrix derivation

    Everything so far has treated $\mathbf{w}^\star=(X^{\!\top}X)^{-1}X^{\!\top}Y$ as the output of a calculus exercise: differentiate a quadratic, set the gradient to zero. There is a second, entirely geometric reading of the same formula, and it is the one that makes the rest of this section — assumptions, diagnostics, $R^2$, inference — fall out almost for free. A deck of regression slides states the object and asks for the derivation without giving it; this subsection supplies it.

    Notation bridge. The source deck writes the estimator as $\hat{\beta} = (X^{\!\top}X)^{-1}X^{\!\top}y$ — the same object this section has been calling $\mathbf{w}^\star$. From here on we follow the source's $\hat{\boldsymbol\beta}$, since the statistical literature (and §3's GLM machinery) uses it universally; read $\hat{\boldsymbol\beta} \equiv \mathbf{w}^\star$ throughout. One further convention change: statistics defines the residual as $\mathbf{e} = \mathbf{y}-\hat{\mathbf{y}}$, which is the negative of §2.6's $e_i = \mathbf{w}^{\!\top}\mathbf{x}_i - y_i$. Every squared quantity (SSE, MSE, $R^2$) is unaffected; only the reported signs flip. On the slide the hat renders as a detached circumflex after the glyph ("βˆ") — a font artefact, not a different symbol.

    2.8.1   Deriving $\hat{\boldsymbol\beta}$ from orthogonality derivation

    Fix shapes first, because every step below is a shape argument in disguise. With $N$ observations and $p = d+1$ parameters (slopes plus intercept):

    ObjectShapeLives in
    $X$ (design matrix)$N \times p$—
    $\mathbf{y}$ (targets)$N \times 1$$\mathbb{R}^N$
    $\hat{\boldsymbol\beta}$$p \times 1$$\mathbb{R}^p$ (parameter space)
    $\hat{\mathbf{y}} = X\hat{\boldsymbol\beta}$$N \times 1$$\operatorname{col}(X) \subset \mathbb{R}^N$, a $p$-dimensional subspace
    $\mathbf{e} = \mathbf{y}-\hat{\mathbf{y}}$$N \times 1$$\operatorname{col}(X)^{\perp}$, an $(N{-}p)$-dimensional subspace

    The key observation: as $\boldsymbol\beta$ ranges over all of $\mathbb{R}^p$, the fitted vector $X\boldsymbol\beta$ traces out exactly the column space of $X$ — the set of all linear combinations of $X$'s $p$ columns. So least squares is not really a search over parameters at all; it is the question

    $$\min_{\mathbf{v}\,\in\,\operatorname{col}(X)} \|\mathbf{y}-\mathbf{v}\|_2^2 ,$$

    and the answer to that question is a fact of Euclidean geometry, not of optimisation: the closest point of a subspace to an external point is its orthogonal projection, and the line joining them is perpendicular to the subspace.

    $\mathbf{e} \perp \operatorname{col}(X)$geometric optimality: if $\mathbf{e}$ had any component inside the subspace, sliding $\hat{\mathbf{y}}$ along that component would strictly shorten $\|\mathbf{e}\|$ — so $\hat{\mathbf{y}}$ would not have been closest
    $\mathbf{x}_{(j)}^{\!\top}\mathbf{e} = 0$ for every column $j=1,\dots,p$"perpendicular to a subspace" = perpendicular to each of its spanning vectors
    $X^{\!\top}\mathbf{e} = \mathbf{0}$stack the $p$ scalar equations; shapes $(p\times N)(N\times 1) \to (p\times 1)$, so this is $p$ equations in $p$ unknowns — exactly enough
    $X^{\!\top}(\mathbf{y} - X\hat{\boldsymbol\beta}) = \mathbf{0}$substitute $\mathbf{e} = \mathbf{y}-X\hat{\boldsymbol\beta}$
    $X^{\!\top}X\,\hat{\boldsymbol\beta} = X^{\!\top}\mathbf{y}$the normal equations — "normal" in the sense of "perpendicular", which is precisely where the name comes from
    $\boxed{\;\hat{\boldsymbol\beta} = (X^{\!\top}X)^{-1}X^{\!\top}\mathbf{y}\;}$multiply by $(X^{\!\top}X)^{-1}$, which exists iff $X$ has full column rank $p$; shapes $(p\times p)(p\times N)(N\times 1)\to(p\times 1)$

    Not one derivative was taken. §2.6.2 and this derivation reach the identical formula from opposite directions — calculus says "the gradient vanishes", geometry says "the residual is perpendicular" — and they must agree, because the gradient of $\|\mathbf{y}-X\boldsymbol\beta\|^2$ is $-2X^{\!\top}\mathbf{e}$.

    2.8.2   The projection (hat) matrix

    Substituting $\hat{\boldsymbol\beta}$ back gives the fitted values as a linear function of $\mathbf{y}$:

    $$\hat{\mathbf{y}} = X\hat{\boldsymbol\beta} = \underbrace{X(X^{\!\top}X)^{-1}X^{\!\top}}_{\textstyle P}\,\mathbf{y}, \qquad P \in \mathbb{R}^{N\times N}.$$

    $P$ is the projection matrix, universally nicknamed the hat matrix because it is the operator that "puts the hat on $\mathbf{y}$". Its complement $M = I_N - P$ produces the residuals: $\mathbf{e} = \mathbf{y}-\hat{\mathbf{y}} = (I_N-P)\mathbf{y} = M\mathbf{y}$. Shapes: $X$ is $(N\times p)$, $(X^{\!\top}X)^{-1}$ is $(p\times p)$, $X^{\!\top}$ is $(p\times N)$ — the product collapses to $(N\times N)$, an operator on target space, not on parameter space.

    Proposition. $P$ is symmetric and idempotent.

    Symmetry $P^{\!\top}=P$. Use $(ABC)^{\!\top}=C^{\!\top}B^{\!\top}A^{\!\top}$ and $(A^{-1})^{\!\top}=(A^{\!\top})^{-1}$:

    $$P^{\!\top} = \big[X(X^{\!\top}X)^{-1}X^{\!\top}\big]^{\!\top} = (X^{\!\top})^{\!\top}\big[(X^{\!\top}X)^{-1}\big]^{\!\top}X^{\!\top} = X\big[(X^{\!\top}X)^{\!\top}\big]^{-1}X^{\!\top} = X(X^{\!\top}X)^{-1}X^{\!\top} = P,$$

    where the last step uses that $X^{\!\top}X$ is itself symmetric: $(X^{\!\top}X)^{\!\top} = X^{\!\top}(X^{\!\top})^{\!\top} = X^{\!\top}X$.

    Idempotency $P^2=P$. Write the product out and cancel the middle pair:

    $$PP = X(X^{\!\top}X)^{-1}\underbrace{X^{\!\top}X}_{\text{cancels}}(X^{\!\top}X)^{-1}X^{\!\top} = X\underbrace{(X^{\!\top}X)^{-1}I_p}_{=(X^{\!\top}X)^{-1}}X^{\!\top} = P.$$

    Corollaries. $M=I-P$ is also symmetric and idempotent ($M^2 = I-2P+P^2 = I-P = M$), the two are orthogonal to each other ($PM = P-P^2 = 0$), and

    $$\operatorname{tr}(P) = \operatorname{tr}\!\big(X(X^{\!\top}X)^{-1}X^{\!\top}\big) = \operatorname{tr}\!\big((X^{\!\top}X)^{-1}X^{\!\top}X\big) = \operatorname{tr}(I_p) = p,$$

    using the cyclic property $\operatorname{tr}(AB)=\operatorname{tr}(BA)$. Hence $\operatorname{tr}(M)=N-p$ — the residual degrees of freedom, the number that will appear as the denominator of every variance estimate in §2.12.

    Why idempotency is the whole story. $P^2=P$ says "projecting something that is already in the subspace does nothing" — apply the shadow-casting operator twice and the shadow does not move. Combined with symmetry it makes $P$ an orthogonal projector rather than a skew one, which is exactly the statement that the projection is along a perpendicular. And because an idempotent matrix has only eigenvalues $0$ and $1$, $\operatorname{tr}(P)=p$ is literally counting eigenvalue-$1$ directions: $P$ keeps $p$ dimensions of $\mathbb{R}^N$ and annihilates the other $N-p$.

    2.8.3   Two orthogonality proofs derivation

    The slide poses both as exercises with no worked answer. Both are two lines once $M=I-P$ is available.

    (a) Residuals are orthogonal to the regressors: $X^{\!\top}\mathbf{e}=\mathbf{0}$.

    $$X^{\!\top}\mathbf{e} = X^{\!\top}(I-P)\mathbf{y} = X^{\!\top}\mathbf{y} - X^{\!\top}X(X^{\!\top}X)^{-1}X^{\!\top}\mathbf{y} = X^{\!\top}\mathbf{y} - I_p X^{\!\top}\mathbf{y} = \mathbf{0}.$$

    Shapes: $(p\times N)(N\times 1) \to (p\times 1)$, so this is $p$ separate scalar orthogonality statements, one per feature.

    (b) Residuals are orthogonal to fitted values: $\mathbf{e}^{\!\top}\hat{\mathbf{y}}=0$.

    $$\mathbf{e}^{\!\top}\hat{\mathbf{y}} = (M\mathbf{y})^{\!\top}(P\mathbf{y}) = \mathbf{y}^{\!\top}M^{\!\top}P\,\mathbf{y} = \mathbf{y}^{\!\top}MP\,\mathbf{y} = \mathbf{y}^{\!\top}(P-P^2)\mathbf{y} = \mathbf{y}^{\!\top}\mathbf{0}\,\mathbf{y} = 0,$$

    using $M^{\!\top}=M$ and then $MP=0$. Note (b) is a consequence of (a): $\hat{\mathbf{y}}$ is a linear combination of the columns of $X$, and $\mathbf{e}$ is perpendicular to every one of them.

    (c) A free corollary — residuals sum to zero. If the model contains an intercept, the all-ones vector $\mathbf{1}$ is one of $X$'s columns, so (a) gives $\mathbf{1}^{\!\top}\mathbf{e} = \sum_i e_i = 0$ automatically. The sample assumption $\mathbb{E}[\varepsilon]=0$ is therefore not something OLS can violate in sample — it is enforced by the algebra, provided you fitted an intercept. That is exactly why the remedy column for that row of the assumptions table reads "include intercept".

    (d) Pythagoras. Since $\mathbf{y}=\hat{\mathbf{y}}+\mathbf{e}$ with the two parts perpendicular, $\|\mathbf{y}\|^2 = \|\hat{\mathbf{y}}\|^2+\|\mathbf{e}\|^2$. Centring $\mathbf{y}$ first turns this into $\text{SST}=\text{SSR}+\text{SSE}$, the decomposition $R^2$ is built on (§2.10).

    2.8.4   The projection made concrete example

    Take §2.7's 3-point fit — $(1,2),(2,2),(3,4)$ — precisely because $N=3$ and $p=2$: the column space is a 2-D plane sitting inside $\mathbb{R}^3$, so the whole picture is drawable.

    $$X = \begin{pmatrix}1&1\\1&2\\1&3\end{pmatrix}_{3\times 2},\qquad \operatorname{col}(X) = \operatorname{span}\!\left\{\begin{pmatrix}1\\1\\1\end{pmatrix},\begin{pmatrix}1\\2\\3\end{pmatrix}\right\},\qquad \mathbf{y}=\begin{pmatrix}2\\2\\4\end{pmatrix}.$$

    From §2.7, $(X^{\!\top}X)^{-1}=\tfrac16\begin{pmatrix}14&-6\\-6&3\end{pmatrix}$, so

    $$P = X(X^{\!\top}X)^{-1}X^{\!\top} = \frac{1}{6}\begin{pmatrix}5&2&-1\\2&2&2\\-1&2&5\end{pmatrix}_{3\times 3}.$$

    Read off the three checks directly:

    PropertyCheckValue
    Symmetric$\max_{ij}|P-P^{\!\top}|$0 (exactly — the matrix above is visibly symmetric)
    Idempotent$\max_{ij}|PP-P|$$3\times10^{-16}$ (floating-point zero)
    Trace = rank$\operatorname{tr}(P)=\tfrac{5+2+5}{6}$2 = $p$ = rank$(X)$
    Complement$\operatorname{tr}(M)=N-p$1

    Applying $P$ and $M$ to $\mathbf{y}$:

    $$\hat{\mathbf{y}} = P\mathbf{y} = \tfrac13\begin{pmatrix}5\\8\\11\end{pmatrix} = \begin{pmatrix}1.6\overline{6}\\2.6\overline{6}\\3.6\overline{6}\end{pmatrix},\qquad \mathbf{e} = M\mathbf{y} = \tfrac13\begin{pmatrix}1\\-2\\1\end{pmatrix}.$$

    Verify the identity $\hat{\mathbf{y}} = X\hat{\boldsymbol\beta}$ against §2.7's $\hat{\boldsymbol\beta}=(\tfrac23,1)$: row 2 gives $\tfrac23 + 1\cdot 2 = \tfrac83$ ✓. And the orthogonality claims, arithmetic in full:

    • $\mathbf{1}^{\!\top}\mathbf{e} = \tfrac13(1-2+1) = 0$ — residuals sum to zero (proof (c)).
    • $(1,2,3)\cdot\mathbf{e} = \tfrac13(1-4+3) = 0$ — orthogonal to the $x$ column too, so $X^{\!\top}\mathbf{e}=\mathbf{0}$ (proof (a)); numerically $\max|X^{\!\top}\mathbf{e}| = 1.4\times10^{-14}$.
    • $\mathbf{e}^{\!\top}\hat{\mathbf{y}} = \tfrac13\cdot\tfrac13(1\cdot5 - 2\cdot 8 + 1\cdot 11) = \tfrac19(5-16+11)=0$ (proof (b)); the computed angle between $\mathbf{e}$ and each column is $90.000°$.
    • Pythagoras: $\|\mathbf{y}\|^2 = 4+4+16 = 24$ and $\|\hat{\mathbf{y}}\|^2+\|\mathbf{e}\|^2 = 23.333+0.667 = 24.000$ ✓ ($\|\mathbf{y}\|=4.899$, $\|\hat{\mathbf{y}}\|=4.830$, $\|\mathbf{e}\|=0.816$).

    Interpretation. $P$ depends on $X$ only — the targets never enter it. That single fact explains most of what follows. The fit's flexibility, the degrees of freedom $N-p$, the leverage of each observation, and the variance of every coefficient are all fixed the moment you choose your design matrix, before you look at a single $y$. It also explains why "add a feature" always weakly increases $R^2$: enlarging $X$ enlarges $\operatorname{col}(X)$, and a point can only get closer to a bigger subspace, never further away (§2.10). What breaks it: if $X$ loses full column rank, $(X^{\!\top}X)^{-1}$ does not exist and $P$ is undefined by this formula — the projection still exists geometrically, but $\hat{\boldsymbol\beta}$ stops being unique (§2.11).

    The diagonal entries $h_{ii}=P_{ii}$ are the leverages: $\partial\hat y_i/\partial y_i = h_{ii}$, i.e. how much observation $i$ drags its own fitted value. They obey $0\le h_{ii}\le 1$ and $\sum_i h_{ii}=p$, so the average leverage is always $p/N$ regardless of the data, and the usual flag is $h_{ii} > 2p/N$. Here $\operatorname{diag}(P) = (5/6,\,2/6,\,5/6) = (0.833,\,0.333,\,0.833)$: the two endpoint observations carry two-and-a-half times the leverage of the middle one, which is the generic behaviour — extreme $x$ values pull hardest. With $N=3$ and $p=2$ the $2p/N = 1.33$ threshold exceeds the maximum possible leverage of 1, so no point can ever be flagged: leverage rules of thumb are meaningless at tiny $N$.

    2.9   OLS assumptions, violations and diagnostics

    The closed form $\hat{\boldsymbol\beta}=(X^{\!\top}X)^{-1}X^{\!\top}\mathbf{y}$ is pure linear algebra and needs nothing but full column rank. Everything beyond the point estimate — standard errors, $t$-tests, confidence intervals, $p$-values — rests on a model of how the data was generated:

    $$\mathbf{y} = X\boldsymbol\beta + \boldsymbol\varepsilon, \qquad \boldsymbol\varepsilon \in \mathbb{R}^{N\times 1},$$

    together with assumptions on $\boldsymbol\varepsilon$. The source deck lists seven:

    1. Linearity / correct specification — the model is linear in the parameters (not necessarily in the features: $x^2$ and $\log x$ are fine as columns), and no relevant variable is omitted.
    2. Independent errors — $\operatorname{Cov}(\varepsilon_i,\varepsilon_j)=0$ for $i\ne j$.
    3. Zero-mean errors — $\mathbb{E}[\boldsymbol\varepsilon]=\mathbf{0}$.
    4. Homoscedasticity — $\operatorname{Var}(\varepsilon_i)=\sigma^2$, the same $\sigma^2$ for every observation.
    5. No perfect multicollinearity — $X$ has full column rank (§2.11).
    6. Exogeneity — $\operatorname{Cov}(X,\boldsymbol\varepsilon)=0$: the regressors carry no information about the error.
    7. Normality of errors — $\boldsymbol\varepsilon \sim \mathcal{N}(\mathbf{0},\sigma^2 I_N)$.

    Assumptions 2–4 combine into the compact statement $\operatorname{Var}(\boldsymbol\varepsilon)=\sigma^2 I_N$: constant variance down the diagonal, zeros off it.

    Adjudication — the deck's error symbol is inconsistent. Slide 1 writes assumption 3 as $E[\varepsilon]=0$ but assumption 6 as $\operatorname{Cov}(X,u)=0$, switching from $\varepsilon$ to $u$ midway through one list, and the transcript flags this as a probable typo. Both symbols denote the same object — the population error term — and the mixture is a transcription slip, not a distinction: $u$ is the econometrics convention, $\varepsilon$ the statistics one, and a single list should commit to one. We use $\boldsymbol\varepsilon$ throughout. Nothing in the mathematics changes; what would be genuinely wrong is to read $u$ as a different quantity from $\varepsilon$ and conclude the deck states eight assumptions about two error terms.

    Which assumptions matter for what is the question students get wrong most often. Assumptions 1, 5 and 6 are needed for $\hat{\boldsymbol\beta}$ to be unbiased — violate them and the point estimate itself is wrong. Assumptions 2 and 4 are needed for the standard-error formula $\sigma^2(X^{\!\top}X)^{-1}$ — violate them and $\hat{\boldsymbol\beta}$ is still unbiased but every $p$-value and confidence interval is untrustworthy. Assumption 7 is needed only for exact small-sample $t$ and $F$ distributions; at large $N$ the CLT rescues inference without it. "My residuals aren't normal" is therefore a much milder problem than "my residuals fan out".

    2.9.1   Violations, detection and remedies

    The deck's full diagnostic table, reproduced with the source's own wording in the middle columns and one added column making the unbiasedness-versus-standard-errors split above explicit:

    AssumptionWhat breaksEffect of violationDetectionRemedy
    Linearity / correct specificationthe estimateBiased modelResidual plots (curvature vs fitted values)Transform, add features
    Independent errorsthe standard errorsIncorrect SEsDurbin–Watson statisticTime-series models, HAC (Newey–West) SEs
    $\mathbb{E}[\varepsilon]=0$the interceptBiased interceptResidual mean ($\approx 0$)Include an intercept
    Homoscedasticitythe standard errorsIncorrect standard errorsBreusch–Pagan test, residual plotsRobust (White/HC) SEs, weighted least squares
    No perfect multicollinearityidentifiabilityCoefficients not identifiableVIF (§2.11)Remove variables, Ridge, PCA
    Exogeneitythe estimateBiased & inconsistent $\hat{\boldsymbol\beta}$Theory, Hausman testInstrumental variables, fixed effects
    Normality of errorssmall-sample inferenceInvalid small-sample inferenceQQ plot, Shapiro–Wilk testBootstrap, transform the response

    The slide abbreviates the homoscedasticity test as "BP test" without expanding it: that is the Breusch–Pagan test, which regresses the squared residuals $e_i^2$ on the regressors and refers $N R^2_{\text{aux}}$ to a $\chi^2_k$ null — literally asking "can the fitted values predict how big the errors are?". Under homoscedasticity they cannot, so $R^2_{\text{aux}}\approx 0$.

    2.9.2   Reading a residual plot example

    The deck's residual-diagnostics slide names five tools — residual plots for pattern detection, QQ plots for normality, studentized residuals for outliers, leverage for unusual $X$ values, and Cook's distance for influence — but shows no plots. Fig. 2.6 supplies them: three synthetic residual sets of $n=60$, each violating a different assumption, with the corresponding formal test statistic computed on the same data.

    Interpretation. The two statistics are not interchangeable — each panel is caught by exactly one of them, which is why the deck lists a different detector per row. Durbin–Watson is $\text{DW} = \sum_{i=2}^{N}(e_i-e_{i-1})^2 / \sum_i e_i^2 \approx 2(1-\hat\rho)$, so $\text{DW}\approx 2$ means no autocorrelation, $\text{DW}\to 0$ means strong positive autocorrelation ($\hat\rho\approx 0.77$ in the right-hand panel), $\text{DW}\to 4$ means negative. Note also the false-positive risk: the autocorrelated panel's Breusch–Pagan $p=0.017$ would "detect" heteroscedasticity that was never simulated — drift in the mean masquerades as drift in the variance. Run the plots and the tests, and diagnose the assumption you actually suspect. On the section's own 5-student fit (§2.7) the residuals give $\text{DW}=1.51$ and sum to $-4\times10^{-12}$ (numerically zero, exactly as proof (c) of §2.8.3 guarantees) — but with $N=5$ no diagnostic has any power, which is the honest reading.

    2.9.3   Outliers, leverage and influence — the rest of slide 6 example

    Residual plots and the two formal tests above cover the first two of the deck's five tools. The remaining three — studentized residuals, leverage and Cook's distance — are named there with no formulas, so here they are, each built from the hat matrix of §2.8.

    Write $h_{ii}=P_{ii}$ for the leverage of observation $i$ (§2.8's warn box) and $\hat\sigma^2=\text{SSE}/(N-p)$. Because $\operatorname{Var}(e_i)=\sigma^2(1-h_{ii})$ — high-leverage points drag the fit toward themselves and so have artificially small raw residuals — the raw $e_i$ are not comparable across observations. Dividing by their own standard deviations fixes that:

    $$\underbrace{r_i = \frac{e_i}{\hat\sigma\sqrt{1-h_{ii}}}}_{\text{internally studentized}},\qquad \underbrace{t_i = \frac{e_i}{\hat\sigma_{(i)}\sqrt{1-h_{ii}}} \sim t_{N-p-1}}_{\text{externally studentized (deleted)}},\qquad D_i = \frac{r_i^2}{p}\cdot\frac{h_{ii}}{1-h_{ii}} .$$

    $\hat\sigma_{(i)}^2$ is the residual variance refitted with observation $i$ removed, which is what makes $t_i$ exactly $t$-distributed: the point being tested no longer contributes to the yardstick it is measured against. Cook's distance $D_i$ multiplies the two ideas — how badly the point is fitted ($r_i^2$) times how much say it has ($h_{ii}/(1-h_{ii})$) — and equals the scaled distance the whole coefficient vector moves when observation $i$ is deleted. The usual flags are $h_{ii}>2p/N$, $|t_i|$ beyond a Bonferroni-corrected $t$ quantile, and $D_i>4/N$.

    Computed on the 10-student model of §2.11 with the collinear $x_3$ dropped ($N=10$, $p=3$, so $\hat\sigma^2=8.815$, mean leverage $p/N=0.3$, flags $h_{ii}>0.6$ and $D_i>0.4$):

    student12345678910
    $e_i$-1.9750.3093.6062.549-5.154-2.6681.9580.5710.5390.265
    $h_{ii}$0.4050.1850.3160.4020.3800.2650.1440.3420.4380.124
    $r_i$ (internal)-0.8630.1151.4681.110-2.204-1.0490.7130.2370.2420.095
    $t_i$ (external)-0.8450.1071.6341.132-3.688-1.0570.6850.2200.2250.088
    $D_i$ (Cook)0.1690.0010.3310.2760.9900.1320.0280.0100.0150.000

    Two checks first: $\sum_i h_{ii} = 3.000 = p$ exactly (§2.8.2), and the largest leverage, student 9's $0.438$, is nowhere near the $0.6$ flag — no observation here is unusual in $X$. Student 5 is a different story. Their raw residual $-5.154$ is the largest, their internally studentized residual $-2.204$ looks borderline, and the deleted version blows up to $-3.688$ once the point stops inflating its own yardstick. Cook's distance $0.990$ is nearly $2.5\times$ the $4/N=0.4$ threshold and $3\times$ the next-largest point's.

    Interpretation. The three tools answer three different questions and only their combination means "influential". Leverage is about $X$ alone (§2.8: $P$ never sees $\mathbf{y}$) — it says how much say a point could have. A studentized residual is about $\mathbf{y}$ alone — it says how badly the point is fitted. Cook's distance multiplies them: a point with huge leverage that happens to sit on the line moves nothing ($r_i\approx0$), and a badly-fitted point at the centre of the $x$ cloud moves little ($h_{ii}$ small). Student 5 is flagged not because they are extreme in study hours or sleep — their leverage $0.380$ is close to the $0.3$ average — but because they score $92$ where the fit predicts $97.2$: high $r$, ordinary $h$. And the discipline the deck implies but does not state: a flag is a question, not a verdict. Here $|t_5|=3.688$ against the Bonferroni-corrected outlier cutoff $t_{1-0.05/(2N),\,N-p-1}=4.317$ — testing the largest of $10$ residuals means allowing for $10$ chances to look extreme, and once you do, student 5 does not clear the bar. Report the fit both with and without them; do not delete.

    2.10   How good is the fit? $R^2$, adjusted $R^2$ and the error metrics

    The deck asks the reader to "understand $R^2$ vs adjusted $R^2$" and to "know MAE, MSE and RMSE" but writes down no formulas at all. This subsection fills that gap and then computes every one of them on the section's existing 5-student exam-score dataset from §2.7, so the numbers can be checked against a fit already in hand.

    Start from the Pythagorean decomposition of §2.8.3(d), applied to the centred target:

    $$\underbrace{\sum_i (y_i-\bar y)^2}_{\text{SST, total}} \;=\; \underbrace{\sum_i (\hat y_i-\bar y)^2}_{\text{SSR, explained}} \;+\; \underbrace{\sum_i (y_i-\hat y_i)^2}_{\text{SSE, residual}},$$ $$R^2 = \frac{\text{SSR}}{\text{SST}} = 1-\frac{\text{SSE}}{\text{SST}}, \qquad R^2_{\text{adj}} = 1-\frac{\text{SSE}/(N-p)}{\text{SST}/(N-1)} = 1-(1-R^2)\frac{N-1}{N-p}.$$

    $R^2$ compares sums of squares; $R^2_{\text{adj}}$ compares mean squares, i.e. it divides each sum by its degrees of freedom, which is the entire difference between them. And the three error metrics, on the same residuals $e_i=y_i-\hat y_i$:

    $$\text{MAE}=\frac1N\sum_i|e_i|,\qquad \text{MSE}=\frac1N\sum_i e_i^2,\qquad \text{RMSE}=\sqrt{\text{MSE}}.$$

    The §2.7 fit was $\widehat{\text{score}} = 29.043 + 4.792\,x_1 + 3.157\,x_2$ over $N=5$ students, $p=3$ parameters. Every quantity below comes from those five residuals:

    $i$$x_1$$x_2$$y$$\hat y$$e=y-\hat y$$|e|$$e^2$
    1265557.569-2.5692.5696.598
    2477070.310-0.3100.3100.096
    3657873.5804.4204.42019.533
    4889592.6352.3652.3655.592
    51069295.906-3.9063.90615.256
    sums13.56947.075

    With $\bar y = 78$, $\text{SST}=\sum(y_i-78)^2 = 1078$ and $\text{SSE}=47.075$, so $\text{SSR}=1030.925$:

    $$R^2 = 1-\frac{47.075}{1078} = 0.9563, \qquad R^2_{\text{adj}} = 1-(1-0.9563)\cdot\frac{5-1}{5-3} = 1-0.04367\cdot 2 = 0.9127,$$ $$\text{MAE}=\frac{13.569}{5}=2.714,\qquad \text{MSE}=\frac{47.075}{5}=9.415,\qquad \text{RMSE}=\sqrt{9.415}=3.068.$$

    For scale: a model that ignores the features entirely and always predicts $\bar y = 78$ scores $\text{MAE}=12.4$, $\text{MSE}=215.6$, $\text{RMSE}=14.683$. The two features cut typical error from about 14.7 points to about 3.1 points.

    2.10.1   Why adjusted $R^2$ exists example

    Add a fourth column to $X$: a binary "attended the optional Friday seminar" indicator, $(1,0,1,0,1)$, deliberately unrelated to exam performance (its correlation with $y$ is $-0.250$, i.e. faintly negative). Refit with $p=4$:

    Model$p$SSE$R^2$$R^2_{\text{adj}}$
    $x_1,x_2$347.0750.95630.9127
    $x_1,x_2$ + junk indicator430.2500.97190.8878
    change+1-16.825+0.0156-0.0249

    $R^2$ went up by $0.0156$ for a predictor with no signal, and adjusted $R^2$ went down by $0.0249$. Neither number is a fluke: §2.8's geometry guarantees the first (a bigger $\operatorname{col}(X)$ cannot be further from $\mathbf{y}$, so SSE can only shrink), and the degrees-of-freedom penalty $\frac{N-1}{N-p}$ jumping from $4/2=2$ to $4/1=4$ guarantees the second. Concretely, the new column would have had to push $R^2$ above $0.9563 \to$ solving $1-(1-R^2)\cdot 4 = 0.9127$ gives the break-even value $R^2 = 0.9782$; the junk feature reached only $0.9719$, so it loses.

    Interpretation. $R^2$ answers "how much of the variance did I account for?" and is monotone in model size, so it can never argue against adding a feature — it is a description, not a model-selection criterion. Adjusted $R^2$ answers "did the feature pay for its own degree of freedom?" and can go down, so it can. MAE, MSE and RMSE answer a third, different question: "how wrong is a typical prediction, in the units of $y$?" — RMSE and MAE are both in points-of-exam-score here, MSE is in points-squared and is therefore never directly interpretable, only comparable. RMSE penalises the large errors quadratically ($3.068$ vs MAE's $2.714$: the gap is the price of student 3's $4.4$-point miss), so choose MAE when outliers are data you distrust and RMSE when large errors genuinely hurt more.

    Three standing traps. (i) $R^2$ is not comparable across different $\mathbf{y}$'s — it is scaled by that dataset's SST, so an $R^2$ of $0.5$ on noisy data may be a far better model than $0.95$ on smooth data. (ii) $R^2_{\text{adj}}$ can go negative, and does so whenever $\text{SSE}/(N-p) > \text{SST}/(N-1)$; with $N=5$ and $p=4$ we were one weak feature away from that. (iii) All five metrics here are in-sample: they are computed on the same five students the coefficients were fitted to and say nothing about generalisation. The out-of-sample versions, and the validation protocol that produces them, are §6's subject.

    2.11   Multicollinearity and the VIF

    Assumption 5 forbids perfect collinearity, and §2.6.2's warning box showed why: with $x_2=2x_1$ exactly, $\det(X^{\!\top}X)=0$ and the inverse does not exist. The practically important case is the near-miss — predictors that are strongly but not perfectly correlated. Then $(X^{\!\top}X)^{-1}$ does exist, OLS returns an answer, and the answer is useless: "high correlation among predictors inflates coefficient variance … unstable coefficients, wider confidence intervals".

    The Variance Inflation Factor quantifies exactly that. Regress predictor $j$ on all the other predictors (not on $y$), obtaining an auxiliary $R^2_j$; then

    $$\text{VIF}_j = \frac{1}{1-R^2_j}, \qquad \text{tolerance}_j = 1-R^2_j = \frac{1}{\text{VIF}_j}.$$

    The deck names VIF as the diagnostic without stating the formula; the formula above is what makes it interpretable, via the identity

    $$\operatorname{Var}(\hat\beta_j) \;=\; \frac{\sigma^2}{(N-1)\,s^2_{x_j}}\cdot\underbrace{\frac{1}{1-R^2_j}}_{\text{VIF}_j}.$$

    Read left to right: the variance of a coefficient is its irreducible floor — driven by the noise level $\sigma^2$, the sample size $N$, and how much the predictor itself varies ($s^2_{x_j}$) — multiplied by the VIF. Hence the name: VIF is literally the factor by which collinearity inflates the variance, and $\sqrt{\text{VIF}_j}$ is the factor by which it inflates the standard error and therefore the width of the confidence interval. $\text{VIF}=1$ means predictor $j$ is orthogonal to the others and costs nothing; the conventional alarm thresholds are $\text{VIF}>5$ (worth investigating) and $\text{VIF}>10$ (serious).

    2.11.1   A computed three-predictor example example

    Five students is too few to fit three predictors, so extend the same story to $N=10$ and add a third feature that is nearly redundant by construction: $x_3$ = hours of group study, which in this cohort tracks $x_1$ = hours of solo study almost exactly.

    student12345678910
    $x_1$ solo study (h)24681035796
    $x_2$ sleep (h)6758676857
    $x_3$ group study (h)2357934685
    $y$ score55707895926274889080

    Pairwise correlations: $\operatorname{corr}(x_1,x_3)=0.9917$, while $\operatorname{corr}(x_1,x_2)=-0.0797$ and $\operatorname{corr}(x_2,x_3)=-0.0895$. The auxiliary regressions give:

    predictorauxiliary $R^2_j$tolerance $1-R^2_j$VIF$_j$SE inflation $\sqrt{\text{VIF}_j}$verdict
    $x_1$ solo study0.98360.016461.077.81severe
    $x_2$ sleep0.01300.98701.011.01clean
    $x_3$ group study0.98370.016361.177.82severe

    Note that $x_2$ is untouched: multicollinearity is a property of a subset of columns, not of the model as a whole, and a clean predictor sitting beside a collinear pair keeps a perfectly usable standard error.

    The variance identity, checked numerically. With $\hat\sigma^2 = 5.6656$, $s^2_{x_1}=6.6667$ and $N=10$:

    $$\operatorname{Var}(\hat\beta_1) = \frac{5.6656}{9\times 6.6667}\times\frac{1}{0.016374} = 0.09443 \times 61.07 = 5.7668,$$

    against the value read straight off $\hat\sigma^2(X^{\!\top}X)^{-1}$: $5.7668$ — agreement to $3\times10^{-14}$. Without the collinearity the variance would have been $0.0944$; the VIF multiplies it by 61.

    What that does to the coefficients. Fit the model with and without $x_3$:

    quantity for $\hat\beta_1$ (solo study)with $x_3$ in the modelwith $x_3$ droppedratio
    estimate10.2895.0222.05×
    standard error2.4010.3856.25×
    variance5.7670.14839.0×
    $t$ statistic4.2813.06—
    $p$ value0.00520.0000036—
    95% CI[4.41, 16.17][4.11, 5.93]—
    CI width11.751.826.46×
    model $R^2$ / $R^2_{\text{adj}}$0.9787 / 0.96810.9613 / 0.9503—

    And the coefficient on $x_3$ itself in the full model is $\hat\beta_3 = -5.968$ ($p=0.069$) — the model claims that group study lowers your exam score by six points an hour. It does not, of course: $x_1$ and $x_3$ move together, so only their sum's effect is identified, and OLS is free to split it into a large positive and a large negative piece that nearly cancel. The full model's $R^2$ is the higher of the two, which is exactly why $R^2$ cannot be used to detect this.

    Interpretation. Collinearity does not bias anything — $\mathbb{E}[\hat{\boldsymbol\beta}]=\boldsymbol\beta$ still holds, and the model's predictions are fine (compare the two $R^2$s: $0.979$ vs $0.961$, both excellent). What it destroys is the ability to attribute effects to individual predictors: 39× the variance means the estimate's standard deviation across repeated samples is $\sqrt{39}=6.25$ times larger, so it wanders 6.25× further from run to run — and on this one run it doubled and produced a sign-flipped partner. The practical rule follows directly: if you only want to predict, high VIFs can be ignored; if you want to interpret a coefficient, they cannot.

    The remedies the deck lists — remove features, combine features, Ridge, PCA — are not interchangeable. Dropping $x_3$ here worked because the two columns measured nearly the same thing; drop the wrong one and you re-introduce omitted-variable bias (assumption 1). Ridge regression keeps every column but adds $\lambda I$ to $X^{\!\top}X$, which makes the inverse well-conditioned at the cost of a small bias — the accepted trade when VIFs are high and every feature is wanted. PCA replaces the collinear block by orthogonal components, buying $\text{VIF}=1$ at the cost of coefficients that no longer refer to named quantities. Ridge and Lasso, the Elastic Net that combines their penalties, and the coefficient paths that distinguish them are §6's subject; PCA is §18's.

    2.12   Inference on the coefficients: $t$, $F$, CIs, $p$-values and power

    $\hat{\boldsymbol\beta}$ is computed from a sample, so it is a random variable: run the experiment again with five different students and you get a different number. Inference is the discipline of saying how different. The deck names the tools — $t$-tests, $F$-tests, confidence intervals, $p$-values, and then point-versus-interval estimation, Type I and II errors, and power — without formulas or worked cases. Here is the whole apparatus, computed end-to-end on the 5-student fit.

    Where the deck's probability essentials live. The deck spends a whole slide on probability prerequisites before it reaches inference, so it is worth saying explicitly which of them this section uses and where the rest are developed, rather than leaving the list unaccounted for.

    • Expectation and variance — the two objects everything below is built from: $\mathbb{E}[\hat{\boldsymbol\beta}]=\boldsymbol\beta$ is what "unbiased" means, and $\operatorname{Var}(\hat{\boldsymbol\beta})=\sigma^2(X^{\!\top}X)^{-1}$ is what every SE, CI and $p$-value is computed from.
    • Covariance vs correlation — same numerator, different scaling: $\operatorname{corr}(u,v)=\operatorname{Cov}(u,v)/(s_u s_v)$. On §2.11's ten students $\operatorname{Cov}(x_1,x_3)=5.889$ hours² and $\operatorname{Cov}(x_2,x_3)=-0.222$ hours², numbers whose size means nothing on its own; dividing by $s_{x_1}=2.582$, $s_{x_2}=1.080$, $s_{x_3}=2.300$ turns them into $0.9917$ and $-0.0895$, which are comparable and unit-free. Covariance carries the units, correlation carries the strength — which is why VIF is defined through an $R^2$ and never through a covariance.
    • The CLT — the reason assumption 7 is the mildest of the seven (§2.9): $\hat{\boldsymbol\beta}$ is a linear function of $\boldsymbol\varepsilon$, so as $N$ grows its sampling distribution becomes normal whatever the errors' own shape, and the $t$/$F$ machinery below becomes asymptotically valid without assuming normal errors. At $N=5$ there is no such rescue, which is exactly why this section keeps flagging its own toy inference as illustrative.
    • Conditional probability, independence and Bayes' theorem — used here only as the assumption $\operatorname{Cov}(\varepsilon_i,\varepsilon_j)=0$ and as the definition of a $p$-value ("probability of the data given $H_0$", never the reverse). The toolkit itself — product rule, sum rule, Bayes' theorem and the prior/likelihood/posterior vocabulary — is developed where it does real work, in §9.
    • The named distributions — this section uses the normal (errors), $t$ (a coefficient, §2.12.1), $F$ (a joint test, §2.12.2), noncentral $t$ (power, §2.12.3) and $\chi^2$ (§2.12.4). The discrete family the slide lists — Bernoulli/binomial, geometric, hypergeometric, negative binomial, Poisson — parameterises response models rather than error models, so it belongs with the GLMs that use it: Bernoulli in §3's logistic likelihood and §9's Naive Bayes, Poisson in §3's count GLM.

    The sampling distribution. Substituting $\mathbf{y}=X\boldsymbol\beta+\boldsymbol\varepsilon$ into the estimator:

    $$\hat{\boldsymbol\beta} = (X^{\!\top}X)^{-1}X^{\!\top}(X\boldsymbol\beta+\boldsymbol\varepsilon) = \boldsymbol\beta + (X^{\!\top}X)^{-1}X^{\!\top}\boldsymbol\varepsilon.$$

    Under assumptions 1–6, $\mathbb{E}[\hat{\boldsymbol\beta}]=\boldsymbol\beta$ (unbiased), and since $\operatorname{Var}(A\boldsymbol\varepsilon)=A\,\sigma^2 I\,A^{\!\top}$ with $A=(X^{\!\top}X)^{-1}X^{\!\top}$,

    $$\operatorname{Var}(\hat{\boldsymbol\beta}) = \sigma^2 (X^{\!\top}X)^{-1} \in \mathbb{R}^{p\times p},\qquad \hat\sigma^2 = \frac{\text{SSE}}{N-p} = \frac{\mathbf{e}^{\!\top}\mathbf{e}}{\operatorname{tr}(M)} .$$

    The divisor $N-p$ is $\operatorname{tr}(M)$ from §2.8.2 — the residual vector lives in an $(N-p)$-dimensional space, so it has that many free coordinates, not $N$. Then $\text{SE}(\hat\beta_j)=\sqrt{\hat\sigma^2[(X^{\!\top}X)^{-1}]_{jj}}$ and, adding assumption 7,

    $$t_j = \frac{\hat\beta_j - \beta_j^{(0)}}{\text{SE}(\hat\beta_j)} \sim t_{N-p}\quad\text{under } H_0:\beta_j=\beta_j^{(0)} \text{ (usually } 0).$$

    2.12.1   Standard errors and $t$-tests, computed example

    For the §2.7 fit: $\text{SSE}=47.075$, $N=5$, $p=3$, hence $N-p=2$ residual degrees of freedom and

    $$\hat\sigma^2 = \frac{47.075}{2} = 23.537, \qquad \hat\sigma = 4.852 .$$

    The diagonal of $(X^{\!\top}X)^{-1}$ is $(8.3961,\ 0.02549,\ 0.19608)$, so for instance

    $$\operatorname{Var}(\hat\beta_1) = 23.537\times 0.02549 = 0.5999,\qquad \text{SE}(\hat\beta_1)=\sqrt{0.5999}=0.7746 .$$

    Assembling the standard regression table, with $t_{0.975,\,2}=4.3027$ giving the CI half-widths:

    coefficientestimateSE$t$$p$ (2-sided)95% CI$H_0:\beta_j=0$
    intercept $\beta_0$29.04314.0582.0660.1748[-31.44, 89.53]not rejected
    $\beta_1$ hours studied4.7920.7756.1870.0251[1.46, 8.12]rejected at 5%
