    $\beta_2$ hours slept3.1572.1481.4690.2795[-6.09, 12.40]not rejected

    Arithmetic for the study-hours row, in full: $t_1 = 4.792/0.7746 = 6.187$; the two-sided $p$ is $2\,P(T_2 > 6.187) = 0.0251$; and the interval is $4.792 \pm 4.3027\times 0.7746 = 4.792 \pm 3.333 = [1.459,\ 8.125]$.

    The CI and the test are the same statement. $H_0:\beta_j=0$ is rejected at level $\alpha$ exactly when the $(1-\alpha)$ confidence interval excludes $0$ — check both rows above: $\beta_1$'s interval $[1.46, 8.12]$ misses zero and $p<0.05$; $\beta_2$'s interval $[-6.09, 12.40]$ straddles zero and $p>0.05$. This is not a coincidence but a definition: the interval is the set of null values that would not be rejected. Note also how wide the intervals are — $\beta_1$ is "significant" yet consistent with anything from 1.5 to 8.1 points per study hour. Point estimation gives one number; interval estimation gives the honest range, and at $N=5$ the honest range is enormous.

    2.12.2   The $F$-test: is the model, as a whole, worth anything?

    The $t$-tests ask $p$ separate questions. The overall $F$-test asks one joint question, $H_0: \beta_1=\beta_2=\cdots=\beta_k=0$ (all slopes zero; the intercept is not on trial), by comparing explained to unexplained mean squares:

    $$F = \frac{\text{SSR}/k}{\text{SSE}/(N-p)} = \frac{R^2/k}{(1-R^2)/(N-k-1)} \sim F_{k,\,N-p} \text{ under } H_0,\qquad k = p-1 .$$

    For the 5-student fit, $\text{SSR}=1030.925$ with $k=2$, $\text{SSE}=47.075$ with $N-p=2$:

    $$F = \frac{1030.925/2}{47.075/2} = \frac{515.463}{23.537} = 21.900 \quad\text{on } (2,2)\text{ df},\qquad p = 0.0437 .$$

    Cross-check via the $R^2$ form: $\dfrac{0.9563/2}{0.04367/2} = 21.900$ ✓. So the pair of features jointly explains significantly more than nothing at the 5% level, even though only one of the two individual $t$-tests cleared the same bar.

    Significant $F$, insignificant $t$'s — the classic diagnostic pattern. When the $F$-test rejects but no (or few) individual coefficients do, one of two things is happening. Either the predictors are collinear, so the joint effect is well determined while the split between them is not (§2.11 is the pure case: there, $\hat\beta_1$'s $t$ fell from 13.06 to 4.28 purely by adding a redundant column). Or the sample is simply too small for per-coefficient precision, which is what is happening here: $\operatorname{corr}(x_1,x_2)=0.139$, so there is essentially no collinearity — the problem is 2 degrees of freedom. The reverse pattern (all $t$'s significant, $F$ not) is essentially impossible and indicates an arithmetic error.

    2.12.3   Type I, Type II and power example

    Every hypothesis test is a decision under uncertainty with two ways to be wrong:

    $H_0$ is true$H_0$ is false
    reject $H_0$Type I error, probability $\alpha$ (a false alarm)correct decision, probability $1-\beta$ = power
    fail to reject $H_0$correct decision, probability $1-\alpha$Type II error, probability $\beta$ (a miss)

    $\alpha$ is chosen by you (conventionally $0.05$); $\beta$ is not chosen — it is whatever the sample size, the noise level and the true effect leave you with. The $p$-value is a third, distinct thing: the probability, assuming $H_0$ is true, of a test statistic at least as extreme as the one observed. It is not the probability that $H_0$ is true, and it is not $\alpha$; $\alpha$ is the threshold, $p$ is the observation compared against it.

    Take $H_0:\beta_1=0$ against the alternative that the true effect equals the fitted $4.792$. With $\text{SE}=0.7746$ the noncentrality parameter is $\lambda = 4.792/0.7746 = 6.187$, and at $\alpha=0.05$ with 2 df the rejection region is $|t| > 4.3027$. Integrating the noncentral $t_2(\lambda)$ density over that region:

    $$\text{power} = 1-\beta = 0.853, \qquad \beta = P(\text{Type II error}) = 0.147 .$$

    Power against smaller true effects, same design:

    true $\beta_1$1234568
    power0.1240.3140.5430.7410.8750.9490.995
    $\beta$ (miss rate)0.8760.6860.4570.2590.1250.0510.005

    At a true effect of 2 points per hour — half what we fitted, still a real effect — this design detects it only 31% of the time. Holding everything else fixed and enlarging the cohort, the sample size needed to reach the conventional 80% power against that effect is $N=9$ (power $0.858$, $\text{SE}(\hat\beta_1)$ falling from $0.775$ to $0.548$).

    Interpretation. The two error rates trade against each other along a fixed curve set by the design: lowering $\alpha$ to $0.01$ widens the acceptance band, which shrinks the red region and grows the purple one. The only way to shrink both at once is to move the two distributions further apart — more data ($\text{SE}\propto 1/\sqrt{N}$), less noise ($\sigma$), or more spread-out predictors ($s^2_{x_j}$), which are precisely the three terms in §2.11's variance identity. This is also the honest reading of a non-significant result: $\beta_2$'s $p=0.28$ does not say sleep has no effect on exam scores; with power around $0.31$ against a plausible effect, it says this experiment could not have told the difference. "Absence of evidence is not evidence of absence" is a statement about $\beta$, not about $\alpha$.

    Every $p$-value in this subsection assumes assumptions 2, 4 and 7 hold. They are not checkable at $N=5$ — five residuals cannot reveal heteroscedasticity or non-normality — so the correct posture is that these numbers illustrate the machinery, not that they license a claim about students. Two further habits worth building: run $k$ tests at $\alpha=0.05$ and you expect $0.05k$ false positives by construction (multiple-comparison correction, not covered here); and statistical significance is not effect size — $\hat\beta_1 = 4.792$ points per hour is the number that matters practically, $t=6.19$ merely says it is distinguishable from zero.

    2.12.4   The other two tests on the list: $\chi^2$ and Kolmogorov–Smirnov example

    The deck's inference slide names four "important tests": $t$ (compare means), $F$ (compare variances / overall regression significance), $\chi^2$ (variance, independence and goodness-of-fit) and, under nonparametric inference, the Kolmogorov–Smirnov test. The first two are §2.12.1–2.12.2. The other two have already appeared here in passing — Breusch–Pagan refers $NR^2_{\text{aux}}$ to a $\chi^2$ null (§2.9.1), and §3's Wald and likelihood-ratio tests will be $\chi^2$ too — but neither has been stated in its own right, so both are closed out here.

    Adjudication — the deck's spelling. Slide 9 writes "Kolmogorov Smirnov" with a space; the test is named for two people, Andrey Kolmogorov and Nikolai Smirnov, so the conventional rendering is the hyphenated "Kolmogorov–Smirnov". A typographic slip in the source, not a different test; we use the hyphenated form throughout.

    $\chi^2$, three uses, one statistic. The chi-square distribution with $k$ degrees of freedom is the law of a sum of $k$ squared independent standard normals, which is why it turns up wherever squared deviations are added up.

    • A variance. For an iid normal sample, $\dfrac{(N-1)s^2}{\sigma_0^2}\sim\chi^2_{N-1}$ under $H_0:\sigma^2=\sigma_0^2$. Inverting it gives the CI $\left[\frac{(N-1)s^2}{\chi^2_{0.975,\,N-1}},\ \frac{(N-1)s^2}{\chi^2_{0.025,\,N-1}}\right]$, which is asymmetric — variances are.
    • Independence, and goodness-of-fit. Both are the same arithmetic, $\chi^2=\sum_{\text{cells}}\frac{(O-E)^2}{E}$, differing only in where the expected counts $E$ come from: from the product of the margins ($E_{ij}=R_iC_j/n$, $\mathrm{df}=(r-1)(c-1)$) for independence, and from a hypothesised distribution ($\mathrm{df}=\text{cells}-1-\#\text{parameters estimated}$) for goodness-of-fit.

    (i) A variance. The ten exam scores of §2.11 have $s^2=177.38$ (i.e. $s=13.32$ marks). The department claims its papers are calibrated to $\sigma=10$:

    $$\chi^2 = \frac{9\times 177.38}{100} = 15.964 \ \text{ on } 9\ \text{df},\qquad p_{\text{2-sided}} = 0.135,$$

    with the 95% acceptance region $[2.700,\ 19.023]$ — $15.964$ sits inside it, so the claim survives. The 95% CI for $\sigma^2$ is $[83.9,\ 591.2]$, i.e. $\sigma\in[9.2,\ 24.3]$: ten observations pin a variance down barely at all.

    (ii) Independence. A $2\times2$ table of 100 students, revision attendance against pass/fail:

    passedfailedrow total
    attended revision30 (22.5)20 (27.5)50
    skipped revision15 (22.5)35 (27.5)50
    column total4555100

    Expected counts (italic) are $E_{ij}=R_iC_j/n$, e.g. $50\times45/100=22.5$. Then

    $$\chi^2 = \frac{7.5^2}{22.5}+\frac{7.5^2}{27.5}+\frac{7.5^2}{22.5}+\frac{7.5^2}{27.5} = 2.5+2.045+2.5+2.045 = 9.091 \ \text{ on } 1\ \text{df},\qquad p = 0.0026,$$

    so attendance and outcome are not independent in this sample.

    (iii) Goodness-of-fit. Are 100 grades spread evenly over four bands? Observed $(32,28,22,18)$ against $E=25$ each:

    $$\chi^2 = \frac{49+9+9+49}{25} = 4.64 \ \text{ on } 3\ \text{df},\qquad p = 0.200,$$

    so uniformity is not refuted: an imbalance of $32$ against $18$ across four bands is well within what 100 coin-flips-into-four-buckets produces by chance.

    Kolmogorov–Smirnov. The one test here that assumes no distribution family at all — hence "nonparametric". It compares the empirical CDF $F_N(x)=\frac1N\#\{i: x_i\le x\}$ with a reference CDF $F_0$ by their largest vertical gap:

    $$D_N = \sup_x\,\big|F_N(x)-F_0(x)\big| ,$$

    whose null distribution depends on $N$ alone, not on $F_0$. The two-sample version replaces $F_0$ by a second empirical CDF and asks whether two samples came from the same law. It is the formal counterpart of the QQ plot that the assumptions table offers for normality of errors (§2.9.1) — the QQ plot shows you where the fit fails, KS reduces the same comparison to one number.

    Run it on the three residual sets of Fig. 2.6, each against a normal with the sample's own scale, and put it beside the Shapiro–Wilk values from the same data:

    panel ($n=60$)KS $D$KS $p$Shapiro–Wilk $p$Breusch–Pagan $p$Durbin–Watson
    healthy0.1210.3210.5010.6571.99
    heteroscedastic0.1710.0540.0270.000951.74
    autocorrelated0.2770.000150.3230.0170.46

    Two-sample KS between the healthy and heteroscedastic residuals gives $D=0.233$, $p=0.076$.

    Interpretation. This table is the best argument in the section for running more than one diagnostic. Read the heteroscedastic row: Shapiro–Wilk rejects normality at 5% ($p=0.027$) and KS does not ($p=0.054$) — both are looking at the right thing, since scaling a normal by a varying factor produces heavy tails, and they simply differ in power. Now read the autocorrelated row, and read it sceptically: KS returns $p=0.00015$ for a series whose marginal distribution is exactly normal by construction. That is not a normality failure, it is KS's own assumption failing — the null distribution of $D_N$ assumes independent draws, and $\hat\rho\approx0.77$ means these 60 points carry far less information than 60 independent ones, so the empirical CDF wanders further than the null allows. It is the same false positive as the Breusch–Pagan $p=0.017$ in the same column, from the same cause. A second caveat pulls the other way: the scale here is estimated from the same sample the test is applied to, which makes the quoted KS $p$-values conservative (the Lilliefors correction exists precisely for that). The rule that survives both: a distributional test only tests the assumption you named if the other assumptions hold, so establish independence first (Durbin–Watson), then constant variance (Breusch–Pagan), then shape (QQ, Shapiro–Wilk, KS) — in that order.

    Forward bridge — the same three tests, one level up. Everything in §2.12 depends on $\hat{\boldsymbol\beta}$ being exactly normal, which follows from linearity plus assumption 7. Generalised linear models (§3) have no closed form and no exact normal sampling distribution, so each tool is replaced by its large-sample analogue: the $t$-test on $\hat\beta_j/\text{SE}$ becomes the Wald test, $(\hat\beta_j/\text{SE})^2 \sim \chi^2_1$, with the standard errors read off the inverse Fisher information instead of $\hat\sigma^2(X^{\!\top}X)^{-1}$; and the overall $F$-test becomes the likelihood-ratio test, comparing model deviances against a $\chi^2$ null. Confidence intervals, $p$-values, Type I/II errors and power carry over unchanged in meaning — only the reference distribution changes.

    §2.12's whole regression table — coefficients, SEs, $t$, $p$, CIs, the overall $F$ — and §2.11's VIF diagnostics are both one library call away in practice; this is the interview-ready version of everything derived by hand above.

    Code — statsmodels OLS summary and VIF (statsmodels) 
    import statsmodels.api as sm
from statsmodels.stats.outliers_influence import variance_inflation_factor
import numpy as np

X = np.array([[2, 6], [4, 7], [6, 5], [8, 8], [10, 6]], dtype=float)
y = np.array([55, 70, 78, 95, 92], dtype=float)

X_sm = sm.add_constant(X)          # statsmodels does NOT add an intercept automatically -- easy to forget
model = sm.OLS(y, X_sm).fit()
print(model.summary())             # coef, SE, t, P>|t|, 95% CI per row, plus the overall F-statistic -- all of §2.12 in one call

# VIF is computed on the design matrix WITH the constant included, one column index at a time
vifs = [variance_inflation_factor(X_sm, i) for i in range(X_sm.shape[1])]
# vifs[0] is the VIF of the constant column (ignore it); read vifs[1:] against the >5 / >10 thresholds of §2.11

    sm.add_constant is easy to skip and silently fits a no-intercept model with biased slopes; variance_inflation_factor takes the whole design matrix plus a column index rather than two separate feature arrays, so omitting the constant column understates every VIF in the list.

    2.13   Summary

    Three algorithms, one score $\mathbf{w}^{\!\top}\mathbf{x}$: the perceptron applies the delta rule $\mathbf{w}\leftarrow\mathbf{w}+y\mathbf{x}$ on every misclassified point and is only guaranteed to terminate on linearly separable data; pocket adds a running best-so-far tracker so there is always a well-defined answer even when the data is not separable; linear regression drops the sign and solves the mean-squared-error objective exactly via the normal equations, $\mathbf{w}^\star=(X^{\!\top}X)^{-1}X^{\!\top}Y$, provided $X$ has full column rank. All three reappear later: perceptron's mistake-driven update is the ancestor of gradient descent (§4); the closed-form MSE solution is what ridge regression regularises (§6); and the linear score itself is what logistic regression squashes through a sigmoid (§3).

    The second half of the section reads the same estimator statistically rather than algorithmically. Geometrically, $\hat{\boldsymbol\beta}$ is whatever makes the residual perpendicular to $\operatorname{col}(X)$, and the operator that performs the projection is the hat matrix $P=X(X^{\!\top}X)^{-1}X^{\!\top}$ — symmetric, idempotent, with $\operatorname{tr}(P)=p$ and $\operatorname{tr}(I-P)=N-p$, which is where every degrees-of-freedom divisor in the section comes from. Seven assumptions turn that algebra into inference; violating them costs you either unbiasedness (linearity, exogeneity, rank) or trustworthy standard errors (independence, homoscedasticity), and residual plots plus Durbin–Watson, Breusch–Pagan, Shapiro–Wilk, Kolmogorov–Smirnov and VIF are how you find out which — with leverage, studentized residuals and Cook's distance answering the separate question of which observations are driving the fit. Fit quality is reported by $R^2$ (monotone in model size, so useless for selection), $R^2_{\text{adj}}$ (degrees-of-freedom-penalised, so usable), and MAE/MSE/RMSE in the units of $y$. Coefficient inference is one formula, $\operatorname{Var}(\hat{\boldsymbol\beta})=\sigma^2(X^{\!\top}X)^{-1}$, unfolded into $t$-tests, confidence intervals, the joint $F$-test, the $\chi^2$ and Kolmogorov–Smirnov tests that complete the deck's list, and the Type I/Type II/power triangle — with multicollinearity acting on all of them through the single multiplier $\text{VIF}_j=1/(1-R^2_j)$.

    Practice 2.3 — is the point $\mathbf{x}=(1,-2,3)$ (augmented) correctly classified by $\mathbf{w}=(1,2,1)$ from the §2.3 example, if its true label is $y=-1$?

    Score $= \mathbf{w}^{\!\top}\mathbf{x} = 1\cdot1 + 2\cdot(-2) + 1\cdot3 = 1-4+3=0$. By the sign convention $\operatorname{sign}(0)=-1$, predicted $\hat y=-1=y$. Correctly classified — but only by the convention; a score of exactly $0$ means the point sits exactly on the decision boundary, so this is a boundary case, not a confidently correct one.

    Practice 2.4 — why can't pocket simply keep the current $\mathbf{w}$ every step instead of tracking a separate best-so-far?

    Because the current $\mathbf{w}$ after a PLA update is not guaranteed to have lower $E_{\text{in}}$ than before — the update only guarantees fixing the one point it was applied to, and may break others (§2.4's non-separable example: $E_{\text{in}}(\mathbf{w}_t)$ swings between $0.17$ and $0.83$ across steps). If pocket reported "whatever $\mathbf{w}$ we currently hold" at an arbitrary stopping step, it could report a state with $E_{\text{in}}=0.83$ purely by bad luck in when the budget ran out. The separate best-so-far tracker is what makes the reported answer independent of the stopping point.

    Practice 2.5 — for the 2-feature exam-score regression, predict the score for a student who studies 5 hours and sleeps 7 hours.

    Using $\mathbf{w}^\star\approx(29.04,\,4.79,\,3.16)$ from §2.7:

    $$\hat y = 29.04 + 4.79(5) + 3.16(7) = 29.04+23.96+22.10 \approx 75.1.$$

    Sanity check against the table: this sits between the $(4,7)\to70$ and $(6,5)\to78$ rows, which is plausible — 5 hours studied is between those two, and the extra 2 hours of sleep versus the $(6,5)$ row nudges the prediction up slightly relative to interpolating on $x_1$ alone.

    Practice 2.6 — a colleague adds a "attended the optional seminar" flag to the exam-score model and reports that $R^2$ rose from $0.9563$ to $0.9719$. Should the feature stay?

    No — and $R^2$ could never have answered the question. §2.8's geometry guarantees that adding any column enlarges $\operatorname{col}(X)$, and $\mathbf{y}$ cannot be further from a larger subspace, so SSE weakly falls and $R^2$ weakly rises for every feature, signal or noise. Compute the degrees-of-freedom-corrected version instead. With $N=5$:

    $$R^2_{\text{adj}} = 1-(1-R^2)\frac{N-1}{N-p}:\qquad \text{2 features } (p=3):\; 1-0.043668\cdot\tfrac{4}{2} = 0.9127,\qquad \text{3 features } (p=4):\; 1-0.028061\cdot\tfrac{4}{1} = 0.8878 .$$

    Adjusted $R^2$ fell by $0.0249$. The penalty multiplier doubled (from $4/2=2$ to $4/1=4$) because the fourth parameter consumed one of only two remaining degrees of freedom, and the feature's $R^2$ gain of $0.0156$ did not cover that. The break-even point: solving $1-(1-R^2)\cdot 4 = 0.9127$ gives $R^2 = 0.9782$, so the new column needed to reach $0.9782$ and reached only $0.9719$. Independent confirmation that it is noise: its correlation with $y$ is $-0.250$, i.e. faintly negative.

    The general lesson: use $R^2$ to describe a fitted model, never to choose between models of different sizes. Adjusted $R^2$ is the minimum defensible correction; cross-validated out-of-sample error (§6) is the better one, because it penalises complexity by measuring the harm directly instead of assuming a formula for it.

    Practice 2.7 — the overall $F$-test on the exam-score model is significant ($p=0.0437$) but the sleep coefficient's $p$ is $0.2795$. Build its 95% CI and reconcile the two results.

    The interval. $\hat\beta_2 = 3.1569$ with $\text{SE}(\hat\beta_2)=2.1483$ on $N-p = 5-3 = 2$ degrees of freedom, so $t_{0.975,\,2}=4.3027$ and

    $$\text{CI} = 3.1569 \pm 4.3027\times 2.1483 = 3.1569 \pm 9.2433 = [-6.086,\ 12.400].$$

    The interval contains $0$, which is the same statement as $p=0.2795 > 0.05$ — a coefficient is "significant at 5%" precisely when its 95% interval excludes zero. Note its width: $18.5$ points per hour of sleep. That is not evidence that sleep is irrelevant; it is evidence that five students tell you almost nothing about it.

    The reconciliation. $F$ and $t$ ask different questions. $F$ tests $H_0:\beta_1=\beta_2=0$ jointly — "do these two features together beat an intercept-only model?" — and answers yes ($F=21.90$ on $(2,2)$ df). Each $t$ tests $H_0:\beta_j=0$ given the other feature is already in the model — a marginal-contribution question. The joint effect here is carried almost entirely by study hours ($t=6.19$), so the joint test fires while sleep's marginal test does not. There are two standard causes of this pattern, and only one applies: collinearity is not it, since $\operatorname{corr}(x_1,x_2)=0.139$; the cause is low power, with only 2 residual degrees of freedom. Confirmation from §2.12.3: against a true effect of 2 points per hour this design has power $0.31$, so it misses a real effect roughly two times in three.

    Practice 2.8 — from the 3-point example's hat matrix, compute each observation's leverage. Which point does the fit listen to most, and why is the usual $2p/N$ flag useless here?

    Leverage is the diagonal of $P$, so read it straight off $P = \tfrac16\begin{pmatrix}5&2&-1\\2&2&2\\-1&2&5\end{pmatrix}$:

    $$h_{11}=\tfrac56=0.8333,\qquad h_{22}=\tfrac26=0.3333,\qquad h_{33}=\tfrac56=0.8333 .$$

    Check. $\sum_i h_{ii} = \tfrac{5+2+5}{6} = 2 = \operatorname{tr}(P) = p$, exactly as §2.8.2 proves — the leverages of any OLS fit always sum to the number of parameters, so the mean leverage is $p/N = 2/3$ no matter what the data looks like.

    Interpretation. $h_{ii} = \partial\hat y_i/\partial y_i$, so the endpoints at $x=1$ and $x=3$ each pull their own fitted value 2.5 times harder than the middle point at $x=2$: nudge $y_1$ up by one unit and $\hat y_1$ follows by $0.833$, whereas nudging $y_2$ moves $\hat y_2$ by only $0.333$. This is generic — leverage grows with distance from $\bar x$, which is why extreme $x$ values are where fits get hijacked, and why the deck pairs leverage with Cook's distance for influence detection. Row 1 of $P$, $(0.833,\,0.333,\,-0.167)$, also shows the fitted value at $x=1$ borrowing negatively from the far endpoint: pushing $y_3$ up tilts the line and drags $\hat y_1$ down.

    Why the flag is useless. The rule of thumb is $h_{ii} > 2p/N = 2\cdot 2/3 = 1.333$, but leverage is bounded above by $1$, so no observation in this dataset can ever be flagged. Small-$N$, large-$p$ designs push the average leverage $p/N$ toward 1 and make the threshold exceed the maximum possible value — the diagnostic only works when $N \gg p$.

    3   Logistic Regression, GLMs & Statistical Inference

    Section 2 ended with a linear score $z = \boldsymbol{\beta}^{\!\top}\mathbf{x}$ and two things to do with it: threshold it (perceptron) or read it as a real number (regression). This section adds the third and by far the most useful option — squash it into a probability. That single change turns the linear score into a full statistical model: a likelihood, a loss, standard errors, hypothesis tests, and goodness-of-fit statistics. Once the machinery is set up for binary $y$, the same machinery generalises with one substitution — the link function — to counts, ordered categories and unordered categories. That family is the generalised linear model (GLM), and logistic regression is just its most famous member.

    Notation for this section. Following the handwritten source we write coefficients as $\boldsymbol{\beta}$ rather than the $\mathbf{w}$ of §2 — they are the same object. Labels here are $y\in\{0,1\}$ (not the $\pm1$ of the perceptron); the two conventions are reconciled in §3.3. Symbols used throughout:

    • $\mathbf{x} \in \mathbb{R}^{(d+1)\times 1}$ — one augmented feature vector, first entry $x_0=1$ so the intercept lives inside $\boldsymbol{\beta}$.
    • $\mathbf{X} \in \mathbb{R}^{n\times(d+1)}$ — the design matrix, one row per sample.
    • $\boldsymbol{\beta} \in \mathbb{R}^{(d+1)\times1}$ — the coefficient vector.
    • $z = \boldsymbol{\beta}^{\!\top}\mathbf{x}$ (scalar), $\mathbf{z} = \mathbf{X}\boldsymbol{\beta} \in \mathbb{R}^{n\times1}$ — the linear predictor (also written $\eta$ in GLM language).
    • $p = P(y=1\mid\mathbf{x})$ (scalar), $\mathbf{p}\in(0,1)^{n\times1}$ — fitted probabilities.
    • $\ell$ — log-likelihood; $L$ — a loss to be minimised; $\mathcal{L}$ — a likelihood.

    3.1   From score to probability: the sigmoid and the log-odds

    Logistic regression is used to predict the probability of a binary outcome. The construction is two lines:

    $$z = \boldsymbol{\beta}^{\!\top}\mathbf{x}, \qquad p = \sigma(z) = \frac{1}{1+e^{-z}} = \frac{e^{z}}{1+e^{z}}.$$

    The two forms are the same function — multiply numerator and denominator of the first by $e^{z}$. The map $\sigma:\mathbb{R}\to(0,1)$ is the sigmoid (logistic) function: monotone increasing, $\sigma(-\infty)=0$, $\sigma(0)=\tfrac12$, $\sigma(+\infty)=1$.

    Why this particular squasher — inverting it gives the log-odds

    Start from $p = \dfrac{1}{1+e^{-z}}$ and solve for $z$.

    1. Reciprocate: $\dfrac{1}{p} = 1 + e^{-z}$.
    2. Rearrange: $e^{-z} = \dfrac{1}{p} - 1 = \dfrac{1-p}{p}$.
    3. Invert both sides: $e^{z} = \dfrac{p}{1-p}$.
    4. Take logs: $z = \ln\dfrac{p}{1-p}$.

    Hence the model can be written entirely without $\sigma$:

    $$\boxed{\;\log\frac{p}{1-p} = \boldsymbol{\beta}^{\!\top}\mathbf{x}\;}$$

    The quantity $\dfrac{p}{1-p}$ is the odds, and its logarithm is the log-odds or logit — exactly the label the handwritten page attaches with an arrow to that fraction. So logistic regression is linear regression on the log-odds scale. The nonlinearity is entirely in the link, never in the predictor.

    The sigmoid, tabulated. Note that column 4 reproduces column 1 exactly — that is the inversion above.

    $z=\boldsymbol{\beta}^{\!\top}\mathbf{x}$$p=\sigma(z)$odds $p/(1-p)$$\ln[p/(1-p)]$
    $-4$0.0179860.018316$-4$
    $-2$0.1192030.135335$-2$
    $-1$0.2689410.367879$-1$
    $\;\;0$0.5000001.000000$\;\;0$
    $\;\;0.5$0.6224591.648721$\;\;0.5$
    $\;\;1$0.7310592.718282$\;\;1$
    $\;\;2$0.8807977.389056$\;\;2$
    $\;\;4$0.98201454.598150$\;\;4$

    Two identities used constantly below

    (i) Reflection. $1-\sigma(z) = \sigma(-z)$, so $\sigma(z)+\sigma(-z)=1$.

    Proof. $1 - \dfrac{e^{z}}{1+e^{z}} = \dfrac{1+e^{z}-e^{z}}{1+e^{z}} = \dfrac{1}{1+e^{z}} = \sigma(-z)$. $\blacksquare$ Numerically, $\sigma(1.3)+\sigma(-1.3) = 1$ to machine precision.

    (ii) Derivative. $\sigma'(z) = \sigma(z)\,\big(1-\sigma(z)\big) = p(1-p)$.

    Proof. Write $\sigma = (1+e^{-z})^{-1}$. Then $\sigma' = -(1+e^{-z})^{-2}\cdot(-e^{-z}) = \dfrac{e^{-z}}{(1+e^{-z})^{2}} = \dfrac{1}{1+e^{-z}}\cdot\dfrac{e^{-z}}{1+e^{-z}} = \sigma(z)\,\sigma(-z) = p(1-p)$, using (i) in the last step. $\blacksquare$

    The derivative is maximal at $z=0$, where it equals $0.25$, and decays to $0$ in both tails.

    Interpretation. Three consequences follow from the boxed log-odds form, and they are the reason logistic regression survived a century of competitors.

    1. Coefficients are odds multipliers. Increase $x_j$ by one unit, holding everything else fixed: the log-odds increase by $\beta_j$, so the odds get multiplied by $e^{\beta_j}$. With $\beta_j=0.8$ the odds multiply by $2.225541$ (a 123% increase in odds); with $\beta_j=-0.3$ they multiply by $0.740818$ (a 26% decrease).
    2. The decision boundary stays linear. The rule from the source is $p\ge0.5\Rightarrow$ predict $1$, $p<0.5\Rightarrow$ predict $0$. Since $\sigma$ is monotone and $\sigma(0)=\tfrac12$, "$p\ge0.5$" is exactly "$z\ge0$", i.e. $\boldsymbol{\beta}^{\!\top}\mathbf{x}\ge0$ — a hyperplane, the same geometric object as §2's perceptron. Logistic regression buys calibration, not extra flexibility.
    3. Effects are non-linear in probability but linear in log-odds. The same $\Delta z=1$ moves $p$ from $0.5$ to $0.731059$ near the middle, but only from $0.982014$ to $0.993307$ out in the tail. Saturation is a feature: an extra unit of evidence should not matter much once you are already sure.

    Gotcha — $0.5$ is a convention, not a result. The threshold rule quoted above is a separate decision on top of the fitted model. Nothing in the likelihood chooses $0.5$; it is optimal only under symmetric misclassification costs and it is a bad default under class imbalance (§3.10 shows a fitted model with recall $0.1351$ at threshold $0.5$). Choosing the operating point is what the ROC curve is for — see §5.

    3.2   The loss: cross-entropy derived from maximum likelihood derivation

    The handwritten notes state the loss without derivation:

    $$L = -\sum \Big[\, y\log p + (1-y)\log(1-p) \,\Big].$$

    Here is where it comes from. Nothing is assumed except that the $n$ samples are independent given their features.

    Step 1 — write the per-sample probability as one formula. The model says $P(y=1\mid\mathbf{x})=p$ and $P(y=0\mid\mathbf{x})=1-p$. Both cases collapse into a single expression, because an exponent of $0$ kills a factor:

    $$P(y\mid\mathbf{x}) = p^{\,y}\,(1-p)^{\,1-y}, \qquad y\in\{0,1\}.$$

    Check: $y=1$ gives $p^1(1-p)^0=p$; $y=0$ gives $p^0(1-p)^1=1-p$. This is the Bernoulli likelihood.

    Step 2 — likelihood of the whole sample. Independence turns the joint probability into a product:

    $$\mathcal{L}(\boldsymbol{\beta}) = \prod_{i=1}^{n} p_i^{\,y_i}\,(1-p_i)^{\,1-y_i}, \qquad p_i = \sigma(\boldsymbol{\beta}^{\!\top}\mathbf{x}_i).$$

    Step 3 — take logs. $\ln$ is strictly increasing, so it does not move the maximiser; it converts the product into a sum (essential — a product of $n$ numbers each below $1$ underflows for $n$ in the hundreds).

    $$\ell(\boldsymbol{\beta}) = \ln\mathcal{L}(\boldsymbol{\beta}) = \sum_{i=1}^{n}\Big[\, y_i\ln p_i + (1-y_i)\ln(1-p_i) \,\Big].$$

    Step 4 — flip the sign to get a loss. Maximising $\ell$ is minimising $-\ell$:

    $$\boxed{\;L(\boldsymbol{\beta}) = -\sum_{i=1}^{n}\Big[\, y_i\ln p_i + (1-y_i)\ln(1-p_i) \,\Big]\;}$$

    which is precisely the handwritten formula. Dividing by $n$ gives the mean log-loss, the version reported by software; the minimiser is unchanged.

    Why it is called "cross-entropy". For a single sample the true label defines a degenerate distribution $q=(1-y,\;y)$ over $\{0,1\}$ and the model proposes $\hat q=(1-p,\;p)$. The cross-entropy between two distributions is $H(q,\hat q) = -\sum_c q_c\ln\hat q_c$, which for this $q$ is exactly $-[y\ln p+(1-y)\ln(1-p)]$. So "log loss", "binary cross-entropy", "negative Bernoulli log-likelihood" and "logistic loss" are four names for one function.

    Reconciling the two label conventions

    v5 derives the same loss with labels $y\in\{+1,-1\}$ and reaches

    $$E_{\text{in}}(\mathbf{w}) = \frac{1}{n}\sum_{i=1}^{n}\ln\!\Big(1+e^{-y_i\,\mathbf{w}^{\!\top}\mathbf{x}_i}\Big).$$

    This is the same function, not a different one. The bridge is the reflection identity: with $\pm1$ labels the model compresses to $\hat P(y\mid\mathbf{x}) = \sigma(y\,\mathbf{w}^{\!\top}\mathbf{x})$, because $y=+1$ gives $\sigma(z)=p$ and $y=-1$ gives $\sigma(-z)=1-p$. Then $-\ln\sigma(s) = -\ln\frac{1}{1+e^{-s}} = \ln(1+e^{-s})$ with $s=y\,\mathbf{w}^{\!\top}\mathbf{x}$. Mapping $y_{\pm}=2y_{01}-1$ converts one form into the other term by term. Use whichever the surrounding software uses: scikit-learn and the handwritten notes use $\{0,1\}$; margin-based literature (SVM, AdaBoost, §12) uses $\{+1,-1\}$.

    The form $\ln(1+e^{-s})$ is also the numerically safe one: implemented as logaddexp(0, -s) it never evaluates $\ln(0)$, whereas the literal $-[y\ln p+(1-y)\ln(1-p)]$ overflows to infinity as soon as a fitted $p$ rounds to exactly $0$ or $1$. Every compute script in this section uses the stable form.

    3.3   Why not MSE? gap filled

    The source answers this in one line — "MSE doesn't penalize these appropriately and leads to a non-convex optimization problem" — and backs it with a two-row table of predicted/true pairs, but never computes anything. Both halves of the claim are worked out here.

    Claim 1 — the penalties are wrong (the source's table, computed)

    The page's table, with the losses filled in. True label $y=0$ in both rows, so squared error is $(p-0)^2$ and cross-entropy is $-\ln(1-p)$.

    Predicted $p$True $y$squared error $(p-y)^2$cross-entropy $-\ln(1-p)$$|\partial L/\partial z|$, MSE$|\partial L/\partial z|$, CE
    0.9900.9801004.6051700.0196020.990000
    0.5500.3025000.7985080.2722500.550000
    ratio3.24005.76720.07201.8000

    The gradient columns use $\dfrac{\partial}{\partial z}(p-y)^2 = 2(p-y)\,p(1-p)$ and $\dfrac{\partial}{\partial z}\big[-\ln(1-p)\big] = p-y$ (both derived in §3.4).

    Interpretation. Predicting $0.99$ when the truth is $0$ is a confident, catastrophic error; predicting $0.55$ is a mild hedge. Squared error rates the catastrophe as only $3.24\times$ worse than the hedge, and — far more damaging — the learning signal it produces is $0.0720$ times as strong, i.e. 14 times weaker for the worse mistake. The $p(1-p)$ factor, which is the sigmoid's own derivative, throttles the gradient exactly where the model is most confidently wrong. Cross-entropy has no such factor: its gradient is $p-y$, which grows monotonically with the size of the error, so the catastrophe generates $1.8\times$ the signal of the hedge. This is the mechanism behind "doesn't penalize these appropriately".

    Claim 2 — MSE on a sigmoid is non-convex in $\boldsymbol{\beta}$

    Take one sample, one weight, $x=1$, so $z=w$ and $p=\sigma(w)$. For squared error $L_{\text{MSE}} = (p-y)^2$:

    1. First derivative: $\dfrac{dL}{dw} = 2(p-y)\,\dfrac{dp}{dw} = 2(p-y)\,p(1-p)$.
    2. Second derivative, product rule, using $\dfrac{d}{dw}\big[p(1-p)\big] = p(1-p)(1-2p)$: $$\frac{d^2L_{\text{MSE}}}{dw^2} = 2\Big[\big(p(1-p)\big)^{2} + (p-y)\,p(1-p)\,(1-2p)\Big].$$
    3. Set $y=0$ and factor out $p^2(1-p)$, which is positive: $$\frac{d^2L_{\text{MSE}}}{dw^2} = 2p^{2}(1-p)\Big[(1-p) + (1-2p)\Big] = 2p^{2}(1-p)\,(2-3p).$$
    4. This is negative whenever $p>\tfrac23$, i.e. whenever $w > \ln 2 = 0.693147$. At exactly $w=\ln2$ it is $0$.

    By contrast, for cross-entropy with $y=0$, $L_{\text{CE}} = -\ln(1-p)$, and the same two steps give $\dfrac{dL}{dw} = p-y$ and

    $$\frac{d^{2}L_{\text{CE}}}{dw^{2}} = p(1-p) \;>\; 0 \quad\text{for all } w .$$

    In the general $d$-dimensional case this becomes the Hessian $\mathbf{X}^{\!\top}\mathbf{W}\mathbf{X}$ with $\mathbf{W} = \operatorname{diag}\!\big(p_i(1-p_i)\big)$, which is positive semi-definite for any $\boldsymbol{\beta}$ (§3.4) — so cross-entropy is convex, globally.

    Curvature, tabulated (single sample, $x=1$, $y=0$). Sign flip in the MSE column at $w=\ln2$:

    $w$$p=\sigma(w)$$d^2L_{\text{MSE}}/dw^2$$d^2L_{\text{CE}}/dw^2$
    $-2.0$0.119203$+0.041111$0.104994
    $-1.0$0.268941$+0.126183$0.196612

    On the three-point dataset $\mathbf{x}=(1,1,4)$, $\mathbf{y}=(1,0,0)$ swept over $w\in[-6,6]$, the MSE objective has negative curvature over 87.35% of the sweep, while the cross-entropy objective's smallest curvature over the same range is $+0.001686$ — strictly positive everywhere.

    Gotcha — the flat-region trap is worse than the non-convexity. On the same three-point dataset, start optimisation from $w=-5$, where the model assigns $p=(0.006693,\,0.006693,\,0)$ and gets the first point badly wrong. The mean MSE gradient there is $-0.004373$; the mean cross-entropy gradient is $-0.328871$ — 75.21 times larger. With MSE, a badly initialised model does not merely converge to a local optimum, it barely moves at all. This is the same vanishing-gradient mechanism that kills deep sigmoid networks (§15) — here it is caused by the loss, not the depth.

    3.4   The gradient, with shapes derivation

    Neither source derives this: the handwritten page stops at the loss, and v5 states "hence gradient descent" without producing anything to descend on. Here it is, in full, with every shape tracked.

    Scalar chain rule, one sample

    Let $\ell_i = -\big[y_i\ln p_i + (1-y_i)\ln(1-p_i)\big]$ with $p_i = \sigma(z_i)$ and $z_i = \boldsymbol{\beta}^{\!\top}\mathbf{x}_i$. Chain: $\dfrac{\partial\ell_i}{\partial\boldsymbol{\beta}} = \dfrac{\partial \ell_i}{\partial p_i}\cdot\dfrac{\partial p_i}{\partial z_i}\cdot\dfrac{\partial z_i}{\partial\boldsymbol{\beta}}$.

    1. Loss w.r.t. probability. $\dfrac{\partial\ell_i}{\partial p_i} = -\dfrac{y_i}{p_i} + \dfrac{1-y_i}{1-p_i} = \dfrac{-y_i(1-p_i) + (1-y_i)p_i}{p_i(1-p_i)} = \dfrac{p_i - y_i}{p_i(1-p_i)}$  (scalar).
    2. Probability w.r.t. score. $\dfrac{\partial p_i}{\partial z_i} = p_i(1-p_i)$  (scalar, identity (ii) of §3.1).
    3. The cancellation. Multiply (1) and (2): the $p_i(1-p_i)$ factors annihilate, leaving $$\frac{\partial \ell_i}{\partial z_i} = p_i - y_i .$$ This single cancellation is the whole reason cross-entropy is the right loss for a sigmoid: the loss is chosen so that its derivative undoes the link's saturation.
    4. Score w.r.t. coefficients. $\dfrac{\partial z_i}{\partial\boldsymbol{\beta}} = \mathbf{x}_i$, shape $(d{+}1)\times1$.
    5. Combine. $\dfrac{\partial\ell_i}{\partial\boldsymbol{\beta}} = (p_i - y_i)\,\mathbf{x}_i$ — a scalar times a $(d{+}1)\times1$ vector, so shape $(d{+}1)\times1$. ✓

    Matrix form, whole dataset

    Summing step 5 over $i$ and writing it as a matrix product:

    $$\boxed{\;\nabla_{\boldsymbol{\beta}} L = \mathbf{X}^{\!\top}(\mathbf{p} - \mathbf{y})\;}\qquad\text{or, for the mean loss,}\qquad \nabla_{\boldsymbol{\beta}} \bar L = \tfrac{1}{n}\mathbf{X}^{\!\top}(\mathbf{p} - \mathbf{y}).$$
    objectshapemeaning
    $\mathbf{X}$$n \times (d{+}1)$design matrix, augmented with a column of ones
    $\boldsymbol{\beta}$$(d{+}1) \times 1$coefficients
    $\mathbf{z} = \mathbf{X}\boldsymbol{\beta}$$n \times 1$$\big(n\times(d{+}1)\big)\cdot\big((d{+}1)\times1\big)$
    $\mathbf{p} = \sigma(\mathbf{z})$$n \times 1$elementwise, shape preserved
    $\mathbf{p}-\mathbf{y}$$n \times 1$the residual vector
    $\mathbf{X}^{\!\top}(\mathbf{p}-\mathbf{y})$$(d{+}1) \times 1$$\big((d{+}1)\times n\big)\cdot\big(n\times1\big)$ ✓ matches $\boldsymbol{\beta}$
    $\mathbf{W} = \operatorname{diag}\!\big(p_i(1-p_i)\big)$$n \times n$IRLS weights (below)
    $\mathbf{H} = \mathbf{X}^{\!\top}\mathbf{W}\mathbf{X}$$(d{+}1)\times(d{+}1)$Hessian / observed information

    The shape that surprises people. $\nabla_{\boldsymbol{\beta}}L$ has shape $(d{+}1)\times1$ — the same shape as $\boldsymbol{\beta}$, not the shape of the data. It must be so: you can only subtract a gradient from the thing you are updating. If your derivation produces an $n\times1$ object you have forgotten the $\mathbf{X}^{\!\top}$. And note $\mathbf{X}^{\!\top}(\mathbf{p}-\mathbf{y})$ is formally identical to the least-squares gradient $\mathbf{X}^{\!\top}(\hat{\mathbf{y}}-\mathbf{y})$ of §2 — only the definition of the prediction changed. What differs is that there is no closed form: setting $\mathbf{X}^{\!\top}(\sigma(\mathbf{X}\boldsymbol{\beta})-\mathbf{y})=\mathbf{0}$ is transcendental in $\boldsymbol{\beta}$, so there is no pseudo-inverse analogue. Iteration is compulsory.

    The Hessian, and why the problem is easy

    Differentiate the gradient once more. The $i$-th entry of $\mathbf{p}$ depends on $\boldsymbol{\beta}$ only through $z_i$, so $\dfrac{\partial p_i}{\partial\boldsymbol{\beta}^{\!\top}} = p_i(1-p_i)\,\mathbf{x}_i^{\!\top}$ and

    $$\nabla^2_{\boldsymbol{\beta}} L = \sum_{i=1}^{n} p_i(1-p_i)\,\mathbf{x}_i\mathbf{x}_i^{\!\top} \;=\; \mathbf{X}^{\!\top}\mathbf{W}\mathbf{X}, \qquad \mathbf{W}=\operatorname{diag}\big(p_i(1-p_i)\big)\in\mathbb{R}^{n\times n}.$$

    For any vector $\mathbf{v}\in\mathbb{R}^{(d+1)\times1}$: $\mathbf{v}^{\!\top}\mathbf{X}^{\!\top}\mathbf{W}\mathbf{X}\mathbf{v} = \sum_i p_i(1-p_i)\,(\mathbf{x}_i^{\!\top}\mathbf{v})^2 \ge 0$ because every weight $p_i(1-p_i)$ is positive. So the Hessian is positive semi-definite everywhere and the cross-entropy objective is convex: any stationary point is a global minimum, and there are no local minima to get stuck in. That is the formal version of §3.3's Claim 2.

    Two ways to use the gradient

    (a) Gradient descent — $\boldsymbol{\beta} \leftarrow \boldsymbol{\beta} - \eta\,\tfrac1n\mathbf{X}^{\!\top}(\mathbf{p}-\mathbf{y})$. Cheap per step, no matrix inversion, scales to millions of rows; step-size behaviour, momentum and Adam are §4's subject.

    (b) Newton–Raphson / IRLS — $\boldsymbol{\beta} \leftarrow \boldsymbol{\beta} + \big(\mathbf{X}^{\!\top}\mathbf{W}\mathbf{X}\big)^{-1}\mathbf{X}^{\!\top}(\mathbf{y}-\mathbf{p})$. Quadratic convergence in a handful of iterations, but each step costs an $\mathcal{O}(nd^2 + d^3)$ solve. This is what statsmodels and R's glm do, and it hands you the Fisher information for free (§3.9) — which is why classical statistics prefers it.

    3.5   A fitted model, end to end example

    Data. $n=40$ students; features hours (weekly study hours) and att (attendance, scored $0$–$10$); label $y=1$ if the student passed. 26 passed, 14 failed. The design matrix is $\mathbf{X}\in\mathbb{R}^{40\times3}$ (intercept, hours, attendance), so $\boldsymbol{\beta}\in\mathbb{R}^{3\times1}$.

    Step 0 — the gradient at $\boldsymbol{\beta}=\mathbf{0}$. Every $z_i=0$, so every $p_i=0.5$, and the score $\mathbf{X}^{\!\top}(\mathbf{y}-\mathbf{p})$ is $$\mathbf{X}^{\!\top}(\mathbf{y}-\mathbf{p}) = \begin{pmatrix}6.0\\ 54.5\\ 59.0\end{pmatrix} \;(3\times1).$$ All three entries are positive: more hours and more attendance both push toward $y=1$, so the fit will move in that direction. The Fisher information at the same point is $\mathbf{X}^{\!\top}\mathbf{X}/4$ (since $p(1-p)=0.25$ everywhere), i.e. $$\mathbf{I}(\mathbf{0}) = \begin{pmatrix} 10.0 & 48.5 & 65.5\\ 48.5 & 295.0 & 331.875\\ 65.5 & 331.875 & 483.0\end{pmatrix}\;(3\times3).$$

    Step 1 — one gradient-descent step with $\eta=0.1$ on the mean loss. The mean-form gradient is $\tfrac1{40}\mathbf{X}^{\!\top}(\mathbf{p}-\mathbf{y}) = (-0.15,\,-1.3625,\,-1.475)^{\!\top}$, so $$\boldsymbol{\beta}^{(1)} = \mathbf{0} - 0.1\cdot(-0.15,\,-1.3625,\,-1.475)^{\!\top} = (0.015,\;0.13625,\;0.1475)^{\!\top},$$ and the mean loss drops from $\ln 2 = 0.693147$ to $0.612007$.

    Step 2 — Newton–Raphson instead. Five iterations of the trace (the run converged to $\|\Delta\boldsymbol{\beta}\|<10^{-12}$ after 8):

    iter$\boldsymbol{\beta}$ at start of step$\ell(\boldsymbol{\beta})$score $\mathbf{X}^{\!\top}(\mathbf{y}-\mathbf{p})$$\|\Delta\boldsymbol{\beta}\|$

    1$(-2.918696,\;0.360769,\;0.270071)$$-17.384779$$(1.526,\;13.810,\;14.670)$1.630970
    2$(-4.529504,\;0.573035,\;0.412562)$$-15.855238$$(0.419,\;3.777,\;4.037)$0.874621
    3$(-5.393387,\;0.685855,\;0.489640)$$-15.648188$$(0.061,\;0.561,\;0.599)$0.184977
