    $\partial_{\xi_i}\mathcal{L}=C-\alpha_i-\mu_i=0\Rightarrow\alpha_i=C-\mu_i$new stationarity condition from the slack term
    $\mu_i\ge0\Rightarrow\boxed{0\le\alpha_i\le C}$the box constraint — the only change to the dual

    Substituting eliminates $\boldsymbol\xi$ and $\boldsymbol\mu$; the dual objective is exactly the hard-margin dual, with $\alpha_i$ now capped above by $C$ instead of unbounded:

    $$\max_{\boldsymbol\alpha}\ \sum_i\alpha_i-\tfrac12\sum_{i,j}\alpha_i\alpha_jy_iy_j\mathbf{x}_i^\top\mathbf{x}_j \quad\text{s.t. } 0\le\alpha_i\le C,\ \textstyle\sum_i\alpha_iy_i=0.$$

    Three regimes per point, from complementary slackness on both multiplier sets:

    Condition$\alpha_i$Interpretation
    $y_i(\mathbf{w}^\top\mathbf{x}_i+b)>1$$=0$correctly classified, strictly outside the margin
    $y_i(\mathbf{w}^\top\mathbf{x}_i+b)=1$$0<\alpha_i<C$“free” support vector — exactly on the margin
    $y_i(\mathbf{w}^\top\mathbf{x}_i+b)<1$$=C$“bound” support vector — margin violator / outlier
    How $C$ behaves. $C\to\infty$: any slack costs unbounded loss, so the soft-margin problem converges to the hard margin of §17.1 — a narrow margin that overfits to noisy or overlapping points. $C\to0$: slack is essentially free, so the optimiser buys the widest possible margin regardless of violations — heavy underfitting. $C$ is SVM's regularisation knob, directly analogous to $1/\lambda$ in ridge regression: small $C$ = strong regularisation, large $C$ = weak regularisation.
    A worked $C$-sweep on overlapping data — new content, since v5 §11 had zero numerical examples and zero figures. 14 points: 6 positives clustered around $(3,3)$ and 6 negatives — five of them around $({-3},{-3})$ and a sixth already pulled in to $(0.5,{-0.5})$ — plus one deliberate intruder of each label right at the origin (a positive point at $({-0.5},0.5)$ sitting on the negative side, a negative point at $(0.5,{-0.3})$ sitting on the positive side). Fitting a linear-kernel soft-margin SVM at four values of $C$:
    $C$$\mathbf{w}$$b$margin widthtrain acc.#SV (bound / free)
    $0.01$$(0.125,\,0.167)$$0.00$$9.60$92.9%10 (8 / 2)
    $1$$({-0.5},\,1.3)$$-0.10$$1.44$100%4 (2 / 2)
    $100$$({-0.697},\,1.627)$$-0.163$$1.13$100%3 (0 / 3)
    $10^6$$({-0.697},\,1.627)$$-0.163$$1.13$100%3 (0 / 3)

    Reading the sweep: at $C{=}0.01$ the margin is enormous ($9.60$) and eight of the ten support vectors are “bound” ($\alpha_i{=}C$, sitting inside the margin or misclassified) — the optimiser is barely paying for violations, so it buys the widest possible corridor and tolerates real training mistakes (92.9% accuracy, i.e. 1 of 14 points misclassified). At $C{=}1$ the margin shrinks to $1.44$ and training accuracy reaches 100%, with a mix of 2 bound and 2 free support vectors — the two intruders are still “bound” (pinned at $\alpha_i{=}C$, their true regime is a violation the model chooses to tolerate rather than distort $\mathbf{w}$ around). By $C{=}100$ the solution has already converged to its $C\to\infty$ limit: $\mathbf{w},b$ and the margin width are numerically identical at $C{=}100$ and $C{=}10^6$ , and all three remaining support vectors are now “free” ($0<\alpha_i<C$, sitting exactly on the margin with no violation) — the hard-margin regime for this particular dataset. In other words: past a data-dependent threshold, raising $C$ further buys nothing; the useful tuning range for $C$ is bounded above by wherever the hard-margin solution first becomes reachable.

    The same bound/free split the table reads off $\alpha_i$ is available directly from a fitted SVC via dual_coef_.

    Code — reproducing the C-sweep (support-vector regimes) 
    import numpy as np
from sklearn.svm import SVC

for C in [0.01, 1, 100, 1e6]:
    clf = SVC(kernel="linear", C=C).fit(X, y)
    alpha_abs = np.abs(clf.dual_coef_)          # dual_coef_ stores y_i * alpha_i, not alpha_i alone
    n_bound = np.sum(np.isclose(alpha_abs, C))  # alpha_i == C -> "bound" SV, sec 17.7's table
    clf.coef_, clf.intercept_, len(clf.support_), n_bound

    take abs() of dual_coef_ before comparing to C -- its sign encodes the label $y_i$, not the box-constraint regime; free support vectors satisfy 0 < alpha_i < C strictly.

    Fig. 17.4 — the $C$-sweep example at its two extremes. Left ($C{=}0.01$): wide margin, most support vectors are “bound” (orange rings, $\alpha_i{=}C$) — the optimiser tolerates violations freely. Right ($C{=}100$): narrow margin, every support vector is “free” (purple rings, on the margin exactly) — the solution has already reached its hard-margin limit.
    Section recap. The hard-margin SVM (§17.1) maximises $1/\|\mathbf{w}\|$ subject to every point clearing the margin, which convex duality (§17.2) turns into a QP over $\boldsymbol\alpha$ touching the data only through $\mathbf{x}_i^\top\mathbf{x}_j$; complementary slackness (§17.3) shows the solution depends only on the support vectors on the margin. The kernel trick (§17.5) replaces that dot product with $K(\mathbf{x}_i,\mathbf{x}_j)$, buying an implicit (even infinite-dimensional, for RBF) feature-space lift for free, as long as $K$ is Mercer-valid (PSD Gram matrix for every sample — not automatic, as the sigmoid-kernel counterexample shows). The soft margin (§17.7) relaxes hard separation with slack penalised by $C$, recovering the identical dual with only a box constraint $0\le\alpha_i\le C$ added — $C$ is SVM's bias–variance dial, playing the same role $1/\lambda$ plays for ridge regression.

    17.8   Practice

    Practice 17.1 — for the vertical-band hard-margin example (§17.4), verify directly that the point $(6,1)$ is not a support vector
    With $\mathbf{w}=(1,0)$, $b=-2$: $y\cdot(\mathbf{w}^\top\mathbf{x}+b) = (+1)\cdot(1\cdot6+0\cdot1-2) = 4 > 1$. Since the margin value is strictly greater than $1$ (not equal to it), complementary slackness (§17.3) forces $\alpha_i=0$ for this point — it plays no role in $\mathbf{w}$, consistent with it lying well outside the shaded corridor in Fig. 17.1.
    Practice 17.2 — using the closed-form $\mathbf{w}=(1,0)$, $b=-2$ from §17.4, what is the margin width, and how does it compare to the raw gap between the closest positive ($x_1{=}3$) and closest negative ($x_1{=}1$) point?
    Margin width $=2/\|\mathbf{w}\| = 2/1 = 2$. The raw gap between $x_1{=}1$ and $x_1{=}3$ is also exactly $2$ — as it must be, since the max-margin derivation (§17.1) places the boundary and its two margin lines symmetrically between the closest points of each class by construction; the QP's margin width and the visual gap between classes are the same quantity by definition, not a coincidence to be separately checked.
    Practice 17.3 — verify the degree-2 polynomial kernel identity for a fresh pair $\mathbf{x}=(2,-1)$, $\mathbf{x}'=(1,1)$: does $\phi(\mathbf{x})^\top\phi(\mathbf{x}') = (1+\mathbf{x}^\top\mathbf{x}')^2$?
    $\mathbf{x}^\top\mathbf{x}' = 2(1)+({-1})(1) = 1$, so $(1+1)^2=4$. Directly: $\phi(\mathbf{x})^\top\phi(\mathbf{x}') = 1+2(2)(1)+2({-1})(1)+2(2)({-1})(1)(1)+2^2\cdot1^2+({-1})^2\cdot1^2 = 1+4-2-4+4+1 = 4$. Both routes give $4$, confirming the identity (§17.5) on a pair not in the original three checks — the identity holds for any input pair, not just the ones tabulated, because it follows from binomial expansion, not from anything specific to those three examples.
    Practice 17.4 — the sigmoid kernel with $k_1{=}0.5$, $k_2{=}{-}1.0$ produced a Gram matrix with a negative eigenvalue ($-2.827$) on 5 sample points (§17.5). What does that negative eigenvalue mean operationally for an SVM solver handed this $K$?
    A negative eigenvalue means $\mathcal{K}=K(\mathbf{x}_i,\mathbf{x}_j)$ is not positive semi-definite , so by Mercer's condition there is no real feature map $\phi$ with $K(\mathbf{x},\mathbf{x}')=\phi(\mathbf{x})^\top\phi(\mathbf{x}')$ for this specific parameter/data combination. Operationally, the dual's quadratic form $\boldsymbol\alpha^\top H\boldsymbol\alpha$ (with $H_{ij}=y_iy_jK_{ij}$) is then not guaranteed convex — the "maximize" in §17.2's dual QP can have a direction of unbounded increase or multiple local optima, so a solver may fail to converge, return a solution that depends on initialization, or silently return a non-optimal $\boldsymbol\alpha$. Some SVM implementations clip or regularise a non-PSD $K$ to force convexity; this is why the sigmoid kernel is flagged "not PSD in general" rather than banned outright — some $(k_1,k_2,\text{data})$ combinations are fine, but there is no guarantee, unlike the linear, polynomial and RBF kernels.
    Practice 17.5 — in the $C$-sweep worked example (§17.7), why did $C{=}100$ and $C{=}10^6$ produce numerically identical $\mathbf{w}$, $b$, and support vectors?
    Once $C$ is large enough that no assignment of slack is worth it — i.e. the optimal hard-margin solution for this particular dataset requires zero total violation ($\sum_i\xi_i=0$ is achievable, since the two intruder points can each sit exactly on the margin at $\alpha_i All three remaining support vectors at $C{=}100$ are already "free" ($0<\alpha_i
    Practice 17.6 — using the kernel-choice flowchart (Fig. 17.3), which kernel would you reach for first on a dataset you know contains exactly one pairwise-interaction non-linearity (e.g. "risk depends on income times age, and nothing higher-order"), and why not RBF?
    The flowchart's "no, but I know the geometry (fixed-degree polynomial interaction)" branch points to the polynomial kernel with $q{=}2$: $K(\mathbf{x},\mathbf{x}')=(1+\mathbf{x}^\top\mathbf{x}')^2$ exactly captures pairwise products like income$\times$age (as §17.5's degree-2 identity shows, its 6-dim feature map includes every $x_ix_j$ cross term) without paying for the higher-order interactions RBF's infinite expansion would also fit. RBF is the safe default when the non-linearity's shape is unknown, but it comes with an extra hyperparameter $\gamma$ to tune and no guarantee it won't also fit spurious higher-order structure the data doesn't actually have — when the interaction's degree is known in advance, the polynomial kernel is both cheaper to tune (one integer $q$ instead of a continuous $\gamma$) and more interpretable (its feature map is a known, finite list of monomials).

    18   PCA & the Curse of Dimensionality

    Too many features hurt learning long before you fit a single model; Principal Component Analysis (PCA) is the standard fix — find the handful of directions that carry almost all the variance, and throw the rest away.

    Every model covered so far — linear regression's $\mathbf{w}^\top\mathbf{x}$, KNN's raw distances, the kernel machinery of SVMs — assumes the feature vector $\mathbf{x}\in\mathbb{R}^D$ is already a sensible description of the data. This section asks what happens when $D$ itself becomes the problem, and how to compress $D$ down to the directions that actually matter.

    18.1   The curse of dimensionality

    Combinatorial explosion. If you tried to pick the best $d$-feature subset out of $D$ candidate features by brute force, the number of subsets to check is

    $$\binom{D}{d} = O(D^d).$$

    which is already unmanageable for modest $D$:

    $D$$\binom{D}{2}$$\binom{D}{5}$$\binom{D}{10}$
    10452521
    2019015,504184,756
    501,2252,118,76010,272,278,170
    1004,95075,287,52017,310,309,456,440

    By $D=100$, choosing the best 10-feature subset means comparing more candidates than there are seconds since the Big Bang. Greedy alternatives exist — forward search starts from the empty set and adds the single feature that most improves performance at each step; backward search starts from all $D$ features and greedily drops the least useful — but both are heuristics with no optimality guarantee, they just avoid the exhaustive $O(D^d)$ search.

    Distances stop discriminating. The subtler and more damaging effect of high dimension is geometric, not combinatorial. Take $D$ independent coordinates, each with some variance $\sigma^2$. A squared Euclidean distance between two random points is a sum of $D$ i.i.d. terms:

    $$d^2(\mathbf{x},\mathbf{y}) = \sum_{k=1}^{D} (x_k - y_k)^2, \qquad \mathbb{E}[d^2] = D\,\mathbb{E}[(x_1-y_1)^2], \qquad \mathrm{Var}[d^2] = D\,\mathrm{Var}[(x_1-y_1)^2].$$

    By the law of large numbers, the relative spread of $d^2$ around its mean shrinks like

    $$\frac{\mathrm{std}(d^2)}{\mathbb{E}[d^2]} = \frac{\sqrt{D\,\mathrm{Var}[(x_1-y_1)^2]}}{D\,\mathbb{E}[(x_1-y_1)^2]} = O\!\left(\frac{1}{\sqrt{D}}\right) \;\longrightarrow\; 0.$$

    So as $D\to\infty$, every pairwise distance converges to roughly the same value — the nearest and farthest points become statistically indistinguishable.

    Fig. 18.1 — 500 points drawn i.i.d. uniform in $[0,1]^D$; both the relative range $(d_{\max}-d_{\min})/d_{\text{mean}}$ and the relative standard deviation $\mathrm{std}(d)/d_{\text{mean}}$ of all pairwise distances collapse toward zero as $D$ grows from 2 to 1000.

    Concretely, the spread ratio falls from $2.588$ at $D{=}2$ to $0.167$ at $D{=}1000$ — a $15\times$ collapse. This is exactly why KNN's "nearest neighbour" premise degrades in high dimension: once distances stop discriminating, there is no meaningfully "closer" point left to vote with.

    Volume hides at the boundary. A related fact: for a $D$-dimensional unit cube, the probability that a uniformly random point lies within $\varepsilon$ of some face is

    $$1-P[\text{interior}] = 1-(1-2\varepsilon)^D,$$

    since each of the $D$ independent coordinates must individually avoid both boundaries (probability $1-2\varepsilon$ per axis), and all $D$ axes must succeed simultaneously. At $\varepsilon = 0.05$:

    $D$15102050100
    fraction within $5\%$ of a face10.0%41.0%65.1%87.8%99.5%$\approx100\%$

    By $D=100$, essentially every point is near some boundary — there is no meaningful "middle" of the space left. Almost all the volume of a high-dimensional cube lives in a thin shell near its surface.

    Comparing distributions after reduction — adjudicating v5's "KL divergence." v5 §12 heads a subsection "KL divergence — comparing distributions" and then, for checking whether a reduced feature set preserves the original distribution, gives what it calls the "symmetric KL divergence": $$p_1(x)\log\frac{p_1(x)}{p_2(x)} + p_2(x)\log\frac{p_2(x)}{p_1(x)} \quad\text{integrated over } x \qquad\text{(as written in v5)}.$$ This is the symmetrised (Jeffreys) divergence, not the Kullback–Leibler divergence. The true KL divergence is asymmetric — $$\mathrm{KL}(p_1\,\|\,p_2) = \int p_1(x)\,\log\frac{p_1(x)}{p_2(x)}\,dx \;\ne\; \mathrm{KL}(p_2\,\|\,p_1) \text{ in general,}$$ and is not a metric (it fails the triangle inequality and symmetry). v5's formula is the sum $\mathrm{KL}(p_1\|p_2)+\mathrm{KL}(p_2\|p_1)$, which is symmetric by construction — a legitimate quantity for a "how different are these two distributions, order-independent" check. v5's qualifier "symmetric" is doing real work, and the standard name for that object is the Jeffreys divergence; what must not be dropped is the qualifier, because the unqualified "KL divergence" means something else. The distinction matters: $\mathrm{KL}(p_1\|p_2)$ alone answers "how many extra bits does coding $p_1$-data with a $p_2$-optimal code cost," a specific and asymmetric question, and conflating the two loses that meaning entirely.

    18.2   PCA — the variance-maximisation derivation

    Given centred data $\{\mathbf{x}_i\}_{i=1}^{N}$, $\mathbf{x}_i\in\mathbb{R}^D$ (mean already subtracted), PCA looks for the single direction $\mathbf{u}\in\mathbb{R}^D$, $\|\mathbf{u}\|=1$, onto which the projected data has maximum variance. The projection of $\mathbf{x}_i$ onto $\mathbf{u}$ is the scalar $z_i = \mathbf{u}^\top\mathbf{x}_i$, and since the data is centred, $\mathbb{E}[z]=0$, so the variance of the projected scores is

    $$\mathrm{Var}(z) = \frac{1}{N-1}\sum_{i=1}^N z_i^2 = \frac{1}{N-1}\sum_{i=1}^N \mathbf{u}^\top\mathbf{x}_i\mathbf{x}_i^\top\mathbf{u} = \mathbf{u}^\top\left(\frac{1}{N-1}\sum_i \mathbf{x}_i\mathbf{x}_i^\top\right)\mathbf{u} = \mathbf{u}^\top C\,\mathbf{u},$$

    where $C = \tfrac{1}{N-1}\sum_i \mathbf{x}_i\mathbf{x}_i^\top \in \mathbb{R}^{D\times D}$ is the (sample) covariance matrix of the centred data — $\mathbf{u}$ is $(D\times1)$, $C$ is $(D\times D)$, $\mathbf{u}^\top C\mathbf{u}$ is a scalar $(1\times1)$.

    Constrained optimisation. We want $\mathbf{u}^\star = \operatorname*{arg\,max}_{\mathbf{u}}\; \mathbf{u}^\top C\mathbf{u}$ subject to $\mathbf{u}^\top\mathbf{u}=1$ (the constraint is needed because $\mathbf{u}^\top C\mathbf{u}$ is unbounded without it — just scale $\mathbf{u}$ up). Form the Lagrangian: $$\mathcal{L}(\mathbf{u},\lambda) = \mathbf{u}^\top C\mathbf{u} - \lambda(\mathbf{u}^\top\mathbf{u}-1).$$

    Setting the gradient with respect to $\mathbf{u}$ to zero (using $C=C^\top$):

    $$\nabla_{\mathbf{u}}\mathcal{L} = 2C\mathbf{u} - 2\lambda\mathbf{u} = \mathbf{0} \quad\Longrightarrow\quad \boxed{C\mathbf{u} = \lambda\mathbf{u}}.$$

    So the stationary directions are exactly the eigenvectors of $C$, and $\lambda$ is the corresponding eigenvalue. Plugging back in: at any stationary point, $\mathbf{u}^\top C\mathbf{u} = \mathbf{u}^\top(\lambda\mathbf{u}) = \lambda\,\mathbf{u}^\top\mathbf{u} = \lambda$. The variance captured by direction $\mathbf{u}$ equals its eigenvalue. To maximise, pick the eigenvector with the largest eigenvalue $\lambda_1$ — call it $\mathbf{u}_1$, the first principal component (PC1).

    For the second direction $\mathbf{u}_2$: maximise $\mathbf{u}^\top C\mathbf{u}$ again, now under two constraints, $\mathbf{u}^\top\mathbf{u}=1$ and $\mathbf{u}^\top\mathbf{u}_1=0$ (orthogonal to PC1, so it captures genuinely new variance rather than re-explaining PC1's). The Lagrangian picks up a second multiplier $\mu$ for the orthogonality constraint; the stationarity condition becomes $C\mathbf{u} = \lambda\mathbf{u} + \mu\,\mathbf{u}_1$, and left-multiplying by $\mathbf{u}_1^\top$ gives $\mathbf{u}_1^\top C\mathbf{u} = \mu$ (since $\mathbf{u}_1^\top\mathbf{u}=0$); but $\mathbf{u}_1^\top C\mathbf{u} = (C\mathbf{u}_1)^\top\mathbf{u} = \lambda_1\mathbf{u}_1^\top\mathbf{u} = 0$, forcing $\mu=0$. So the constraint again collapses to $C\mathbf{u}=\lambda\mathbf{u}$ — an eigenvector — and among eigenvectors orthogonal to $\mathbf{u}_1$, the one with the largest remaining eigenvalue $\lambda_2$ maximises variance. Repeating this argument $D$ times recovers the entire eigendecomposition, sorted $\lambda_1\ge\lambda_2\ge\cdots\ge\lambda_D\ge0$ (the $\ge0$ holds because $C$ is a covariance matrix, hence positive semi-definite), each $\mathbf{u}_k$ orthogonal to all the others.

    Gotcha — this derivation assumes centred data and comparable feature scales. If the mean is not subtracted first, the "variance" computed above is contaminated by $\mathbb{E}[z]^2$ and the top eigenvector chases the mean instead of the spread. And because $C$ mixes raw feature units, a feature measured in different units (e.g. income in rupees vs age in years) with a larger numeric range will dominate $C$'s diagonal and hijack PC1 for reasons that have nothing to do with genuine correlation structure — exactly the same failure mode flagged for KNN distances. The standard fix is to standardise every feature to zero mean, unit variance before computing $C$, unless the units are already comparable and you specifically want raw-variance weighting.

    18.3   The algorithm — eigendecomposition route

    Stack the $N$ raw points as rows of a data matrix $X\in\mathbb{R}^{N\times D}$.

    PCA via eigendecomposition, with shapes at every step:
    1. Centre. $\bar{\mathbf{x}} = \tfrac{1}{N}\sum_i\mathbf{x}_i \in \mathbb{R}^{D}$; form $X_c = X - \mathbf{1}\bar{\mathbf{x}}^\top$, shape $(N\times D)$, each row now mean-zero.
    2. Covariance. $C = \tfrac{1}{N-1}X_c^\top X_c$, shape $(D\times D) = (D\times N)(N\times D)$.
    3. Eigendecomposition. Solve $C\mathbf{u}_k=\lambda_k\mathbf{u}_k$ for all $D$ pairs, sort $\lambda_1\ge\cdots\ge\lambda_D$; stack the top $d$ eigenvectors as columns of $U_d\in\mathbb{R}^{D\times d}$.
    4. Project. $Z = X_c U_d$, shape $(N\times d) = (N\times D)(D\times d)$ — the compressed representation, $d\ll D$.
    5. Reconstruct (optional). $\hat{X} = \mathbf{1}\bar{\mathbf{x}}^\top + Z U_d^\top$, shape $(N\times D) = (N\times d)(d\times D)$ — back in the original space, but only using the top $d$ directions.

    The five steps above translate directly into numpy, matching the section's own notation ($X_c$, $U_d$, $Z$) exactly.

    Code — PCA from scratch via numpy SVD 
    import numpy as np

def pca_svd(X, d):
    X = np.asarray(X, dtype=float)
    xbar = X.mean(axis=0)                    # (D,)
    Xc = X - xbar                             # center FIRST -- sec 18.2 warn box
    U, S, Vt = np.linalg.svd(Xc, full_matrices=False)   # Xc = U @ diag(S) @ Vt
    U_d = Vt[:d].T                            # (D, d) top-d principal directions
    eigvals = (S ** 2) / (X.shape[0] - 1)     # lambda_k = sigma_k^2 / (N-1), sec 18.4
    Z = Xc @ U_d                              # (N, d) projected scores
    X_hat = xbar + Z @ U_d.T                  # (N, D) reconstruction, sec 18.3 step 5
    return Z, X_hat, eigvals, U_d

Z, X_hat, eigvals, U_d = pca_svd(X, d=1)
explained_ratio = eigvals[:1].sum() / eigvals.sum()

    np.linalg.svd returns Vt (V transposed) -- the principal directions are its ROWS, not V's columns; each u_k's sign is arbitrary (SVD sign ambiguity), only the subspace it spans is unique, so don't expect sign to match across re-runs or against sklearn.

    18.4   PCA via SVD — and why it's usually the better route

    Step 3 above needs the eigendecomposition of a $(D\times D)$ matrix, which costs $O(D^3)$ — a problem in itself when $D$ is large (images, genomics: $D$ in the thousands or millions). The Singular Value Decomposition of the centred data matrix directly gives the same answer without ever forming $C$ explicitly:

    $$X_c = U\,\Sigma\,V^\top, \qquad X_c\;(N\times D),\quad U\;(N\times r),\quad \Sigma\;(r\times r)\text{ diagonal},\quad V^\top\;(r\times D),\quad r=\min(N,D),$$

    with $U^\top U = I_r$, $V^\top V = I_r$ (both orthonormal), and $\Sigma = \mathrm{diag}(\sigma_1\ge\sigma_2\ge\cdots\ge\sigma_r\ge0)$ the singular values.

    Connecting SVD to the eigendecomposition of $C$. $$C = \frac{1}{N-1}X_c^\top X_c = \frac{1}{N-1}(U\Sigma V^\top)^\top(U\Sigma V^\top) = \frac{1}{N-1}V\Sigma U^\top U \Sigma V^\top = V\left(\frac{\Sigma^2}{N-1}\right)V^\top,$$

    using $U^\top U = I_r$. This is exactly an eigendecomposition of $C$ with eigenvectors = columns of $V$ and eigenvalues $\lambda_k = \sigma_k^2/(N-1)$. So the right singular vectors of the centred data matrix are the principal components, and the singular values determine the eigenvalues directly — no $D\times D$ covariance matrix ever needs to be formed.

    Which route to use. When $N \ll D$ (few samples, many features — the exact curse-of-dimensionality regime this section opened with), SVD of $X_c$ ($O(N^2D)$ or cheaper via the $N\times N$ Gram matrix $X_cX_c^\top$) is far cheaper than eigendecomposing the $(D\times D)$ covariance matrix. This is precisely the setting (e.g. gene-expression data with thousands of genes but dozens of patients) where PCA is most needed and the eigendecomposition route is least affordable — SVD is the practical algorithm libraries like scikit-learn actually run.

    In practice nobody hand-rolls the SVD route above — sklearn.decomposition.PCA does it, plus the bookkeeping (mean, whitening, inverse transform) worth knowing for an interview.

    Code — PCA in sklearn (fit/transform, whiten, inverse_transform) 
    from sklearn.decomposition import PCA
from sklearn.preprocessing import StandardScaler
from sklearn.pipeline import make_pipeline

# standardize first when units differ (sec 18.2 warn box) -- else PCA chases raw numeric range
pipe = make_pipeline(StandardScaler(), PCA(n_components=2, whiten=False))
Z = pipe.fit_transform(X)

pca = pipe.named_steps["pca"]
pca.explained_variance_ratio_    # fraction of variance per component (sec 18.6)
pca.components_                  # (n_components, D) rows are the u_k directions
pca.mean_                        # (D,) subtracted before projecting

X_hat_scaled = pca.inverse_transform(Z)   # back to the (still-standardized) input space

    whiten=True additionally divides each score by sqrt(eigenvalue), making every component unit-variance -- useful before scale-sensitive downstream models (e.g. k-means), but it means the raw Z values no longer directly read as "variance captured," and inverse_transform must undo the whitening internally to reconstruct correctly.

    18.5   Worked examples example

    Recomputing v5's two 4-point examples. Four points, already centred: $(2,0),(0,2),(-2,0),(0,-2)$. $$C = \frac{1}{3}\begin{pmatrix}8 & 0\\0 & 8\end{pmatrix} = \begin{pmatrix}2.667&0\\0&2.667\end{pmatrix}, \qquad \lambda_1=\lambda_2=2.667.$$

    Equal eigenvalues confirm the recomputation: with isotropic spread, every unit vector is an eigenvector with the same variance — PCA genuinely has no preferred direction here, matching v5's claim exactly.

    Now skew it: $(3,0),(0,1),(-3,0),(0,-1)$. $$C = \frac{1}{3}\begin{pmatrix}18&0\\0&2\end{pmatrix} = \begin{pmatrix}6.0 & 0\\0 & 0.667\end{pmatrix}, \qquad \lambda_1=6.0,\;\; \lambda_2=0.667,$$ $$\mathbf{u}_1 = (1,0), \qquad \text{variance explained by PC1} = \frac{6.0}{6.0+0.667} = 90.0\%.$$ Both numbers match v5 §12 exactly, confirming the source's worked example.

    Fig. 18.2 — the skewed 4-point example: PC1 (red, along the axis of largest spread, $\lambda_1{=}6.000$) and PC2 (green, orthogonal, $\lambda_2{=}0.667$) drawn through the data mean. PC1 alone captures $90\%$ of the total variance.
    A fresh, richer example — full pipeline on 6 points that are not pre-centred. $$X = \begin{pmatrix}2&1\\3&4\\5&5\\6&7\\8&6\\9&9\end{pmatrix}, \qquad N=6,\;D=2.$$

    Step 1 — centre. $\bar{\mathbf{x}} = (5.5,\; 5.333)$. Subtracting gives $X_c$ with rows summing to zero in each column by construction.

    Step 2 — covariance. $$C = \begin{pmatrix}7.500 & 6.800\\6.800 & 7.467\end{pmatrix}.$$ The large off-diagonal ($6.8$, comparable to the diagonal entries) signals strong positive correlation between $x_1$ and $x_2$ — exactly what the scatter in Fig. 18.3 shows.

    Step 3 — eigendecomposition. $$\lambda_1 = 14.283, \qquad \lambda_2 = 0.683, \qquad \mathbf{u}_1 = (0.7080,\,0.7062), \qquad \mathbf{u}_2=(-0.7062,\,0.7080).$$ $\mathbf{u}_1\approx(0.708,0.706)$ is almost exactly the $45^\circ$ diagonal — unsurprising given how tightly $x_1$ and $x_2$ move together.

    Cross-check — same answer from SVD. Singular values of $X_c$: $\sigma_1=8.451,\,\sigma_2=1.848$. $$\lambda_k = \frac{\sigma_k^2}{N-1}: \quad \frac{8.451^2}{5}=14.283, \qquad \frac{1.848^2}{5}=0.683,$$ matching the eigendecomposition's $\lambda_1,\lambda_2$ to 3 decimal places, and the right singular vectors $V$ match $\mathbf{u}_1,\mathbf{u}_2$ up to sign — confirming §18.4's identity numerically, not just symbolically.

    Sanity check — direct search confirms $\mathbf{u}_1$ truly maximises variance. Sweeping $\mathbf{u}(\theta)=(\cos\theta,\sin\theta)$ over $\theta\in[0,2\pi)$ and evaluating $\mathbf{u}^\top C\mathbf{u}$ directly on a $0.01^\circ$ grid, the maximum is $14.283354$ at $\theta=0.784176$ rad $=44.93^\circ$ — matching $\lambda_1=14.283354$ and $\mathbf{u}_1$'s own angle $\arctan(0.7062/0.7080)=44.9298^\circ$ , an independent numerical confirmation of the Lagrange-multiplier result in §18.2. (Note that $\mathbf{u}_1$ is near the $45^\circ$ diagonal but not on it: the tiny asymmetry $7.500$ vs $7.467$ in $C$'s diagonal tilts it by $0.07^\circ$. A $1^\circ$ sweep grid would have reported a spurious exact $45.0^\circ$.)

    Step 4 — project to $d{=}1$ and reconstruct. Scores $z_i = \mathbf{u}_1^\top(\mathbf{x}_i-\bar{\mathbf{x}})$ range from $-5.538$ (point $(2,1)$) to $5.067$ (point $(9,9)$). Reconstructing $\hat{\mathbf{x}}_i = \bar{\mathbf{x}} + z_i\mathbf{u}_1$ places every point back onto the PC1 line (Fig. 18.3); e.g. $(6,7)\to(6.584,\,6.415)$.

    Fig. 18.3 — the fresh 6-point example: original points (circles), the PC1 axis through the mean (dashed), and each point's reconstruction using only PC1 (crosses, connected by dotted residual lines). Points already near the diagonal (e.g. $(5,5)$) reconstruct almost exactly; points far off it (e.g. $(8,6)$) lose the most.

    18.6   Variance explained and reconstruction error

    The fraction of total variance captured by keeping the top $d$ components is

    $$\text{variance explained ratio} = \frac{\sum_{k=1}^{d}\lambda_k}{\sum_{k=1}^{D}\lambda_k}.$$

    For the fresh example, total variance $= \lambda_1+\lambda_2 = 14.967$ , and PC1 alone already explains $95.4\%$ of it, PC2 the remaining $4.6\%$ — dropping PC2 loses very little.

    Fig. 18.4 — scree plot for the fresh example: bars are per-component variance explained, the line is the running cumulative total. In real (higher-$D$) datasets this is the standard plot for choosing $d$ — keep components up to the "elbow" where the curve flattens.
    A useful identity: discarded eigenvalues predict reconstruction error exactly. The total sum-of-squares reconstruction error over all $N$ points, keeping only the top $d$ components, equals $(N-1)$ times the sum of the discarded eigenvalues: $$\sum_{i=1}^N \|\mathbf{x}_i-\hat{\mathbf{x}}_i\|^2 = (N-1)\sum_{k=d+1}^{D}\lambda_k.$$ Checked numerically on the fresh example: discarding PC2 ($\lambda_2=0.6833$), the identity predicts $(6-1)\times0.6833 = 3.4166$; the recomputed reconstruction errors sum to $0.3553+0.6751+0.0137+0.6837+1.6734+0.0154=3.4166$ , and dividing by $N=6$ gives the mean-squared reconstruction error $0.5694$ , matching to 4 decimal places. This is why "variance explained" and "reconstruction error" are two names for the same trade-off: maximising captured variance is identical to minimising squared reconstruction error, and both are read directly off the eigenvalues you threw away — no need to re-run PCA at every candidate $d$.

    Reading the elbow off a scree plot (Fig. 18.4) by eye is fine for a report; in a pipeline, target a cumulative-variance threshold directly.

    Code — choosing n_components (cumulative variance / auto) 
    from sklearn.decomposition import PCA
import numpy as np

pca_full = PCA().fit(X)                        # fit with all components first, D of them
cum = np.cumsum(pca_full.explained_variance_ratio_)
d_95 = np.searchsorted(cum, 0.95) + 1           # smallest d with cumulative variance >= 95%

# or let sklearn resolve it directly: n_components as a float = variance target, not a count
pca_auto = PCA(n_components=0.95).fit(X)
pca_auto.n_components_                          # the resolved integer d

    PCA(n_components=0.95) picks the smallest d hitting 95% cumulative variance automatically -- the reconstruction-error identity of sec 18.6 is exactly why this is a well-posed target: variance kept and SSE lost are the same trade-off read two ways.

    18.7   When PCA fails

    • Non-linear structure. PCA finds the best linear subspace. Data that lies on a curved manifold (e.g. a "Swiss roll" or a circular arc) has directions of large variance that cut straight through the manifold rather than following it — projecting collapses points that were actually far apart along the manifold onto nearby positions in $d$-space. Non-linear methods (kernel PCA, t-SNE, UMAP, autoencoders) exist precisely to handle this; plain PCA has no way to detect it beyond an unusually flat variance-explained curve.
    • Variance $\ne$ discriminative signal. PCA is entirely unsupervised — it never looks at labels. If class separation happens to lie along a low-variance direction (imagine two tight, well-separated clusters stacked close together, with each cluster individually elongated along an unrelated axis), PCA will keep the elongated axis and discard exactly the direction that would have made classification trivial. Supervised dimensionality reduction (e.g. LDA, which explicitly maximises between-class separation) is the fix when the downstream task is classification, not PCA.
    • Scale sensitivity. As flagged in the §18.2 warn box, PCA on unstandardised features with different units effectively re-derives "which feature has the largest numeric range," not "which features are genuinely correlated." Always standardise unless the units are already comparable and the raw-variance weighting is intentional.
    • Interpretability cost. Each principal component is a linear combination of every original feature (all $D$ entries of $\mathbf{u}_k$ are typically non-zero), so "PC1" rarely has a clean real-world meaning the way an original feature (e.g. "age") does — a real cost when the reduced features must be explained to a non-technical audience.

    18.8   Bridge to clustering

    The distance-concentration problem in §18.1 is not just a KNN issue — it is exactly why clustering algorithms that rely on distance (k-means' Euclidean objective, distance-based membership) also degrade in high dimension, and why the choice of distance metric itself (plain Euclidean vs Mahalanobis, which accounts for feature correlation) becomes a live design decision rather than a formality once $D$ grows. PCA is one standard pre-processing step before clustering high-dimensional data for exactly this reason.

    Section recap. High dimension hurts two ways: combinatorial (feature-subset search is $O(D^d)$) and geometric (pairwise distances concentrate, $O(1/\sqrt D)$ relative spread — Fig. 18.1). PCA fights the geometric problem by finding the $d\ll D$ directions of maximum variance: Lagrange multipliers show these are exactly the top-$d$ eigenvectors of the covariance matrix $C$ (§18.2), computable either by eigendecomposing $C$ directly (§18.3, $O(D^3)$) or, more cheaply when $D$ is large, via the SVD of the centred data matrix (§18.4, eigenvalues $=\sigma_k^2/(N-1)$). Variance explained and reconstruction error are the same quantity read two ways (§18.6). PCA is linear, unsupervised, and scale-sensitive — know its failure modes (§18.7) before reaching for it.

    18.9   Practice

    Practice 18.1 — verify $\mathbf{u}_1$ is a unit vector and that $C\mathbf{u}_1=\lambda_1\mathbf{u}_1$ for the skewed 4-point example
    $\mathbf{u}_1=(1,0)$: $\|\mathbf{u}_1\|=\sqrt{1^2+0^2}=1$, confirmed unit-norm. Applying $C$: $$C\mathbf{u}_1 = \begin{pmatrix}6.0&0\\0&0.667\end{pmatrix}\begin{pmatrix}1\\0\end{pmatrix} = \begin{pmatrix}6.0\\0\end{pmatrix} = 6.0\begin{pmatrix}1\\0\end{pmatrix} = \lambda_1\mathbf{u}_1,$$ so the eigenvector equation holds exactly, as the §18.2 derivation requires.
    Practice 18.2 — for the fresh 6-point example, what does $\mathbf{u}_2^\top C\mathbf{u}_2$ evaluate to, and why is that the minimum, not the maximum, over unit vectors?
    $\mathbf{u}_2^\top C\mathbf{u}_2 = \lambda_2 = 0.683$ by the same identity used for $\mathbf{u}_1$ in §18.2 ($\mathbf{u}^\top C\mathbf{u}=\lambda$ at any eigenvector). Since $D{=}2$ here, there are only two orthogonal directions total, and $\mathbf{u}_1$ was chosen as the one maximising variance ($\lambda_1=14.283$) — the direction orthogonal to it is automatically the remaining one, which for a 2D problem is also the global minimiser of $\mathbf{u}^\top C\mathbf{u}$ over unit vectors (there is nowhere left for it to be but the smallest eigenvalue). In $D>2$, $\mathbf{u}_2$ is only the maximiser among directions orthogonal to $\mathbf{u}_1$, not the global minimiser — that role falls to $\mathbf{u}_D$.
    Practice 18.3 — using the reconstruction-error identity of §18.6, predict the total SSE if you kept zero principal components (project every point to the mean)
    Keeping $d=0$ components means every $\lambda_k$ for $k=1,\dots,D$ is "discarded," so the identity gives total SSE $=(N-1)\sum_{k=1}^{D}\lambda_k = (N-1)\times\text{total variance}$. For the fresh example: $(6-1)\times14.967=74.833$ . This is just the total sum-of-squared-deviations from the mean, $\sum_i\|\mathbf{x}_i-\bar{\mathbf{x}}\|^2$ — consistent, since with zero components every reconstruction $\hat{\mathbf{x}}_i$ collapses to $\bar{\mathbf{x}}$ itself, and the identity should reduce to exactly that baseline.
    Practice 18.4 — a dataset has $D=3$ features: "salary in rupees" (range ~500,000), "age in years" (range ~40), and "years of education" (range ~15). You run PCA directly on the raw values. What goes wrong, and what's the fix?
    The covariance matrix's diagonal entries scale with the square of each feature's numeric range, so "salary" alone will dominate every entry of $C$ by several orders of magnitude over "age" or "education." PC1 will point almost exactly along the salary axis regardless of whether salary is actually the most informative direction of joint variation — this is the §18.2 warn-box failure mode. The fix: standardise each feature to zero mean and unit variance (z-score) before computing $C$ (equivalently, run PCA on the correlation matrix rather than the covariance matrix), so all three features start on a comparable numeric footing and PCA reflects genuine co-variation, not unit choice.
    Practice 18.5 — why does distance concentration (§18.1, Fig. 18.1) make PCA's job simultaneously more important and more surprising in very high dimension?
    More important: once $D$ is large enough that pairwise distances have nearly collapsed (Fig. 18.1 shows the relative spread falling to $0.167$ by $D{=}1000$ ), any downstream distance-based method — KNN, k-means — is starved of usable signal; reducing to the handful of dimensions that actually carry variance is what restores distances to being meaningful again. More surprising: the concentration argument in §18.1 assumed i.i.d., uncorrelated coordinates — but real high-dimensional data (images, gene expression) is rarely i.i.d.; it typically has a small number of true underlying degrees of freedom (an "intrinsic dimensionality" $d^\ast \ll D$) with the remaining dimensions highly correlated or redundant. That is exactly the regime PCA exploits: a handful of large eigenvalues and a long tail of near-zero ones (as in Fig. 18.4's scree shape), so the "everything is equidistant" pessimism of §18.1 is often defeated in practice once you work in the $d^\ast$ components that actually vary.

    19   Clustering I: k-Means, Distances & Fuzzy Membership

    Nobody hands you the groups. Clustering asks a dataset to confess its own structure — and the entire answer hinges on two choices you make before any algorithm runs: what counts as close, and what shape a group is allowed to have.

    Almost everything up to here has been supervised: a label $y$ told the model what "right" meant. The exception was §18's PCA, which needs no labels — but there the compressed features were still on their way to a labelled model, and §18 closed by warning that once $D$ is large, pairwise distances concentrate and stop discriminating. That warning is the hinge into this section: everything below is built out of distances, and now there is no label left to correct them. We are given only

    $$\mathcal{X} = \{\mathbf{x}_1, \mathbf{x}_2, \ldots, \mathbf{x}_n\} \subset \mathbb{R}^{p},$$

    and asked to partition it into $k$ groups. Here $n$ is the number of observations, $p$ the number of features, and the data matrix $\mathbf{X}$ has shape $(n \times p)$ — row $i$ is the feature vector $\mathbf{x}_i^\top$ of shape $(1 \times p)$. There is no $\mathbf{y}$. There is no test set with the truth on it. The only thing that can be optimised is a statement about the data's own geometry.

    Notation map. The deck writes the data set as $X=\{x_1,\ldots,x_n\}\subset R^p$, cluster sets as $S_j$ (slide 16) and later $C_j$ (slide 18), centres as $\mu_j^k$ with "$j$th cluster, $k$th iteration" (slide 15), and the fuzzy objective in terms of $\mathbf{J}_m(U,\mathbf{V})$ with prototypes $\mathbf{V}$ (slide 33). This section keeps those symbols but sets them in the global notation of these notes: bold lowercase $\mathbf{x}_i$ for a data vector, bold uppercase $\mathbf{X},\mathbf{U},\mathbf{V}$ for matrices, and $\boldsymbol\mu_j^{(t)}$ for the $j$-th centre at iteration $t$ — because the deck's slide 27 overloads $k$ as an iteration counter while every other slide uses $k$ for the number of clusters.

    19.1   The unsupervised setting, and the deck's Netflix question

    The deck motivates clustering with a picture of twelve anonymous users and the question "Can we group them?". The whole point of that slide is that the picture contains no grouping. What creates a grouping is a feature — the deck spends three consecutive title slides shouting "Feature! Feature! Feature" for exactly this reason. Choose age and you slice the users one way; choose average episode rating and you slice them another; choose both and you get a genuine two-dimensional partition.

    Clustering. Given $\mathcal{X}\subset\mathbb{R}^p$ and an integer $k$, find a partition $\mathcal{X} = C_1 \cup C_2 \cup \cdots \cup C_k$ with $C_i \cap C_j = \varnothing$ for $i \ne j$, such that points inside a cluster are homogeneous and points in different clusters are not.

    Homogeneity: "If the distance between two observations is small, they are homogeneous." That single sentence is the entire modelling assumption — and it is why the next subsection is about distances rather than about algorithms.

    The tiger-census slide makes the feature-engineering point without any equations: to cluster tigers you do not cluster photographs, you cluster the pugmark geometry — the pentagon of four toe pads plus the pad apex, and the lengths and angles between them. Raw pixels are not a feature space in which "distance small" means "same tiger". A good feature map is what makes clustering possible at all; the algorithm is the easy part.

    Fig. 19.1 — The deck's Netflix example made numeric: 150 synthetic users with an age and an average episode rating. (a) what the algorithm actually sees; (b) the deck's "group by age" cut — three vertical slabs that throw the rating axis away and split the top-middle blob in half; (c) k-means with $k=3$ on both standardised features recovers the three generating groups exactly. Black crosses are the final centroids.

    Interpretation. Panel (b) is not a strawman — it is what happens whenever you cluster on a subset of the available features. The three age slabs put users drawn from the $9.4$-star and the $7.2$-star generating groups into the same slab whenever their ages happen to agree. Panel (c) uses the same points and the same $k$, and reaches purity $1.0$ against the generating groups versus $0.9533$ when the very same k-means is run on the raw (unstandardised) columns . The difference between those two runs is one line of preprocessing; see the scaling warning in §19.2.

    19.2   Homogeneity: choosing a distance

    Slide 19 lists the candidates — Euclidean, Manhattan, Chessboard, Cosine, Correlation, "…" — and stops there. Below, each is defined, computed on one shared pair of vectors, and given the situation it is actually for. The $L_p$ family and cosine distance were already introduced as KNN's design choice; they are restated here because the deck's list adds correlation and Mahalanobis, and because in clustering the metric decides the shape of a cluster rather than the identity of a neighbour. Throughout, $\mathbf{x},\mathbf{y}\in\mathbb{R}^{p}$ are two observations, both of shape $(p \times 1)$, and $\mathbf{d}=\mathbf{x}-\mathbf{y}$ has shape $(p\times 1)$.

    Metric axioms. $d(\cdot,\cdot)$ is a metric iff (i) $d(\mathbf{x},\mathbf{x})=0$ and $d(\mathbf{x},\mathbf{y})>0$ for $\mathbf{x}\ne\mathbf{y}$; (ii) $d(\mathbf{x},\mathbf{y}) = d(\mathbf{y},\mathbf{x})$; (iii) $d(\mathbf{x},\mathbf{z}) \le d(\mathbf{x},\mathbf{y}) + d(\mathbf{y},\mathbf{z})$. Cosine and correlation distances violate (iii) and are therefore dissimilarities, not metrics — which matters, because a triangle-inequality violation can make a "nearest centroid" assignment behave non-geometrically.

    19.2.1   The $L_p$ family, cosine and correlation

    Take the concrete pair $\mathbf{x}=(2,5,1,0,3)^\top$ and $\mathbf{y}=(4,1,1,2,0)^\top$ in $\mathbb{R}^5$, so $\mathbf{d}=(-2,4,0,-2,3)^\top$:

    NameFormulavalue on $(\mathbf{x},\mathbf{y})$Use it when
    Euclidean $L_2$$\sqrt{\sum_{q=1}^{p}(x_q-y_q)^2}$$\sqrt{33}=5.7446$continuous features on comparable scales; the only metric for which the cluster mean is optimal
    Manhattan $L_1$$\sum_{q=1}^{p}|x_q-y_q|$$11$outlier-heavy data, or features that move independently (counts, grid moves)
    Chessboard $L_\infty$$\max_q |x_q-y_q|$$4$"worst single coordinate" logic — tolerance/QC style rules
    Cosine$1-\dfrac{\mathbf{x}^\top\mathbf{y}}{\lVert\mathbf{x}\rVert\,\lVert\mathbf{y}\rVert}$$1-0.4780=0.5220$only direction matters, not magnitude: TF-IDF text, sparse high-dimensional vectors
    Correlation$1-\mathrm{corr}(\mathbf{x},\mathbf{y})$$1-(-0.3085)=1.3085$shape-of-profile matching with the level removed: gene expression, time-series shapes
    Mahalanobis$\sqrt{(\mathbf{x}-\boldsymbol\mu)^\top\boldsymbol\Sigma^{-1}(\mathbf{x}-\boldsymbol\mu)}$see §19.2.2correlated features, or clusters with genuinely different spreads

    The intermediate quantities behind the cosine and correlation rows, so they can be checked by hand: $\mathbf{x}^\top\mathbf{y}=14$, $\lVert\mathbf{x}\rVert=6.2450$, $\lVert\mathbf{y}\rVert=4.6904$, $\bar{x}=2.2$, $\bar{y}=1.6$ . Note the sign: these two vectors point roughly the same way ($\cos = +0.478$) yet their deviations from their own means are anti-correlated ($\mathrm{corr}=-0.3085$), so the correlation distance exceeds $1$. Cosine and correlation are not interchangeable.

    Fig. 19.2 — The unit ball $\{\mathbf{z}: d(\mathbf{0},\mathbf{z})=1\}$ is the shape of a metric's opinion about "equally far". Darker shading = smaller distance. Manhattan gives a diamond, Euclidean a circle, Chessboard a square; cosine has no ball at all — its level sets are rays through the origin, so a point at radius $0.1$ and one at radius $10$ in the same direction are at distance $0$ from each other.

    Interpretation. For any $\mathbf{d}$, $\;\lVert\mathbf{d}\rVert_\infty \le \lVert\mathbf{d}\rVert_2 \le \lVert\mathbf{d}\rVert_1$ — here $4 \le 5.7446 \le 11$ . So swapping $L_2$ for $L_1$ rescales all distances upward, but not uniformly: it inflates them most for points that differ in many coordinates a little, and least for points that differ in one coordinate a lot. That is precisely why $L_1$ is the robust choice — a single wild coordinate cannot dominate a sum of absolute values the way it dominates a sum of squares.

    Gotcha — units decide your clustering before the algorithm does. Re-express feature 2 of the pair above in a unit $100\times$ smaller (say, rating on a 0–1000 scale instead of 0–10). The Euclidean distance jumps from $5.7446$ to $400.02$, and feature 2 alone now supplies $99.99\%$ of the squared distance . Every other feature has been silently deleted. k-means on the raw Netflix columns is exactly this failure in miniature: age has standard deviation $12.06$ and rating $0.94$ , a $12.8\times$ ratio, so raw-scale k-means is $164\times$ more sensitive to age than to rating in the squared metric — hence its purity of $0.9533$ versus $1.0$ after standardising. Standardise, or use Mahalanobis.

    19.2.2   Mahalanobis distance — filling the deck's gap

    Slide 21 shows a small round magenta prototype on the left, a wide flat green ellipse on the right, an "Unknown" point at the bottom, and asserts: "Mahalanobis distance may give that Prototype-2 is closer to the unknown." No formula, no covariance matrix and no numbers appear anywhere on the slide. Here is the missing content.

    Mahalanobis distance from a point $\mathbf{x}$ $(p\times 1)$ to a prototype with mean $\boldsymbol\mu$ $(p\times1)$ and covariance $\boldsymbol\Sigma$ $(p\times p)$, symmetric positive definite:

    $$d_M(\mathbf{x},\boldsymbol\mu) \;=\; \sqrt{(\mathbf{x}-\boldsymbol\mu)^{\top}\, \boldsymbol\Sigma^{-1}\,(\mathbf{x}-\boldsymbol\mu)}.$$

    Shapes at every step. $(\mathbf{x}-\boldsymbol\mu)$ is $(p\times1)$; transposing gives $(1\times p)$; $\boldsymbol\Sigma^{-1}$ is $(p\times p)$. The chain $(1\times p)\cdot(p\times p)\cdot(p\times1)$ contracts to $(1\times 1)$, i.e. a scalar — the squared Mahalanobis distance $d_M^2$. Setting $\boldsymbol\Sigma=\mathbf{I}_p$ recovers Euclidean exactly, so Mahalanobis is a strict generalisation.

    Worked example (slide 21, made numeric).

    Prototype-1 (the tight magenta blob): $\boldsymbol\mu_1=(2,6)^\top$, $\boldsymbol\Sigma_1=\begin{pmatrix}1&0\\0&1\end{pmatrix}$ — standard deviations $(\sigma_{x_1},\sigma_{x_2})=(1,1)$.
    Prototype-2 (the wide flat green ellipse): $\boldsymbol\mu_2=(8,6)^\top$, $\boldsymbol\Sigma_2=\begin{pmatrix}16&0\\0&2.25\end{pmatrix}$ — standard deviations $(4,\,1.5)$, i.e. an ellipse $8$ wide and $3$ tall.
    Unknown point: $\mathbf{u}=(4.5,\,4)^\top$.

    Step 1 — the two difference vectors, each $(2\times1)$.

    $$\mathbf{u}-\boldsymbol\mu_1 = \begin{pmatrix}2.5\\-2\end{pmatrix},\qquad \mathbf{u}-\boldsymbol\mu_2 = \begin{pmatrix}-3.5\\-2\end{pmatrix}.$$

    Step 2 — plain Euclidean (i.e. pretend $\boldsymbol\Sigma=\mathbf{I}$).

    $$d_E(\mathbf{u},\boldsymbol\mu_1)=\sqrt{2.5^2+2^2}=\sqrt{10.25}=3.2016,\qquad d_E(\mathbf{u},\boldsymbol\mu_2)=\sqrt{3.5^2+2^2}=\sqrt{16.25}=4.0311.$$

    Euclidean says Prototype-1 — matching the deck's slide 20 conclusion for the Euclidean picture.

    Step 3 — invert the covariances. Both are diagonal, so inversion is elementwise:

    $$\boldsymbol\Sigma_1^{-1}=\begin{pmatrix}1&0\\0&1\end{pmatrix},\qquad \boldsymbol\Sigma_2^{-1}=\begin{pmatrix}1/16&0\\0&1/2.25\end{pmatrix} =\begin{pmatrix}0.0625&0\\0&0.4444\end{pmatrix}.$$

    Step 4 — the quadratic forms $(1\times2)(2\times2)(2\times1)\to(1\times1)$. For a diagonal $\boldsymbol\Sigma$ the quadratic form is just a sum of per-coordinate terms $(\Delta_q)^2/\sigma_q^2$:

    $$d_M^2(\mathbf{u},\boldsymbol\mu_1)=\frac{2.5^2}{1}+\frac{(-2)^2}{1}=6.25+4=10.25 \;\Rightarrow\; d_M=3.2016,$$ $$d_M^2(\mathbf{u},\boldsymbol\mu_2)=\frac{(-3.5)^2}{16}+\frac{(-2)^2}{2.25} =0.7656+1.7778=2.5434 \;\Rightarrow\; d_M=1.5948.$$

    Step 5 — the verdict. $1.5948 < 3.2016$: Mahalanobis says Prototype-2. The ranking has flipped.

    Fig. 19.3 — Slide 21 redrawn with numbers. Shaded rings are the $1\sigma$, $2\sigma$ and $3\sigma$ contours of each prototype's covariance. In plain Euclidean terms the Unknown is $3.20$ from Prototype-1 and $4.03$ from Prototype-2; measured in each prototype's own standard deviations it is $3.20$ from Prototype-1 but only $1.59$ from Prototype-2 — the Unknown sits inside Prototype-2's $2\sigma$ ellipse and outside Prototype-1's $3\sigma$ circle.

    Interpretation. Mahalanobis answers a different question from Euclidean. Euclidean asks "how many metres away is it?"; Mahalanobis asks "how surprising is it, given how much this cluster normally varies?" A displacement of $3.5$ along an axis where the cluster routinely varies by $\sigma=4$ is unremarkable ($0.875\sigma$), whereas a displacement of $2.5$ along an axis where the cluster only varies by $\sigma=1$ is a $2.5\sigma$ event. The flip is not a trick — it is the correct answer to the question "which population was this point more likely drawn from?", and it is exactly the term that appears in the exponent of a multivariate Gaussian density, which is why Gaussian mixture models are the natural generalisation of k-means.

    Adjudication. The deck hedges: "Mahalanobis distance may give that Prototype-2 is closer". The hedge is warranted — whether the flip happens depends entirely on the covariances, which the slide never supplies. It does not happen merely because Prototype-2's ellipse is flat; it happens because Prototype-2's overall scale is larger. If instead $\boldsymbol\Sigma_2=\mathrm{diag}(16,\,0.25)$ (same width, four times flatter), then $d_M^2(\mathbf{u},\boldsymbol\mu_2)=0.7656+16=16.77$, $d_M=4.095$, and Prototype-1 wins under Mahalanobis too. The picture alone cannot settle it; only the numbers can.

    19.2.3   Correlated features and whitening

    When $\boldsymbol\Sigma$ is not diagonal, Mahalanobis also decorrelates. Write the eigendecomposition $\boldsymbol\Sigma = \mathbf{Q}\boldsymbol\Lambda\mathbf{Q}^\top$ with $\mathbf{Q}$ $(p\times p)$ orthonormal and $\boldsymbol\Lambda$ $(p\times p)$ diagonal, and define the whitening matrix $\mathbf{W}=\boldsymbol\Sigma^{-1/2}=\mathbf{Q}\boldsymbol\Lambda^{-1/2} \mathbf{Q}^\top$, shape $(p\times p)$. Then

    $$d_M^2(\mathbf{x},\boldsymbol\mu)=(\mathbf{x}-\boldsymbol\mu)^\top\mathbf{W}^\top\mathbf{W} (\mathbf{x}-\boldsymbol\mu)=\bigl\lVert \mathbf{W}(\mathbf{x}-\boldsymbol\mu)\bigr\rVert_2^2,$$

    i.e. Mahalanobis distance is ordinary Euclidean distance after whitening. With $\boldsymbol\Sigma=\begin{pmatrix}4&3.6\\3.6&4\end{pmatrix}$ (eigenvalues $0.4$ and $7.6$ along the $(-1,1)/\sqrt2$ and $(1,1)/\sqrt2$ directions), the two points $(3,3)^\top$ and $(3,-3)^\top$ are at identical Euclidean distance $4.2426$ from the origin, but at Mahalanobis distances $1.5390$ and $6.7082$ respectively — a $4.36\times$ gap, because one lies along the correlation ridge and the other cuts across it. Whitening turns them into $(1.088,1.088)^\top$ and $(4.743,-4.743)^\top$, whose Euclidean norms reproduce those two numbers exactly.

    19.2.4   Geodesic distance on a manifold

    Slide 22 draws a wavy blob, a point $\underline{x}$ with a dashed circle labelled $N(x)=\epsilon$, a second point $y$, a green curve joining them along the blob, and the captions "Shortest path along the manifold, Geodesic distance" and "Local neighborhood of $x$". No neighbourhood graph, no shortest-path construction and no formula are given. The missing recipe is the one at the heart of Isomap:

    Geodesic distance via an $\epsilon$-graph.

    1. Neighbourhoods. For each $\mathbf{x}_i$ define $N_\epsilon(\mathbf{x}_i)=\{\mathbf{x}_j : \lVert\mathbf{x}_i-\mathbf{x}_j\rVert_2 \le \epsilon\}$ — this is the slide's $N(x)=\epsilon$.
    2. Graph. Build a weighted graph $G$ on the $n$ points with an edge $i\!-\!j$ whenever $\mathbf{x}_j\in N_\epsilon(\mathbf{x}_i)$, weight $=\lVert\mathbf{x}_i-\mathbf{x}_j\rVert_2$. Short hops are trusted (locally the manifold looks flat); long hops are simply not drawn.
    3. Shortest path. $d_{\text{geo}}(\mathbf{x}_i,\mathbf{x}_j)$ is the Dijkstra shortest-path length in $G$. This is a metric on the connected component containing both points, and it converges to the true manifold geodesic as $n\to\infty$, $\epsilon\to0$.

    Worked example. Sample $n=120$ points along a "C"-shaped arc of radius $2$ (the manifold), with Gaussian jitter $\sigma=0.05$. Take $\epsilon=0.45$, giving a graph of mean degree $10$. Endpoints $\mathbf{x}$ and $\mathbf{y}$ sit at the two open ends of the C.

    • Straight-line (chord) distance: $\lVert\mathbf{x}-\mathbf{y}\rVert_2 = 3.0769$.
    • Geodesic distance: $8.9502$, realised by a $26$-hop path around the arc.
    • Ratio $= 2.909$.

    So a Euclidean clusterer thinks the two ends of the C are the third-closest thing in the dataset; a geodesic clusterer knows they are the two most distant points on it.

    Fig. 19.4 — Slide 22 made computable. (a) the local neighbourhood $N(x)=\epsilon$ and the $\epsilon$-graph it generates; (b) the chord ($3.08$, dashed red) versus the geodesic ($8.95$, solid green) — a factor of $2.91$.

    Gotcha — $\epsilon$ is not free. Too small and the graph disconnects: at $\epsilon=0.20$ only $21$ of the $120$ points are reachable from the source and $d_{\text{geo}}=\infty$ for the rest. Too large and the graph "short-circuits" across the gap, so the geodesic collapses back toward the chord ($8.69$ at $\epsilon=1.2$, on its way to $3.08$). The same $\epsilon$/neighbourhood tension reappears as DBSCAN's $\epsilon$ and MinPts; it is the single most fragile knob in the whole density/manifold family.

    19.3   The k-means objective

    Slide 16 states the goal in words — "k-means tries to minimize the within cluster sum of distance squares" — and then writes:

    $$\arg\min_{s}\;\sum_{i=1}^{n}\sum_{x \in S_j}\bigl\lVert x_i-\mu_j\bigr\rVert^2 .$$

    Adjudication of the slide's objective. As printed this expression does not typecheck, in three ways, and the transcript flags all three: (i) the $\arg\min$ is over a lowercase $s$ that appears nowhere else, while the cluster sets are $S_j$; (ii) the outer sum runs over $i=1,\dots,n$ (all points) while the inner sum runs over $x\in S_j$ with $j$ never bound by any sum — so every point would be counted $|S_j|$ times; (iii) the summand uses $x_i$ although the inner index is $x$. The intended and standard object is a minimisation over the partition, with the outer sum over clusters:

    $$\boxed{\;J(\mathcal{C},\boldsymbol\mu)=\sum_{j=1}^{k}\ \sum_{\mathbf{x}_i\in C_j} \bigl\lVert\mathbf{x}_i-\boldsymbol\mu_j\bigr\rVert_2^2,\qquad \{\hat{\mathcal{C}},\hat{\boldsymbol\mu}\}=\arg\min_{\mathcal{C},\boldsymbol\mu} J. \;}$$

    This is the within-cluster sum of squares (WCSS). Slide 16 also draws only two cylinders where the neighbouring slides draw three — cosmetic, but worth not copying into an exam answer.

    Two families of unknowns appear in $J$: the discrete assignment (which $C_j$ each point belongs to) and the continuous centres $\boldsymbol\mu_j\in\mathbb{R}^p$, stacked as a matrix $\mathbf{M}$ of shape $(k\times p)$. Minimising over both jointly is NP-hard even for $k=2$ in the plane, so we alternate: fix one family, solve the other exactly.

    19.3.1   Why the centroid is the mean — full derivation

    Proposition. For a fixed cluster $C=\{\mathbf{x}_1,\dots,\mathbf{x}_m\}\subset\mathbb{R}^p$, the unique minimiser of $f(\boldsymbol\mu)=\sum_{i=1}^{m}\lVert\mathbf{x}_i-\boldsymbol\mu\rVert_2^2$ is the sample mean $\boldsymbol\mu^\star=\frac1m\sum_{i=1}^m\mathbf{x}_i$.

    Proof, with shapes. Write the squared norm as an inner product:

    $$f(\boldsymbol\mu)=\sum_{i=1}^{m}(\mathbf{x}_i-\boldsymbol\mu)^\top(\mathbf{x}_i-\boldsymbol\mu), \qquad (1\times p)\cdot(p\times 1)\to \text{scalar}.$$

    Step 1 — gradient of one term. Expanding, $(\mathbf{x}_i-\boldsymbol\mu)^\top(\mathbf{x}_i-\boldsymbol\mu) =\mathbf{x}_i^\top\mathbf{x}_i-2\boldsymbol\mu^\top\mathbf{x}_i+\boldsymbol\mu^\top\boldsymbol\mu$, so with $\nabla_{\boldsymbol\mu}(\boldsymbol\mu^\top\mathbf{a})=\mathbf{a}$ and $\nabla_{\boldsymbol\mu}(\boldsymbol\mu^\top\boldsymbol\mu)=2\boldsymbol\mu$,

    $$\nabla_{\boldsymbol\mu}\lVert\mathbf{x}_i-\boldsymbol\mu\rVert_2^2 = -2\mathbf{x}_i+2\boldsymbol\mu = -2(\mathbf{x}_i-\boldsymbol\mu),\qquad (p\times 1).$$

    Step 2 — sum and set to zero.

    $$\nabla_{\boldsymbol\mu} f = -2\sum_{i=1}^{m}(\mathbf{x}_i-\boldsymbol\mu) = -2\sum_{i=1}^{m}\mathbf{x}_i + 2m\boldsymbol\mu \;\overset{!}{=}\;\mathbf{0} \quad\Longrightarrow\quad \boldsymbol\mu^\star=\frac1m\sum_{i=1}^{m}\mathbf{x}_i .$$

    Step 3 — it is a minimum, not a saddle. The Hessian is $\nabla^2_{\boldsymbol\mu} f = 2m\,\mathbf{I}_p$, shape $(p\times p)$, with all eigenvalues $2m>0$, so $f$ is strictly convex and $\boldsymbol\mu^\star$ is the unique global minimiser. $\blacksquare$

    Gotcha — the mean is $L_2$-specific. Minimising $\sum_i\lVert\mathbf{x}_i-\boldsymbol\mu \rVert_1$ gives the coordinate-wise median; minimising the $L_\infty$ version gives the midpoint of the enclosing box. So "k-means with Manhattan distance" — assign by $L_1$ but update with the mean — optimises no single objective and can oscillate. Use k-medians ($L_1$ assign, median update) or k-medoids/PAM (centre must be an actual data point) instead. Concretely, for the four points $(1,1),(2,1),(9,1),(2,9)$ the mean is $(3.5,3)$ with total $L_1$ cost $23$, while the median $(2,1)$ has total $L_1$ cost $16$ — the mean is $44\%$ worse under the metric you claimed to be using.

    19.3.2   Lloyd's algorithm and why it stops

    Lloyd's algorithm (the deck's four steps, slide 28).

    1. Initialise. Choose $k$ initial means $\boldsymbol\mu_1^{(0)},\dots,\boldsymbol\mu_k^{(0)}$ "randomly generated within the data domain".
    2. Assign. $c(i)=\arg\min_{j}\lVert\mathbf{x}_i-\boldsymbol\mu_j^{(t)}\rVert_2^2$ for every $i$; set $C_j^{(t)}=\{i : c(i)=j\}$. Cost $O(nkp)$ — the full distance matrix is $(n\times k)$.
    3. Update. $\boldsymbol\mu_j^{(t+1)}=\dfrac{1}{|C_j^{(t)}|}\sum_{i\in C_j^{(t)}}\mathbf{x}_i$. Cost $O(np)$.
    4. Repeat steps 2–3 until the assignment stops changing. Slide 27 phrases the stopping rule as: "Do until the centers in $k^{th}$ step is same as the centers in $(k-1)^{th}$ step."

    Per-iteration cost $O(nkp)$; total $O(nkpT)$ for $T$ iterations.

    Convergence. Lloyd's algorithm terminates after finitely many iterations at a local minimum of $J$.

    Proof. (a) The assignment step cannot increase $J$: for each $i$ it replaces $\lVert\mathbf{x}_i-\boldsymbol\mu_{c_{\text{old}}(i)}\rVert^2$ by the minimum over $j$ of $\lVert\mathbf{x}_i-\boldsymbol\mu_j\rVert^2$, which is $\le$ the old term. (b) The update step cannot increase $J$: by the Proposition of §19.3.1 the mean is the exact minimiser of each cluster's contribution with the assignment held fixed. (c) $J\ge0$ and depends on the configuration only through the assignment, of which there are at most $k^n$ — finitely many. A non-increasing sequence over a finite set that strictly decreases whenever the assignment changes must stop changing. $\blacksquare$

    What the proof does not give you. Nothing here says the limit is the global minimum; only that it is a fixed point. §19.5 quantifies how bad that can get.

    Code — Lloyd's algorithm from scratch (numpy) 
    import numpy as np

def kmeans_lloyd(X, k, n_iter=100, seed=0):
    """Assign/update halves matching Sec 19.3.2 exactly, including the
    slide-27 stopping rule (assignment unchanged between iterations)."""
    rng = np.random.default_rng(seed)
    n, p = X.shape
    mu = X[rng.choice(n, size=k, replace=False)].copy()  # mu_j^(0), (k, p)
    assign_prev = None
    for t in range(n_iter):
        # assign step: c(i) = argmin_j ||x_i - mu_j||^2, cost O(nkp)
        dist2 = ((X[:, None, :] - mu[None, :, :]) ** 2).sum(axis=2)  # (n, k)
        assign = dist2.argmin(axis=1)

        if assign_prev is not None and np.array_equal(assign, assign_prev):
            break  # centers at step t == centers at step t-1 (slide 27)

        # update step: mu_j is the mean of its assigned points, cost O(np)
        for j in range(k):
            members = X[assign == j]
            if len(members):           # guard an empty cluster (bad seed)
                mu[j] = members.mean(axis=0)
        assign_prev = assign

    wcss = dist2[np.arange(n), assign].sum()  # J after the final assignment
    return assign, mu, wcss

    Recompute the full $(n\times k)$ distance matrix every assign step (never reuse a stale one) and always guard the empty-cluster case -- a bad k-means++ draw can leave a centroid with zero members, and members.mean() on an empty slice is a silent NaN.
