    20.8.4   Why k-means is EM in disguise

    Slide 72 asserts "$K$-means is special case" and stops. Here is the argument.

    Claim. Constrain the mixture to equal weights $\pi_k=1/K$ and shared isotropic covariance $\boldsymbol\Sigma_k=\sigma^2\mathbf{I}$. Then as $\sigma^2\to 0^{+}$, EM's E step becomes hard nearest-centroid assignment and its M step becomes the cluster mean — i.e. Lloyd's algorithm.

    Proof. Under the constraint the responsibility is

    $$\gamma_{ik}=\frac{\exp\bigl(-\lVert\mathbf{x}_i-\boldsymbol\mu_k\rVert^2/2\sigma^2\bigr)} {\sum_{j}\exp\bigl(-\lVert\mathbf{x}_i-\boldsymbol\mu_j\rVert^2/2\sigma^2\bigr)},$$

    because the constants $(2\pi\sigma^2)^{-d/2}$ and $1/K$ cancel between numerator and denominator. Let $k^\star=\arg\min_j\lVert\mathbf{x}_i-\boldsymbol\mu_j\rVert^2$ and divide top and bottom by the $k^\star$ term:

    $$\gamma_{ik}=\frac{\exp\bigl(-(\delta_k-\delta_{k^\star})/2\sigma^2\bigr)} {\sum_j\exp\bigl(-(\delta_j-\delta_{k^\star})/2\sigma^2\bigr)}, \qquad \delta_k:=\lVert\mathbf{x}_i-\boldsymbol\mu_k\rVert^2 .$$

    Every exponent with $k\ne k^\star$ has $\delta_k-\delta_{k^\star}>0$ (assuming no ties), so as $\sigma^2\to0^{+}$ that term $\to e^{-\infty}=0$; the $k^\star$ term is $e^{0}=1$. Hence $\gamma_{ik}\to\mathbb{1}[k=k^\star]$ — a hard assignment to the nearest centroid, which is k-means' assign step. Substituting a $0/1$ $\gamma$ into the M step gives $\boldsymbol\mu_k = \frac{1}{\lvert C_k\rvert}\sum_{i\in C_k}\mathbf{x}_i$ — k-means' update step. And the expected complete-data log-likelihood reduces to $-\frac{1}{2\sigma^2}\sum_k\sum_{i\in C_k}\lVert\mathbf{x}_i-\boldsymbol\mu_k\rVert^2 + \text{const}$, so maximising it is minimising WCSS. $\blacksquare$

    Numerically. Freeze $\mu=(2,6)$ on the same six points and shrink $\sigma^2$; watch $\gamma_{i1}$ harden.

    $\sigma^2$$x{=}1$$x{=}2$$x{=}3$$x{=}7$$x{=}8$$x{=}9$
    4.000.9525740.8807970.7310590.0474260.0179860.006693
    1.000.9999940.9996650.9820140.0000060.0000000.000000
    0.251.0000001.0000001.0000000.0000000.0000000.000000

    By $\sigma^2 = 0.25$ every responsibility is $0$ or $1$ to six decimals: soft clustering has become crisp clustering.

    Interpretation. $\sigma^2$ is a softness dial. Large $\sigma^2$: every point partly belongs to every cluster, boundaries are fuzzy, and the model tolerates overlap. Small $\sigma^2$: hard boundaries, k-means. This is the same crisp-versus-fuzzy axis that fuzzy c-means parameterises with its exponent $m$, arrived at from probability rather than from a modified objective. So k-means is not a rival to GMM — it is the zero-temperature, equal-weight, spherical corner of it.

    20.8.5   What the extra generality buys, and what it costs

    Fig. 20.11 — $250$ points: one elongated, correlated cluster ($180$ pts) and one small compact cluster ($70$ pts). k-means reaches purity $0.768$; a full-covariance GMM reaches $1.000$. Right: the monotone log-likelihood of §20.8.3.
    covariance typefree parameters ($K=2$, $d=2$)cluster shapes
    spherical, $\sigma_k^2\mathbf{I}$7circles, sizes may differ
    diagonal9axis-aligned ellipses
    tied, shared $\boldsymbol\Sigma$8identical ellipses
    full, per-component $\boldsymbol\Sigma_k$11arbitrary ellipses

    Slide 70 assumes "diagonal covariance, known variance, same for all clusters" — the cheapest row but one, which is exactly the assumption that collapses to k-means.

    Gotcha — the likelihood is unbounded. Put $\boldsymbol\mu_k$ exactly on a data point and let $\lvert\boldsymbol\Sigma_k\rvert\to0$: that component's density at that point diverges and $\ell\to+\infty$. So the MLE does not exist for full-covariance GMMs; EM finds a local maximum and you must guard against the degenerate one. Standard fixes: add a small ridge to the covariance diagonal (scikit-learn's reg_covar), restrict the covariance type, or use MAP with an inverse-Wishart prior. If a run reports a component with a single member and a near-singular covariance, it has collapsed — restart it.

    Second gotcha — choosing $K$. $\ell$ increases monotonically with $K$, so you cannot pick $K$ by likelihood. Penalise it: $\mathrm{BIC}=-2\ell+P\log n$ with $P$ the free-parameter count. On the Fig. 20.11 data BIC is $2227.93$ at $K=1$, $1696.15$ at $K=2$ and $1728.89$ at $K=3$ — minimised at the true $K=2$.

    Code — GaussianMixture with BIC model selection (sklearn) 
    import numpy as np
from sklearn.mixture import GaussianMixture

bic = []
k_range = range(1, 7)
for k in k_range:
    gmm = GaussianMixture(
        n_components=k,
        covariance_type="full",  # spherical | diag | tied | full (Sec 20.8.5)
        reg_covar=1e-6,           # ridge on the covariance diagonal -- guards
        random_state=0,           # against the unbounded-likelihood collapse
    ).fit(X)
    bic.append(gmm.bic(X))       # -2*loglik + P*log(n); LOWER is better

best_k = list(k_range)[int(np.argmin(bic))]
gmm = GaussianMixture(n_components=best_k, covariance_type="full",
                       reg_covar=1e-6, random_state=0).fit(X)

resp = gmm.predict_proba(X)  # (n, k) soft responsibilities, gamma_ik
hard = gmm.predict(X)         # argmax(resp, axis=1), the crisp labels

    Never select $K$ by raw log-likelihood -- it only ever increases with $K$ (§20.8.5's first gotcha); BIC's $P\log n$ penalty is what gives it an interior minimum, and reg_covar is the practical fix for the degenerate-covariance collapse in the second.

    20.9   Internal validation: is the clustering any good?

    Slide 73 poses the question and leaves it hanging; slide 74 answers with two indices. Internal evaluation judges a clustering using only the data that was clustered — no labels required.

    Davies–Bouldin index. With $n$ clusters (the slide's symbol; it means the number of clusters, not the number of points), $c_i$ the centroid of cluster $i$, and $\sigma_i$ the average distance from cluster $i$'s members to $c_i$:

    $$DB=\frac{1}{n}\sum_{i=1}^{n}\max_{j\ne i}\left(\frac{\sigma_i+\sigma_j}{d(c_i,c_j)}\right).$$

    Each term is a worst-case "how much do my spread and my neighbour's spread eat the gap between us" ratio. Lower is better; $DB\ge0$, and $DB=0$ would mean zero-spread clusters infinitely far apart.

    Dunn index:

    $$D=\frac{\displaystyle\min_{1\le i<j\le n} d(i,j)}{\displaystyle\max_{1\le k\le n} d'(k)},$$

    where $d(i,j)$ is the inter-cluster distance (we use the minimum point-pair distance) and $d'(k)$ the intra-cluster distance (we use the cluster's diameter, the maximum point-pair distance inside it). Higher is better.

    Silhouette. For point $i$ in cluster $C_{(i)}$:

    $$a(i)=\frac{1}{\lvert C_{(i)}\rvert-1}\sum_{j\in C_{(i)},\,j\ne i} d(i,j),\qquad b(i)=\min_{C_k\ne C_{(i)}}\ \frac{1}{\lvert C_k\rvert}\sum_{j\in C_k} d(i,j),$$ $$s(i)=\frac{b(i)-a(i)}{\max\{a(i),b(i)\}}\in[-1,1],\qquad S=\frac{1}{n}\sum_{i=1}^{n} s(i).$$

    $a$ is cohesion (mean distance to my own cluster), $b$ is separation (mean distance to the nearest other cluster). By convention $s(i)=0$ for a singleton cluster. Higher is better.

    20.9.1   All three computed by hand on six points

    v5 defines $a(i)$, $b(i)$ and $s(i)$ and then never computes one. Here is the arithmetic in full, on a set small enough to check with a pencil.

    Data. $A(1,1), B(1,2), C(2,1)$ in cluster $1$; $D(6,1), E(6,2), F(7,1)$ in cluster $2$.

    Centroids and spreads. $c_1=\bigl(\tfrac{1+1+2}{3},\tfrac{1+2+1}{3}\bigr)=(1.333333, 1.333333)$ and $c_2=(6.333333, 1.333333)$, so $d(c_1,c_2)=5.0$ exactly. Distances to $c_1$: $\lVert A-c_1\rVert=\sqrt{(1/3)^2+(1/3)^2}=0.471405$, $\lVert B-c_1\rVert=\sqrt{(1/3)^2+(2/3)^2}=0.745356$, $\lVert C-c_1\rVert=0.745356$, so

    $$\sigma_1=\frac{0.471405+0.745356+0.745356}{3}=0.654039,\qquad \sigma_2=0.654039 \text{ (by symmetry)}.$$

    Davies–Bouldin. With only two clusters the $\max_{j\ne i}$ has a single candidate:

    $$R_{12}=\frac{\sigma_1+\sigma_2}{d(c_1,c_2)}=\frac{1.308078}{5.0}=0.261616 \;\Rightarrow\; DB=\tfrac12(0.261616+0.261616)=0.261616.$$

    Cross-checked against sklearn.metrics.davies_bouldin_score: identical.

    Dunn. Minimum inter-cluster distance: the closest cross pair is $C(2,1)$–$D(6,1)$ at $4.0$. Maximum intra-cluster diameter: $B$–$C$ (and $E$–$F$) at $\sqrt{1^2+1^2}=1.414214$. So $D=4.0/1.414214=2.828426$.

    Silhouette, point by point. For $A$: $a(A)=\tfrac{d(A,B)+d(A,C)}{2}=\tfrac{1+1}{2}=1.0$; $b(A)=\tfrac{d(A,D)+d(A,E)+d(A,F)}{3}=\tfrac{5.0+5.099020+6.0}{3}=5.366340$; hence $s(A)=\tfrac{5.366340-1.0}{5.366340}=0.813653$.

    point$a(i)$$b(i)$$s(i)$
    A1.0000005.3663400.813653
    B1.2071075.3939270.776210
    C1.2071074.3743690.724050
    D1.0000004.6996730.787219
    E1.2071074.7407080.745374
    F1.2071075.6942540.788013

    $S=\tfrac16(0.813653+\cdots+0.788013)=0.772420$, matching sklearn.metrics.silhouette_score exactly.

    Contrast — a deliberately bad partition of the same six points, $\{A,B,E\}$ vs $\{C,D,F\}$: $DB$ rises from $0.261616$ to $1.764353$, Dunn falls from $2.828426$ to $0.196116$, and mean silhouette collapses from $0.772420$ to $0.016059$.

    Interpretation. All three indices move together and by a lot — an order of magnitude for Dunn and for the silhouette — which is what a usable index should do. Note what each one is sensitive to: $DB$ uses centroids and average spreads, so it is a "typical case" measure; Dunn uses the single closest cross pair and the single widest intra pair, so it is a pure worst-case measure and one bridging point destroys it; silhouette is computed per point, so it is the only one of the three that tells you which points are badly placed. That per-point detail is why silhouette is the practical default.

    20.9.2   Sweeping $k$ on a shared dataset

    Fig. 20.12 — A $90$-point, three-blob dataset clustered with k-means for $k=2\ldots7$. WCSS shows an elbow at $k=3$; Davies–Bouldin is minimised at $k=3$; Dunn and mean silhouette are maximised at $k=3$. The last panel shows the per-point silhouettes at $k=3$.
    $k$WCSSDavies–Bouldin ↓Dunn ↑mean silhouette ↑
    2261.2060.6945200.3941030.553014
    348.6440.3308860.6346640.754883
    439.5960.6608510.1304050.629290
    533.1660.8430070.0396520.490480
    627.2090.9781550.0620510.375172
    724.2150.9161640.0494530.365833

    Interpretation. WCSS alone would not settle it — it keeps falling ($48.6\to39.6\to33.2$), and the "elbow" at $k=3$ is a judgement call about curvature. The three proper indices are unambiguous: all three peak (or trough) at $k=3$, and the drop from $k=3$ to $k=4$ is severe (Dunn falls by a factor of nearly $5$, because splitting a real blob creates two clusters that almost touch, which is exactly the quantity Dunn's numerator measures). This is v5's Fig 19.4 claim — "here $k=4$ wins" — replaced with actual computed evidence, on data where the answer is known.

    Gotcha — internal indices have model bias baked in. $DB$, Dunn and silhouette are all distance-based and all reward compact, well-separated, roughly spherical clusters. Run them on Fig. 20.1's two moons and they will prefer k-means' wrong answer to DBSCAN's right one, because DBSCAN's crescents have huge intra-cluster diameters. Never use an internal index to compare a density-based clustering against a centroid-based one; use them to tune $k$ within one algorithm family, or use a density-aware index (DBCV). Also: silhouette costs $O(n^2)$ distances — subsample for large $n$.

    20.10   External validation: comparing against known labels

    "In external evaluation, clustering results are evaluated based on data that was not used for clustering, such as known class labels". The deck then shows the classification confusion matrix and the $F$-measure:

    $$P=\frac{TP}{TP+FP},\qquad R=\frac{TP}{TP+FN},\qquad F_\beta=\frac{(\beta^2+1)\,P\,R}{\beta^2 P + R}.$$

    Adjudication — you cannot apply the classification confusion matrix directly. These formulas are the classification metrics of §5, and slide 75 prints the familiar $2\times2$ TP/FN/FP/TN block (with no row or column headers, so its orientation is ambiguous — the standard convention is rows $=$ actual, columns $=$ predicted). But a clustering has no class names: the algorithm outputs "cluster 0, cluster 1, cluster 2", not "cats, dogs". There is no canonical way to say which cluster is the "positive" class, and permuting the cluster labels must not change the score.

    The standard repair, and the one the slide's own reference (Manning, Raghavan & Schütze, Introduction to Information Retrieval, Ch. 16/20) uses, is pair counting: evaluate over the $\binom{n}{2}$ pairs of points, not over points.

    Pair-counted confusion matrix. For each unordered pair $\{i,j\}$:

    same class (truth)different class
    same clusterTP — correctly groupedFP — wrongly grouped
    different clusterFN — wrongly separatedTN — correctly separated

    $TP+FP+FN+TN=\binom{n}{2}$. Then $P$, $R$, $F_\beta$ as above, plus the Rand index $RI=(TP+TN)/\binom{n}{2}$ — pairwise accuracy. This construction is permutation-invariant in the cluster labels, as required.

    Worked example. $8$ users, ground-truth classes $y=(0,0,0,0,1,1,1,1)$, clustering output $C=(0,0,0,1,1,1,1,2)$.

    contingencyclass 0class 1row total
    cluster 0303
    cluster 1134
    cluster 2011

    Counting the pairs. $\binom{8}{2}=28$ pairs in total. Same-cluster pairs: $\binom{3}{2}+\binom{4}{2}+\binom{1}{2}=3+6+0=9$. Of those, the $3$ pairs inside cluster 0 are all class-0 (TP), and inside cluster 1 the $3$ class-1 members give $\binom{3}{2}=3$ TP while the lone class-0 member forms $3$ mixed pairs (FP). So $TP=3+3=6$ and $FP=3$. Same-class pairs in truth: $\binom{4}{2}+\binom{4}{2}=12$, so $FN=12-6=6$, and $TN=28-6-3-6=13$.

    TPFPFNTN$P$$R$$F_1$$F_{0.5}$$F_2$$RI$
    636130.6666670.5000000.5714290.6250000.5263160.678571

    For reference, the chance-corrected scores on the same partition are $\mathrm{ARI}=0.322581$ and $\mathrm{NMI}=0.494110$.

    Interpretation. Precision $0.667$ > recall $0.500$: this clustering is conservative — when it puts two users together it is usually right, but it splits many pairs that belong together (the class-1 users are spread over clusters 1 and 2). $\beta$ picks your side of that trade, exactly as in §5: $\beta<1$ (here $F_{0.5}=0.625$) leans toward precision, $\beta>1$ ($F_2=0.526$) toward recall. Use $\beta>1$ when missing a true grouping is expensive (deduplicating customer records), $\beta<1$ when a spurious merge is expensive (merging two patients' medical histories).

    Why the chance-corrected versions matter: the Rand index here is $0.679$, which sounds decent — but a random partition into $3$ clusters already scores well above $0$ on RI, because most pairs are genuinely different-class and land in TN for free. ARI subtracts that expected-by-chance baseline and reports $0.323$, a much more honest number. Report ARI or NMI, not raw RI.

    20.11   Choosing an algorithm

    Fig. 20.13 — Clustering-algorithm decision flowchart. Every path terminates in the same validation step.
    algorithmneeds $k$?cluster shapenoise handlingtypical costmain risk
    k-meansyesconvex, similar sizenone — every point assigned$O(nkdI)$local optima; outlier drag
    DBSCANnoarbitraryexplicit noise class$O(n\log n)$ indexed, $O(n^2)$ otherwiseone global density scale
    AGNES / DIANAno (cut later)linkage-dependentnone$O(n^2)$–$O(n^3)$no backtracking; memory
    BIRCHPhase 2 doesspherical leaf entriessmall outlier entries can be pruned$O(n)$, one scanorder-sensitive; numeric only
    CUREyesnon-sphericalshrinking damps outliers$O(s^2\log s)$ on a sampletwo extra knobs $c,\alpha$
    GMM / EMyes (or BIC)ellipticallow-likelihood points flagged$O(nKd^2I)$degenerate covariances; local optima

    Recap. Four definitions of "cluster" appeared in this section, and each brings its own algorithm and its own failure mode.

    • Density (DBSCAN): a cluster is a maximal density-connected set. Needs $(\varepsilon,\text{MinPts})$; finds arbitrary shapes; reports noise; assumes one density scale. The deck's example recomputes to $2$ clusters $+$ $1$ noise point at $\varepsilon=2$, MinPts $=3$.
    • Hierarchy (AGNES/DIANA): a cluster is a node of a merge tree. Needs a linkage, not a $k$; single chains, complete compacts; $O(n^2)$ memory kills it above $\sim10^4$ points.
    • Summary (BIRCH, CURE): compress first, cluster the summaries. CF additivity $(N,\overrightarrow{LS},SS)$ makes merges $O(d)$; CURE's $c$ representatives $+$ $\alpha$-shrink buy shape and outlier robustness.
    • Probability (GMM/EM): a cluster is a mixture component. Soft memberships, elliptical shapes, $K$ chosen by BIC; k-means is its $\sigma^2\to0$, equal-weight, isotropic limit.
    • Validation: internal ($DB\downarrow$, Dunn$\uparrow$, silhouette$\uparrow$) with no labels; external via pair-counted $P/R/F_\beta$ and chance-corrected ARI when labels exist.

    Adjudication — the deck's closing claim. Slide 77 ends: "Different clustering may result in different patterns, but the most consistent pattern is the correct distribution". Consistency across algorithms and across restarts is strong evidence for structure, and instability is strong evidence against it — but it is not proof of correctness. Two counter-cases: (i) all distance-based methods share the same spherical bias, so they can agree on the same wrong answer, as Fig. 20.1's k-means panels show; (ii) on uniform noise, every run of k-means with a fixed seed returns the same partition, perfectly consistent and completely meaningless. Use consistency as one signal, alongside an internal index, a stability analysis (bootstrap the data and measure ARI between runs), and — always — domain sense.

    20.12   Practice

    Practice 20.1 — With $\varepsilon=2$ and MinPts $=4$ instead of $3$, reclassify the 11 points of §20.4.1.

    The neighbourhood sizes do not change (they depend only on $\varepsilon$): P1, P2, Q1, Q3, Q5 have $\lvert N_\varepsilon\rvert = 3$ and P3, P4, P5, Q2, Q4 have $4$; N1 has $1$.

    Raising MinPts to $4$ leaves exactly four core points: P3, P4, Q2, Q4. Running the algorithm:

    • P3 is core; $N_\varepsilon(\text{P3})=\{$P1, P3, P4, P5$\}$ seeds the cluster. P4 is also core, and its neighbourhood adds P2. Result $C_1=\{$P1,…,P5$\}$, with P1, P2, P5 now border points instead of core.
    • Q2 is core; $N_\varepsilon(\text{Q2})=\{$Q1, Q2, Q4, Q5$\}$; Q4 is core and adds Q3. Result $C_2=\{$Q1,…,Q5$\}$, with Q1, Q3, Q5 as border points.
    • N1 has $\lvert N_\varepsilon\rvert = 1$ and is in no core point's ball → noise.

    The compute run confirms: $2$ clusters, $4$ core points, $1$ noise point . Lesson: the partition is unchanged, but the core/border composition changed completely — $10$ core points became $4$. MinPts controls how much of a cluster is "load-bearing", and a cluster held up by four core points is far more fragile to a small perturbation of the data than one held up by ten.

    Practice 20.2 — Show that a border point can legitimately belong to two clusters, and explain what implementations do about it.

    Construction ($d=1$, $\varepsilon=1$, MinPts $=4$). Seven points on a line:

    point$a_1$$a_2$$a_3$$b$$c_1$$c_2$$c_3$
    $x$0.00.40.81.82.83.23.6
    $\lvert N_\varepsilon\rvert$3343433

    Only $a_3$ and $c_1$ reach $4$, so those two are the only core points. Check them: $N_\varepsilon(a_3)=\{a_1,a_2,a_3,b\}$ (since $\lvert 0.8-0.0\rvert=0.8\le1$ and $\lvert 1.8-0.8\rvert=1.0\le1$) and $N_\varepsilon(c_1)=\{b,c_1,c_2,c_3\}$ (since $\lvert 2.8-1.8\rvert = 1.0 \le 1$ and $\lvert 3.6-2.8\rvert=0.8\le1$).

    Now $\lvert N_\varepsilon(b)\rvert = 3 < 4$, so $b$ is not core — yet $b$ lies inside the $\varepsilon$-ball of both core points $a_3$ and $c_1$ . And $a_3$ is not density-reachable from $c_1$: the only route runs through $b$, which is not core, so no hop may start there. Hence $\{a_1,a_2,a_3,b\}$ and $\{b,c_1,c_2,c_3\}$ are two different clusters, each of which legitimately contains $b$.

    The formal definition (§20.3) then puts $b$ in both clusters by maximality — a contradiction with "partition". Every implementation resolves it by visit order: whichever cluster expands to $b$ first claims it — our run, sweeping left to right, gives $b$ to the $a$-cluster . Consequence: DBSCAN's core-point and noise assignments are deterministic, but border assignments are not. If your downstream analysis is sensitive to a handful of boundary points, either report them separately or use a variant (DBSCAN* treats all border points as noise, which restores determinism).

    Practice 20.3 — Compute the complete-linkage merge sequence for the four-object matrix, then explain why single and complete give different topologies.

    Matrix (§20.6.4): $d(A,B)=1$, $d(A,C)=4$, $d(A,D)=5$, $d(B,C)=2$, $d(B,D)=6$, $d(C,D)=3$.

    Step 1. Minimum off-diagonal is $d(A,B)=1$ → merge at height $1$.
    Step 2. Complete update: $D(\{AB\},C)=\max(4,2)=4$; $D(\{AB\},D)=\max(5,6)=6$; $D(C,D)=3$ unchanged. Minimum is $3$ → merge $C,D$ at height $3$.
    Step 3. $D(\{AB\},\{CD\})=\max(4,5,2,6)=6$ → merge at height $6$.
    Heights: $1, 3, 6$.

    Why different from single ($1,2,3$)? After the first merge the two rules disagree about $\{AB\}$ vs $C$: single says $\min(4,2)=2$ (it sees only the short $B$–$C$ edge), complete says $\max(4,2)=4$ (it insists the whole merged cluster stay tight, and $A$ is $4$ from $C$). So single merges $\{AB\}$ with $C$ next, producing a chain $A\!-\!B\!-\!C\!-\!D$; complete instead prefers the cheaper $C$–$D$ pair and ends with two balanced 2-clusters. Single linkage cares about the nearest bridge, complete about the worst diameter — so single propagates through thin connections and complete refuses them.

    Practice 20.4 — Given $\mathrm{CF}=(5,(16,30),(54,190))$, compute the centroid and radius without touching the points. Then merge it with $\mathrm{CF}'=(5,(36,17),(262,65))$ and give the merged radius.

    Scalar $SS = 54+190 = 244$ (see the adjudication in §20.7.1).

    Centroid: $\bar{\mathbf{x}}=\overrightarrow{LS}/N = (16,30)/5 = (3.2, 6.0)$.

    Radius: $R=\sqrt{SS/N - \lVert\bar{\mathbf{x}}\rVert^2} =\sqrt{244/5 - (3.2^2+6.0^2)} = \sqrt{48.8-46.24}=\sqrt{2.56}=1.6$.

    Merge by additivity: $\mathrm{CF}_{\text{merged}} = (5+5,\ (16+36,\ 30+17),\ (54+262,\ 190+65)) = (10,\ (52,47),\ (316,255))$.

    Merged scalar $SS = 316+255 = 571$; merged centroid $=(52,47)/10=(5.2,4.7)$; merged radius $=\sqrt{571/10 - (5.2^2+4.7^2)} = \sqrt{57.1 - (27.04+22.09)} = \sqrt{57.1-49.13} = \sqrt{7.97} = 2.823119$.

    Point: the merged radius ($2.823$) is much larger than either child's, which is exactly the quantity a CF-tree tests against its threshold $T$ before absorbing a point or an entry — and it was computed with six additions and one square root, never revisiting the ten points.

    Practice 20.5 — One EM E-step by hand: $x=5$, two 1-D components with $\mu=(2,6)$, $\sigma^2=2$ each, $\pi=(0.5,0.5)$. Find $\gamma$. Then say what happens to $\gamma$ as $\sigma^2\to 0$.

    Densities (the $1/\sqrt{2\pi\sigma^2}=1/3.5449$ factor cancels in the ratio, but keep it for clarity):

    $\mathcal{N}(5\mid 2,2)=\frac{1}{3.5449}e^{-(5-2)^2/4}=\frac{1}{3.5449}e^{-2.25}=0.029733$; $\mathcal{N}(5\mid 6,2)=\frac{1}{3.5449}e^{-(5-6)^2/4}=\frac{1}{3.5449}e^{-0.25}=0.219696$.

    $p(5)=0.5(0.029733)+0.5(0.219696)=0.124714$, so

    $$\gamma_1=\frac{0.5(0.029733)}{0.124714}=0.119203,\qquad \gamma_2=0.880797 .$$

    (These are the same two numbers that appear, mirrored, in the $x=3$ row of §20.8.3's table — because $x=3$ is $1$ away from $\mu_1$ and $3$ away from $\mu_2$, the mirror situation.

    As $\sigma^2\to0$: the ratio becomes $\gamma_1=\bigl(1+e^{(\delta_1-\delta_2)/2\sigma^2}\bigr)^{-1}$ with $\delta_1=9,\delta_2=1$, so the exponent $\to+\infty$ and $\gamma_1\to0$, $\gamma_2\to1$: a hard assignment to the nearer mean, i.e. k-means (§20.8.4). At $\sigma^2=0.25$ the computed responsibility is already $0$ to six decimals.

    Practice 20.6 — Two clusters $\{(0,0),(0,2)\}$ and $\{(6,0),(6,2)\}$. Compute $DB$, Dunn and the silhouette of $(0,0)$.

    Centroids: $c_1=(0,1)$, $c_2=(6,1)$; $d(c_1,c_2)=6$.

    Spreads: each point is $1$ from its centroid, so $\sigma_1=\sigma_2=1$.

    Davies–Bouldin: $R_{12}=(1+1)/6=0.333333$; with two clusters $DB=\tfrac12(0.333333+0.333333)=0.333333$.

    Dunn: minimum inter-cluster distance is $6$ (e.g. $(0,0)$ to $(6,0)$); maximum intra-cluster diameter is $2$. $D=6/2=3.0$.

    Silhouette of $(0,0)$: $a=d\bigl((0,0),(0,2)\bigr)=2$; $b=\tfrac12\bigl(d((0,0),(6,0))+d((0,0),(6,2))\bigr)=\tfrac12(6+\sqrt{40})=\tfrac12(6+6.324555) =6.162278$; so $s=\frac{6.162278-2}{6.162278}=0.675445$.

    Sanity check against §20.9.1's example: there $DB=0.261616$ and Dunn $=2.828426$ for a configuration with the same gap-to-spread flavour; here the clusters are more elongated ($a=2$ vs $a=1$) so the silhouette is lower ($0.675$ vs $0.814$) even though the centroid gap is larger. Elongation costs you on every distance-based index — the §20.9.2 warning in miniature.

    Practice 20.7 — A clustering of 6 points gives clusters $\{1,2,3\},\{4,5,6\}$; the true classes are $\{1,2,4\},\{3,5,6\}$. Compute pair-counted $TP,FP,FN,TN$, then $P$, $R$, $F_1$ and the Rand index.

    $\binom{6}{2}=15$ pairs. Same-cluster pairs: $\binom32+\binom32 = 3+3 = 6$, namely $\{1,2\},\{1,3\},\{2,3\},\{4,5\},\{4,6\},\{5,6\}$. Same-class pairs: also $6$, namely $\{1,2\},\{1,4\},\{2,4\},\{3,5\},\{3,6\},\{5,6\}$.

    TP = same cluster and same class = $\{1,2\}$ and $\{5,6\}$ → $TP=2$.
    FP = same cluster, different class = $6-2=4$ (namely $\{1,3\},\{2,3\},\{4,5\},\{4,6\}$).
    FN = different cluster, same class = $6-2=4$ (namely $\{1,4\},\{2,4\},\{3,5\},\{3,6\}$).
    TN = $15-2-4-4=5$.

    $P=\frac{2}{2+4}=0.333333$; $R=\frac{2}{2+4}=0.333333$; $F_1=\frac{2PR}{P+R}=0.333333$; $RI=\frac{2+5}{15}=0.466667$.

    Interpretation. $F_1=1/3$ is barely better than the pairwise coin-flip, and the Rand index's $0.467$ flatters it — which is the §20.10 warning in action: RI gives free credit for the $5$ TN pairs. The clustering has correctly recovered only $2$ of the $6$ true co-membership relations, mostly because point $3$ and point $4$ are each in the wrong group.

    21   Decision Playbook & Exam Cheat Sheet

    §20 closed the last piece of new material — how to tell whether a clustering is any good — and with it the technical content of these notes. Everything in this section has already been derived somewhere else in these notes. Nothing new is introduced here — not one formula, not one number. What this section adds is routing: given a problem, or given an exam question, which of the previous twenty sections do you open? It is built from v5's night-before cheat sheet, extended with the material v5 never had (gradient boosting, XGBoost, SMOTE, SHAP, DBSCAN, GMM, deep architectures) and with the six topics v5's cheat sheet silently dropped (evaluation metrics, pocket, kernels, the soft-margin $C$, bagging/OOB, and the whole of deep learning).

    How to read this section. Three kinds of artefact, used for three different moments:
    • Flowcharts (§21.1–§21.3) — for the moment a new dataset lands on your desk and you have to pick a family before you have tuned anything.
    • The formula sheet (§21.5) — for the moment an exam says "state" or "derive". Each row is the minimum you must be able to write down cold; the section reference is where the derivation lives.
    • The anchor table and the gotcha table (§21.6–§21.7) — for the moment you have written an answer and want to check it is not nonsense. Every anchor is a number recomputed here and cross-checked against the section it came from.
    Provenance discipline for a recap section. A cheat sheet that disagrees with the sections it summarises is worse than no cheat sheet. Every number below is produced by work/computes/s21_anchors.py, which (a) recomputes the value from scratch and (b) reads the peer section's own JSON and asserts agreement. All nineteen cross-checks currently pass — if a peer section changes a worked example, the script fails loudly rather than leaving a stale digit here. Two anchors below (§19's and §20's) are computed on a four-point toy set of this section's own, small enough to do in your head, rather than on §19/§20's larger worked datasets; the cross-check for §19 is therefore made separately, by independently recomputing the $k{=}1$ WCSS of §19's eight-point example as $100.75$ and matching it against §19's own stored value .

    21.1   The master model-selection flowchart

    The chart below is deliberately ordered by how expensive the decision is to reverse. Q1 (are there labels?) cannot be reversed at all — it is a property of the data. Q2 (what kind of target) fixes the loss function and therefore the whole optimisation story. Only at Q3 does the question become "which model", and by then most of the search space is already gone. Q4 and Q5 are drawn at the bottom not because they come last in importance but because they apply to every leaf.

    Fig. 21.1 — The master model-selection flowchart. Leaf labels carry the section that derives the method.
    Interpretation. Read the chart as a constraint propagator, not as a recommendation engine. Each question deletes branches; it never scores them. The chart will happily route a 200-row tabular problem to gradient boosting if you answer Q3 with "medium" — the guard against that is the regime map of §21.3, which says what the row and feature counts alone already forbid. And the chart deliberately has no "deep learning" branch for tabular data: on tabular problems, boosted trees remain the default, and a neural net is a considered deviation, not a starting point.
    The three ways this chart is abused.
    • Answering Q1 "no" when the answer is "not yet". Unlabelled data is not the same as an unsupervised problem. If the business question is "which customers will churn", that is supervised with a labelling cost, and clustering will not answer it — it will answer a different question fluently.
    • Skipping Q2 for classification. "Two or more classes" hides a fork: one label per row (softmax) versus several labels per row (K independent one-vs-rest sigmoids). Getting this wrong makes the probabilities not sum to 1 — or forces them to, wrongly.
    • Treating Q4/Q5 as post-processing. Imbalance handling changes the training loop (resampling must live inside the CV fold, §21.7), and an explainability requirement can veto the model family outright. Both belong at model-choice time.

    21.2   The mini-flowchart gallery

    Each section carries its own decision rule for one narrow choice. Collected on one page, they are the second half of the playbook: Fig. 21.1 gets you to a family, the gallery gets you through the settings inside it.

    Fig. 21.2 — Twelve per-topic decision rules on one page. Each card condenses the decision flowchart of the named section; the section itself carries the reasoning.
    Interpretation. Notice how many cards reduce to the same underlying question — "what does an error cost?" The metric card, the imbalance card and the $F_\beta$ choice are three faces of one asymmetry: $\beta > 1$ weights recall, $\beta < 1$ weights precision, and moving the decision threshold is the cheapest lever for either. Likewise the regularisation card and the validation card are one question in two costumes: how much of the data are you willing to spend to find out whether the model is memorising?

    21.3   What the shape of the data already decides

    Before any of the flowchart's questions, two integers constrain the answer: $n$, the number of labelled rows, and $d$, the number of raw features. The VC analysis of §7 turns them into a hard admissibility line. For a linear model in $d$ dimensions $d_{VC} = d + 1$, and the practical rule of thumb is $n \gtrsim 10\,d_{VC}$; at $d_{VC} = 11$ that is $n \gtrsim 110$ for a usable estimate, and $n \gtrsim 1100$ before the bound itself becomes non-vacuous.

    Fig. 21.3 — Admissible regions in the $(n, d)$ plane. The red line is the $n = 10\,d_{VC}$ rule of thumb for a linear model, $d_{VC} = d+1$.
    Interpretation. The shaded region is not "impossible" — it is "impossible without an additional assumption". Every technique that lets you work above the line is a way of smuggling in prior information: $L_1$ says most coefficients are zero, PCA says the signal lives in a low-dimensional subspace, a convolution says the signal is translation-equivariant, a kernel with a small bandwidth says the target is smooth. That is why the $d \gg n$ box says "regularise hard or get more rows" and not "use a bigger model".
    The line moves for non-linear models — usually upward. $d_{VC} = d+1$ is the linear value. A depth-$k$ tree, an RBF-kernel SVM or a neural net has a far larger effective capacity, so the honest version of the line for those families sits well above the red one drawn here. Reading Fig. 21.3 as "I have $n = 10(d+1)$ rows, so a random forest is safe" is exactly backwards: it is the linear model that is safe there.

    21.4   Model comparison at a glance

    One row per family: what it assumes, whether it needs the features rescaled, what it costs, and what it gives you for free. "Scaling" means: does a monotone rescaling of one feature change the fitted model?

    FamilyCore assumptionNeeds feature scaling?Train cost Predict costGives youWhere
    Linear / logistic regressiontarget is (log-odds) linear in $\mathbf{x}$ Only for the penalty and for GD conditioning$O(nd^2 + d^3)$ closed form $O(d)$signed coefficients, standard errors, $p$-values §2, §3
    k-NNnear in distance $\Rightarrow$ near in labelYes — distance is unit-dependent$O(1)$ (store)$O(nd)$ per query a non-parametric boundary of any shape§8
    Naive Bayesfeatures conditionally independent given $y$No $O(nd)$$O(d)$calibrated-ish scores from tiny data §9
    Decision tree (CART)axis-aligned rectangles sufficeNo — splits are rank-based$O(dn\log n)$$O(\text{depth})$ a readable rule list, native missing-value handling§10
    Random forest / baggingbase learner is low-bias, high-varianceNo $O(B\,d_{\text{try}} n\log n)$$O(B\cdot\text{depth})$ OOB error for free, permutation importances§11
    AdaBoostweak learners beat chance on every reweightingNo $O(T\cdot\text{stump})$$O(T)$margins that keep improving after zero training error§12
    Gradient boosting / XGBoostloss is differentiable; additive fit is enoughNo $O(M\,d\,n\log n)$$O(M\cdot\text{depth})$ state-of-the-art tabular accuracy, missing-value default directions§13
    SVM (kernel)large margin in some feature spaceYes — the kernel is a distance$O(n^2)$ to $O(n^3)$$O(n_{SV}\,d)$ sparse support-vector solution, max-margin guarantee§17
    Neural networka composition of simple functions fits; lots of data Yes — plus normalisation layers$O(\text{epochs}\cdot n\cdot|W|)$ $O(|W|)$representation learning on raw signals§15, §16
    PCAvariance $=$ signal; directions are orthogonalYes $O(nd^2)$ or $O(nd\,k)$ via SVD$O(dk)$ decorrelated axes, an explained-variance curve§18
    k-meansclusters are isotropic blobs of similar sizeYes $O(Ink d)$$O(kd)$a centroid you can describe §19
    DBSCANclusters are dense regions separated by sparse onesYes $O(n\log n)$ with an index—arbitrary shapes plus an explicit noise label§20
    GMM (EM)data drawn from a mixture of GaussiansYes $O(Ink d^2)$ full covariance$O(kd^2)$ soft memberships, a likelihood you can compare across $k$§20
    Interpretation. The "needs scaling" column is the single most useful column in practice, because it is the one that silently breaks pipelines. Everything that computes a distance or an inner product (k-NN, SVM, PCA, k-means, DBSCAN, GMM, any penalised linear model) is unit-sensitive; everything that computes a threshold on one feature at a time (trees and every ensemble of trees) is not. That single distinction explains why swapping a random forest for an SVM without adding a scaler tends to destroy the result.

    21.5   The formula sheet

    Rows are grouped the way the exam groups them. Each row is the smallest complete statement of the result: enough to recognise it, enough to start a derivation from, and a pointer to the section where the derivation lives.

    21.5.1   Part I — trees, probability, structure

    NameStatementWatch out forWhere
    Entropy$E(S) = -\sum_c p_c \log_2 p_c$; binary maximum $1$ bit at $p = 0.5$ base-2 logs, else "bits" is wrong§10
    Information gain$IG(S,A) = E(S) - \sum_v \frac{|S_v|}{|S|}E(S_v)$ the $|S_v|/|S|$ weights are mandatory; an unweighted average is the classic error §10
    Gini$G(S) = 1 - \sum_c p_c^2$; binary $2p(1-p)$ Gini and entropy can rank two splits differently§10
    Gain ratio$GR = IG / SI$, $\;SI = -\sum_v \frac{|S_v|}{|S|}\log_2\frac{|S_v|}{|S|}$ only fix for many-valued attributes; $SI \to 0$ makes $GR$ explode§10
    Cost-complexity pruning$R_\alpha(T) = R(T) + \alpha|T|$; prune the weakest link as $\alpha$ grows$\alpha$ is chosen on validation data, never on training§10
    Bayes$P(h \mid D) = \dfrac{P(D\mid h)P(h)}{P(D)}$ $P(D)$ is a normaliser — never needed for an argmax§9
    MLE / MAP (Bernoulli)$\hat\theta_{MLE} = \frac{n_H}{n_H+n_T}$; $\hat\theta_{MAP} = \frac{n_H+\alpha_H}{n_H+\alpha_H+n_T+\alpha_T}$; Laplace is $\alpha = 1$ MAP $\to$ MLE as $n$ grows; the prior is pseudo-counts§9
    Naive Bayes$\hat y = \arg\max_y P(y)\prod_i P(x_i\mid y)$; $2N+1$ parameters; the log-odds is linear in $\mathbf{x}$one zero count zeroes the whole product — smooth§9
    Bayes-net factorisation$P(X_1,\dots,X_n) = \prod_i P(X_i\mid \mathrm{Pa}(X_i))$ parameter count $\sum_i 2^{|\mathrm{Pa}(X_i)|}$ for binary nodes§9
    d-separationchain and fork block when the middle node is observed; a collider blocks unless it or a descendant is observedthe collider rule runs the other way — that is "explaining away"§9
    EME-step: fill hidden values with their expectations under the current parameters. M-step: re-fit by MLE. The likelihood never decreases. "never decreases" $\neq$ "reaches the global maximum"§9, §20

    21.5.2   Part II — linear models, theory, optimisation

    NameStatementWatch out forWhere
    Perceptron / delta ruleon a misclassified point, $\mathbf{w} \leftarrow \mathbf{w} + y\mathbf{x}$terminates only if the data are separable — otherwise use pocket §2
    Pocketrun PLA, but keep the best-so-far $\mathbf{w}$ by full-sample $E_{in}$ each candidate costs a full pass over the data§2
    Linear regression$\mathbf{w}^\star = (\mathbf{X}^\top\mathbf{X})^{-1}\mathbf{X}^\top \mathbf{y} = \mathbf{X}^{+}\mathbf{y}$, with $\mathbf{X}$ of shape $(n \times (d{+}1))$, $\mathbf{y}$ of shape $(n \times 1)$, $\mathbf{w}$ of shape $((d{+}1) \times 1)$ needs $\mathbf{X}$ of full column rank; collinearity $\Rightarrow$ ridge§2
    Sigmoid / logit$\sigma(s) = \frac{1}{1+e^{-s}}$, $\;1-\sigma(s) = \sigma(-s)$, $\;\sigma'(s) = \sigma(s)(1-\sigma(s)) \le 0.25$ $\sigma(0) = 0.5$ ; the $0.25$ cap is the vanishing-gradient seed§3, §15
    Cross-entropy$E_{in} = \frac1N\sum_i \ln\!\big(1 + e^{-y_i\mathbf{w}^\top\mathbf{x}_i}\big)$ with $y_i \in \{-1,+1\}$; equivalently $-\frac1N\sum_i [y_i\ln p_i + (1-y_i)\ln(1-p_i)]$ with $y_i\in\{0,1\}$the two label conventions give the same loss, not the same formula §3
    Logistic gradient$\nabla_{\boldsymbol\beta} L = \frac1N\mathbf{X}^\top(\mathbf{p} - \mathbf{y})$; shapes $((d{+}1)\times n)(n\times1) = ((d{+}1)\times1)$ same shape as linear regression's — that is not a coincidence, both are GLMs§3
    Softmax$p_k = e^{z_k}/\sum_j e^{z_j}$; shift-invariant in $\mathbf{z}$ one label per row. K independent labels $\Rightarrow$ K sigmoids (OvR)§3
    Poisson GLM$\ln \mathbb{E}[y\mid\mathbf{x}] = \boldsymbol\beta^\top\mathbf{x}$; $e^{\beta_j}$ is a rate multiplierassumes mean $=$ variance; check for overdispersion §3
    Gradient descent$\mathbf{w} \leftarrow \mathbf{w} - \eta\nabla E_{in}(\mathbf{w})$ on $L(w)=w^2$ from $w=1$: $\eta = 0.1 \Rightarrow 0.8$ , $\eta = 0.5 \Rightarrow 0$ , $\eta = 1.1 \Rightarrow -1.2$ (diverging)§4
    Momentum$\mathbf{v}_t = \gamma\mathbf{v}_{t-1} + \nabla L$; $\mathbf{w} \leftarrow \mathbf{w} - \eta\mathbf{v}_t$ effective step is $\eta/(1-\gamma)$ on a consistent direction§4
    Adam$\hat m_t = m_t/(1-\beta_1^t)$, $\hat v_t = v_t/(1-\beta_2^t)$, $\mathbf{w} \leftarrow \mathbf{w} - \eta\,\hat m_t/(\sqrt{\hat v_t}+\epsilon)$ at $t=1$ the correction divisors are $1-\beta_1 = 0.1$ and $1-\beta_2 = 0.001$ — without them the first steps are ~10x and ~1000x too small§4
    Confusion metrics$P = \frac{TP}{TP+FP}$, $R = \frac{TP}{TP+FN}$, $\text{Spec} = \frac{TN}{TN+FP}$, $F_\beta = \frac{(1+\beta^2)PR}{\beta^2P+R}$ $\beta > 1$ favours recall, $\beta < 1$ favours precision§5
    ROCsweep the threshold, plot $TPR = R$ against $FPR = \frac{FP}{FP+TN}$; AUC $=$ P(random positive scored above random negative) AUC ignores calibration and flatters imbalanced problems — use PR-AUC there§5
    Bias–variance$E_{out} = \mathbb{E}_\mathbf{x}[\text{Bias}^2] + \mathbb{E}_\mathbf{x}[\text{Var}] + \sigma^2$ the expectations are over different things: $\mathbb{E}_\mathcal{D}$ vs $\mathbb{E}_\mathbf{x}$§6
    Ridge (Tikhonov)$\mathbf{w}_{\text{reg}} = (\mathbf{Z}^\top\mathbf{Z} + \lambda \mathbf{I})^{-1}\mathbf{Z}^\top\mathbf{y}$; singular value $s$ shrinks by $s^2/(s^2+\lambda)$ at $s = 3, \lambda = 2$ the factor is $0.8182$ — small directions shrink most§6
    Lasso$\min E_{in} + \lambda\|\mathbf{w}\|_1$; the corner of the $L_1$ ball sets coefficients exactly to zerono closed form; unstable choice among correlated features §6
    Hoeffding$P[|E_{in}-E_{out}| > \epsilon] \le 2e^{-2\epsilon^2 N}$; with $M$ hypotheses, $2Me^{-2\epsilon^2N}$$\epsilon=0.1, N=200 \Rightarrow 0.0366$ ; $N \ge 265$ for a 1% bound§7
    VC bound$E_{out} \le E_{in} + \sqrt{\frac{8}{N}\ln\frac{4m_\mathcal{H}(2N)}{\delta}}$; $m_\mathcal{H}(N) \le \sum_{i=0}^{d_{VC}}\binom{N}{i}$ $d_{VC}=11, N=1000, \delta=0.05 \Rightarrow \epsilon = 0.7508$ — the bound is true and useless§7
    VC dimension$d_{VC} = k-1$ where $k$ is the smallest break point; $d$-D perceptron gives $d_{VC} = d+1$the proof has two directions and you need both§7
    SVM primal$\min \frac12\|\mathbf{w}\|^2 + C\sum_i \xi_i$ s.t. $y_i(\mathbf{w}^\top\mathbf{x}_i + b) \ge 1 - \xi_i$, $\xi_i \ge 0$ $C\sum\xi_i$ is hinge loss; large $C$ $\to$ hard margin§17
    SVM dual$\max_{\boldsymbol\alpha}\sum_i\alpha_i - \frac12\sum_{i,j}\alpha_i\alpha_j y_i y_j K(\mathbf{x}_i,\mathbf{x}_j)$ s.t. $\sum_i \alpha_i y_i = 0$, $0 \le \alpha_i \le C$ the box constraint $\alpha_i \le C$ is the only thing slack changes in the dual §17
    Margin / kernelswidth $= 2/\|\mathbf{w}\|$, $\mathbf{w} = \sum_{SV}\alpha_i y_i \mathbf{x}_i$; RBF $K = e^{-\gamma\|\mathbf{x}-\mathbf{x}'\|^2}$, polynomial $K = (1 + \mathbf{x}^\top\mathbf{x}')^q$a valid kernel needs a PSD Gram matrix (Mercer) §17
    PCAtop-$d$ eigenvectors of $\mathbf{C} = \frac{1}{N-1}\mathbf{X}_c^\top\mathbf{X}_c$ (shape $(D\times D)$), or the top-$d$ right singular vectors of $\mathbf{X}_c$; $\lambda_k$ is the variance along PC$_k$centre first; scale first if units differ§18

    NameStatementWatch out forWhere
    Bagging / OOBP(a given row is left out of one bootstrap sample) $= (1-1/m)^m \to 1/e = 0.3679$ already $0.3487$ at $m=10$ and $0.3677$ at $m=1000$ ; OOB is a free validation set§11
    Correlated-average variance$\mathrm{Var}(\bar f) = \rho\sigma^2 + \frac{1-\rho}{B}\sigma^2$at $\rho = 0.3, \sigma^2 = 1, B = 100$: $0.307$ , against $0.01$ if the trees were independent. The floor $\rho\sigma^2 = 0.3$ is why feature subsampling exists§11
    Majority vote (Condorcet)$P(\text{ensemble right}) = \sum_{k > B/2}\binom{B}{k}p^k (1-p)^{B-k}$ for independent learners$p = 0.7$: three learners give $0.784$ , eleven give $0.9218$ . At $p = 0.45$ and $B = 101$ the vote gives $0.1562$ — worse than one learner§11
    AdaBoost$\epsilon_t = \sum_i w_i \mathbb{1}[h_t(\mathbf{x}_i)\neq y_i]$, $\;\alpha_t = \frac12\ln\frac{1-\epsilon_t}{\epsilon_t}$, $\;Z_t = 2\sqrt{\epsilon_t(1-\epsilon_t)}$, $\;w_i \leftarrow w_i e^{-\alpha_t y_i h_t(\mathbf{x}_i)}/Z_t$ at $\epsilon_t = 0.3$: $\alpha_t = 0.4236$ , $Z_t = 0.9165$ , misclassified weights scale by $2.3333$ . $\epsilon_t = 0.5 \Rightarrow \alpha_t = 0$ §12
    Boosting error boundtraining error $\le \prod_t Z_t = \prod_t 2\sqrt{\epsilon_t(1-\epsilon_t)}$this is why $Z_t$ is derived; each factor is $< 1$ whenever $\epsilon_t < 0.5$§12
    Gradient boosting$F_m(\mathbf{x}) = F_{m-1}(\mathbf{x}) + \nu\,\gamma_m h_m(\mathbf{x})$, with $h_m$ fitted to the pseudo-residual $r_{im} = -\big[\partial\ell(y_i,F)/\partial F\big]_{F=F_{m-1}}$ for squared loss the pseudo-residual is the residual; for every other loss it is not §13

    XGBoost similarity & gain$\text{Sim}_j = \dfrac{(\sum_{i\in I_j} g_i)^2} {\sum_{i\in I_j} h_i + \lambda}$; $\;\text{Gain} = \text{Sim}_L + \text{Sim}_R - \text{Sim}_{\text{root}} - \gamma$numerator is the square of the sum, never the sum of squares; $\gamma$ prunes by making Gain negative§13
    SMOTE$\mathbf{x}_{\text{new}} = \mathbf{x}_i + \lambda(\mathbf{x}_{nn} - \mathbf{x}_i)$, $\lambda \sim U(0,1)$, $\mathbf{x}_{nn}$ a minority $k$-NN of $\mathbf{x}_i$ from $(2,3)$ toward $(6,5)$ at $\lambda = 0.25$: $(3.0, 3.5)$ . Interpolation only — never extrapolates§14
    Shapley value$\phi_i = \sum_{S\subseteq F\setminus\{i\}} \frac{|S|!\,(|F|-|S|-1)!}{|F|!}\big[f(S\cup\{i\}) - f(S)\big]$ efficiency: $f(\mathbf{x}) = \phi_0 + \sum_i\phi_i$. With $\phi_0 = 50$ and $\sum\phi_i = 30$ the prediction must be $80$ §14
    Backprop$\boldsymbol\delta^{(L)} = \nabla_{\mathbf{a}}L \odot \phi'(\mathbf{z}^{(L)})$; $\boldsymbol\delta^{(l)} = \big(\mathbf{W}^{(l+1)\top}\boldsymbol\delta^{(l+1)}\big)\odot \phi'(\mathbf{z}^{(l)})$; $\nabla_{\mathbf{W}^{(l)}}L = \boldsymbol\delta^{(l)}\mathbf{a}^{(l-1)\top}$, shapes $(n_l\times 1)(1\times n_{l-1}) = (n_l\times n_{l-1})$ the gradient always has the same shape as the parameter — use that as your check§15
    Vanishing gradientsa chain of $L$ sigmoids attenuates by at most $0.25^L$ $L = 5$: $9.766\times10^{-4}$ ; $L = 20$: $9.095\times10^{-13}$ §15
    Conv arithmetic$n_{\text{out}} = \left\lfloor\frac{n + 2p - k}{s}\right\rfloor + 1$; params $= (k^2 C_{\text{in}} + 1)C_{\text{out}}$ $n=32,k=3,s=1,p=0 \Rightarrow 30$ ; $p=1 \Rightarrow 32$ ; $k=5,s=2,p=0 \Rightarrow 14$ . A $3\times3\times3\to64$ layer has $1792$ parameters§16
    Attention$\mathrm{Attn}(\mathbf{Q},\mathbf{K},\mathbf{V}) = \mathrm{softmax} \!\left(\frac{\mathbf{Q}\mathbf{K}^\top}{\sqrt{d_k}}\right)\mathbf{V}$; shapes $(n\times d_k)(d_k\times n) = (n\times n)$, then $(n\times n)(n\times d_v) = (n\times d_v)$ the $1/\sqrt{d_k}$ scale is $0.125$ at $d_k = 64$ ; drop it and softmax saturates§16
    k-means$J = \sum_k\sum_{\mathbf{x}_i\in C_k}\|\mathbf{x}_i - \boldsymbol\mu_k\|^2$; the $L_2$-optimal centre is the mean$J$ decreases monotonically but only to a local minimum; $L_1$ would give the median§19
    Fuzzy c-means$J_m = \sum_i\sum_k u_{ik}^m\|\mathbf{x}_i - \mathbf{v}_k\|^2$, $\sum_k u_{ik} = 1$, $m > 1$$m \to 1$ recovers crisp k-means; large $m$ makes everything equally a member of everything§19
    Mahalanobis$d^2(\mathbf{x},\mathbf{y}) = (\mathbf{x}-\mathbf{y})^\top\mathbf{S}^{-1} (\mathbf{x}-\mathbf{y})$$\mathbf{S} = \mathbf{I}$ recovers Euclidean; it can reverse a Euclidean ranking§19
    DBSCANcore point: $|N_\varepsilon(p)| \ge \text{MinPts}$ (the point itself counts); border: non-core but inside a core's $\varepsilon$-ball; else noise self-counting is the classic off-by-one: with MinPts $= 3$ a point needs itself plus two neighbours §20
    GMM / EME: $\gamma_{ik} = \frac{\pi_k\mathcal{N}(\mathbf{x}_i\mid \boldsymbol\mu_k,\boldsymbol\Sigma_k)}{\sum_j \pi_j\mathcal{N}(\mathbf{x}_i\mid \boldsymbol\mu_j,\boldsymbol\Sigma_j)}$. M: re-fit $\pi_k,\boldsymbol\mu_k,\boldsymbol\Sigma_k$ with weights $\gamma_{ik}$k-means is the hard-assignment, shared-spherical-covariance limit §20
    Silhouette$s(i) = \frac{b(i)-a(i)}{\max(a(i),b(i))} \in [-1,1]$ on two well-separated pairs, $a = 1$ , $b = 5.5$ , $s = 0.8182$ §20
    Davies–Bouldin / DunnDB $= \frac1k\sum_i\max_{j\neq i}\frac{\sigma_i+\sigma_j} {d(c_i,c_j)}$ (lower is better); Dunn $= \frac{\min\text{ inter-cluster}}{\max\text{ intra-cluster}}$ (higher is better)opposite directions — say which one you are optimising§20

Its first checkbox also read "know one numerical example for every section" — self-refuting, since nine of v5's sections contained no numerical example at all. Both are repaired above: every family in Fig. 21.1 now has a row here, and §21.6 gives one recomputed anchor per section.

    §14SHAP efficiency: $\phi_0 = 50$, $\sum_i\phi_i = 30$ $80$ the one identity that lets you check any SHAP output
    §15max of $\sigma'$ $0.25$ ten sigmoid layers attenuate to $9.537\times10^{-7}$
    §16output size of a $5\times5$ stride-2 conv on $32\times32$ $14$ the floor is where off-by-one errors live
    §17hard-margin SVM on a vertical band (positives $x_1 \ge 3$, negatives $x_1 \le 1$) width $= 2$ $\mathbf{w} = (1,0)$ , $b = -2$ , boundary $x_1 = 2$; width $= 2/\|\mathbf{w}\|$
    §18PC1 variance explained for eigenvalues $\{6, 2/3\}$ $0.90$ ratio of eigenvalues, not of singular values
    §19WCSS of $\{(0,0),(1,0)\}$ and $\{(5,0),(6,0)\}$ at $k=2$ vs $k=1$ $1.0$ vs $26.0$ the elbow, on four points you can do in your head
    §20silhouette of a point in that same two-cluster toy set $0.8182$ $a = 1$ , $b = 5.5$ — one subtraction and one division
    Interpretation. The table is a self-test, not a reference. If you can only recognise $0.3679$ you have learnt a fact; if you can rederive it as $\lim_m (1-1/m)^m$ you have learnt why bagging gets a validation set for free. The same distinction separates recognising $\alpha_t = 0.4236$ from being able to say that it comes from setting $\frac{d}{d\alpha}\big[(1-\epsilon)e^{-\alpha} + \epsilon e^{\alpha}\big] = 0$.

    21.7   Common gotchas

    Every row below is a mistake that produces a plausible-looking number rather than an error message. Those are the expensive ones.

    GotchaWhat it looks likeThe fix§
    Unweighted information gain$IG$ computed as a plain average of child entropies; the number is bigger and the ranking of splits can flipalways weight by $|S_v|/|S|$ §10
    Accuracy on imbalanced dataa classifier that predicts the majority class on a 99:1 split scores $0.99$ with recall $0$ report recall/precision or PR-AUC; state the prevalence§5, §14
    $F_\beta$ directionquoting $F_2$ when false alarms are the problem on the fraud table $F_{0.5} = 0.7692$ $> F_1 = 0.7273$ $> F_2 = 0.6897$ because precision $>$ recall here§5
    Preprocessing before splittingscaler, imputer, feature selector or SMOTE fitted on all rows; CV score becomes fictionfit every transformer inside the training fold only — see Fig. 21.4§6, §14
    Tuning on the test seta "test" score that keeps improving as you try more hyperparametersthree-way split, or nested CV; touch test once§6
    Forgetting to scale for distance methodsk-NN, SVM, k-means, PCA and DBSCAN silently ranked by whichever feature has the biggest unitsstandardise, or use Mahalanobis §8, §17, §18, §19
    MinPts off-by-oneDBSCAN cluster counts that do not match the reference the point itself counts toward MinPts§20
    Sum of squares vs square of sumXGBoost similarity computed as $\sum g_i^2$ instead of $(\sum g_i)^2$; leaves with cancelling residuals get a high score $\text{Sim} = (\sum g_i)^2/(\sum h_i + \lambda)$§13
    Reading $\lambda$ as harmlessthe same split scores $+0.375$ at $\lambda = 0$ and $-0.375$ at $\lambda = 1$ — i.e. it flips from "make the split" to "do not"$\lambda$ and $\gamma$ are structural, not cosmetic; tune them§13
    Voting with bad learnersensembling 101 learners at $p = 0.45$ gives $0.1562$ majority voting amplifies whichever side of $0.5$ the base learner is on§11
    SMOTE on the validation rowssynthetic minority points interpolated across the train/val boundary; recall looks fine, production recall does notresample inside the fold; §14's own experiment shows the inflated $F_1$§14
    Adam without bias correctionfirst steps ~$10\times$ too small; the run looks "slow to start" rather than brokendivide by $1-\beta_1^t$ and $1-\beta_2^t$§4
    Conv floor divisionan "obvious" output size that is one off, then a shape error three layers later$\lfloor (n+2p-k)/s\rfloor + 1$; check $32 \to 14$ at $k=5,s=2$§16
    Softmax where OvR belongsmulti-label problems forced to have probabilities summing to 1one label per row $\Rightarrow$ softmax; several $\Rightarrow$ K sigmoids §3

    21.7.1   The leakage gotcha, demonstrated

    The "preprocessing before splitting" row deserves its own experiment, because it is the one mistake that reliably survives peer review. Take $n = 60$ rows and $d = 400$ features drawn as pure Gaussian noise, with labels drawn independently of the features. There is, by construction, nothing to learn: the true accuracy of any classifier is $0.5$ .

    Now select the $10$ features with the largest between-class mean difference, and run $5$-fold cross-validation with a nearest-class-centroid classifier. Do the selection before splitting and the CV accuracy is $75.0\%$ . Redo the selection inside each training fold and it collapses to $40.0\%$ — scattered around chance, as it must be. The gap is $35.0$ percentage points of pure fiction.

    Fig. 21.4 — The same six operations in two orders. Left leaks; right does not. The two result boxes are the same data and the same classifier.
    Interpretation. Notice what leaked: not the labels of the validation rows, but a statistic of them. Choosing which columns to keep is a fit, and any fit that has seen the validation rows contaminates the estimate. This is why the rule is stated as "everything that learns anything from the data goes inside the fold", not "do not look at the labels" — the selector never touched the validation labels during scoring, and the score was still fiction. Note also the direction: the honest run came out below chance ($40\%$ across folds ), which at $n=60$ is ordinary sampling noise around $0.5$ and is exactly the kind of unimpressive result an honest protocol produces.
    The leakage number is seed-dependent — the phenomenon is not. With another random seed the inflated figure will move by several points in either direction, and the honest figure will wander around $0.5$. What does not change is the sign and rough size of the gap: selecting $10$ of $400$ noise features on all the data manufactures an apparent signal every time. Do not quote $75.0\%$ as a constant; quote the mechanism.

    The leak-free order of Fig. 21.4's right-hand pipeline is exactly what a coding-round interview expects you to type from memory. Here is that pipeline as one runnable template.

    Code — the master interview pipeline: preprocess -> select -> model -> GridSearchCV (sklearn) 
    import numpy as np
from sklearn.compose import ColumnTransformer
from sklearn.pipeline import Pipeline
from sklearn.impute import SimpleImputer
from sklearn.preprocessing import StandardScaler, OneHotEncoder
from sklearn.feature_selection import SelectKBest, f_classif
from sklearn.linear_model import LogisticRegression
from sklearn.model_selection import GridSearchCV, StratifiedKFold

numeric_cols = ["age", "income"]         # scale: needed by every distance- or
categorical_cols = ["region", "plan"]    # gradient-based method -- k-NN, SVM,
                                          # PCA, k-means, GMM, linear/logistic
                                          # (Sec 21.4's "needs scaling" column)

numeric_pipe = Pipeline([
    ("impute", SimpleImputer(strategy="median")),
    ("scale", StandardScaler()),
])
categorical_pipe = Pipeline([
    ("impute", SimpleImputer(strategy="most_frequent")),
    ("onehot", OneHotEncoder(handle_unknown="ignore")),
])
# every imputer/scaler/encoder below is fit on the TRAIN FOLD ONLY --
# GridSearchCV's cv loop enforces that automatically, which is the one-line
# fix for the leakage measured in Fig. 21.4
preprocess = ColumnTransformer([
    ("num", numeric_pipe, numeric_cols),
    ("cat", categorical_pipe, categorical_cols),
])

pipe = Pipeline([
    ("preprocess", preprocess),
    ("select", SelectKBest(score_func=f_classif, k=10)),  # or SelectFromModel(...)
    ("model", LogisticRegression(max_iter=1000)),
    # swap "model" for the family Fig. 21.1 routed you to -- Sec 21.4 rows:
    #   LogisticRegression / SVC(kernel=...)   -> needs scaling (kept above)
    #   RandomForestClassifier() / GB variants -> scaling irrelevant, but the
    #                                              ColumnTransformer still
    #                                              handles missing + categoricals
])

param_grid = {
    "select__k": [5, 10, 20],
    "model__C": [0.01, 0.1, 1, 10],        # LogisticRegression / SVC
    # "model__n_estimators": [100, 300],  # swap in for RF / GB instead
}

cv = StratifiedKFold(n_splits=5, shuffle=True, random_state=0)
search = GridSearchCV(pipe, param_grid, cv=cv, scoring="f1", n_jobs=-1)
search.fit(X_train, y_train)   # fit ONCE on train; touch X_test only to score

    Everything inside pipe refits per fold under GridSearchCV -- imputer, scaler, selector and model all see only that fold's training rows, which is the structural fix for the §21.7 leakage experiment, not a coding-style preference.

    # the feature-selection toolkit -- three families, all swap into the "select" slot above
from sklearn.feature_selection import RFE, RFECV, SelectFromModel, mutual_info_classif
from sklearn.ensemble import RandomForestClassifier

# filter   : score each feature alone -- fast, ignores interactions
#            SelectKBest(f_classif) above; use mutual_info_classif for non-linear links
# embedded : the model's own coefficients/importances prune for free during the fit
sel_embed = SelectFromModel(RandomForestClassifier(n_estimators=200, random_state=0),
                            threshold="median")   # or L1: LogisticRegression(penalty="l1", solver="liblinear")
# wrapper  : RFE -- fit, drop the weakest feature(s), refit; most faithful, most expensive
sel_rfe  = RFE(LogisticRegression(max_iter=1000), n_features_to_select=10, step=1)
sel_auto = RFECV(LogisticRegression(max_iter=1000), cv=5, scoring="f1")  # CV picks how many to keep

    Interview map -- filter: univariate scores (cheap, blind to interactions); embedded: L1 / tree importances (free with the fit, §11.7's MDI bias applies); wrapper: RFE/RFECV (respects the model, costs O(d) refits). Name the family you chose and why -- and note that whichever you pick sits inside the pipeline, so selection refits per fold and never sees validation rows.

    21.8   The ensemble-library row

    Fig. 21.1's "gradient boosting" leaf hides a three-way choice. §13 derives the differences in full from the handwritten comparison table; the one-row version for the playbook is:

    CatBoostLightGBMXGBoost
    Tree growthsymmetric — the same split condition at every node of a level leaf-wise — grow whichever single leaf reduces loss mostlevel-wise / depth-wise
    Categoricalspass the raw categories ininteger encoding required one-hot encoding
    Row samplingMVS / uniform: keep every high-error point, sample the rest with probability $\propto |g_i|$GOSS: keep the top $a\%$ by $|g_i|$, randomly sample $b\%$ of the restbootstrap, e.g. subsample = 0.8
    Pick it whenmany high-cardinality categorical features $n$ is large and training time mattersyou want the most-documented default

    (hand p16; derivations, the missing-value default-direction rule and the source's transcription issues are all handled in §13)

    Leaf-wise growth is the trade. LightGBM's leaf-wise strategy reaches a lower training loss per tree than level-wise growth, and overfits faster for exactly the same reason: nothing stops it from growing one deep, thin branch that memorises a handful of rows. The handwritten notes flag the fix directly — cap max_depth or num_leaves. This is the same bias–variance dial as tree depth in §10, wearing a library-specific name.

    21.9   Answering an exam question

    The four verbs.
    • "State" — the boxed formula plus the meaning of every symbol. One line of definitions is not padding; an unnamed symbol is an unearned mark.
    • "Derive" — a chain of equalities with a justification beside each step. Start from something you are allowed to assume (a loss, a model, an axiom), end at the boxed result, and never skip the step where a term vanishes — that is usually the step being examined.
    • "Compute" — show the intermediate values, not just the answer. Carry four decimals and state the units or the base of the logarithm.
    • "Compare / when would you use" — this is Fig. 21.1 in prose: name the deciding property of the data, then the consequence. "The classes are 99:1, so accuracy is uninformative ($0.99$ for the trivial classifier) and I report recall at a tuned threshold."
    Assumptions are marks. Three that are almost always worth writing: "assuming $\mathbf{X}^\top\mathbf{X}$ is invertible", "assuming the data are linearly separable", "assuming the samples are i.i.d.". Each one is the hypothesis of a theorem you are about to use.

    21.10   The night-before checklist

    • One numerical example per section — the twenty anchors of §21.6 — reproduced on paper, not recognised on a page.
    • Two derivations you can write cold from a blank sheet: AdaBoost's $\alpha_t$ and the bias–variance split. They exercise the two moves every other derivation uses — differentiate-and-set-to-zero, and add-and-subtract.
    • Every shape, every time. If linear algebra appears, annotate shapes; a shape mismatch is the fastest self-check you own.
    • The subscripts on expectations: $\mathbb{E}_\mathcal{D}$ averages over datasets, $\mathbb{E}_\mathbf{x}$ over inputs. Swapping them turns bias into variance.
    • The VC $d_{VC} = d+1$ proof, both directions: exhibit $d+1$ shattered points, then show $d+2$ are linearly dependent.
    • The three things that must live inside a CV fold: imputation, scaling/selection, and resampling (§21.7).
    • The Part I anchors: $IG = 0.3219$ , MAP $= 7/15$ , storm-net $P(S\mid T) = 0.7161$ , EM $0.6 \to 0.8 \to 0.84 \to \cdots \to 0.85$ . The Part II anchors: OOB $= 0.3679$ , $\alpha_t(0.3) = 0.4236$ , $w^\star = 0.75$ , silhouette $= 0.8182$ .
    Adjudication — the clustering deck's closing claim. The source deck ends with: "Different clustering may result in different patterns, but the most consistent pattern is the correct distribution." The first half is right and important — clustering is exploratory, and the algorithm you pick is part of the answer you get. The second half is too strong as written: consistency across algorithms is evidence for a structure, not proof that it is correct. Two algorithms sharing the same bias (k-means and GMM with spherical covariances both prefer round, similarly-sized clusters) will agree with each other and be wrong together on a crescent-shaped dataset. The defensible statement is: a structure that survives a change of algorithm, a change of distance and a change of $k$ is worth investigating; nothing about internal validation alone makes it "correct".
    Section recap.
    • Fig. 21.1 routes a problem to a model family by asking the irreversible questions first: labels, then target type, then data shape, with imbalance and explainability as always-on side constraints.
    • Fig. 21.2 collects the twelve per-topic decision rules; Fig. 21.3 shows what $n$ and $d$ already forbid before any tuning, via the $n \gtrsim 10\,d_{VC}$ rule.
    • §21.5 is the formula sheet: Part I, Part II, and a third block for everything v6 added (GB/XGBoost, SMOTE, SHAP, DBSCAN, GMM, backprop, conv arithmetic, attention).
    • §21.6 gives one recomputed anchor per section, all cross-checked against the owning section's own compute output.
    • §21.7 and Fig. 21.4 catalogue the mistakes that return plausible numbers rather than errors — with a leakage experiment on pure noise scoring $75.0\%$ instead of chance.
    • Nothing here is new. If a row surprises you, that row's section is the one to reread.
    Interpretation. The playbook's real claim is that model selection is mostly elimination, and that the eliminations are driven by properties of the data and of the cost of errors — not by which algorithm is fashionable. The gotcha table is the other half of the same claim: most bad results in practice are not bad models, they are good models measured wrongly.

    21.11   Practice

    Practice 21.1 — A fraud screen scores TP $=40$, FP $=10$, FN $=20$, TN $=930$. The reviewing team says a false alarm costs about four times what a missed fraud costs. Which summary metric do you report, what is its value, and what would you have reported if the costs were reversed?

    False alarms (FP) dominating means precision matters more than recall, so use $F_\beta$ with $\beta < 1$. The conventional choice is $\beta = 0.5$.

    From the table: $P = \frac{40}{40+10} = 0.8$ , $R = \frac{40}{40+20} = 0.6667$ .

    $$F_{0.5} = \frac{(1+0.25)\,PR}{0.25P + R} = \frac{1.25 \times 0.8 \times 0.6667} {0.25\times 0.8 + 0.6667} = 0.7692.$$

    So report $F_{0.5} = 0.7692$ . If the costs were reversed (missed frauds expensive), you would report $F_2 = 0.6897$ , and $F_1 = 0.7273$ sits between them. The ordering $F_{0.5} > F_1 > F_2$ holds here because $P > R$; if recall exceeded precision the ordering would reverse.

    Worth saying out loud: accuracy on this table is $0.97$ , which is useless — with $60$ true frauds among $1000$ cases, predicting "never fraud" already scores $0.94$.

    Practice 21.2 — You are handed 500 labelled rows with 20,000 features (a gene-expression panel), a binary outcome, and a requirement that the clinician can see why each prediction was made. Walk Fig. 21.1 and Fig. 21.3 and state your plan.

    Q1: labels exist $\Rightarrow$ supervised. Q2: binary target $\Rightarrow$ classification, logit link. Q3: tabular, and $n = 500$ is small.

    Fig. 21.3 first. $d = 20{,}000 \gg n = 500$, so the point sits far above the $n = 10\,d_{VC}$ line — for a linear model $d_{VC} = d+1 = 20{,}001$, which would demand $n \gtrsim 200{,}010$ rows by the practical rule (at $d_{VC} = 11$ the same rule reads $n \gtrsim 110$ ). Unregularised fitting is meaningless: the data are separable by accident.

    Plan. (i) $L_1$-penalised logistic regression, or $L_1$ pre-screening followed by a small model — the sparsity assumption is the extra information that makes the regime workable. (ii) Nested cross-validation: the feature selection and the penalty search must both happen inside the outer folds, otherwise you get the §21.7 result — an apparent $75.0\%$ on data with no signal. With $n=500$, use $K = 5$ or $10$. (iii) Explainability: lasso coefficients are directly readable, which satisfies the requirement without SHAP; if a boosted model later wins on accuracy, add SHAP and check the efficiency identity $f(\mathbf{x}) = \phi_0 + \sum_i \phi_i$. (iv) Scale the features before penalising — the penalty is unit-sensitive (§21.4).

    What you do not do: reach for a deep net. Fig. 21.3 puts this point in the "regularise hard or get more rows" region, and a network adds parameters to a problem whose difficulty is that it already has too many.

    Practice 21.3 — An AdaBoost round returns weighted error $\epsilon_t = 0.3$. Compute $\alpha_t$, the normaliser $Z_t$, and the factor by which a misclassified point's weight grows. What happens at $\epsilon_t = 0.5$, and what would you do at $\epsilon_t = 0.7$?

    $\alpha_t = \tfrac12\ln\frac{1-\epsilon_t}{\epsilon_t} = \tfrac12\ln\frac{0.7}{0.3} = 0.4236$ .

    $Z_t = 2\sqrt{\epsilon_t(1-\epsilon_t)} = 2\sqrt{0.21} = 0.9165$ .

    A misclassified point has $y_i h_t(\mathbf{x}_i) = -1$, so its unnormalised weight is multiplied by $e^{+\alpha_t}$ while a correct point is multiplied by $e^{-\alpha_t}$. The ratio of the two multipliers is $e^{2\alpha_t} = \frac{1-\epsilon_t}{\epsilon_t} = 2.3333$ : after this round a misclassified point carries $2.3333$ times the weight of a correct one, relative to before.

    At $\epsilon_t = 0.5$, $\alpha_t = \tfrac12\ln 1 = 0$ — the learner is a coin flip and gets zero say; the weights are unchanged and the round is wasted.

    At $\epsilon_t = 0.7$ the formula gives $\alpha_t < 0$, which is meaningful: the learner is anti-correlated with the truth, and a negative $\alpha_t$ simply votes against it. Standard implementations instead flip the learner's sign (equivalently, treat $\epsilon_t \to 1-\epsilon_t$) or abort the round. Also note $Z_t = 0.9165$ again — the error bound $\prod_t Z_t$ is symmetric about $\epsilon_t = 0.5$.

    Practice 21.4 — Three independent classifiers each get 70% of cases right and vote by majority. What is the ensemble's accuracy? Repeat for eleven classifiers, and for 101 classifiers that are each right only 45% of the time. What is the moral?

    Majority correct means at least $\lfloor B/2\rfloor + 1$ of $B$ are right: $P = \sum_{k > B/2}\binom{B}{k}p^k(1-p)^{B-k}$.

    $B = 3$, $p = 0.7$: $\binom{3}{2}(0.7)^2(0.3) + (0.7)^3 = 3(0.49)(0.3) + 0.343 = 0.441 + 0.343 = 0.784$ , a gain of $0.084$ over one classifier.

    $B = 11$, $p = 0.7$: $0.9218$ . Adding learners keeps helping, with diminishing returns.

    $B = 101$, $p = 0.45$: $0.1562$ — far worse than the $0.45$ of a single learner.

    Moral. Majority voting is an amplifier, not a fixer: it drives the ensemble toward whichever side of $0.5$ the base learner sits on. It also assumes independence, which real bagged learners violate — that is precisely the $\rho$ in $\mathrm{Var} = \rho\sigma^2 + \frac{1-\rho}{B}\sigma^2$, which at $\rho = 0.3$, $B = 100$ leaves $0.307$ instead of the independent-case $0.01$ . Random forests attack $\rho$ (feature subsampling) precisely because $B$ alone cannot get past the $\rho\sigma^2$ floor.

    Practice 21.5 — One XGBoost leaf holds residuals $\{1.0, 0.5, 1.5\}$ under squared loss. Compute $G$, $H$, the leaf weight and the similarity score at $\lambda = 1$. Then evaluate splitting it into $\{1.0, 0.5\}$ and $\{1.5\}$, at $\lambda = 1$ and at $\lambda = 0$.

    For squared loss $\ell = \tfrac12(y - F)^2$: $g_i = -(y_i - F_i) = -r_i$ and $h_i = 1$. So $G = -(1.0+0.5+1.5) = -3.0$ and $H = 3$ .

    Leaf weight. $w^\star = -G/(H+\lambda) = 3/(3+1) = 0.75$ . With $\lambda = 0$ it would be $3/3 = 1.0$ , exactly the mean residual — so $\lambda$ shrinks the leaf output toward zero by the factor $H/(H+\lambda) = 3/4$.

    Similarity. $\text{Sim} = G^2/(H+\lambda) = 9/4 = 2.25$ .

    The split, $\lambda = 1$. Left $G_L = -1.5$, $H_L = 2$: $\text{Sim}_L = 2.25/3 = 0.75$ . Right $G_R = -1.5$, $H_R = 1$: $\text{Sim}_R = 2.25/2 = 1.125$ . Using §13's convention $\text{Gain} = \text{Sim}_L + \text{Sim}_R - \text{Sim}_{\text{root}} - \gamma$ with $\gamma = 0$:

    $$\text{Gain} = 0.75 + 1.125 - 2.25 = -0.375.$$

    Negative — XGBoost refuses the split.

    The same split, $\lambda = 0$. $\text{Sim}_{\text{root}} = 9/3 = 3.0$, $\text{Sim}_L = 2.25/2 = 1.125$, $\text{Sim}_R = 2.25/1 = 2.25$, so Gain $= 1.125 + 2.25 - 3.0 = +0.375$ — the split is now made.

    Interpretation. $\lambda$ penalises leaves with few observations hardest, because it is added to $H$, which for squared loss is just the leaf's row count. Splitting off a single point buys a lot of apparent similarity at $\lambda=0$ and almost none at $\lambda=1$. That is the entire mechanism by which $\lambda$ controls tree structure — not just leaf values.

    Practice 21.6 — A colleague reports 5-fold CV accuracy of 75% on a 60-row, 400-feature dataset, having first kept the 10 most discriminative features. Nothing else was tuned. What do you say?

    Say: that number is not an estimate of anything. The feature selection saw all 60 rows, including the rows used for validation in every fold. Selecting 10 columns out of 400 by between-class mean difference is a fit with a huge search space; on pure noise it manufactures exactly this result — $75.0\%$ in the §21.7 experiment, on data built to have no signal at all.

    The test. Move the selection inside the fold and rerun. In the experiment that drops the score to $40.0\%$ , i.e. chance ($0.5$ ) within sampling noise at this $n$; per-fold values were $0.3333, 0.5833, 0.4167, 0.4167, 0.25$ . A drop of that size is diagnostic of leakage, not of a bad model.

    What is defensible instead. Nested CV: an inner loop that selects features and tunes, an outer loop that only scores. Plus a permutation test — shuffle the labels and rerun the whole pipeline; if the shuffled score matches the real one, there was never any signal. And with $n = 60$ and $d = 400$, Fig. 21.3 says the honest ceiling is low no matter what: the point sits deep in the $d \gg n$ region.

    Section sources: v5 §20 (formula cheat sheet, ported and extended); hand p16 (ensemble library comparison, derived in §13); the clustering lecture deck slide 77 (clustering summary, adjudicated in §21.10); all anchor values recomputed in work/computes/s21_anchors.py and cross-checked against §5, §7, §9, §10, §11, §12, §13, §14, §18, §20.

    22   The Coding Test: pandas & Modelling Drills (Timed Test Format)

    §21 ends with a routing question — which model do I reach for? — and a template pipeline you should be able to type from memory. This section is the other half of that sentence: the two hours in front of a laptop where the marks are actually awarded, and where nobody asks you to derive anything. It is built entirely from one source, a Jupyter notebook the user wrote for themselves — Timed Data-Science Test — Python Reference Kit, 75 cells, 45 of them code — restructured for the page and, crucially, re-executed. Nothing conceptual is re-derived here; every model named links back to the section that derives it.

    The format this section is built around. The kit's opening cell quotes the interview-experience document verbatim:
    • "3 questions each for 160 marks — goal is to check your pandas (data manipulation and cleaning) and modelling skills. Q1: one table divided into 4 subparts + 3 other different tables. Q2: one dataset, do further cleaning. Q3: apply a model on cleaned data, train/val/test given, minimum RMSE to pass the test cases."
    • "You were allowed to use documentation of pandas, scikit-learn etc. No AI apps were allowed."
    So: §22.1 = Q1 (stack, join, derive, aggregate, reshape), §22.2 = Q2 (clean), §22.5 = Q3 (model until the RMSE threshold falls), §22.6 = the cheat sheets to skim the morning of the test, §22.7 = the operating procedure for the two hours themselves. Practice drills are in §22.8.
    Two subsections here are not from the notebook. §22.3 (datetime and time-series preprocessing) is built from a second user-supplied source — a preprocessing cheat-sheet of 38 numbered points, cited as — because a date column appears in every one of Q1, Q2 and Q3 and the kit treats it only in passing. §22.4 (XGBoost on time series) follows it, because a forecasting variant of Q3 breaks the split, the cross-validation and the feature construction all at once, and none of those breakages raise an error. Both are computed in work/computes/s22_timeseries.py; the conceptual treatment of boosting stays in §13, and §13.13 has the general xgboost workflow this section deliberately does not repeat.

    The kit's own strategic advice, and the only sentence in it worth memorising as a sentence: "the modelling question is where the pass/fail test-cases live (minimum RMSE). Get a working end-to-end baseline submission first, then go back and improve. A mediocre model that runs beats a great model that errors out."

    Two things were repaired before anything was quoted.

Every line the file wrapped at roughly column 72 lost the space at the wrap point, in markdown and in code alike: interview-experience, pandas(data manipulation, # plainvertical stack, and — fatally — for f inglob.glob(...), which is a SyntaxError.
