    22.1   Q1 — Data manipulation: one table in four subparts, plus three lookups

    The described question is the classic stack the fragments, enrich by joining lookups, then aggregate pattern. The kit builds a synthetic version so every later snippet has real data underneath it, which is also the right habit in the test: if you are unsure what a call does, make a five-row frame and try it rather than reasoning about it.

    Code — cell 1: imports, display options, seed 
    import warnings, sys
warnings.filterwarnings("ignore")

import numpy as np
import pandas as pd

pd.set_option("display.max_columns", 50)
pd.set_option("display.width", 160)
pd.set_option("display.float_format", lambda v: f"{v:,.4f}")

np.random.seed(23)
print("python", sys.version.split()[0], "| pandas", pd.__version__, "| numpy", np.__version__)

    Set the float format once and every frame you print for the rest of the paper is readable; graders read your notebook, not just your answers. Seed everything that can be seeded — a result you cannot reproduce on re-run is a result you cannot defend.

    22.1.1   The fixtures

    Code — cell 3: the "one table split into 4 subparts" and the 3 lookup tables 
    # ---- The "one table split into 4 subparts" (e.g. one file per quarter) ----
def make_sales(quarter, n, start):
    return pd.DataFrame({
        "order_id":  [f"O{quarter}{i:04d}" for i in range(n)],
        "cust_id":   np.random.randint(1, 60, n),
        "prod_id":   np.random.randint(1, 25, n),
        "order_date": pd.to_datetime(start) + pd.to_timedelta(np.random.randint(0, 89, n), unit="D"),
        "units":     np.random.randint(1, 12, n),
        "unit_price": np.round(np.random.uniform(50, 900, n), 2),
        "discount":  np.round(np.random.choice([0, 0, 0, .05, .1, .2], n), 2),
    })

sales_q1 = make_sales(1, 250, "2024-01-01")
sales_q2 = make_sales(2, 300, "2024-04-01")
sales_q3 = make_sales(3, 280, "2024-07-01")
sales_q4 = make_sales(4, 320, "2024-10-01")

# ---- The "3 other different tables" (lookups / dimensions) ----
customers = pd.DataFrame({
    "cust_id": np.arange(1, 61),
    "cust_name": [f"Cust_{i}" for i in range(1, 61)],
    "region_id": np.random.randint(1, 6, 60),
    "signup_date": pd.to_datetime("2021-01-01") + pd.to_timedelta(np.random.randint(0, 1200, 60), unit="D"),
    "segment": np.random.choice(["SMB", "Mid", "Enterprise"], 60, p=[.5, .3, .2]),
})

products = pd.DataFrame({
    "prod_id": np.arange(1, 26),
    "category": np.random.choice(["Electronics", "Apparel", "Home", "Grocery"], 25),
    "cost": np.round(np.random.uniform(30, 600, 25), 2),
})

regions = pd.DataFrame({
    "region_id": [1, 2, 3, 4, 5],
    "region": ["North", "South", "East", "West", "Central"],
    "country": ["IN", "IN", "IN", "IN", "IN"],
})

print(sales_q1.shape, customers.shape, products.shape, regions.shape)
sales_q1.head(3)

    Shapes: (250, 7), (60, 5), (25, 3), (5, 3) . Note the deliberate trap the fixture builds in: cust_id is drawn from randint(1, 60), which stops at 59, so customer 60 never orders and every per-customer aggregate has 59 rows , not 60. Row counts that are "one short" are usually a half-open range, not a bug.

    22.1.2   Stack the four subparts

    pd.concat with keys= is the safe version: it keeps a label saying which fragment each row came from, which is usually worth a mark and always worth it for debugging. Sanity-check the schemas before concatenating — all four fragments here share a column list and the stack lands at (1150, 8) : the 7 original columns plus quarter, and 1150 = 250 + 300 + 280 + 320 rows . Check that arithmetic every single time.

    Code — cell 5: stack with keys=, keeping the fragment label 
    parts = {"Q1": sales_q1, "Q2": sales_q2, "Q3": sales_q3, "Q4": sales_q4}

# Sanity check FIRST: do the fragments actually share a schema?
for k, v in parts.items():
    print(k, v.shape, list(v.columns) == list(sales_q1.columns))

sales = (pd.concat(parts, names=["quarter", "row_id"])   # MultiIndex: (quarter, original index)
           .reset_index(level="quarter")                 # promote 'quarter' to a column
           .reset_index(drop=True))
print("\nstacked:", sales.shape)
sales.head(3)

    Passing a dict to concat gets you the provenance column for free — one call instead of four assigns. The alternative one-liner pd.concat([...], ignore_index=True) throws that information away.

    Code — cell 6: concat variants, schema diff, and reading many files 
    # Variants worth knowing
pd.concat([sales_q1, sales_q2], ignore_index=True)          # plain vertical stack
pd.concat([sales_q1, sales_q2], axis=1)                     # side-by-side (aligns on index!)
pd.concat([sales_q1, sales_q2], join="inner")               # keep only common columns

# If the fragments have MISMATCHED columns, find the difference before concatenating:
print(set(sales_q1.columns) ^ set(sales_q2.columns))        # symmetric difference == {} means identical

# Reading many files at once (very common phrasing: "combine different files into one dataframe")
import glob
sales = pd.concat((pd.read_csv(f).assign(src=f) for f in glob.glob("data/sales_*.csv")),
                  ignore_index=True)

    The symmetric difference ^ on two column sets is the fastest schema diff there is — empty set means identical . .assign(src=f) inside the generator is the file-level provenance column.

    Cell 6 is a live landmine — verified. Its last statement rebinds sales, the frame every downstream cell depends on. Run top-to-bottom with no data/ directory and the glob is empty, so pandas raises ValueError: No objects to concatenate ; the exception at least stops you. The dangerous case is the one where the glob does match something: sales is silently replaced by a frame with different columns, and §22.1.3's join, §22.1.4's derived columns and every aggregate after them are computed on the wrong table without a single error message. The fix is one character of discipline — name the demo variable something else (sales_from_files = pd.concat(...)). This is the "Q1 failure mode" the kit's own test-day rule 3 is about: print df.shape after every transformation.

    22.1.3   Join the lookup tables

    Two habits that save you in a timed test: validate= makes pandas raise if the join is not the cardinality you assumed ("m:1", "1:1", "1:m"), and indicator=True tells you which rows failed to match. Here all 1150 rows match on all three joins , with 0 unmatched customers and an anti-join of 0 rows , and the joined frame is (1150, 16) — same row count as the input, which is the whole point of checking.

    Code — cell 8: three left joins with validate= and indicator= 
    df = (sales
      .merge(customers, on="cust_id", how="left", validate="m:1", indicator="m_cust")
      .merge(products,  on="prod_id", how="left", validate="m:1")
      .merge(regions,   on="region_id", how="left", validate="m:1")
)

print(df["m_cust"].value_counts().to_dict())          # want: all 'both'
print("unmatched customers:", (df["m_cust"] != "both").sum())
df = df.drop(columns="m_cust")
df.head(3)

    Say this out loud in the interview: left join to preserve the fact table, validate="m:1" to assert the lookup is unique, indicator to prove nothing fell through. Three arguments, three marks.

    Code — cell 9: join mechanics, anti-join, and merge_asof 
    # Join mechanics you may need to vary
a, b = sales_q1.head(5), customers.head(5)

pd.merge(a, b, on="cust_id", how="inner")                       # inner / left / right / outer / cross
pd.merge(a, b, left_on="cust_id", right_on="cust_id")           # different key names
pd.merge(a, b, on="cust_id", suffixes=("_sales", "_cust"))      # control overlapping col names
a.set_index("cust_id").join(b.set_index("cust_id"), how="left") # .join() = index-based merge

# Multi-key join
# df1.merge(df2, on=["cust_id", "order_date"], how="left")

# Anti-join: rows in `sales` with no matching customer
missing = sales.merge(customers, on="cust_id", how="left", indicator=True)
missing = missing[missing["_merge"] == "left_only"]
print("anti-join rows:", len(missing))

# Nearest-key / as-of join (time series: attach the most recent price before each order)
prices = (pd.DataFrame({"order_date": pd.date_range("2024-01-01", periods=12, freq="MS"),
                        "fx_rate": np.round(np.random.uniform(80, 88, 12), 2)}))
asof = pd.merge_asof(sales.sort_values("order_date"), prices.sort_values("order_date"),
                     on="order_date", direction="backward")
asof[["order_id", "order_date", "fx_rate"]].head(3)

    merge_asof is the one nobody remembers and it is exactly what "attach the prevailing rate/price at the time of the order" means. Both frames must be sorted on the key first, or it raises; here it leaves 0 unmatched rows .

    22.1.4   Derive columns

    Chain with .assign() — it keeps the pipeline readable and avoids SettingWithCopyWarning. Inside assign, refer to columns created earlier in the same call through the lambda d: argument, not through the outer name; that is what makes net_rev visible to margin two lines later.

    Code — cell 11: .assign() chain, np.select, cut/qcut 
    df = df.assign(
    gross      = lambda d: d["units"] * d["unit_price"],
    net_rev    = lambda d: d["gross"] * (1 - d["discount"]),
    cogs       = lambda d: d["units"] * d["cost"],
    margin     = lambda d: d["net_rev"] - d["cogs"],
    margin_pct = lambda d: np.where(d["net_rev"] > 0, (d["net_rev"] - d["cogs"]) / d["net_rev"], np.nan),
    month      = lambda d: d["order_date"].dt.to_period("M").dt.to_timestamp(),
    dow        = lambda d: d["order_date"].dt.day_name(),
    tenure_days= lambda d: (d["order_date"] - d["signup_date"]).dt.days,
)

# Conditional columns, three ways (np.select is the one to remember for >2 branches)
df["size_band"] = np.select(
    [df["net_rev"] < 1_000, df["net_rev"] < 5_000, df["net_rev"] >= 5_000],
    ["small", "medium", "large"],
    default="unknown",
)
df["is_discounted"] = np.where(df["discount"] > 0, 1, 0)
df["cat_short"] = df["category"].map({"Electronics": "ELEC", "Apparel": "APP",
                                      "Home": "HOME", "Grocery": "GROC"})

# Binning
df["rev_decile"] = pd.qcut(df["net_rev"], 10, labels=False, duplicates="drop")  # equal-count
df["price_bin"]  = pd.cut(df["unit_price"], bins=[0, 200, 500, 1000],
                          labels=["low", "mid", "high"])                        # fixed edges

df[["order_id", "net_rev", "margin_pct", "size_band", "rev_decile"]].head(3)

    np.where for two branches, np.select for more, .map(dict) for a lookup — and qcut = equal counts, cut = equal (or specified) edges. Mixing those two up is a standard trap. duplicates="drop" stops qcut raising when a distribution has ties at a quantile boundary.

    Interpretation. The three derived rows come out as O10000: net revenue 768.82, margin 35.25%, band small, decile 2; O10001: 6430.75, 50.41%, large, decile 9; O10002: 2622.12, 43.38%, medium, decile 5 . Across all 1150 orders the bands split 638 medium / 326 small / 186 large on total net revenue of 3,106,922.13 . Worth noticing before you build a margin report on it: 429 of the 1150 rows have negative margin, because cost is drawn independently of unit_price. That is a fixture artefact, not a finding — but in a real Q1 it is precisely the sanity check that separates "I computed the column" from "I looked at the column".

    22.1.5   Group-by: aggregate, transform, filter

    Three modes, three output shapes. Knowing which one the question wants is most of the mark:

    NeedMethodOutput rows
    One number per group.agg()one per group
    Broadcast a group stat back onto every row.transform()same as input
    Keep/drop whole groups by a condition.filter()subset of input
    Code — cell 13: named aggregation 
    # --- agg: named aggregation gives clean column names in one shot ---
summary = (df.groupby(["region", "category"], as_index=False)
             .agg(orders      = ("order_id", "nunique"),
                  customers   = ("cust_id", "nunique"),
                  units       = ("units", "sum"),
                  revenue     = ("net_rev", "sum"),
                  avg_ticket  = ("net_rev", "mean"),
                  median_disc = ("discount", "median"),
                  margin      = ("margin", "sum"))
             .assign(margin_pct=lambda d: d["margin"] / d["revenue"])
             .sort_values("revenue", ascending=False))
summary.head(5)

    Named aggregation (new=("col", "func")) is the only form that gives you flat, readable column names in one shot — no MultiIndex to flatten afterwards. Memorise the tuple order: source column first, function second.

    NorthHome8615558226,175.082,629.940.0054,328.060.2402

    The full table is 20 rows by 10 columns — 5 regions × 4 categories, complete, which is itself worth checking: a missing cell means a combination that never occurred, and whether that should appear as a zero row is a question you should answer out loud rather than let groupby answer for you.

    Code — cell 14: transform, ranking, top-N per group, filter, first/last per group 
    # --- transform: % of group total, group mean, group z-score ---
df["rev_share_in_region"] = df["net_rev"] / df.groupby("region")["net_rev"].transform("sum")
df["region_avg_rev"]      = df.groupby("region")["net_rev"].transform("mean")
df["rev_z_in_region"]     = (df["net_rev"] - df.groupby("region")["net_rev"].transform("mean")) \
                            / df.groupby("region")["net_rev"].transform("std")

# --- rank within group, and top-N per group (extremely common exam ask) ---
df["rank_in_region"] = df.groupby("region")["net_rev"].rank(method="dense", ascending=False)
top3 = (df.sort_values("net_rev", ascending=False)
          .groupby("region", as_index=False)
          .head(3)[["region", "order_id", "net_rev"]])

# Equivalent, often cleaner:
top3_alt = df.loc[df.groupby("region")["net_rev"].rank(method="first", ascending=False) <= 3]

# --- filter: keep only regions with more than 250 orders ---
big_regions = df.groupby("region").filter(lambda g: len(g) > 250)

# --- first / last row per group (e.g. each customer's latest order) ---
latest = df.sort_values("order_date").groupby("cust_id", as_index=False).last()
first_order = df.loc[df.groupby("cust_id")["order_date"].idxmin()]

print(top3.shape, big_regions["region"].nunique(), latest.shape, first_order.shape)
top3.head(4)

    Two idioms for top-N per group: sort_values → groupby → head(n), and rank(method="first") <= n. Prefer method="first" when you must return exactly n rows; method="dense" can return more when there are ties. The idxmin/idxmax + .loc pattern is how you get the whole row at a group extremum, not just the value.

    Interpretation. top3 is 15 rows × 3 columns — 3 per region for 5 regions, the arithmetic you should do before looking. The leaders are O40158 in North at 9787.80, O20249 in East at 9624.89, O20060 in South at 9596.62 and O40103 in Central at 9388.83 . The rank-based variant returns the same 15 rows but keeps all 33 columns — a boolean mask on the original frame, not a projection. .filter() keeps just 1 region with more than 250 orders , and both per-customer reductions return 59 rows for the reason flagged in §22.1.1. The transform check that costs nothing: within-region revenue shares must sum to exactly the number of regions, and they sum to 5.0 .
    Code — cell 15: several aggregations per column, flattening MultiIndex columns, custom agg 
    # --- multiple aggs per column, then flatten the MultiIndex columns ---
multi = df.groupby("region").agg({"net_rev": ["sum", "mean", "std"], "units": ["sum", "max"]})
multi.columns = ["_".join(c) for c in multi.columns]     # flatten: net_rev_sum, net_rev_mean, ...
multi = multi.reset_index()

# --- custom aggregation function ---
def rev_per_unit(g):
    return g["net_rev"].sum() / g["units"].sum()

custom = df.groupby("region").apply(rev_per_unit).rename("rev_per_unit").reset_index()
multi.merge(custom, on="region").head()

    ["_".join(c) for c in multi.columns] is the flatten idiom — learn it as one token. Note why rev_per_unit needs .apply rather than .agg: it is a ratio of two different columns' sums, so it needs the whole group frame, not one Series. In pandas ≥ 2.2 this .apply also emits a DeprecationWarning about include_groups; the kit's blanket filterwarnings("ignore") hides it, which is fine in a test and a bad habit everywhere else.

The mean ticket barely moves across regions (2,652.98 to 2,773.47) while total revenue varies twofold (418,794.47 to 830,187.77) : the regions differ in volume, not in basket size. That is exactly the sentence a Q1 sub-part asking "comment on the regional pattern" wants, and you can only write it because you asked for sum and mean in the same block. Note also that rev_per_unit (440.69–462.06) is not the same as net_rev_mean / units_mean — a ratio of sums is not a mean of ratios, and picking the wrong one is a classic silent error.

    22.1.6   Reshape: pivot, melt, stack/unstack, crosstab

    pivot_table = long → wide with aggregation; melt = wide → long. Those two cover about 90% of what gets asked.

    Code — cell 17: pivot_table with margins 
    # long -> wide
wide = pd.pivot_table(df, index="region", columns="category", values="net_rev",
                      aggfunc="sum", fill_value=0, margins=True, margins_name="TOTAL")
wide

    margins=True gives you the row and column totals for free — and the grand-total cell is a free consistency check against df["net_rev"].sum(). fill_value=0 matters: an absent combination is a zero, not a NaN, in a revenue report.

    Revenue by region × category, with margins
    category totalApparelElectronicsGroceryHomeTOTAL
    all regions927,945.18561,334.80837,440.61780,201.533,106,922.13

    The pivot is 6 × 5 (5 regions + TOTAL row, 4 categories + TOTAL column) and its grand total, 3,106,922.13 , equals df["net_rev"].sum() exactly. That equality is the cheapest proof available that the pivot did not silently drop rows, and it takes one line to state in the answer.

    Code — cell 18: melt, stack/unstack, crosstab 
    # wide -> long
long = (wide.drop(index="TOTAL", errors="ignore")
            .drop(columns="TOTAL", errors="ignore")
            .reset_index()
            .melt(id_vars="region", var_name="category", value_name="net_rev"))

# stack / unstack operate on the index instead of columns
s = df.groupby(["region", "category"])["net_rev"].sum()
s.unstack(fill_value=0)          # -> wide DataFrame
s.unstack().stack()              # -> back to Series

# counts / proportions cross-tab
pd.crosstab(df["region"], df["segment"], normalize="index").round(3)

    Drop the margins before melting or "TOTAL" becomes a category level — the single most common reshape bug. errors="ignore" makes the drop idempotent so the cell survives a re-run. normalize="index" gives row proportions, normalize="columns" column proportions, normalize=True the whole-table share; state which one you used.

    Round-tripping wide → long gives 20 rows × 3 columns , matching the 5 × 4 unstacked block — the same 20 cells in two layouts. The segment mix per region is quite uneven: SMB runs from 48.1% in South to 75.6% in North, and Enterprise from 6.2% in West to 26.5% in East . Each row sums to 1 by construction, which is what normalize="index" buys you and what makes rows comparable across regions of different sizes.

    Code — cell 19: the region × month reporting matrix 
    # Monthly revenue matrix (region x month) — the classic "reporting table" output
monthly = (df.pivot_table(index="region", columns="month", values="net_rev",
                          aggfunc="sum", fill_value=0)
             .rename(columns=lambda c: c.strftime("%Y-%m")))
monthly.iloc[:, :6]

    rename(columns=lambda c: c.strftime(...)) is how you turn timestamp column labels into something a human (or a CSV) can read. Do it after the pivot, never before — string months sort lexicographically, and "2024-10" would land between "2024-01" and "2024-02" if you had already converted.

    The matrix is 5 × 12 , one column per month of 2024; Central's first six months run 30,270.66 / 56,982.01 / 36,704.74 / 50,932.06 / 47,206.37 / 42,312.91 .

    22.1.7   Time-series style operations

    shift / diff / pct_change / rolling — always sort first, and always use the groupby(...) versions so values do not leak across entities. That last point is the same rule as §21.7's leakage rule wearing different clothes: a shift computed on an unsorted or ungrouped frame quietly imports the previous region's last month into this region's first month.

    Code — cell 21: lag, delta, percent change, rolling mean, cumulative sum, index; resampling 
    ts = (df.groupby(["region", "month"], as_index=False)["net_rev"].sum()
        .sort_values(["region", "month"]))

g = ts.groupby("region")["net_rev"]
ts["prev_month"] = g.shift(1)
ts["mom_change"] = g.diff(1)
ts["mom_pct"]    = g.pct_change(1)
ts["roll3_mean"] = g.transform(lambda s: s.rolling(3, min_periods=1).mean())
ts["cum_rev"]    = g.cumsum()
ts["yoy_index"]  = g.transform(lambda s: s / s.iloc[0])

# Resampling (needs a DatetimeIndex)
daily = df.set_index("order_date")["net_rev"].resample("D").sum()
weekly = daily.resample("W").sum()

ts.head(6)

    The first row of every group is NaN for shift, diff and pct_change — three NaNs in row 1 here , and that is correct, not a bug to fill. min_periods=1 makes the rolling mean start at row 1 instead of row 3; say which convention you chose. resample needs a DatetimeIndex, which is why the set_index is there.

Read the columns as a set. mom_pct swings between +88.2% and −35.6% in consecutive months while roll3_mean stays in a 41k–48k band — the month-on-month series is dominated by noise, the rolling mean is the signal, and that contrast is the reason both columns exist. yoy_index is just net_rev / first month, so it reads as a growth multiple against the base month; cum_rev ends the six months at 264,408.75. The panel is 60 rows × 9 columns (5 regions × 12 months), and the daily resample yields 363 days , not 366: resample("D") spans first-to-last order date, so a missing day at either end is invisible unless you check.

    22.1.8   Strings, dates and selection

    These are exactly the "do you actually know pandas" marks.

    Code — cell 23: .str accessor and mixed-format date parsing 
    s = pd.Series([" Delhi ", "MUMBAI", "bangalore", "Chennai-600001", None, "pune"])

s.str.strip().str.title()                         # ' Delhi ' -> 'Delhi'
s.str.lower().str.replace(r"[^a-z]", "", regex=True)
s.str.contains("ai", case=False, na=False)        # na=False stops NaN blowing up the mask
s.str.split("-", expand=True)                     # -> DataFrame of parts
s.str.extract(r"(\d{6})")                         # regex capture group -> pincode
s.str.len()
s.fillna("unknown").str.startswith("p")

d = pd.to_datetime(pd.Series(["2024-01-05", "05/02/2024", "March 3, 2024", "garbage"]),
                   format="mixed", errors="coerce", dayfirst=False)
print(d.dt.year.tolist(), d.dt.quarter.tolist(), d.dt.is_month_end.tolist())
d.dt.strftime("%Y-%m-%d").tolist()

    na=False in str.contains is the one-argument fix for "cannot mask with NA" — without it the resulting mask has NaNs and indexing blows up. errors="coerce" is the same idea for dates: junk becomes NaT instead of an exception that kills the cell.

    Interpretation. The parsed dates come back as ['2024-01-05', '2024-05-02', '2024-03-03', NaT] , i.e. 1 of 4 unparseable . Look hard at the second one: 05/02/2024 became 5 February… no — it became 2 May, because dayfirst=False puts it in Q2. The same string with dayfirst=True is a different date, and there is no way for pandas to know which you meant. In a test, parse with an explicit dayfirst and write one sentence saying which convention you assumed; that sentence is worth more than the code. Meanwhile str.extract(r"(\d{6})") pulls 600001 out of "Chennai-600001" and returns NaN everywhere else , which is exactly the behaviour you want from a capture group.
    Code — cell 24: selection idioms, row-wise apply, explode 
    # Selection idioms you should not have to think about
df.loc[df["region"].eq("North") & df["net_rev"].gt(5000), ["order_id", "net_rev"]].head(2)
df.query("region == 'North' and net_rev > 5000").head(2)
df[df["category"].isin(["Home", "Apparel"])].head(2)
df[df["net_rev"].between(1000, 2000)].head(2)
df.nlargest(3, "net_rev")[["order_id", "net_rev"]]
df.sort_values(["region", "net_rev"], ascending=[True, False]).head(2)

# apply along rows is SLOW — prefer vectorised. Use only when unavoidable:
df.head(100).apply(lambda r: r["units"] * r["unit_price"], axis=1).head(2)

# explode a list-column into rows
tmp = pd.DataFrame({"id": [1, 2], "tags": [["a", "b"], ["c"]]})
tmp.explode("tags")

    The .loc[mask] and .query() forms select the same 49 rows ; use whichever reads better, but remember &/| need parentheses around each comparison, which is precisely the annoyance .query() removes. apply(..., axis=1) is the slow path — it exists in this cell to be named and avoided.

    22.2   Q2 — Data cleaning

    The reported question: "you will be given one dataset, on that you need to do further cleaning." The kit prescribes a fixed order, and the order is the answer — it is fast and nothing gets missed:

    1. Profile — shape, dtypes, nulls, duplicates, cardinality, value counts, describe
    2. Fix dtypes — numbers stored as text, dates as text, IDs as ints
    3. Standardise text/categories — case, whitespace, synonyms, rare levels
    4. Duplicates — exact and key-level
    5. Missing values — decide per column, not globally
    6. Outliers / impossible values — domain rules first, statistics second
    7. Re-profile to confirm
    The golden rule, stated by the kit itself: any imputation or scaling that learns from the data must be fitted on train only and applied to val/test — inside a Pipeline, not on the full frame. §21.7's experiment measures what happens when you ignore this: selecting features on all the rows before cross-validating pure noise produced 75.0% apparent accuracy against a true 50%. The same mechanism applies to a median imputer, and it is easy to see the leaked statistic here — the median of num_3 is −0.0765 computed on the training rows and −0.0483 computed on all rows , a difference of 0.0283 that is a function of the validation rows. §14 makes the identical argument for SMOTE: resampling must happen inside the fold, never on the frame you are about to split.
    Code — cell 26: a deliberately messy dataset 
    # ---- A deliberately messy dataset ----
n = 900
messy = pd.DataFrame({
    "cust_id":  np.random.randint(1000, 1200, n),
    "name":     np.random.choice([" Ravi Kumar", "PRIYA S ", "amit  shah", "Neha", None], n),
    "city":     np.random.choice(["Delhi", "delhi ", "DELHI", "Mumbai", "mumbai", "Bangalore",
                            "Bengaluru", "?", None], n),
    "gender":   np.random.choice(["M", "F", "male", "female", "m", "f", "U", None], n),
    "age":      np.random.choice([23, 31, 45, 52, -5, 199, np.nan, 38, 29], n),
    "income":   np.random.choice(["45,000", "62000", "1,20,000", "  85000 ", "N/A", "", None], n),
    "joined":   np.random.choice(["2021-03-01", "01/04/2022", "15-06-2020", "not available", None], n),
    "score":    np.round(np.random.normal(600, 80, n), 1),
    "segment":  np.random.choice(["SMB", "smb", "Mid", "Enterprise", "ENT", "misc", "xx"], n),
    "target":   np.random.normal(0, 1, n),
})
# inject extra pathologies
messy.loc[np.random.choice(n, 60, replace=False), "score"] = np.nan
messy.loc[np.random.choice(n, 15, replace=False), "score"] = 9999           # sentinel outliers
messy = pd.concat([messy, messy.sample(40, random_state=1)], ignore_index=True)   # dup rows
messy["constant_col"] = 1                                              # zero-variance column
messy.head(5)

    Every pathology a Q2 can contain, in one frame: whitespace and case variants, synonyms (Bengaluru/Bangalore), a junk level ("?"), impossible numerics (-5, 199), thousands separators in Indian and Western formats, three date formats plus a sentence, a 9999 sentinel, exact duplicate rows and a zero-variance column. Read it as a checklist of what to look for.

    22.2.1   Profile — always run this block first

    Code — cell 28: the reusable profile() helper 
    def profile(d: pd.DataFrame) -> pd.DataFrame:
    out = pd.DataFrame({
        "dtype":    d.dtypes.astype(str),
        "n_null":   d.isna().sum(),
        "pct_null": (d.isna().mean() * 100).round(2),
        "n_unique": d.nunique(dropna=True),
        "sample":   [d[c].dropna().iloc[0] if d[c].notna().any() else None for c in d.columns],
    })
    return out.sort_values("pct_null", ascending=False)

print("shape:", messy.shape, "| exact duplicate rows:", messy.duplicated().sum())
profile(messy)

    Type this from memory in the first two minutes of Q2 and re-run it after every stage. It is five lines and it answers "what is wrong with this data" faster than any amount of scrolling. Sorting by pct_null puts the decisions you have to make at the top.

    Profile of messy: 940 rows × 11 columns, 40 exact duplicate rows

    nameobject18719.894free text, needs normalising

    Read the two integer dtypes. cust_id is int32 while constant_col is int64 in the same frame , because the legacy np.random.randint returns a C long (32-bit on Windows) whereas a Python literal 1 becomes the platform default, int64 . Harmless here; not harmless when the two frames you are about to merge were built on different machines. Print df.dtypes for both key columns before every merge — see §22.6.7.
    Code — cell 29: describe for numerics and objects 
    messy.describe(include="number").T          # numeric summary: look for impossible min/max
messy.describe(include="object").T          # top / freq: look for case variants and junk levels

    Two different questions. The numeric one is about min/max being physically possible; the object one is about unique being far larger than the number of things that actually exist.

    Code — cell 30: value counts on the suspicious categoricals 
    for c in ["city", "gender", "segment"]:
    print(f"--- {c} ---")
    print(messy[c].value_counts(dropna=False).head(10), "\n")

    dropna=False is the whole point — you want the null count sitting in the same table as the levels, not hidden. Counting nulls separately is how people lose track of them.

    The counts make the damage concrete: city carries delhi  114, None 113, Delhi 110, ? 110, Mumbai 110, Bangalore 105, Bengaluru 94, mumbai 93, DELHI 91 — 8 non-null levels describing 3 cities. That ratio, not the null count, is the thing to report.

    22.2.2   Fix dtypes

    Code — cell 32: money-as-text and mixed-format dates 
    clean = messy.copy()

# Money/number strings: strip currency, commas, spaces, then coerce. errors='coerce' -> NaN not crash
clean["income"] = (clean["income"].astype("string")
                                  .str.replace(r"[^0-9.\-]", "", regex=True)
                                  .replace("", np.nan)
                                  .pipe(pd.to_numeric, errors="coerce"))

# Mixed date formats: 'mixed' handles per-element parsing; junk becomes NaT
clean["joined"] = pd.to_datetime(clean["joined"], format="mixed", dayfirst=True, errors="coerce")

# Downcast / categorise for memory and for sklearn
clean["cust_id"] = clean["cust_id"].astype("int32")
print(clean[["income", "joined"]].dtypes)
print("income parsed:", clean["income"].notna().mean().round(3),
      "| joined parsed:", clean["joined"].notna().mean().round(3))

    The regex [^0-9.\-] — keep digits, dot and minus, delete everything else — handles currency symbols, commas and stray spaces in one pass, and it handles the Indian 1,20,000 grouping that a naive replace(",", "")-then-int also handles but that locale-based parsing does not. Always print the parse rate afterwards; a silent errors="coerce" that turned 40% of a column into NaN is worse than a crash.

    Interpretation. income becomes Int64 and joined becomes datetime64[ns] , with parse rates of 0.552 and 0.582 . Those look alarming until you check them against the fixture: the income column was drawn from 7 values of which "N/A", "" and None are unparseable, so ≈4/7 ≈ 0.57 is the expected rate, and joined was drawn from 5 values of which 2 are unusable, so ≈3/5. The parse rate is doing its job — it tells you the coercion destroyed nothing it should have kept. The Indian-format string 1,20,000 survives as 120000 in 117 rows , which is the single result most worth spot-checking by eye.

    22.2.3   Standardise strings and collapse category variants

    Code — cell 34: normalise, map synonyms, bucket rare levels 
    def norm_text(s: pd.Series) -> pd.Series:
    return (s.astype("string")
             .str.strip()
             .str.replace(r"\s+", " ", regex=True)
             .str.lower())

clean["name"] = norm_text(clean["name"]).str.title()
clean["city"] = norm_text(clean["city"]).replace({"?": pd.NA, "": pd.NA})

# Synonym mapping (the thing graders look for)
clean["city"]   = clean["city"].replace({"bengaluru": "bangalore"})
clean["gender"] = norm_text(clean["gender"]).map(
    {"m": "M", "male": "M", "f": "F", "female": "F"}).fillna("Unknown")
clean["segment"] = norm_text(clean["segment"]).map(
    {"smb": "SMB", "mid": "Mid", "enterprise": "Enterprise", "ent": "Enterprise"})

# Rare / unknown levels -> 'Other' (prevents one-hot explosion and test-set unseen categories)
freq = clean["segment"].value_counts(normalize=True)
rare = freq[freq < 0.02].index
clean["segment"] = clean["segment"].where(~clean["segment"].isin(rare), "Other").fillna("Other")

print(clean["city"].value_counts(dropna=False).to_dict())
print(clean["gender"].value_counts().to_dict())
print(clean["segment"].value_counts().to_dict())

    Three separate operations that people conflate: normalise (case, whitespace) is mechanical; map synonyms (bengaluru → bangalore) is a domain judgement you must state; bucket rare levels into Other is a modelling decision that also protects you against unseen test categories. Note that .map() returns NaN for anything not in the dict — that is a feature: unmapped junk becomes missing and then becomes Other/Unknown explicitly, rather than surviving as a level.

    Interpretation. City goes from 8 levels to 3 — delhi 315, mumbai 203, bangalore 199, with 223 now explicitly NA because "?" was recognised as a missing-value marker rather than a city . Gender collapses to F 346 / M 345 / Unknown 249 : note that "U" and None both land in Unknown, which is a decision — if "U" means declined to answer and None means not collected, those are different and you should keep them apart. Segment ends as Other 282 / SMB 268 / Enterprise 254 / Mid 136 , and the largest level is now the bucket, because misc and xx together outweigh any real level. When Other wins, say so — it means the category was never usable as given.

    22.2.4   Duplicates

    Code — cell 36: exact duplicates and key-level duplicates 
    print("exact dups:", clean.duplicated().sum())
clean = clean.drop_duplicates().reset_index(drop=True)

# Key-level duplicates: same customer appearing twice — keep the most recent record
key_dups = clean.duplicated(subset=["cust_id"], keep=False).sum()
print("rows involved in cust_id duplication:", key_dups)

dedup_by_key = (clean.sort_values("joined")
                     .drop_duplicates(subset=["cust_id"], keep="last"))
print("after key dedup:", dedup_by_key.shape)

    keep=False in duplicated flags every row involved in a duplication, not just the extra copies — that is the number you report. And sort_values(...).drop_duplicates(keep="last") is the idiomatic "keep the most recent record per key"; the sort is what makes "last" mean anything.

    Do not run the key-level dedup reflexively. Exact duplicates here are 40 rows , and dropping them takes the frame to 900 × 11 — that is unambiguous repair. But 897 of the 900 rows are involved in cust_id duplication, and deduplicating by key would leave 197 rows , discarding 78% of the data. Here cust_id is simply not a primary key — it is a customer attribute of a transaction table. Establish what one row means before you dedupe on anything, and in a test say it in the notebook: "cust_id repeats by design; deduplicating on it would be wrong." This is why the kit computes dedup_by_key into a separate variable and never uses it.

    22.2.5   Impossible values and outliers

    Order matters: kill domain-impossible values first — they poison every statistic you would use to detect statistical outliers — then treat the outliers. Prefer clipping/winsorising over dropping rows in a test; dropping rows can break a required output row-count.

    Code — cell 38: domain rules, IQR, z-score, winsorising, log transform 
    # 1) Domain rules -> NaN
clean.loc[~clean["age"].between(0, 100), "age"] = np.nan
clean.loc[clean["score"] >= 9000, "score"] = np.nan          # 9999 sentinel
clean.loc[clean["income"] <= 0, "income"] = np.nan

# 2) IQR rule
def iqr_bounds(s, k=1.5):
    q1, q3 = s.quantile([.25, .75])
    iqr = q3 - q1
    return q1 - k * iqr, q3 + k * iqr

lo, hi = iqr_bounds(clean["score"].dropna())
print(f"IQR bounds for score: {lo:.1f} .. {hi:.1f} | flagged: {(~clean['score'].between(lo, hi)).sum()}")

# 3) Z-score rule
z = (clean["score"] - clean["score"].mean()) / clean["score"].std()
print("z>3 count:", (z.abs() > 3).sum())

# 4) Treatment — winsorise at the 1st/99th percentile (keeps the row, tames the tail)
clean["score_w"] = clean["score"].clip(*clean["score"].quantile([.01, .99]))
clean["income_w"] = clean["income"].clip(upper=clean["income"].quantile(.99))

# 5) Log transform for right-skewed money variables
clean["log_income"] = np.log1p(clean["income_w"])
print("skew before/after:", round(clean["income"].skew(), 2), round(clean["log_income"].skew(), 2))

    clip(*s.quantile([.01, .99])) is the whole of winsorising in one expression — the star unpacks the two-element quantile Series into lower, upper. np.log1p, not np.log, because incomes of 0 are legal and log(0) = -inf would poison the column.

    Interpretation. The 9999 sentinel is the important one: it was not a null, so the profile did not flag it, and it would have dragged the mean and inflated the standard deviation of score — which is why domain rules must run before the z-score rule. Once removed, the IQR fence sits at 382.9 … 816.9 and the cell prints 78 flagged points while the z > 3 rule flags 1 . That 78-versus-1 gap is a bug in the diagnostic, and worth dissecting (see the warning below). On the age column, 195 rows carried the impossible values −5 or 199 , all now NaN. Finally the log transform takes income's skew from 0.45 to 0.08 : a real improvement, but note the starting skew was only 0.45 — this fixture's income is nearly symmetric, so if you had reported "log-transform fixed the severe skew" you would have been describing a problem that was not there.
    The outlier count the kit prints is wrong, and the mechanism is one line long. ~s.between(lo, hi) is True for NaN, because between returns False for a missing value and the negation flips it. So the 78 "flagged" points are 73 nulls plus only 5 genuine out-of-fence values . Five out of 827 non-null scores is 0.60% , which is exactly what theory predicts: for roughly Gaussian data the upper fence here sits at +2.674σ , and P(|Z| > 2.674) ≈ 0.7%. The z-score rule reports 1 because a comparison against NaN is False, so nulls are silently excluded there — the two rules disagreed only about missing values, never about outliers. The fix is (~s.between(lo, hi)) & s.notna(), and the habit is: any ~ applied to a comparison on a column with nulls needs a & s.notna() beside it.

    22.2.6   Missing values — pick a strategy per column

    The per-column decision table
    SituationReasonable choice
    Numeric, roughly symmetricmean
    Numeric, skewed or has outliersmedian (default choice in a test)
    Categoricalmode, or an explicit "Missing" level
    Missingness itself is informativeadd an is_missing indicator flag
    Grouped structure (city, segment)group-wise median via transform
    More than 60–70% missingusually drop the column, and say why
    Time seriesffill / bfill / interpolate
    Code — cell 40: re-profile before deciding 
    # quick view of what's left
profile(clean).head(8)

    Re-profiling between stages is not ceremony: the null counts have moved, because the domain rules in §22.2.5 converted impossible values into missing ones.

    And they moved a lot. income is now 44.56% null (401 rows), up from 14.79%; age is 30.78% null (277 rows), up from 10.11%; joined is 42.0%; city 23.56% . Every one of those increases is work you did — replacing junk with an honest NaN. If you report the null percentages from the first profile you will be describing a dataset that no longer exists.

    Code — cell 41: flags, simple fills, group-wise fill, dropping useless columns 
    work = clean.copy()

# Flag before filling — the flag is often predictive
for c in ["income", "score", "age"]:
    work[f"{c}_was_na"] = work[c].isna().astype("int8")

# Simple fills
work["age"] = work["age"].fillna(work["age"].median())

# Group-wise fill with a global fallback (the version that scores well)
work["income"] = (work.groupby("segment")["income"]
                      .transform(lambda s: s.fillna(s.median()))
                      .fillna(work["income"].median()))

# Categorical: explicit level beats silent mode-filling
work["city"] = work["city"].fillna("Missing")

# Time-series style
# work = work.sort_values("joined")
# work["score"] = work["score"].ffill().bfill()
# work["score"] = work["score"].interpolate(method="linear", limit_direction="both")

# Drop columns that are useless: all-null, constant, or >70% missing
drop_cols = [c for c in work.columns
             if work[c].nunique(dropna=True) <= 1 or work[c].isna().mean() > 0.7]
print("dropping:", drop_cols)
work = work.drop(columns=drop_cols)
print("remaining nulls:", int(work.isna().sum().sum()), "| shape:", work.shape)

    Three things worth a mark each: the _was_na flag before the fill (the missingness is often the signal); the group-wise median with a .fillna(global_median) fallback for groups that are entirely missing; and an explicit "Missing" level for categoricals rather than silently pushing everything to the mode.

    Interpretation. Only constant_col is dropped , leaving 900 × 16 . But 1505 nulls remain , and the useful question is where: income_w 401, log_income 401, joined 378, name 179, score 73, score_w 73 . Every one is a column the cell never addressed — the derived _w/log_ columns were built before the fill and so kept the original holes, and joined, name and score were simply never in the fill list. That is the ordering trap of Q2 in miniature: derive after you impute, or impute everything you derived. Note too that the group-wise income fill worked precisely because segment had already been repaired in §22.2.3 — filling by a column that still had 7 junk levels would have produced 7 different medians.

    22.2.7   sklearn imputers — the leakage-safe way

    SimpleImputer / KNNImputer / IterativeImputer inside a ColumnTransformer learn their statistics on fit and reuse them on transform. This is what you want the moment the question hands you separate train/val/test files — which, per the format quote, it does.

    Code — cell 43: ColumnTransformer with imputers, scaler, one-hot; KNNImputer 
    from sklearn.impute import SimpleImputer, KNNImputer
from sklearn.preprocessing import StandardScaler, OneHotEncoder, OrdinalEncoder
from sklearn.compose import ColumnTransformer
from sklearn.pipeline import Pipeline

num_demo = ["age", "income", "score"]
cat_demo = ["city", "gender", "segment"]

# GOTCHA: pandas' nullable "string"/"Int64" dtypes use pd.NA, which sklearn cannot evaluate
# ("TypeError: boolean value of NA is ambiguous"). Convert to plain object/float + np.nan first.
sk_ready = clean.copy()
for c in cat_demo:
    sk_ready[c] = sk_ready[c].astype(object).where(sk_ready[c].notna(), np.nan)

num_pipe = Pipeline([("imp", SimpleImputer(strategy="median")),
                     ("sc",  StandardScaler())])
cat_pipe = Pipeline([("imp", SimpleImputer(strategy="most_frequent")),
                     ("oh",  OneHotEncoder(handle_unknown="ignore", sparse_output=False))])

demo_pre = ColumnTransformer([("num", num_pipe, num_demo),
                              ("cat", cat_pipe, cat_demo)], remainder="drop")

X_demo = demo_pre.fit_transform(sk_ready)
print("encoded shape:", X_demo.shape)
print("first 8 feature names:", list(demo_pre.get_feature_names_out())[:8])

# KNN imputation when columns are correlated (slower, sometimes worth it)
knn_out = KNNImputer(n_neighbors=5).fit_transform(sk_ready[num_demo])
print("knn-imputed nulls left:", int(np.isnan(knn_out).sum()))

    Two things to carry away. get_feature_names_out() is how you map encoded columns back to human names — without it, coefficient and importance tables are unreadable. And remainder="drop" versus "passthrough" is a decision, not a default: dropping silently discards every column you forgot to list.

    Interpretation. Three numeric and three categorical columns encode to 13 features on 900 rows : 3 numeric passthroughs plus 3 city + 3 gender + 4 segment dummies, named num__age, num__income, num__score, cat__city_bangalore, cat__city_delhi, cat__city_mumbai, cat__gender_F, cat__gender_M, … . The KNNImputer leaves 0 nulls . Note the column count is a check you can do before running: if it comes out at 14 you have a level you did not know about, and if it comes out at 12 a level vanished. And note what KNNImputer assumes — it is §8's k-NN with the same requirement, that the columns be on comparable scales, so it belongs after a scaler, not before one.
    handle_unknown="ignore" — remember this one. If a category appears in test but not in train, OneHotEncoder raises by default and your submission cell dies at the last moment. Verified: encoding an unseen level with the default handle_unknown="error" raises ValueError , while handle_unknown="ignore" emits an all-zeros row [0.0, 0.0] and carries on. The ordinal equivalent is OrdinalEncoder(handle_unknown="use_encoded_value", unknown_value=-1). This is a guaranteed occurrence when the rare levels of §22.2.3 were bucketed on train only, so treat it as mandatory boilerplate rather than a defensive extra.
    Two pandas/sklearn interface details, adjudicated. (i) The kit's comment on cell 43 warns that pandas' nullable string/Int64 dtypes carry pd.NA, which raises "boolean value of NA is ambiguous" inside sklearn. That is sound advice, and note it converts only the categorical columns — income stays Int64 and is handled by SimpleImputer without complaint on this stack (pandas 2.3.3, scikit-learn 1.9.0 ). Convert both kinds if you want the code to be portable. (ii) Cell 38's line clean.loc[clean["income"] <= 0, "income"] = np.nan builds a nullable boolean mask that contains pd.NA wherever income is missing. On this stack .loc accepts it , but the defensive form costs six characters and never surprises you: clean.loc[(clean["income"] <= 0).fillna(False), "income"] = np.nan.

    22.2.8   Missingness mechanisms — MCAR / MAR / MNAR

    §22.2.6 chose a fill per column and §22.2.7 chose an estimator to do the filling. Neither answers the prior question: why is this value missing? The answer decides whether dropping the rows is honest, whether imputing them is honest, and whether either can be honest at all. Three mechanisms, one sentence each.

    • MCAR — missing completely at random. The probability of being missing does not depend on anything, observed or unobserved. Example: a temperature sensor dies on random days, so those readings are absent for reasons that have nothing to do with the temperature or with anything else in the table. The observed rows are a genuine random sample of all rows.
    • MAR — missing at random, which is a badly-named "missing at random given the observed data". The probability of being missing depends on columns you can see. Example: income is missing far more often for young respondents — and age is in the table, so the missingness is fully predictable from data you have.
    • MNAR — missing not at random. The probability of being missing depends on the missing value itself. Example: high earners decline to state their income, so whether income is present depends on how large income is — the one thing you cannot look up.

    The distinction is not academic bookkeeping. Under MCAR, throwing the rows away costs you power and nothing else. Under MAR, throwing them away biases every estimate, but conditioning on the observed cause repairs it. Under MNAR nothing in the dataset repairs it.

    Code — construct all three mechanisms on one column, then diagnose them 
    rng = np.random.default_rng(514)
n   = 6000
age    = rng.integers(20, 70, n).astype(float)
income = 180.0 + 7.5 * age + rng.normal(0, 55, n)     # income genuinely rises with age
sensor = rng.normal(50, 10, n)                        # an unrelated observed column

expit = lambda z: 1 / (1 + np.exp(-z))
p_mcar = np.full(n, 0.30)                                     # nothing predicts it
p_mar  = 0.62 * expit(-(age - 42) / 7.0)                      # the YOUNG skip the question
p_mnar = 0.62 * expit((income - np.median(income)) / 60.0)    # HIGH EARNERS hide the answer

for tag, p in [("mcar", p_mcar), ("mar", p_mar), ("mnar", p_mnar)]:
    hidden = rng.random(n) < p
    df[f"income_{tag}"] = np.where(hidden, np.nan, income)
    df[f"m_{tag}"]      = hidden.astype(int)          # the missingness INDICATOR

df["age_band"] = pd.cut(df["age"], [19, 30, 42, 55, 70])

# --- Diagnostic 1: null rate by observed group. A flat column is consistent with MCAR. ---
df.groupby("age_band", observed=True)[["m_mcar", "m_mar", "m_mnar"]].mean()

# --- Diagnostic 2: correlate the indicator with every observed column. ---
for tag in ["mcar", "mar", "mnar"]:
    print(tag, df[f"m_{tag}"].corr(df["age"]), df[f"m_{tag}"].corr(df["sensor"]))

# --- Diagnostic 3 (a t-test version of the same idea) ---
# stats.ttest_ind(df.loc[df["m_x"] == 1, "age"], df.loc[df["m_x"] == 0, "age"], equal_var=False)

    The two diagnostics are the same question asked twice: does knowing whether the value is missing tell me anything about the columns I can see? Run them on every column with non-trivial nulls, and run them against the target too — a missingness indicator that predicts y is the strongest possible argument for keeping the flag as a feature (§22.2.6). Neither diagnostic requires the true values, which is exactly why neither can settle the MNAR question.

    Null rate by age band, all three mechanisms, n = 6000
    age bandMCAR null rateMAR null rateMNAR null rate
    20–300.28970.56840.0754
    31–420.29220.41700.1910
    43–550.28060.15700.3682
    56–690.30100.03920.5386
    spread (max − min)0.02040.52920.4632
    corr(indicator, age)0.0018−0.45980.3925
    corr(indicator, sensor)−0.01470.0114−0.0046
    overall null rate0.29100.27800.3078
    Interpretation — what the diagnostics can and cannot see. The MCAR column is flat: 0.2806 to 0.3010 across bands, a spread of 0.0204 that is pure sampling noise, and its indicator correlates 0.0018 with age and −0.0147 with the unrelated sensor. That is what "no observable structure" looks like, and it is the only one of the three claims the data can support. The MAR and MNAR columns both show a violent gradient — spreads of 0.5292 and 0.4632 — so both are decisively not MCAR, and any test you run will say so. But look at what you cannot do: nothing in this table separates the second column from the third. Both correlate strongly with age, in opposite directions, which looks like a distinguishing fact but is not — MNAR's indicator correlates with age only because income correlates with age at 0.8925 , so hiding high incomes hides old respondents as a side effect. Had the sign of the income effect been reversed, MNAR would have produced MAR's exact signature. MNAR is untestable from the data alone. The only evidence that separates them is the values you do not have, and the only substitute for those values is domain reasoning: "was this question refused, or was it never asked?" — a question about the data-collection process, not about the dataframe.
    What each mechanism does to the mean, and whether conditioning repairs it. True mean 511.206
    mechanismobserved mean
    (= listwise deletion)    		 biasafter group-wise fill
    (mean within age band)    		 biasverdict
    MCAR511.017−0.189 511.432+0.226unbiased either way
    MAR541.498+30.292 511.178−0.029bias removed by conditioning on age
    MNAR476.434−34.772 502.720−8.486bias reduced, not removed
    Interpretation. Three readings, in increasing order of how much they matter. (i) Under MCAR, dropping the missing rows leaves the mean at 511.017 against a truth of 511.206 — an error of 0.189 on 6000 rows, i.e. nothing. Listwise deletion is safe here in the sense of unbiased; it still costs 29.1% of the sample and therefore power. (ii) Under MAR, the observed mean is 541.498, biased upward by 30.292 — because the young are missing and the young earn less, so the survivors are older and richer. Filling with the overall mean cannot help: it fills in that same wrong number. Filling within age_band drives the bias to −0.029, essentially zero. This is the entire practical content of MAR: the bias is a function of a column you have, so conditioning on that column removes it — which is what groupby("segment").transform(lambda s: s.fillna(s.median())) in §22.2.6, and IterativeImputer in §22.2.7, are actually for. (iii) Under MNAR, the observed mean is 476.434, biased downward by 34.772, and conditioning on age recovers only three-quarters of it: 8.486 of bias survives, because within any age band it is still the higher earners who are missing. No richer imputer fixes this — KNNImputer and IterativeImputer both learn from the observed rows, and the observed rows are the non-representative ones. One more thing every imputation does, visible even under MCAR: mean-filling drops the column's standard deviation from 122.568 to 103.756 , because 29% of the values are now identical. The mean survives; the variance, and every correlation and standard error computed from it, does not.
    What to actually do — and to say.
    If you believe…DoDo not
    MCARListwise deletion is defensible if you can afford the rows; otherwise impute (median) and add the _was_na flag anyway assume MCAR by default — it is the strongest assumption of the three and the least often true
    MARImpute conditionally on the observed cause — group-wise median, IterativeImputer, or a model — and always keep the missing-indicator, which lets a model recover any residual effect drop the rows: deletion is biased under MAR, and that is the case this framework exists for
    MNARModel the mechanism (selection models, pattern-mixture) or, in a test, do the honest cheap thing: keep the indicator, state the assumption, and run a sensitivity analysis — impute the missing incomes at the observed mean, and again at the 75th percentile, and report how much the conclusion moves report a single imputed estimate as if it were the answer

    Two structural rules carry over unchanged. Whichever branch you take, the imputer must be fitted on train only and applied to validation and test — §22.2.7's ColumnTransformer, not a fill on the full frame; the median of a column is a statistic like any other and leaks like any other (§21.7). And when the missingness is correlated with a rare class, imputation interacts with resampling: fit the imputer inside the fold and resample inside the fold, in that order, exactly as §14 requires of SMOTE. The sentence for the interview: "I can show this is not MCAR — the null rate runs from 0.57 to 0.04 across age bands. I cannot show whether it is MAR or MNAR, because that depends on the values I do not have; I have assumed MAR, imputed within age band, kept the indicator, and here is the sensitivity of the result to that assumption."

    22.3   Datetime & time-series preprocessing

    Q1 and Q2 both hand you a date column, and in both of them the date column is the one people lose marks on — not because the calls are hard, but because a date is the only dtype where doing nothing silently gives you a column of text that still prints like a date. This subsection is built from a second source: a preprocessing cheat-sheet the user assembled from a working chat, 38 numbered points plus a "15 syntaxes to memorise" list. The code is kept as the chat wrote it; every behavioural claim with an observable consequence was re-executed by work/computes/s22_timeseries.py on pandas 2.3.3 / numpy 2.5.2 , and every place where the environment does something the chat did not mention — the isocalendar() dtype, the ISO week-year, what rolling("7D") demands of its index, the frequency-alias deprecation — is adjudicated in a box where it arises.

    The one mental rule the whole subsection collapses into:
    pd.to_datetime() make it a datetime →.dt pull parts out →subtraction make durations →groupby + diff/shift/transform make within-entity history →rolling/resample change the frequency
    Everything in §22.3 is one of those five moves. If you can name which move a question is asking for, the syntax is a lookup; if you cannot, no amount of syntax helps.

    22.3.1   Convert and validate

    A column of dates arrives as object — Python strings that happen to look like dates — and pandas will happily sort them lexicographically, compare them as text and refuse to subtract them. The first line of any date work is df["date"].dtype; the second is pd.to_datetime.

    Code — convert, with an explicit format and a coercion policy 
    # Step 0: what have I actually got?
print(df["date"].dtype)          # object  -> text; datetime64[ns] -> a real datetime

# Plain conversion (pandas infers the format from the first non-null values)
df["date"] = pd.to_datetime(df["date"])

# With a KNOWN format — faster, and it refuses to guess wrong on ambiguous dates
df["date"] = pd.to_datetime(df["date"], format="%d-%m-%Y")

# Date + time together
df["ts"] = pd.to_datetime(df["ts"], format="%d-%m-%Y %H:%M:%S")

# Invalid dates (31-02-2025 does not exist) -> NaT instead of an exception
df["date"] = pd.to_datetime(df["date"], errors="coerce")
print("parse rate:", df["date"].notna().mean())      # ALWAYS print this

# Build a single Timestamp, or stitch a date column and a time column together
pd.Timestamp("2025-03-15")
pd.to_datetime(df["date"].astype(str) + " " + df["time"].astype(str))

    errors="coerce" is the difference between a cell that dies and a cell that reports. But it is only half the discipline: coercion is silent, so the parse rate is the other half. On the four-element probe ["15-03-2025", "31-02-2025", "01-12-2025", "not a date"] the coerced parse rate is 0.5 — two NaT , one for an impossible day-of-month and one for prose. Say which is which: a date that failed because February has no 31st is a data-entry bug; a date that failed because the cell says "not available" is a missing value.

    The format codes worth memorising
    CodeMeansExampleCodeMeansExample
    %dday of month, zero-padded15 %Hhour, 24-hour clock18
    %mmonth number03 %Ihour, 12-hour clock06
    %Y4-digit year2025 %Mminute30
    %y2-digit year25 %Ssecond45

    Two of those collide in a way worth saying out loud: %m is the month and %M is the minute, %y is two digits and %Y is four. A format string that swaps either pair does not error — it produces plausible, wrong dates.

    Without errors="coerce" the whole cell dies. The same probe run with the default errors="raise" gives ValueError: day is out of range for month, at position 1 — informative (it even names the offending position) but fatal in a timed test. The pattern is: coerce first to keep moving, then go back and look at what became NaT. NaN is a missing numeric, NaT is a missing datetime; they behave the same way under isna() and they are not interchangeable in a fillna.

    22.3.2   Component extraction

    A raw timestamp is almost useless to a model — 1.7 billion nanoseconds since 1970 is a number with no structure a tree can split on usefully. What carries signal is the parts: which month, which day of week, which hour.

    Code — the .dt accessor, and the two flags that earn marks 
    d = df["order_ts"]                       # dtype must be datetime64[ns] or .dt raises

df["year"]      = d.dt.year
df["month"]     = d.dt.month             # 1..12
df["day"]       = d.dt.day
df["dayofweek"] = d.dt.dayofweek         # Monday=0 ... Sunday=6
df["day_name"]  = d.dt.day_name()        # 'Saturday'  (text — for reading, not for modelling)
df["hour"]      = d.dt.hour
df["minute"]    = d.dt.minute
df["second"]    = d.dt.second
df["quarter"]   = d.dt.quarter           # Jan->1, Apr->2, Jul->3, Oct->4
df["week"]      = d.dt.isocalendar().week            # ISO week-of-year, NOT dayofweek
df["month_name"]= d.dt.month_name()
df["period_m"]  = d.dt.to_period("M")    # 2025-01-15 -> 2025-01, for monthly group-bys

# The two binary flags that appear in every fraud / demand question
df["is_weekend"] = (d.dt.dayofweek >= 5).astype(int)
df["is_night"]   = ((d.dt.hour >= 0) & (d.dt.hour < 6)).astype(int)

    Learn dayofweek's convention as a fact: Monday = 0 , so weekend is >= 5. Half the weekend flags written under time pressure are off by one because the author assumed Sunday = 0. And day_name() returns text: fine in a report, a 7-level categorical in a model — prefer the integer plus the cyclical encoding of §22.3.6.

    Every component of one timestamp, 2025-03-15 18:30:45
    callvaluecallvaluecallvalue
    .dt.year2025 .dt.dayofweek5 .dt.quarter1
    .dt.month3 .dt.day_name()Saturday .dt.isocalendar().week11
    .dt.day15 .dt.hour18 .dt.month_name()March
    .dt.minute30 .dt.second45 .dt.to_period("M")2025-03
    Two things about isocalendar() that the cheat-sheet does not mention, both verified. (i) It returns a DataFrame with columns ['year', 'week', 'day'] , and week comes back as UInt32 — pandas' nullable integer, which survives arithmetic as UInt32 and carries pd.NA rather than np.nan. That is the same "boolean value of NA is ambiguous" landmine as §22.2.7; call .astype(int) before handing the column to numpy, sklearn or xgboost. (ii) The ISO week-year is not the calendar year: 2025-12-31 is ISO 2026, week 1 , while 2025-01-01 is ISO 2025, week 1. Grouping by (dt.year, isocalendar().week) therefore splits the last week of December across two years; group by isocalendar().year or not at all.

    22.3.3   Durations — the features that actually predict

    Raw dates rarely predict anything; elapsed time does. "Account was created on 2019-04-02" is a fact about the calendar; "this transaction happened 3 days after the account was created" is a fraud feature. Subtracting two datetime64[ns] columns gives a timedelta64[ns] , which then needs its own accessor to become a number.

    Code — timedeltas, recency, age features 
    # datetime - datetime = timedelta  (a duration, not a point in time)
gap = df["purchase_date"] - df["signup_date"]      # dtype: timedelta64[ns]

df["days_since_signup"]  = gap.dt.days                        # WHOLE days, truncated
df["days_exact"]         = gap.dt.total_seconds() / 86400     # fractional days
df["hours_since_signup"] = gap.dt.total_seconds() / 3600
df["mins_since_signup"]  = gap.dt.total_seconds() / 60

# Recency against 'now'
today = pd.Timestamp.today()                       # or pd.Timestamp.now() for date+time
df["customer_age_days"] = (today - df["signup_date"]).dt.days

# Age-at-event: the single most reusable fraud/churn feature
df["account_age_days"] = (df["transaction_date"] - df["account_created"]).dt.days

# Per-customer lifetime, in one aggregation
life = df.groupby("cust_id")["order_date"].agg(["min", "max"])
life["lifetime_days"] = (life["max"] - life["min"]).dt.days

    Check the arithmetic once by hand so you trust it forever: 2025-01-01 to 2025-01-15 is 14 days , not 15 — a difference counts intervals, not endpoints. pd.Timestamp.today() makes your notebook irreproducible: re-run it tomorrow and every recency feature shifts by one. In a graded test freeze it — REF = pd.Timestamp("2026-01-01") — and say in one line that you did.

    Interpretation — .dt.days versus .dt.total_seconds(), the distinction that costs a mark. For a duration of 2 days 6 hours: .dt.days returns 2 , because it reports the whole-day component and throws the remainder away; .dt.total_seconds() / 86400 returns 2.25 , and / 3600 returns 54.0 hours , / 60 3240.0 minutes . The rule: .dt.days is a truncation, so any gap shorter than a day becomes 0 and any sub-day variation vanishes. On transaction-level data — where the interesting gaps are minutes — .dt.days silently produces a column of zeros, which is exactly the failure Practice 22.4 walks into deliberately. Use total_seconds() whenever the resolution of the question is finer than a day.

    22.3.4   Filter, sort, and the groupby().last() trap

    Code — comparisons against strings, between, multi-key sorting 
    # A datetime column compares directly against a date STRING — pandas parses the right-hand side
df[df["date"] >= "2025-01-01"]

# Two-sided: each condition needs its own parentheses, because & binds tighter than >=
df[(df["date"] >= "2025-01-01") & (df["date"] <= "2025-03-31")]

# The interview-friendly form — inclusive on BOTH ends
df[df["date"].between("2025-01-01", "2025-03-31")]

# Sorting: single key, descending, and the multi-key form that everything downstream depends on
df.sort_values("date")
df.sort_values("date", ascending=False)
df.sort_values(["cust_id", "date"])          # entity first, time second — memorise this order

# Earliest / latest
df["date"].min(), df["date"].max()
df.groupby("cust_id")["date"].min()          # first order per customer

    between is inclusive at both ends by default (inclusive="both"); if the question says "in Q1" that is what you want, if it says "before April" it is not. And sort_values(["cust_id", "date"]) — entity first, time second — is the precondition for every single call in §22.3.5. Type it before you need it.

    groupby().last() does not mean "latest" — demonstrated. last() returns the last row in the current ordering, which is chronological only if you sorted. On a five-row frame where customer 1's rows appear in the order 2025-03-05, 2025-01-10, 2025-02-14, the unsorted groupby("cust_id")["date"].last() returns 2025-02-14 for customer 1 , while the true maximum is 2025-03-05 . Customer 2 comes out right by luck , which is what makes this bug so durable: it is wrong for some groups, so a spot-check passes. Two fixes, and prefer the second: df.sort_values(["cust_id","date"]).groupby("cust_id").last(), or just use .max(), which does not care about order at all. The same argument applies to .first(), to drop_duplicates(keep="last") (§22.2.4) and to .nth().

    22.3.5   Group-temporal patterns: transform, diff, shift

    This is where datetime preprocessing stops being clerical. Three patterns cover the fraud and churn questions almost completely, and all three are the same shape: sort by [entity, time] → group by entity → apply a within-group temporal operator.

    Code — time-since-first, time-since-previous, and the lag column 
    df = df.sort_values(["cust_id", "txn_time"])        # NOT optional

# (1) transform("min"): broadcast each customer's FIRST event onto all their rows
df["first_txn"]        = df.groupby("cust_id")["txn_time"].transform("min")
df["days_since_first"] = (df["txn_time"] - df["first_txn"]).dt.days

# (2) groupby -> diff: time since this customer's PREVIOUS transaction (the fraud feature)
df["gap"]         = df.groupby("cust_id")["txn_time"].diff()
df["gap_minutes"] = df["gap"].dt.total_seconds() / 60
df["gap_days"]    = df["gap"].dt.total_seconds() / 86400

# (3) groupby -> shift: the previous VALUE, per customer (the lag feature)
df["prev_amount"]  = df.groupby("cust_id")["amount"].shift(1)
df["amount_delta"] = df["amount"] - df["prev_amount"]

# Per-customer lifetime in one line
(df.groupby("cust_id")["txn_time"].agg(["min", "max"])
   .assign(lifetime_days=lambda d: (d["max"] - d["min"]).dt.days))

    The pattern to say out loud is groupby → diff → dt.total_seconds. Three failure modes, all silent: forgetting the sort (gaps become nonsense), forgetting the groupby (the first row of each customer imports the previous customer's timestamp), and using .dt.days on minute-scale gaps (a column of zeros — §22.3.3).

    The three operators on one five-row frame, sorted by [cust_id, date]
    cust_iddateamountdays_since_first gap_daysprev_amount
    12025-01-1075.000——
    12025-02-1440.003535.075.00
    12025-03-05100.005419.040.00
    22025-01-20250.000——
    22025-02-28310.003939.0250.00
    Interpretation. Read the two — cells in the gap_days column: they are NaT at the first row of each group , exactly as they should be — a first transaction has no predecessor. That is the same structural NaN as §22.1.7's shift column, and the same advice applies: do not fillna(0) it. A gap of zero means "two transactions at the same instant", which is a strong fraud signal; a gap of NaN means "this is the customer's first transaction", which is a different and also useful signal. Encode it as gap_days.isna() and leave the number missing — xgboost learns a default direction for it (§13.13) and so does HistGradientBoosting. Note also that customer 1's days_since_first (0, 35, 54) is cumulative while gap_days (—, 35, 19) is incremental: they answer "how long have they been with us" and "how bursty are they", and a good feature set carries both.

    22.3.6   Cyclical encoding: why December must sit next to January

    Month, day-of-week and hour are cyclical: after 12 comes 1, after 23:00 comes 00:00. Encoded as plain integers, the model is told that December and January are 11 units apart — further apart than January and December's actual neighbour, and further than any other pair in the year. The fix is to place the value on a circle.

    Code — sin/cos encoding for month and hour 
    df["month_sin"] = np.sin(2 * np.pi * df["month"] / 12)
df["month_cos"] = np.cos(2 * np.pi * df["month"] / 12)

df["hour_sin"]  = np.sin(2 * np.pi * df["hour"] / 24)
df["hour_cos"]  = np.cos(2 * np.pi * df["hour"] / 24)

df["dow_sin"]   = np.sin(2 * np.pi * df["dayofweek"] / 7)
df["dow_cos"]   = np.cos(2 * np.pi * df["dayofweek"] / 7)

    Both components are required — sin alone maps March and September to the same value, and the pair is what makes the map injective. The denominator is the period: 12 for months, 24 for hours, 7 for weekdays, 365.25 for day-of-year. Getting it wrong (dividing hours by 12) folds the circle in half and makes 3am identical to 3pm.

    What the encoding buys, in distances
    pairraw integer distancedistance in (sin, cos) spacewhat it should be
    December → January110.5176adjacent
    January → February10.5176adjacent
    January → July62.0000opposite (the diameter)
    23:00 → 00:00230.2611adjacent
    00:00 → 01:0010.2611adjacent
    Interpretation. December sits at (sin, cos) = (0.0, 1.0) and January at (0.5, 0.866) , a distance of 0.5176 — identical to the January–February distance , because every adjacent pair on a 12-point circle is the same chord, $\,2\sin(\pi/12)$. The raw integers said 11 and 1 . Opposite months land at exactly 2.0 , the diameter of the unit circle. The hour version is the same story with a smaller chord because the circle has 24 points rather than 12. Who needs this. Distance- and coefficient-based models — k-NN (§8), k-means (§19), linear and penalised regression (§2, §6), neural nets (§4) — need it badly, because "11 apart" enters the arithmetic literally. A tree does not strictly need it: it can carve month into {12} ∪ {1,2} with two splits. But it must spend those splits, and on a shallow tree or a small dataset that is a real cost — which is why the encoding stays in §22.4's XGBoost feature set even though it is not, strictly, necessary there.

    22.3.7   Resample, rolling and lag features

    Code — changing frequency, windowed statistics, and lags 
    # --- resample: aggregate the series into a DIFFERENT frequency (needs a DatetimeIndex) ---
daily   = df.set_index("date")["sales"].resample("D").sum()
monthly = df.set_index("date")["sales"].resample("ME").sum()      # "ME" = month END
weekly  = df.set_index("date")["sales"].resample("W").sum()
hourly  = df.set_index("ts")["amount"].resample("h").mean()

# --- rolling: a window that slides with the row ---
daily.rolling(7).sum()          # COUNT-based: the last 7 ROWS
daily.rolling("7D").sum()       # TIME-based: the last 7 DAYS (needs a sorted DatetimeIndex)
daily.rolling(7, min_periods=1).mean()

# --- lags, per entity ---
df["prev_amount"] = df.groupby("cust_id")["amount"].shift(1)
df["lag_2"]       = df.groupby("cust_id")["amount"].shift(2)

    Count-based versus time-based is the whole point of the pair, and it only shows up when the index has holes. rolling(7) asks "the last seven observations"; on a series with missing days that can span a month. rolling("7D") asks "the last seven days" and gives you however many observations that happens to be — which is almost always the question a business asks.

    Count-based versus time-based, on a series with a five-day hole
    datevalue.rolling(3).sum().rolling("3D").sum()why they differ
    2025-01-0110—10time windows default to min_periods=1
    2025-01-0220—30same
    2025-01-03306060agree: 3 rows = 3 days here
    2025-01-09409040the hole: 3 rows reaches back to Jan 2; 3 days reaches nothing
    2025-01-105012090same cause
    2025-01-1160150150agree again once 3 rows span 3 days
    Interpretation. On 2025-01-09 the count-based window returns 90 — it has silently reached across a five-day gap and summed 20 + 30 + 40, values from a week earlier. The time-based window returns 40, because in the previous three days nothing else happened. Neither is "correct"; they answer different questions, and the one you want in a "sales in the last week" feature is almost always the time-based one. Resampling to a complete daily grid first is the third option: resample("D") on this series produces 11 rows , 5 of them zeros — after which rolling(3) and rolling("3D") agree by construction. State which you did: "I resampled to a complete daily index so that count-based and time-based windows coincide" is one sentence and removes the entire ambiguity.
    Three ways a window bites, all verified.
    • Time-based rolling needs a datetime index. Call .rolling("3D") on an integer-indexed Series and you get ValueError: window must be an integer 0 or greater — a confusing message, because the real complaint is about the index, not the window.
    • And it must be sorted. Shuffle the index and the same call raises ValueError: index values must be monotonic . This one is a gift: pandas refuses rather than computing something meaningless. Count-based rolling(3) on the same shuffled index computes happily and returns garbage.
    • A window that includes the present row is leakage. rolling(7).mean() at row t includes yt itself. If y is your target, that feature contains one-seventh of the answer. Every rolling feature built from the target must be .shift(1).rolling(k), never .rolling(k) — §22.4.1 measures what the difference is worth, and §21.7 is the general statement of the rule.
    Frequency aliases moved, and the chat is on the right side of it. The chat gives monthly as "ME", weekly as "W" and hourly as "h", which is correct for pandas ≥ 2.2. The older "M" and "H" still run on pandas 2.3.3 but emit FutureWarning: 'M' is deprecated and will be removed in a future version, please use 'ME' instead . Note that §22.6.1's pandas cheat-table, which is quoted from the reference kit, still shows resample("M") — that row is reproduced as the kit wrote it, and "ME" is what you should type. A blanket warnings.filterwarnings("ignore") at the top of a notebook hides exactly this class of message, which is the argument against putting one there.

    22.3.8   NaT, and missingness as a feature

    Code — count it, flag it, and think before you fill it 
    print(df["date"].isna().sum())                      # NaT counts as missing

# The flag is often more predictive than anything you could impute
df["date_missing"] = df["date"].isna().astype(int)

# Filling is a DECISION, not a default. These are all defensible — and all different:
df["date"].ffill()                                   # carry the previous known date forward
df["date"].fillna(df["date"].min())                  # treat unknown as "as early as possible"
df["date"].fillna(pd.Timestamp("2000-01-01"))        # a sentinel — visible, and a lie

# Aggregations skip NaT silently, which is usually what you want and always worth checking
df["date"].mean()

    On a five-element probe with two NaT , .mean() returns 2025-01-31 — the mean of the three observed dates, with no warning that 40% of the column was dropped. That is the same silent-exclusion behaviour as §22.2.5's z-score rule.

    The missing-indicator is a feature, not bookkeeping. A null last_login usually means "never logged in"; a null churn_date usually means "has not churned". In both cases the missingness is the label-adjacent information, and the imputed value is noise. Create date_missing before you fill anything — §22.2.6's _was_na flags are the same move — and read §22.2.8 for the framework that tells you when filling is safe at all.

    22.3.9   The strftime trap

    "Convert 15 March 2025 to 03/15/2025" is a trick question. strftime goes datetime → text; to_datetime goes text → datetime. They are inverses, and only one of them is preprocessing. Verified: d.dt.strftime("%m/%d/%Y") produces "03/15/2025" with dtype object , after which .dt.year raises AttributeError: Can only use .dt accessor with datetimelike values . You have converted a working datetime column back into strings and lost every operation in this subsection. The answer to give: "If the requirement is display, strftime at the very end, on a copy, in the output frame only. If the requirement is modelling, keep datetime64[ns] — a datetime has no display format, and formatting it is not a transformation of the data." Round-tripping it back with to_datetime restores datetime64[ns] but is two wasted operations and one chance to mis-parse.
    The same trap in miniature: .dt.date. It returns Python datetime.date objects in an object column , so you lose the .dt accessor exactly as with strftime. .dt.normalize() does what you almost always meant — it zeroes the time and stays datetime64[ns] , giving 2025-03-15 00:00:00 . Prefer it whenever you want to drop the clock but keep the column usable.

    22.3.10   The workflow, and the 15 syntaxes

    The datetime pipeline, in the order you run it. 
    # 1. What is it?
print(df["date"].dtype)

# 2. Make it a datetime, and survive the junk
df["date"] = pd.to_datetime(df["date"], format="%d-%m-%Y", errors="coerce")
print("parse rate:", df["date"].notna().mean())

# 3. Handle what became NaT — flag it, decide about it, do not blind-fill it
df["date_missing"] = df["date"].isna().astype(int)

# 4. Sort, if anything downstream is temporal
df = df.sort_values(["cust_id", "date"])

# 5. Extract the parts
df["year"]  = df["date"].dt.year
df["month"] = df["date"].dt.month
