df["dow"]   = df["date"].dt.dayofweek
df["is_weekend"] = (df["dow"] >= 5).astype(int)

# 6. Durations and recency — usually the strongest features in the set
df["days_since_signup"] = (df["date"] - df["signup_date"]).dt.days
df["gap_days"] = df.groupby("cust_id")["date"].diff().dt.total_seconds() / 86400

# 7. Cyclical encoding for the periodic parts
df["month_sin"] = np.sin(2 * np.pi * df["month"] / 12)
df["month_cos"] = np.cos(2 * np.pi * df["month"] / 12)

# 8. Lag / rolling, if the question is a forecast   (shift BEFORE you roll — §22.3.7)
df["lag_1"]      = df.groupby("cust_id")["amount"].shift(1)
df["roll7_mean"] = (df.groupby("cust_id")["amount"]
                      .transform(lambda s: s.shift(1).rolling(7).mean()))

# 9. Drop the raw datetime if the model cannot use it
X = df.drop(columns=["date", "signup_date"])

    Nine steps, and the order is load-bearing: sorting after building lags is wrong, extracting parts before coercing raises, and dropping the raw column before you have finished deriving from it is the one mistake you cannot undo without re-parsing.

    The 15 syntaxes to have in muscle memory
    #CallWhen
    1pd.to_datetime(s)text → datetime, always first
    2pd.to_datetime(s, errors="coerce")junk becomes NaT instead of an exception
    3pd.to_datetime(s, format="%d-%m-%Y")the format is known — faster and unambiguous
    4s.dt.year / .dt.month / .dt.daycalendar parts
    5s.dt.dayofweek (Mon=0) / .dt.day_name()weekday effects, weekend flags
    6s.dt.hour / .dt.quarter / .dt.isocalendar().weekintraday, quarterly, weekly grain
    7(end - start).dt.dayswhole-day durations
    8(end - start).dt.total_seconds() / 3600sub-day durations — hours, minutes
    9df[df["date"].between(a, b)]date-range filter, inclusive both ends
    10df.sort_values(["id", "date"])entity first, time second — before anything temporal
    11g["date"].min() / .max()first and last event per entity
    12g["date"].transform("min")broadcast the first event back onto every row
    13g["t"].diff().dt.total_seconds() / 60minutes since this entity's previous event
    14g["x"].shift(1)lag feature, per entity
    15s.set_index("date").rolling("7D") / .resample("D")window and re-grid the series

    Rows 12–15 are the ones that separate a candidate who has "used pandas" from one who has built features — recency, lifetime aggregation, the groupby-diff and the shifted rolling window. They are also the four that leak if you get the sort or the shift wrong, which is why §22.4 spends its first subsection on nothing else.

    22.4   XGBoost on time series

    §13 derives what XGBoost is — second-order boosting with a regularised structure score — and §13.13 gives the general practice: no scaling, native categoricals, learned default directions for missing values, and which importance lens to trust. None of that is repeated here. This subsection is about the one thing a time-series question changes: the rows are not exchangeable. Every standard habit that assumes they are — shuffled cross-validation, a random train/test split, a rolling mean over the whole column — becomes a leak, and the leak is invisible because the score improves.

    Everything below runs on one deterministic fixture: three stores × 730 daily observations, built from a linear trend, a weekly profile, an annual sinusoid, a nominal store and an ordinal size, plus Gaussian noise with σ = 4.0 — which is the RMSE floor no model can beat. The panel is 2190 rows × 4 columns spanning 2022-01-01 to 2023-12-31 , computed in work/computes/s22_timeseries.py on xgboost 3.4.0 .

    Code — the fixture: trend + weekly + annual + nominal + ordinal + noise 
    rng    = np.random.default_rng(2207)
DATES  = pd.date_range("2022-01-01", periods=730, freq="D")
STORES = {"North": 20.0, "South": 0.0, "East": -10.0}          # nominal: arbitrary offsets
SIZES  = ["S", "M", "L", "XL"]                                  # ORDINAL: S < M < L < XL
SIZE_EFF = {"S": 0.0, "M": 4.0, "L": 9.0, "XL": 15.0}           # monotone in the order
DOW_EFF  = np.array([-4., -3., -1., 0., 3., 12., 10.])          # Mon..Sun

frames = []
for st, off in STORES.items():
    t  = np.arange(len(DATES), dtype=float)
    sz = rng.choice(SIZES, len(DATES), p=[.40, .30, .20, .10])
    y  = (100.0
          + 0.05 * t                                                    # trend
          + DOW_EFF[DATES.dayofweek.values]                             # weekly seasonality
          + 6.0 * np.sin(2 * np.pi * DATES.dayofyear.values / 365.25)   # annual seasonality
          + off
          + np.array([SIZE_EFF[s] for s in sz])
          + rng.normal(0, 4.0, len(DATES)))                             # irreducible noise
    frames.append(pd.DataFrame({"date": DATES, "store": st, "size": sz,
                                "sales": np.round(y, 2)}))

panel = (pd.concat(frames, ignore_index=True)
           .sort_values(["store", "date"]).reset_index(drop=True))

    Building the fixture with named effects means every later number has an expected value you can check against. The weekly profile is visible in the raw data before any modelling — Saturday averages 138.42 against Monday's 121.95 — and the ordinal effect is monotone in the size order, S 124.27 < M 127.51 < L 133.98 < XL 138.57 . Do this profiling before you fit anything: if a feature you believe in shows no gradient in a group-by, it will show none in the model either.

    22.4.1   From a series to a supervised frame

    XGBoost has no concept of time. It sees a table of rows and predicts one column from the others, so the entire craft is in constructing that table: each row must carry, as features, only information that existed strictly before the instant its target refers to. Three families do the work — lags, shifted windows, and calendar/cyclical parts.

    Code — the feature builder (lags, shifted rolling stats, calendar, cyclical) 
    def build_features(df: pd.DataFrame) -> pd.DataFrame:
    d = df.sort_values(["store", "date"]).copy()          # entity first, time second
    g = d.groupby("store", observed=True)["sales"]        # NEVER leak across entities

    # --- lags: the value itself, k periods ago ---
    for L in (1, 7, 14, 28):
        d[f"lag_{L}"] = g.shift(L)

    # --- windows: shift(1) FIRST so the window excludes the present row ---
    d["roll7_mean"]  = g.transform(lambda s: s.shift(1).rolling(7).mean())
    d["roll7_std"]   = g.transform(lambda s: s.shift(1).rolling(7).std())
    d["roll28_mean"] = g.transform(lambda s: s.shift(1).rolling(28).mean())

    # --- calendar parts (§22.3.2) ---
    d["dow"]        = d["date"].dt.dayofweek
    d["month"]      = d["date"].dt.month
    d["quarter"]    = d["date"].dt.quarter
    d["weekofyear"] = d["date"].dt.isocalendar().week.astype(int)   # UInt32 -> int, §22.3.2
    d["is_weekend"] = (d["dow"] >= 5).astype(int)

    # --- cyclical encoding (§22.3.6) ---
    d["dow_sin"]   = np.sin(2 * np.pi * d["dow"] / 7)
    d["dow_cos"]   = np.cos(2 * np.pi * d["dow"] / 7)
    d["month_sin"] = np.sin(2 * np.pi * d["month"] / 12)
    d["month_cos"] = np.cos(2 * np.pi * d["month"] / 12)

    # --- feature TYPES, handled per kind (§22.4.2) ---
    d["store_cat"] = d["store"].astype("category")                              # nominal
    d["size_ord"]  = pd.Categorical(d["size"], categories=SIZES,
                                    ordered=True).codes                          # ordinal
    return d

FEATS = ["lag_1", "lag_7", "lag_14", "lag_28", "roll7_mean", "roll7_std", "roll28_mean",
         "dow", "month", "quarter", "weekofyear", "is_weekend",
         "dow_sin", "dow_cos", "month_sin", "month_cos", "store_cat", "size_ord"]

feat     = build_features(panel)
model_df = feat.dropna(subset=FEATS)      # the warm-up rows have no history

    Three details carry the whole subsection. groupby("store") before every shift: without it, store North's first row inherits store East's last value. The transform(lambda s: s.shift(1).rolling(7)...) ordering: shift then roll, so the window ends at t−1. And dropna, not fillna(0): the first 28 rows of each store genuinely have no 28-day history, and a zero there teaches the model that the series occasionally collapses. It costs 84 rows of 2190 , leaving 2106 — 3 stores × 28 warm-up days, arithmetic worth checking.

    A rolling window that includes the present row is a leak — measured. Replace s.shift(1).rolling(7).mean() with s.rolling(7).mean() and the seven-day mean at row t contains yt with weight 1/7. Its correlation with the target rises from 0.8668 to 0.8869 and the test RMSE improves from 5.229 to 4.6805 , a phantom gain of 0.55 . Notice the shape of the bug: it does not crash, it does not warn, and the held-out score rewards it — the feature is computable at scoring time only if you already know the answer. This is §21.7's rule in its time-series costume, and it is the single most common way a forecasting notebook lies to its author. The audit: for every feature, ask "at the moment I must predict yt, is this column knowable?" If the answer needs yt, delete it.

    22.4.2   Feature types: continuous, nominal, ordinal

    The three kinds need three different treatments, and only one of them is the treatment a linear model would want.

    What to do with each kind of column, and why
    KindExample hereTreatmentWhy
    Continuouslag_1, roll7_mean Nothing. Feed them raw — no scaling, no log trees split on thresholds; any monotone map moves the threshold with the data and leaves every split decision identical
    Nominal (no order)store .astype("category") + enable_categorical=True; or one-hot for few levels the booster partitions the level set directly, so it never has to invent an ordering that does not exist
    Ordinal (ordered)size: S < M < L < XL ordered integer codes, pd.Categorical(..., ordered=True).codes the order is information: one split size_ord >= 2 isolates {L, XL}. One-hot would need three splits to say the same thing
    Code — declaring the three kinds to xgboost 
    # Continuous: nothing to do.

# Nominal -> pandas category dtype, and tell the booster to use it
df["store_cat"] = df["store"].astype("category")

# Ordinal -> ordered codes. Passing `categories=` fixes the order EXPLICITLY;
# without it pandas sorts alphabetically and you get L < M < S < XL, which is nonsense.
df["size_ord"] = pd.Categorical(df["size"], categories=["S", "M", "L", "XL"],
                                ordered=True).codes          # S=0, M=1, L=2, XL=3

model = xgb.XGBRegressor(
    n_estimators=800, learning_rate=0.05, max_depth=5,
    subsample=0.9, colsample_bytree=0.9, reg_lambda=1.0,
    enable_categorical=True, tree_method="hist",     # required for category dtype
    early_stopping_rounds=50, eval_metric="rmse", random_state=0,
)

    The categories= argument is the whole ordinal trick, and it is also the bug: pd.Categorical(s, ordered=True) without it sorts the labels alphabetically — for sizes that gives L < M < S < XL, an order that is worse than no order at all. Spell the sequence out, every time. And keep the same categories= list for train, validation and test, or the same label maps to different codes in different splits.

    Interpretation — two claims, both measured on this fixture. (i) Scaling is exactly a no-op. Standardising all seven continuous lag/rolling features changes the test RMSE by 0.000000 — 5.229 either way . Not "approximately unchanged": bit-identical, because standardisation is strictly monotone and the histogram bin boundaries move with it. Any minute spent on a StandardScaler here is a minute not spent on features. (ii) The order in the ordinal code is worth something. Replacing the ordered codes S=0, M=1, L=2, XL=3 with the order-destroying map S=2, M=0, L=3, XL=1 raises test RMSE from 5.229 to 5.4412 , a loss of 0.2121 . The mechanism is exactly one split: with the true order, size_ord >= 2 separates the two high-effect levels in a single cut; scrambled, {L, XL} is {3, 1} and no single threshold isolates it. A deep enough tree recovers the partition eventually — which is why the loss is 0.21 and not 2 — but it spends depth to do it, and depth is the budget you are regularising.

    22.4.3   Splitting in time — and what shuffled CV does to your score

    There is exactly one legitimate split: train on the past, validate on the future. Not train_test_split(..., shuffle=True), not KFold(shuffle=True), not stratify=. The reason is not purity — it is that lag features make neighbouring rows near-duplicates of each other, so a shuffled fold puts row t in training and row t+1 in validation, and row t+1's lag_1 is row t's target.

    Code — the date-boundary split, and TimeSeriesSplit for CV 
    # --- the split: three contiguous blocks, cut on DATES, never on row positions ---
TEST_START = pd.Timestamp("2023-10-04")     # last 90 days
VAL_START  = pd.Timestamp("2023-07-06")     # the 90 days before that

tr = model_df[model_df["date"] <  VAL_START]
va = model_df[(model_df["date"] >= VAL_START) & (model_df["date"] < TEST_START)]
te = model_df[model_df["date"] >= TEST_START]

# --- cross-validation: forward chaining, never shuffling ---
from sklearn.model_selection import TimeSeriesSplit
tscv = TimeSeriesSplit(n_splits=5)          # fold k trains on [0..i_k], tests on (i_k..j_k]
for tr_i, te_i in tscv.split(X):            # X must be sorted by date first
    ...

# WRONG, and it will look better:
# KFold(n_splits=5, shuffle=True).split(X)

    Cut on dates, not on iloc positions: with a panel of three stores, "the last 267 rows" is the last 89 days of one store, not the last 89 days of all three. The split here is 1569 / 270 / 267 rows — note the val and test blocks are ~90 days × 3 stores, and that they are contiguous in time with no overlap. TimeSeriesSplit trains on an expanding window by default, so early folds have little data and score worse; that is a feature, not noise, and it is why its fold spread is wider.

    Shuffled 5-fold versus forward-chaining 5-fold, same features, same model, same rows
    schemefold 1fold 2fold 3fold 4fold 5mean RMSE
    KFold(shuffle=True)4.40414.22704.74094.62174.60784.5203
    TimeSeriesSplit(5)5.26924.80467.78225.91734.47095.6489
    Shuffled K-fold reports 4.5203 where forward chaining reports 5.6489 — a gap of 1.1286 RMSE , or 20.0% optimism . The referee is the genuinely held-out future block, which scores 5.547 — within 0.10 of forward chaining and 1.03 worse than the shuffled estimate. So the forward-chaining number is the honest one and the shuffled number is a fantasy you would have carried into the report. Two further tells that the shuffled estimate is broken: its fold-to-fold spread is far tighter (4.23–4.74 against 4.47–7.78), because every fold has been handed neighbours of its own validation rows; and it gets better as you add more lag features, which is the opposite of what a leak-free score does. Sentence for the interview: "I used TimeSeriesSplit because with lag features a shuffled fold trains on rows adjacent to the rows it validates on — here that was worth 20% of the RMSE."

    22.4.4   Regression: the baselines you are expected to beat

    A forecast is never scored against nothing. Before any model, compute the two baselines every interviewer has in mind — and be ready for the possibility that they are hard to beat, because on a strongly seasonal series they usually are.

    Code — the three baselines, then the model, with early stopping on the temporal fold 
    # rmse(a, b) is the two-line helper of §22.5.1: float(np.sqrt(mean_squared_error(a, b)))

# --- baselines, in order of how embarrassing it is to lose to them ---
rmse_mean     = rmse(te["sales"], np.full(len(te), tr["sales"].mean()))  # the mean predictor
rmse_naive    = rmse(te["sales"], te["lag_1"])       # "tomorrow = today"
rmse_seasonal = rmse(te["sales"], te["lag_7"])       # "next Tuesday = last Tuesday"

# --- the model: early stopping watches the TEMPORAL validation block ---
reg = xgb.XGBRegressor(
    n_estimators=800, learning_rate=0.05, max_depth=5,
    subsample=0.9, colsample_bytree=0.9, reg_lambda=1.0,
    enable_categorical=True, tree_method="hist",
    early_stopping_rounds=50, eval_metric="rmse", random_state=0,
).fit(tr[FEATS], tr["sales"],
      eval_set=[(va[FEATS], va["sales"])], verbose=False)

print("stopped at iteration", reg.best_iteration)
print("test RMSE", rmse(te["sales"], reg.predict(te[FEATS])))

    The eval_set must be the future validation block, never a random slice — early stopping is model selection, and selecting on shuffled rows imports the same 20% optimism §22.4.3 measured. Requesting 800 trees and stopping at 137 is the desired outcome: you set n_estimators generously and let the validation curve decide, rather than guessing the number.

    Test-block RMSE, 2023-10-04 to 2023-12-31 (267 rows), σnoise = 4.0
    predictortest RMSEvs seasonal naivereading
    Train mean 21.9673+150.4%the zero-information reference
    Naive, yt−1 11.3232+29.1%worse than seasonal — the weekly cycle dominates
    7-day rolling mean 8.8332+0.7%smooths the noise, erases the weekly cycle
    Seasonal naive, yt−7 8.7725—the number to beat
    XGBoost, 18 features 5.5470−36.8%beats it, and lands 1.39× the noise floor
    Interpretation. The ordering of the baselines is the finding. Seasonal naive (8.7725) beats plain naive (11.3232) because the day-of-week swing (Monday 121.95 to Saturday 138.42 ) is larger than one day's drift, so "same day last week" is a better guess than "yesterday". Reporting that comparison — not just the winner — is what shows you understand the series. XGBoost reaches 5.5470 , 36.8% below the seasonal naive , against an irreducible floor of 4.0; so it has captured roughly three-quarters of the available headroom and the remaining 1.55 is mostly level-tracking error. Its top features are the two shifted rolling means (roll28_mean 0.2609, roll7_mean 0.2494 ) followed by lag_7 — i.e. the windows supply the level and lag_7 plus is_weekend supply the shape, which is exactly the decomposition the fixture was built from. Train RMSE 2.7592 against test 5.5470 is the usual boosted-tree gap; early stopping at 137 of 800 rounds is what kept it from being much larger.

    22.4.5   Classification: direction and events

    The same frame answers "will it go up?" or "will an event occur?" — swap the estimator, swap the metrics, and remember that the threshold is a decision you make, not a constant sklearn hands you.

    Code — direction classification, AUC/F1, threshold from the PR curve 
    df["up"] = (df["sales"] > df["lag_1"]).astype(int)      # the event: today beat yesterday

clf = xgb.XGBClassifier(
    n_estimators=600, learning_rate=0.05, max_depth=4,
    subsample=0.9, colsample_bytree=0.9, reg_lambda=1.0,
    enable_categorical=True, tree_method="hist",
    early_stopping_rounds=50, eval_metric="logloss", random_state=0,
).fit(tr[FEATS], tr["up"], eval_set=[(va[FEATS], va["up"])], verbose=False)

proba = clf.predict_proba(te[FEATS])[:, 1]
print("AUC:", roc_auc_score(te["up"], proba))

# Pick the threshold on the VALIDATION block, then apply it to test — never both on test
prec, rec, thr = precision_recall_curve(va["up"], clf.predict_proba(va[FEATS])[:, 1])
f1s  = 2 * prec * rec / (prec + rec + 1e-12)
cut  = thr[int(np.nanargmax(f1s[:-1]))]
print("F1 at tuned cut:", f1_score(te["up"], (proba >= cut).astype(int)))

# For a rare event (fraud, churn, stock-out) add:  scale_pos_weight = n_neg / n_pos

    Two disciplines the regression version does not need. The label must be built from lag_1 so it is defined at the same instant as the features — and then lag_1 stays in the feature set, which is legitimate: it is known before yt. And the threshold is chosen on validation and reported on test; choosing and reporting on the same rows is the fit §22.5.8 warns about.

    Interpretation. The classes are near-balanced by construction — 51.8% up in train, 49.1% in test — and the model reaches AUC 0.9308 with F1 0.8582 at the default 0.5 cut . Where does 0.93 come from? Almost entirely from the weekly cycle: a classifier given day-of-week alone already scores AUC 0.7127 , because Friday-to-Saturday is nearly always an up-day and Sunday-to-Monday nearly always a down-day. Say that — a direction model that beats chance on a seasonal series has not discovered anything about momentum. And the honest negative result: the F1-maximising threshold picked on validation is 0.525 , and applying it to test gives F1 0.8438 , worse than the 0.8582 the untuned 0.5 achieves. That is the expected outcome in this regime: with balanced classes and a well-calibrated model, 0.5 is already near-optimal, so the tuned cut is fitting validation noise and does not transfer. Threshold tuning earns its keep when the classes are skewed or the costs are asymmetric — a 99:1 fraud problem — and there you also swap ROC-AUC for average precision.

    22.4.6   Recursive multi-step forecasting

    Everything above is one step ahead: predict yt given real observations up to t−1. A question asking for the next fortnight cannot work that way, because yt+1's lag_1 is yt, which does not exist yet. You feed the prediction back in.

    Code — the recursive loop 
    H = 14
history = train_series["sales"].tolist()      # the real past
preds   = []

for h in range(H):
    row = future_calendar.loc[[h]].copy()     # calendar features are known in advance
    row["lag_1"] = history[-1]                # ...but the lags come from what we predicted
    row["lag_7"] = history[-7]
    yhat = float(model.predict(row[RFEATS])[0])
    preds.append(yhat)
    history.append(yhat)                      # feed it back — errors compound from here

    Design the feature set for the loop, not the other way round: every feature must be reconstructible from predicted history plus the calendar. A roll28_mean is fine (rebuild it from history); a feature depending on some other series' future value is not. The alternative to recursion is direct multi-step — train a separate model per horizon with target y.shift(-h) — which avoids compounding at the cost of H models.

    Interpretation. Over a 14-day horizon the recursive forecast scores RMSE 5.6913 against the seasonal-naive 7.6127 on the same fortnight — still a win, but a thinner one than the 36.8% of the one-step problem, and that shrinkage is the compounding. The step-by-step absolute errors are 3.06 at h = 1 and 4.10 at h = 14 , with no monotone blow-up in between — because the calendar features keep re-anchoring the weekly shape even as the level estimate drifts. The rule to state: quote one-step accuracy and multi-step accuracy separately, and never let a one-step RMSE stand in for a forecast that will actually be run H steps out.

    22.4.7   The trend a tree cannot climb

    This is the one structural limitation of boosted trees on time series, and it is a guaranteed interview question. A tree predicts the mean of a training leaf, so its output is bounded by [min(y_train), max(y_train)]. Confront it with a series that has drifted beyond anything it saw and it does not extrapolate the trend — it flatlines at the top of its range.

    Code — the failure, and the two fixes 
    # A 600-day series with a strong trend (+0.25/day). Train on the first 400 days,
# so every test row sits ABOVE the training range.
XF  = ["t", "dow", "month", "dow_sin", "dow_cos", "month_sin", "month_cos", "size_ord"]
etr, ete = north.iloc[:400], north.iloc[400:]

# (a) the failure — raw target
raw = xgb.XGBRegressor(...).fit(etr[XF], etr["sales"])

# (b) FIX 1 — difference the target, model the change, re-integrate
north["dy"] = north["sales"].diff()                    # stationary: no trend left
dm    = xgb.XGBRegressor(...).fit(etr[XF].iloc[1:], north["dy"].iloc[1:400])
dhat  = dm.predict(ete[XF])
yhat  = ete["sales"].shift(1) + dhat                   # re-integrate off the last KNOWN value

# (c) FIX 2 — detrend: fit the trend, boost the residual, add the trend back
trend = LinearRegression().fit(etr[["t"]], etr["sales"])
res   = xgb.XGBRegressor(...).fit(etr[XF], etr["sales"] - trend.predict(etr[["t"]]))
yhat2 = trend.predict(ete[["t"]]) + res.predict(ete[XF])

    Both fixes work by handing the unbounded part of the signal to something that can extrapolate — a difference (which is stationary, so no extrapolation is needed) or an explicit linear trend — and leaving the booster only the bounded, seasonal remainder. That division of labour is the whole idea; it is also what a classical decomposition, and Prophet, and any "linear trend + residual model" hybrid is doing.

    600-day series, trend +0.25/day; train = first 400 days, test = last 200. Training tops out at y = 205.42 ; the test block reaches 247.97
    modeltest RMSEmax predictionwhat happened
    XGBoost on the raw target 31.0383199.679 flatlines: never predicts above 199.68 although the truth reaches 247.97
    XGBoost + lag_1, lag_7 27.1793—lags do not rescue you — the lags are out of range too
    Ridge on the same features 4.9629249.637 a linear model extends the line, and the truth is a line
    FIX 1 — differenced target, one-step re-integration 8.6049245.063−72.3% RMSE
    FIX 2 — detrend, boost the residual, add the trend back 4.6877246.193−84.9% ; essentially the noise floor
    FIX 1, anchored once and cumulatively summed 46.7924—worse than doing nothing — see the warning below
    Interpretation. Read row 1 as a diagnosis, not a score. The raw model's maximum prediction over 200 test days is 199.679 while its own last training-row prediction is 186.503 : it has run out of leaves and is now returning a constant, so its mean prediction sits 27.175 below the truth — a pure, one-directional bias, which is what distinguishes extrapolation failure from ordinary error. The level rose 74.084 between the two blocks and the model captured almost none of it. Row 2 kills the reflex answer: adding lag features does not fix this (27.1793), because lag_1 in the test block is itself outside the range of lag_1 in training, so the same threshold saturation applies one level down. Row 3 is the contrast that names the cause — the generating trend is exactly linear, so Ridge nails it at 4.9629, and this is the honest answer to "when would you not use a boosted tree". Rows 4–5 are the fixes: the first difference has mean 0.2187 and standard deviation 10.929 on train — a stationary series with no trend to extrapolate — and detrending recovers the fitted slope 0.2488 against a true 0.25, landing at 4.6877, inside a whisker of the σ = 4.0 floor.
    Re-integration is where differencing goes wrong. Predicting the 200 test differences and anchoring once — y_last_train + np.cumsum(dhat) — gives RMSE 46.7924 , worse than the un-differenced model it was meant to fix. The arithmetic is exact: the predicted differences carry a bias of −0.1739 per step , and 200 steps of it accumulate to a terminal drift of −34.773 . A cumulative sum integrates the bias linearly in the horizon while the noise only grows as its square root, so any systematic error in a difference model becomes the dominant term for long horizons. The rule: re-anchor on the last observed value at every step you can (one-step-ahead scoring, or a rolling re-fit), and if you genuinely must integrate H steps, report the drift as an explicit uncertainty rather than a point forecast.
    §22.4 recap — the six sentences.
    1. Build the frame, not the model. Lags, .shift(1).rolling(k) windows, calendar parts, cyclical pairs — grouped by entity, sorted by time.
    2. Feature types: continuous raw (scaling changed RMSE by 0.000000 ), nominal as category + enable_categorical, ordinal as ordered codes (worth 0.21 RMSE here ).
    3. Split on dates only. Shuffled 5-fold read 4.5203 where forward chaining read 5.6489 and the true future read 5.547 — 20.0% optimism .
    4. Beat the seasonal naive, and quote it. 8.7725 → 5.5470 here , against a noise floor of 4.0 .
    5. Multi-step is a different number. Recursive H = 14 gave 5.6913 where one-step gave 5.5470 .
    6. Trees cannot climb a trend. Difference or detrend, model the remainder, re-integrate against the last observed value .
    For importances, feature selection and the general xgboost workflow see §13.13; for the Pipeline/ColumnTransformer skeleton this all sits inside, §21 — with cv=TimeSeriesSplit(...) substituted for KFold at every point where §21 writes one.

    22.5   Q3 — Modelling to beat a minimum RMSE

    The reported question: "apply a model on cleaned data where train, val and test datasets were given and kept some minimum RMSE to pass the test cases." The metric is $\text{RMSE} = \sqrt{\frac{1}{n}\sum_{i=1}^{n}(y_i - \hat{y}_i)^2}$, in the units of the target, and the run order under time pressure is fixed:

    1. Load train/val/test, confirm the target column and that test has no target
    2. Baseline: predict the train mean → gives you the RMSE you must beat
    3. Build a Pipeline(preprocessor, model), fit on train, score on val
    4. Try 4–5 models in a loop, pick the best val RMSE
    5. Light hyper-parameter search on the winner
    6. Refit on train+val, predict test, write the output file in the exact required format
    7. Only then go back and add feature engineering

    Never touch the test set for anything except predict. The pipeline object that makes steps 3–5 safe is the one in §21.7 — ColumnTransformer → selector → estimator inside GridSearchCV, so every transformer refits per fold. This section does not repeat that template; it exercises it.

    Code — cell 46: build a realistic train/val/test split with mixed dtypes and missingness 
    from sklearn.datasets import make_regression
from sklearn.model_selection import train_test_split, KFold, cross_val_score, GridSearchCV, RandomizedSearchCV
from sklearn.linear_model import LinearRegression, Ridge, Lasso, ElasticNet
from sklearn.ensemble import RandomForestRegressor, GradientBoostingRegressor, HistGradientBoostingRegressor
from sklearn.tree import DecisionTreeRegressor
from sklearn.metrics import mean_squared_error, mean_absolute_error, r2_score, mean_absolute_percentage_error
from sklearn.dummy import DummyRegressor
from sklearn.inspection import permutation_importance

# ---- Build a realistic train / val / test split with mixed dtypes and missing values ----
N = 3000
Xn, y = make_regression(n_samples=N, n_features=8, n_informative=6, noise=18.0, random_state=0)
data = pd.DataFrame(Xn, columns=[f"num_{i}" for i in range(8)])
data["cat_a"] = np.random.choice(["a", "b", "c", "d"], N)
data["cat_b"] = np.random.choice(["x", "y", "z"], N, p=[.6, .3, .1])
data["target"] = y + data["cat_a"].map({"a": 20, "b": -10, "c": 5, "d": 0}).to_numpy()
data.loc[np.random.choice(N, 200, replace=False), "num_3"] = np.nan       # missingness in features

train_full, test = train_test_split(data, test_size=0.2, random_state=7)
train, val = train_test_split(train_full, test_size=0.25, random_state=7)   # 60/20/20
test_features = test.drop(columns="target")                                 # what you'd actually be given
y_test_true = test["target"]                                                # hidden in the real test

TARGET = "target"
print("train", train.shape, "| val", val.shape, "| test", test_features.shape)

    The two-step split is the standard way to hit 60/20/20: hold out 20% for test, then take 25% of the remaining 80% for validation. Keep train_full around — step 6 refits on it. And note test_features has one column fewer than train; if your test file has the same width as your train file, the target is in it and you should ask why.

    Shapes: train (1800, 11), val (600, 11), test features (600, 10) , with 109 missing num_3 values in train .

    22.5.1   The baseline is the number to beat

    Code — cell 47: rmse/report helpers and the mean baseline 
    def rmse(y_true, y_pred) -> float:
    # sklearn >= 1.4 has root_mean_squared_error; this works on every version
    return float(np.sqrt(mean_squared_error(y_true, y_pred)))

def report(name, y_true, y_pred):
    print(f"{name:<28} RMSE={rmse(y_true, y_pred):9.3f}  "
          f"MAE={mean_absolute_error(y_true, y_pred):8.3f}  "
          f"R2={r2_score(y_true, y_pred):6.3f}")

X_tr, y_tr = train.drop(columns=TARGET), train[TARGET]
X_va, y_va = val.drop(columns=TARGET),   val[TARGET]

# ---- Step 2: baseline. This is the number the threshold is usually set just below. ----
dummy = DummyRegressor(strategy="mean").fit(X_tr, y_tr)
report("BASELINE (train mean)", y_va, dummy.predict(X_va))

    Writing rmse by hand rather than reaching for root_mean_squared_error costs one line and works on every sklearn version — worth it when you cannot install anything and do not know the grader's version. DummyRegressor takes X only to learn its shape; it is the honest zero-information reference.

    Interpretation. The baseline scores RMSE 137.646, MAE 109.921, R² −0.001 on validation . Three things follow. (i) The RMSE of the mean predictor is (almost exactly) the standard deviation of the target — 139.781 on train — so you can predict the baseline before fitting anything. (ii) R² ≈ 0 by definition: R² is measured against exactly this predictor, so "R² = 0" and "no better than the mean" are the same statement. (iii) A tiny negative R² is expected, because the mean was computed on train and scored on val. If your first real model does not beat 137.646, the bug is in the code, not in the model.

    22.5.2   One preprocessor for every model

    Code — cell 49: two ColumnTransformers — scaled, and lean for trees 
    num_cols = X_tr.select_dtypes(include=np.number).columns.tolist()
cat_cols = X_tr.select_dtypes(exclude=np.number).columns.tolist()
print("numeric:", num_cols, "\ncategorical:", cat_cols)

preprocess = ColumnTransformer([
    ("num", Pipeline([("imp", SimpleImputer(strategy="median")),
                      ("sc",  StandardScaler())]), num_cols),
    ("cat", Pipeline([("imp", SimpleImputer(strategy="most_frequent")),
                      ("oh",  OneHotEncoder(handle_unknown="ignore", sparse_output=False))]), cat_cols),
])

# Tree models don't need scaling; a separate lean preprocessor is slightly faster/better for them
preprocess_tree = ColumnTransformer([
    ("num", SimpleImputer(strategy="median"), num_cols),
    ("cat", Pipeline([("imp", SimpleImputer(strategy="most_frequent")),
                      ("oh",  OneHotEncoder(handle_unknown="ignore", sparse_output=False))]), cat_cols),
])

    select_dtypes to build the column lists means the pipeline survives a schema change; hard-coded lists do not. The two-preprocessor split is the practical form of §21.4's "needs scaling" column: linear/penalised/distance methods do, trees do not.

    The split is 8 numeric columns and 2 categorical .

    22.5.3   The bake-off

    Code — cell 51: fit eight candidate pipelines, score on validation 
    candidates = {
    "LinearRegression":   (preprocess,      LinearRegression()),
    "Ridge(alpha=1)":     (preprocess,      Ridge(alpha=1.0, random_state=0)),
    "Lasso(alpha=0.1)":   (preprocess,      Lasso(alpha=0.1, random_state=0, max_iter=5000)),
    "ElasticNet":         (preprocess,      ElasticNet(alpha=0.1, l1_ratio=0.5, random_state=0, max_iter=5000)),
    "DecisionTree":       (preprocess_tree, DecisionTreeRegressor(max_depth=8, random_state=0)),
    "RandomForest":       (preprocess_tree, RandomForestRegressor(n_estimators=300, min_samples_leaf=2,
                                                                  n_jobs=-1, random_state=0)),
    "GradientBoosting":   (preprocess_tree, GradientBoostingRegressor(random_state=0)),
    "HistGradientBoost":  (preprocess_tree, HistGradientBoostingRegressor(random_state=0)),
}

results = []
fitted = {}
for name, (pre, est) in candidates.items():
    pipe = Pipeline([("pre", pre), ("model", est)]).fit(X_tr, y_tr)
    fitted[name] = pipe
    results.append({"model": name,
                    "train_rmse": rmse(y_tr, pipe.predict(X_tr)),
                    "val_rmse":   rmse(y_va, pipe.predict(X_va)),
                    "val_r2":     r2_score(y_va, pipe.predict(X_va))})

board = pd.DataFrame(results).sort_values("val_rmse").reset_index(drop=True)
board

    A dict of (preprocessor, estimator) pairs plus a five-line loop is the entire bake-off. Keep the fitted pipelines in fitted — you will want the winner again in two cells, and refitting it is wasted minutes. Recording train RMSE alongside val is what turns a leaderboard into a diagnosis.

    Validation leaderboard, eight candidates
    #modeltrain_rmseval_rmseval_R²diagnosis
    1Lasso(alpha=0.1)17.779618.12210.9827train ≈ val ⇒ fit is honest
    2LinearRegression17.770018.13340.9826same, unpenalised
    3Ridge(alpha=1)17.770118.13720.9826same
    4ElasticNet19.047819.62280.9797over-penalised at α=0.1
    5HistGradientBoost10.867029.21360.9549train ≪ val ⇒ overfitting
    6GradientBoosting19.924330.30150.9515overfitting, milder
    7RandomForest18.893439.81510.9163averaging cannot fix extrapolation
    8DecisionTree38.991967.65490.7583bad on both ⇒ underfit and unstable

    Read the leaderboard as a diagnosis, not a ranking — train_rmse ≈ val_rmse, both high → underfitting; train_rmse ≪ val_rmse → overfitting; trees beating linear by a lot → non-linearity and interactions matter; linear beating trees → the relationship is smooth, so try polynomial features on the linear model.

    Interpretation. Linear models win, and the best tree ensemble is 61% worse — 29.2136 against 18.1221 — against a baseline of 137.646, i.e. a 7.6-fold reduction . That is not a fluke: the data comes from make_regression, which is exactly linear plus Gaussian noise, so the linear hypothesis class contains the truth and everything else is paying a variance premium for flexibility it cannot use. HistGradientBoosting's train RMSE of 10.8670 against val 29.2136 is the textbook overfit signature. The single DecisionTree at 38.9919 train / 67.6549 val is bad on both — a depth-8 axis-aligned staircase cannot represent a smooth 8-dimensional linear surface. The interview sentence: "trees lost because the generating function is linear; I would expect the ordering to invert on data with interactions or thresholds."

    22.5.4   Cross-validate, then tune

    Code — cell 53: 5-fold CV on the winner 
    best_name = board.loc[0, "model"]
print("best on val:", best_name)

# Cross-validation gives a more stable estimate than a single val split
cv = KFold(n_splits=5, shuffle=True, random_state=0)
cv_rmse = -cross_val_score(fitted[best_name], train_full.drop(columns=TARGET), train_full[TARGET],
                           scoring="neg_root_mean_squared_error", cv=cv, n_jobs=-1)
print(f"5-fold CV RMSE: {cv_rmse.mean():.3f} +/- {cv_rmse.std():.3f}")

    sklearn's scorers are always "higher is better", hence neg_root_mean_squared_error and the leading minus. Passing the whole pipeline to cross_val_score is what keeps the imputer and scaler inside the fold — passing a pre-transformed matrix instead is the leak of §21.7.

    The winner is Lasso(alpha=0.1) and 5-fold CV on train+val gives RMSE 17.962 ± 0.602 . Compare that spread to the gaps at the top of the leaderboard: positions 1, 2 and 3 are separated by 0.015 RMSE, well inside a ±0.602 fold-to-fold standard deviation. They are tied. Announcing Lasso as "the best model" on a 0.015 margin is exactly the over-claim a good interviewer probes; the defensible statement is "the three linear models are indistinguishable, I will take the penalised one for stability".

    Code — cell 55: GridSearchCV for Ridge, RandomizedSearchCV for RF 
    # GridSearchCV = exhaustive (use when the grid is small)
ridge_grid = GridSearchCV(
    Pipeline([("pre", preprocess), ("model", Ridge(random_state=0))]),
    param_grid={"model__alpha": [0.01, 0.1, 1, 10, 50, 100]},
    scoring="neg_root_mean_squared_error", cv=cv, n_jobs=-1,
).fit(X_tr, y_tr)
print("Ridge best:", ridge_grid.best_params_, f"CV RMSE={-ridge_grid.best_score_:.3f}")

# RandomizedSearchCV = sample the space (use when the grid is big / time is short)
rf_search = RandomizedSearchCV(
    Pipeline([("pre", preprocess_tree), ("model", RandomForestRegressor(random_state=0, n_jobs=-1))]),
    param_distributions={
        "model__n_estimators":     [200, 400, 600],
        "model__max_depth":        [None, 8, 14, 20],
        "model__min_samples_leaf": [1, 2, 4, 8],
        "model__max_features":     ["sqrt", 0.5, 1.0],
    },
    n_iter=12, scoring="neg_root_mean_squared_error", cv=3, n_jobs=-1, random_state=0,
).fit(X_tr, y_tr)
print("RF best:", rf_search.best_params_, f"CV RMSE={-rf_search.best_score_:.3f}")

    The "step__param" double-underscore naming is the whole trick of tuning inside a pipeline — and it nests, so "pre__num__imp__strategy" tunes the imputer too. Grid when the space is small and you want exhaustiveness; randomized when it is large and you want coverage per minute — n_iter=12 here samples 12 of 144 combinations.

    Code — cell 56: grid-search HistGradientBoosting; score all three tuned models 
    # HistGradientBoosting is the fastest strong learner in plain sklearn (no xgboost/lightgbm needed)
hgb_search = GridSearchCV(
    Pipeline([("pre", preprocess_tree),
              ("model", HistGradientBoostingRegressor(random_state=0, early_stopping=True))]),
    param_grid={"model__learning_rate": [0.05, 0.1],
                "model__max_leaf_nodes": [31, 63],
                "model__min_samples_leaf": [10, 20],
                "model__l2_regularization": [0.0, 1.0]},
    scoring="neg_root_mean_squared_error", cv=3, n_jobs=-1,
).fit(X_tr, y_tr)
print("HGB best:", hgb_search.best_params_, f"CV RMSE={-hgb_search.best_score_:.3f}")

tuned = {"Ridge_tuned": ridge_grid.best_estimator_,
         "RF_tuned":    rf_search.best_estimator_,
         "HGB_tuned":   hgb_search.best_estimator_}
for k, m in tuned.items():
    report(k, y_va, m.predict(X_va))

    HistGradientBoostingRegressor is the answer to "what if xgboost is not installed" — histogram binning, native missing-value handling, and no scaling needed. best_estimator_ is already refitted on the full training set by default (refit=True), so you can predict with it immediately.

    Tuning outcomes
    searchbest paramsCV RMSEval RMSEval MAEval R²
    Ridge, grid of 6alpha = 0.1 18.032 18.13414.6320.983
    RF, 12 random drawsn_estimators=200, min_samples_leaf=1, max_features=0.5, max_depth=20 46.863 40.43431.1940.914
    HGB, grid of 16lr=0.1, max_leaf_nodes=31, min_samples_leaf=10, l2=1.0 34.558 29.19522.9610.955
    Interpretation. Tuning moved almost nothing, and that is the finding . Ridge picks the smallest useful alpha (0.1) because there is nothing to regularise away — 6 of 8 features are genuinely informative and n ≫ d, so the penalty can only add bias. The tuned RF lands at val RMSE 40.434, worse than the untuned RF's 39.8151 : the randomized search optimised 3-fold CV RMSE, a different (and noisier) objective than the single validation split, so a small reversal is expected and is not a bug. Note also the RF's CV RMSE (46.863) is far worse than its val RMSE (40.434) — 3-fold CV trains on two-thirds of the data, and trees are data-hungry. Time-management reading: the tuning in these two cells bought 0 RMSE over the untuned linear model and cost the most compute in the notebook. In a timed test, tune after the submission file exists.

    22.5.5   Diagnostics — where is the error coming from?

    Code — cell 58: pick the final model; actual-vs-predicted, residual and histogram panels 
    import matplotlib
matplotlib.use("Agg")
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt

final_name = min(tuned, key=lambda k: rmse(y_va, tuned[k].predict(X_va)))
final_model = tuned[final_name]
pred_va = final_model.predict(X_va)
resid = y_va - pred_va
print("chosen:", final_name, f"| val RMSE={rmse(y_va, pred_va):.3f}")

fig, ax = plt.subplots(1, 3, figsize=(15, 4))
ax[0].scatter(pred_va, y_va, s=8, alpha=.5); ax[0].plot(*[[y_va.min(), y_va.max()]] * 2, "r--")
ax[0].set_xlabel("predicted"); ax[0].set_ylabel("actual"); ax[0].set_title("Actual vs Predicted")
ax[1].scatter(pred_va, resid, s=8, alpha=.5); ax[1].axhline(0, color="r", ls="--")
ax[1].set_xlabel("predicted"); ax[1].set_ylabel("residual"); ax[1].set_title("Residuals (want: no pattern)")
ax[2].hist(resid, bins=40); ax[2].set_title("Residual distribution (want: centred, symmetric)")
plt.tight_layout(); plt.show()

    Three panels, three questions: is it calibrated (points on the 45° line), is there structure left (residuals vs fitted should be a formless band — a funnel is heteroscedasticity, a curve is a missing non-linearity, §2), are the errors symmetric (a skewed residual histogram usually means the target should have been log-transformed). Selecting final_name with min(...) rather than hard-coding it is the habit that survives a re-run on different data.

    Interpretation (the section carries no figures, so here are the numbers the three panels encode). The chosen model is Ridge_tuned at val RMSE 18.134 . Residual mean 0.2243 against a residual standard deviation of 18.1475 — centred, i.e. no systematic bias; residual skew −0.0051 — symmetric, so panel 3 is the bell you want and there is nothing for a log-transform to fix; and the correlation between residual and prediction is 0.0456 — panel 2 is a formless band. Note that resid_std ≈ RMSE here because the mean residual is near zero; RMSE² = bias² + variance of the residual, so a large gap between them is itself a diagnostic.
    Code — cell 59: permutation importance 
    # Permutation importance works for ANY model and is the safe answer in an interview
perm = permutation_importance(final_model, X_va, y_va, n_repeats=5,
                              random_state=0, scoring="neg_root_mean_squared_error")
imp = (pd.DataFrame({"feature": X_va.columns, "importance": perm.importances_mean})
         .sort_values("importance", ascending=False).reset_index(drop=True))
imp.head(10)

    Model-agnostic, computed on validation data, and measured in units of the metric you care about — which is why it is the safe answer when someone asks "how do you know which features matter". Contrast with tree MDI importance, which is computed on training data and biased toward high-cardinality features.

    Code — cell 60: coefficients mapped back to encoded feature names 
    # Coefficients (linear) / feature_importances_ (trees), mapped back to encoded names
lin = Pipeline([("pre", preprocess), ("model", Ridge(alpha=1.0))]).fit(X_tr, y_tr)
names = lin.named_steps["pre"].get_feature_names_out()
coefs = pd.Series(lin.named_steps["model"].coef_, index=names).sort_values(key=np.abs, ascending=False)
coefs.head(8)

    sort_values(key=np.abs) sorts by magnitude while keeping the sign visible — the one-liner people write three lines for. Coefficients are only comparable across features because the pipeline standardised them first; on raw units they measure the unit, not the effect.

    Permutation importance (val, RMSE units) beside standardised Ridge coefficients
    featurepermutation importanceRidge coefficient
    num_2109.869592.1298
    num_188.580274.8927
    num_045.445643.4791
    num_632.534235.4496
    num_530.164629.9395
    num_419.619824.7131
    cat_a5.554916.5650 (level a)
    num_30.0016—

    Interpretation. The two rankings agree on the top six, which is the reassuring case — a disagreement would mean either collinearity (coefficients unstable) or a non-linear effect the linear model is not seeing. Read the bottom three rows carefully: num_3, num_7 and cat_b have importances of 0.0016, −0.0205 and −0.0363 . Negative permutation importance means shuffling the column made the model slightly better, i.e. the column carries no signal and its contribution is noise; it is the correct read, not a bug. And the fixture agrees: make_regression(n_features=8, n_informative=6) built exactly two uninformative columns, and cat_b was never used in the target formula — the two are num_3 and num_7. The diagnostic recovered the ground truth exactly. cat_a, which does shift the target by up to 30 units, ranks 7th with importance 5.5549: small, because its four levels are balanced and its variance contribution is modest next to six informative Gaussian features.

    22.5.6   Feature engineering, target transforms and blending

    Code — cell 62: interactions, ratios, missingness flags; polynomial features 
    def add_features(d: pd.DataFrame) -> pd.DataFrame:
    d = d.copy()
    d["num_0_x_1"]  = d["num_0"] * d["num_1"]            # interaction
    d["num_0_sq"]   = d["num_0"] ** 2                     # non-linearity
    d["ratio_2_5"]  = d["num_2"] / (d["num_5"].abs() + 1e-6)
    d["num_sum"]    = d[[f"num_{i}" for i in range(8)]].sum(axis=1)
    d["num_3_isna"] = d["num_3"].isna().astype(int)       # missingness flag
    return d

Xtr_f, Xva_f = add_features(X_tr), add_features(X_va)
num_f = Xtr_f.select_dtypes(include=np.number).columns.tolist()
pre_f = ColumnTransformer([
    ("num", SimpleImputer(strategy="median"), num_f),
    ("cat", Pipeline([("imp", SimpleImputer(strategy="most_frequent")),
                      ("oh",  OneHotEncoder(handle_unknown="ignore", sparse_output=False))]), cat_cols)])

fe_model = Pipeline([("pre", pre_f),
                     ("model", HistGradientBoostingRegressor(random_state=0))]).fit(Xtr_f, y_tr)
report("HGB + engineered features", y_va, fe_model.predict(Xva_f))

# Polynomial features for linear models (degree 2 only — degree 3 explodes)
from sklearn.preprocessing import PolynomialFeatures
poly = Pipeline([("pre", preprocess),
                 ("poly", PolynomialFeatures(degree=2, include_bias=False)),
                 ("model", Ridge(alpha=10))]).fit(X_tr, y_tr)
report("Ridge + poly(2)", y_va, poly.predict(X_va))

    Note the + 1e-6 in the denominator — engineered ratios are the number-one source of inf in a submission file, and one inf makes every sklearn estimator raise. add_features being a function applied to train and val separately is what stops the engineering itself becoming a leak.

    Code — cell 64: target transform via TransformedTargetRegressor, and a blend 
    # Target transform, done correctly (TransformedTargetRegressor handles the inverse for you)
from sklearn.compose import TransformedTargetRegressor
shifted = y_tr - y_tr.min() + 1                     # log1p needs non-negative input
ttr = TransformedTargetRegressor(
    regressor=Pipeline([("pre", preprocess_tree), ("model", HistGradientBoostingRegressor(random_state=0))]),
    func=np.log1p, inverse_func=np.expm1).fit(X_tr, shifted)
pred_back = ttr.predict(X_va) + y_tr.min() - 1
report("HGB on log1p(target)", y_va, pred_back)

# Simple blend of the tuned models
blend_va = np.mean([m.predict(X_va) for m in tuned.values()], axis=0)
report("BLEND (mean of 3 tuned)", y_va, blend_va)

    TransformedTargetRegressor exists so you cannot forget the inverse — the mistake it prevents (scoring RMSE on the log scale, or reporting expm1-free predictions) is worth the whole question. The manual + y_tr.min() - 1 undoes the shift that made the target non-negative; if you shift, write the un-shift on the same screen.

    The four "unlock the RMSE" attempts, against the untouched references
    attemptval RMSEval MAEval R²verdict
    Ridge_tuned (reference) 18.13414.6320.983the model to beat
    Ridge + poly(2) 18.60414.9720.982worse — 120 spurious terms
    HGB plain (reference) 29.21422.6260.955—
    HGB + engineered features 26.62820.9240.963helps HGB by 2.59, still far behind Ridge
    HGB on log1p(target) 31.72923.9600.947worse — target was already symmetric
    Blend of the 3 tuned 25.47320.0700.966worse than its own best member
    Every one of the kit's "usual RMSE unlocks" fails here — and each failure has a diagnosable cause. Polynomial expansion takes the 15 encoded columns to 135 , i.e. it adds 120 squares and pairwise products to a problem that is exactly linear: pure variance, no bias reduction, hence 18.604 > 18.134. The log-target transform hurts (31.729 against 29.214) because the residual skew was already −0.0051 — a transform that fixes skew can only damage a symmetric target. The blend hurts most instructively: averaging Ridge (18.134) with RF (40.434) and HGB (29.195) gives 25.473, worse than the best member, because a mean is only a good combiner when the members are comparably good and their errors are uncorrelated. Rule: blend models that are close on the leaderboard, never a winner with two losers. Feature engineering is the one that works, and only for the model that could not see the interactions itself. The lesson to carry into the test is not "these techniques do not work" — it is that you find out by measuring on validation, one change at a time, and you keep the change only if the number moves.

    If you still cannot beat the threshold, the kit's checklist: (1) is the metric right — RMSE on the original scale, so np.expm1 before scoring if you trained on log1p(y); (2) any leakage of the target into the features (an ID that encodes the target, a post-outcome column); (3) are train/val/test preprocessed identically — fit on train, transform the rest; (4) is the target skewed — train on log1p(y) and invert; (5) are outliers in y dominating the squared error — clip extreme targets or try HuberRegressor; (6) try HistGradientBoostingRegressor with a lower learning rate and more iterations; (7) blend the top 2–3 models.

    22.5.7   Refit on train+val, predict test, write the submission

    Code — cell 66: clone, refit on all labelled data, write submission.csv 
    from sklearn.base import clone

X_full, y_full = train_full.drop(columns=TARGET), train_full[TARGET]

# clone() copies the winning pipeline's *settings* without its fitted state, so the refit
# on train+val is clean. Never hard-code the model name here — take whatever won on val.
final = clone(final_model).fit(X_full, y_full)
test_pred = final.predict(test_features)
print("refit model:", final_name)

submission = pd.DataFrame({"id": test_features.index, "prediction": test_pred})
submission.to_csv("submission.csv", index=False)

print(submission.head(), "\nrows:", len(submission))
print(f"\n[only possible because this is synthetic] true test RMSE = {rmse(y_test_true, test_pred):.3f}")
print(f"baseline test RMSE = {rmse(y_test_true, np.full(len(y_test_true), y_full.mean())):.3f}")

    clone() then .fit() is the safe refit: same hyperparameters, no leftover fitted state. index=False in to_csv is the difference between a file the grader's harness reads and one it rejects — and printing submission.head() plus the row count is how you prove, in the notebook, that the format is right.

    Interpretation. Refit on all 2400 labelled rows, the submission is 600 rows — matching test_features exactly — and the true test RMSE is 17.897 against a test baseline of 142.881 . Two numbers worth internalising. First, test RMSE (17.897) came in below validation RMSE (18.134) — not because the model improved on unseen data, but because both are noisy estimates from 600 rows and the difference is well inside the ±0.602 fold-to-fold spread measured earlier. Do not report that gap as a finding. Second, the refit on train+val bought 0.05 RMSE over predicting with the train-only fit (17.947 ): a real but tiny gain, because 1800 rows was already plenty for 10 features. On a smaller or wider dataset that same step is worth much more — which is why it stays in the recipe.

    22.5.8   If the question turns out to be classification

    Same skeleton, different estimator and metrics. Two things that specifically earn marks: class_weight="balanced" for imbalance, and tuning the decision threshold instead of accepting 0.5.

    Code — cell 68: logistic regression pipeline and the full metric set 
    from sklearn.linear_model import LogisticRegression
from sklearn.ensemble import RandomForestClassifier, HistGradientBoostingClassifier
from sklearn.metrics import (accuracy_score, precision_score, recall_score, f1_score,
                             roc_auc_score, confusion_matrix, classification_report,
                             precision_recall_curve, roc_curve)
from sklearn.model_selection import StratifiedKFold

y_bin_tr = (y_tr > y_tr.median()).astype(int)
y_bin_va = (y_va > y_tr.median()).astype(int)

clf = Pipeline([("pre", preprocess),
                ("model", LogisticRegression(max_iter=2000, class_weight="balanced"))]).fit(X_tr, y_bin_tr)

proba = clf.predict_proba(X_va)[:, 1]
pred = (proba >= 0.5).astype(int)
print("accuracy :", round(accuracy_score(y_bin_va, pred), 4))
print("precision:", round(precision_score(y_bin_va, pred), 4))
print("recall   :", round(recall_score(y_bin_va, pred), 4))
print("f1       :", round(f1_score(y_bin_va, pred), 4))
print("roc_auc  :", round(roc_auc_score(y_bin_va, proba), 4))
print("\nconfusion matrix [[TN FP],[FN TP]]:\n", confusion_matrix(y_bin_va, pred))

    Note the binarisation uses y_tr's median for both splits — using each split's own median would be a leak, and a subtle one. max_iter=2000 is there because the default 100 does not converge on scaled data of this size; a convergence warning in your notebook reads as carelessness.

    Code — cell 69: threshold tuning on the precision-recall curve 
    # Threshold tuning: pick the cut-off that maximises F1 rather than defaulting to 0.5
prec, rec, thr = precision_recall_curve(y_bin_va, proba)
f1s = 2 * prec * rec / (prec + rec + 1e-12)
best_i = int(np.nanargmax(f1s[:-1]))
print(f"best threshold={thr[best_i]:.3f} -> F1={f1s[best_i]:.4f} (vs {f1_score(y_bin_va, pred):.4f} at 0.5)")

# Imbalanced data toolkit, briefly:
#   class_weight="balanced" (LogReg, RF, SVC)  -> reweight the loss
#   scale_pos_weight = n_neg/n_pos             -> xgboost/lightgbm
#   stratify=y in train_test_split, StratifiedKFold in CV
#   score with roc_auc / average_precision, NOT accuracy
print(classification_report(y_bin_va, (proba >= thr[best_i]).astype(int), digits=3))

    f1s[:-1] — precision_recall_curve returns one more precision/recall point than it returns thresholds, so the last element has no threshold and indexing thr[best_i] would go out of range without the slice. The + 1e-12 guards the all-zeros-prediction endpoint where precision and recall are both 0.

    Interpretation. At the default 0.5 cut-off: accuracy 0.9550, precision 0.9667, recall 0.9446, F1 0.9555, ROC-AUC 0.9943, confusion matrix [[283, 10], [17, 290]] . Moving the threshold to 0.306 raises F1 to 0.9603 from 0.9555 — a gain of 0.0047 . Small, and honestly so: the classes here are balanced by construction (a median split) and the model is already excellent, which is precisely the regime where threshold tuning has least to offer. Say the mechanism anyway — lowering the threshold trades precision for recall, and the optimum sits below 0.5 whenever recall is the scarcer of the two. On a 99:1 fraud problem the same move is worth tens of F1 points, and there class_weight="balanced" and PR-AUC replace accuracy entirely.
    Threshold tuning on validation is a fit. The 0.306 above was chosen by maximising F1 on the same validation rows the F1 is then reported on, so 0.9603 is optimistic in exactly the way §21.7 describes. In a test, say so, or pick the threshold on an inner fold. It is the cheapest sentence of methodological credit available in the whole paper.

    22.6   Cheat sheets

    22.6.1   The 25 pandas calls that cover most of a test

    Skim this the morning of the test
    #CallWhat it is for
    1pd.read_csv(f, sep=",", parse_dates=["d"], dtype={"id": str}, na_values=["N/A", "?", ""])read, typing and null-marking in one shot
    2df.shape / df.info() / df.describe(include="all") / df.head()first look
    3df.isna().sum() / df.duplicated().sum() / df.nunique() / df["c"].value_counts(dropna=False)the profile block
    4pd.concat([a, b], ignore_index=True)stack rows
    5a.merge(b, on="k", how="left", validate="m:1", indicator=True)join, asserted
    6df.assign(new=lambda d: ...)chainable new column
    7np.where(cond, x, y) / np.select([c1, c2], [v1, v2], default=v3)conditional columns
    8df.groupby("g", as_index=False).agg(x=("c", "sum"), y=("c", "nunique"))named aggregation
    9df.groupby("g")["c"].transform("mean")broadcast back to rows
    10df.groupby("g")["c"].rank(ascending=False)top-N per group
    11pd.pivot_table(df, index=, columns=, values=, aggfunc=, fill_value=0)long → wide
    12df.melt(id_vars=, var_name=, value_name=)wide → long
    13s.unstack() / s.stack() / pd.crosstab(a, b, normalize="index")index-side reshape, contingency
    14df.sort_values([...], ascending=[...]) / df.nlargest(n, "c")ordering
    15df.loc[mask, cols] / df.query("a > 1 and b == 'x'") / df["c"].isin([...]) / .between(lo, hi)selection
    16pd.to_numeric(s, errors="coerce") / pd.to_datetime(s, format="mixed", errors="coerce")dtype repair
    17s.str.strip().str.lower().str.replace(r"\D", "", regex=True).str.extract(r"(\d+)")string cleaning
    18s.dt.year / .dt.month / .dt.day_name() / .dt.to_period("M")date parts
    19df.drop_duplicates(subset=[...], keep="last")dedupe by key
    20df.fillna(v) / df.dropna(subset=[...]) / s.ffill() / s.interpolate()missing values
    21s.clip(lo, hi) / pd.cut(s, bins) / pd.qcut(s, q)winsorise and bin
    22df.groupby("g")["c"].shift(1) / .diff() / .pct_change() / .rolling(3).mean() / .cumsum()time-series columns
    23df.set_index("d").resample("M").sum()resample
    24pd.merge_asof(a, b, on="t", direction="backward")as-of join
    25df.to_csv("out.csv", index=False)write the submission

    22.6.2   numpy essentials

    The numpy calls a pandas question still needs
    #CallWhen
    1a.reshape(-1, 1) / a.reshape(3, -1)sklearn wants 2-D; -1 means "infer this axis"
    2a.ravel() / a.flatten()collapse to 1-D — ravel is a view, flatten a copy
    3a.Ttranspose; the fix for a shape error that is off by a swap
    4np.concatenate([a, b], axis=0)join arrays along an existing axis
    5np.vstack([a, b]) / np.hstack([a, b])stack rows / columns without thinking about axis
    6np.where(cond, x, y)vectorised if-else, two branches
    7np.select([c1, c2], [v1, v2], default=v3)vectorised if-elif-else, more than two branches
    8np.clip(a, lo, hi)winsorise; cap an impossible range
    9np.percentile(a, [1, 50, 99]) / np.quantile(a, .99)fence values for outlier rules
    10np.nanmean(a) / np.nansum / np.nanstdthe same statistic when NaNs are present and must be skipped
    11np.argsort(a) / np.argmax / np.argminyou need the position, not the value — top-k, best fold
    12np.unique(a, return_counts=True)levels and their frequencies on a raw array
    13np.isnan(a) / np.isclose(a, b)never test NaN or a float with ==
    14np.log1p(a) / np.expm1(a)log transform that tolerates 0, and its exact inverse
    15broadcasting rule: compare shapes right-to-left; each pair must be equal or one of them 1(n, 3) with (3,) works; (n, 3) with (n,) does not — reshape to (n, 1)

    Row 15 is the one that costs minutes rather than marks. When a numpy operation raises operands could not be broadcast together, print both shapes and align them right-to-left before changing anything: nine times in ten the fix is a single [:, None].

    22.6.3   pandas: transform and reshape

    Column surgery and layout changes, in the order you tend to need them
    #CallWhen
    1df.astype({"id": "int32", "city": "category"})fix dtypes in bulk; category for low-cardinality text
    2df.assign(new=lambda d: ...)add columns without breaking the chain
    3s.map({"a": 1, "b": 2})dictionary lookup; unmapped values become NaN (usually what you want)
    4s.replace({"bengaluru": "bangalore"})collapse synonyms, leaving everything else alone
    5pd.cut(s, bins=[0, 200, 500])bin on fixed edges you choose
    6pd.qcut(s, 10, labels=False, duplicates="drop")bin into equal counts — deciles
    7pd.get_dummies(df, columns=[...], drop_first=True)quick one-hot outside a pipeline; drop_first only for linear models
    8a.merge(b, on="k", how="left", validate="m:1")join, with the cardinality asserted
    9pd.concat([a, b], ignore_index=True)stack rows; axis=1 to stack columns (aligns on index!)
    10pd.pivot_table(df, index=, columns=, values=, aggfunc=)long → wide with aggregation
    11df.melt(id_vars=, var_name=, value_name=)wide → long
    12s.unstack() / df.stack()the same move on the index instead of the columns
    13df.explode("tags")one list-valued cell becomes one row per element
    14df.duplicated(subset=[...], keep=False).sum()count every row involved in a duplication, not just the copies
    15s.value_counts(normalize=True, dropna=False)level shares with nulls visible — the single most useful profiling call
    16df.query("a > 1 and b == 'x'")readable filter without the parentheses & demands
    17df.nlargest(5, "revenue") / nsmallesttop-k rows, faster and clearer than sort-then-head

    22.6.4   The missingness toolkit

    Detect, decide, fill — and the arguments that change the answer
    #CallWhen
    1df.isna().sum() / df.isna().mean()counts, then rates — the rate is the one you report
    2df["c"].notna().mean()parse rate after a to_numeric/to_datetime coercion
    3df["c_was_na"] = df["c"].isna().astype("int8")the indicator — create it before any fill (§22.2.8)
    4s.fillna(value)fill with a constant or a statistic you computed on train
    5s.fillna(s.median()) vs s.fillna(s.mean())median when skewed or outlier-prone (the test-day default); mean when symmetric
    6g["c"].transform(lambda s: s.fillna(s.median()))group-wise fill — the MAR repair of §22.2.8; chain .fillna(global) for empty groups
    7s.ffill(limit=2) / s.bfill(limit=2)carry forward/back in a sorted time series; limit stops a stale value propagating forever
    8df.dropna(subset=["y"])drop rows missing the target — almost always right
    9df.dropna(thresh=5)keep rows with at least 5 non-null values, instead of all-or-nothing
    10df.dropna(axis=1, thresh=int(0.3 * len(df)))drop columns that are more than 70% empty
    11s.interpolate(method="linear", limit_direction="both")fill an interior gap in a numeric series by straight line
    12s.interpolate(method="time")the time-series one: interpolates proportionally to the actual elapsed time — requires a DatetimeIndex, and differs from "linear" whenever the index is unevenly spaced
    13SimpleImputer(strategy="median") inside a ColumnTransformerthe leakage-safe version of rows 4–6 (§22.2.7)
    14KNNImputer / IterativeImputerwhen columns are correlated and the fill is worth the time; scale first for KNN
    15leave it as NaNxgboost, LightGBM and HistGradientBoosting learn a default direction per split — imputing first throws that information away

    Row 12 is the row people miss. method="linear" ignores the index entirely and spaces the fill evenly by position, so on a series with a five-day hole it fills as though the gap were one step wide; method="time" weights by the real interval. On an evenly-spaced daily index they are identical, which is why the bug survives testing (§22.3.7).

    22.6.5   The sklearn skeleton — memorise this shape

    pre = ColumnTransformer([
    ("num", Pipeline([("imp", SimpleImputer(strategy="median")),
                      ("sc",  StandardScaler())]), num_cols),
    ("cat", Pipeline([("imp", SimpleImputer(strategy="most_frequent")),
                      ("oh",  OneHotEncoder(handle_unknown="ignore",
                                            sparse_output=False))]), cat_cols),
])
pipe = Pipeline([("pre", pre), ("model", Ridge())])
gs = GridSearchCV(pipe, {"model__alpha": [0.1, 1, 10]},
                  scoring="neg_root_mean_squared_error", cv=5, n_jobs=-1).fit(X_tr, y_tr)
rmse = np.sqrt(mean_squared_error(y_va, gs.predict(X_va)))

    Nine lines. They are the same nine lines as §21.7's master pipeline with the selector removed and the estimator swapped for a regressor — refer to that box for the classification form, the feature-selection slot (SelectKBest / SelectFromModel / RFECV) and the reason the whole thing must sit inside GridSearchCV rather than around it.

    Which metric, and its sklearn scoring string
