    22.6.7   Gotchas that cost marks

    Each row re-tested on pandas 2.3.3 / scikit-learn 1.9.0
    GotchaThe fixVerified behaviour
    SettingWithCopyWarning — you sliced, then assigned .loc[mask, col] = v, or .copy() first —
    df.append no longer existspd.concat hasattr(pd.DataFrame, "append") is False
    inplace=True is not faster and breaks chainingavoid it—
    Merging on columns of different dtypes (int64 vs object) cast the key first adjudicated: it does not match silently — pandas raises ValueError: You are trying to merge on int64 and object columns
    groupby drops NaN keys by defaultgroupby(..., dropna=False) 1 group vs 2 groups on the same 3-row frame
    Float equalitynp.isclose, not == 0.1 + 0.2 == 0.3 is False; np.isclose is True
    Chained indexing df[df.a > 1]["b"] = 0 does nothinga single .loc chained form left the column untouched; .loc form wrote [0, 99, 99]
    Fitting a scaler/imputer on the full dataset before splitting = leakage everything that learns goes inside the fold the leaked statistic is visible: num_3 median −0.0765 (train) vs −0.0483 (all) ; §21.7 measures the damage
    OneHotEncoder without handle_unknown="ignore" set it, always raises ValueError on an unseen level; "ignore" emits all-zeros
    Scoring RMSE on a transformed target without inverting TransformedTargetRegressorsee §22.5.6
    One row of the kit's gotcha list is wrong, and it matters. The kit writes that merging on columns with different dtypes "silently matches nothing". On pandas 2.3.3 it does the opposite: merge raises ValueError: You are trying to merge on int64 and object columns for key 'k' . The advice — cast the key first — is still right; the failure mode is loud, not silent, which is better news than the kit thought. The genuinely silent version of this bug is different and still real: keys that are both strings but differ in whitespace or case ("A1 " vs "A1") match nothing and raise nothing. That is what indicator=True is for.

    22.6.8   Statistics one-liners

    from scipy import stats
stats.ttest_ind(a, b, equal_var=False)        # two-sample t-test (Welch)
stats.ttest_rel(before, after)                # paired t-test
stats.ttest_1samp(x, popmean=0)
stats.chi2_contingency(pd.crosstab(a, b))     # independence of two categoricals
stats.shapiro(x) / stats.normaltest(x)        # normality
stats.levene(a, b)                            # equal variance
stats.mannwhitneyu(a, b)                      # non-parametric two-sample
stats.ks_2samp(a, b)                          # same distribution?
stats.pearsonr(x, y) / stats.spearmanr(x, y)
stats.norm.cdf(z) / stats.norm.ppf(0.975)     # 1.959964

    — and stats.norm.ppf(0.975) does return 1.959964 , the number behind every 95% interval you will ever quote.

    Reading a hypothesis test: p < α ⇒ reject H₀. Type I = false positive (reject a true H₀, probability α); Type II = false negative (probability β; power = 1 − β). Linear regression assumptions, asked in almost every one of these interviews: linearity, independence of errors, homoscedasticity, normality of residuals, no perfect multicollinearity — checked with residual plots, Durbin–Watson, Breusch–Pagan, a Q–Q plot, and VIF (VIF > 5–10 ⇒ multicollinearity). Ridge vs Lasso: both add a penalty to shrink coefficients; Ridge (L2, α·Σβ²) shrinks toward zero but never to zero, which suits correlated predictors, while Lasso (L1, α·Σ|β|) can set coefficients exactly to zero and so performs selection; ElasticNet mixes both. Conditional probability: P(A|B) = P(A∩B)/P(B), Bayes P(A|B) = P(B|A)P(A)/P(B) — for the classic disease/test question, build the 2×2 table with a concrete population of 100,000 rather than manipulating symbols under time pressure.

    Code — cell 71: the VIF snippet interviewers ask about 
    # VIF — the exact snippet interviewers ask about
def vif_table(X: pd.DataFrame) -> pd.DataFrame:
    from sklearn.linear_model import LinearRegression
    Xn = X.select_dtypes(include=np.number).dropna()
    rows = []
    for c in Xn.columns:
        r2 = LinearRegression().fit(Xn.drop(columns=c), Xn[c]).score(Xn.drop(columns=c), Xn[c])
        rows.append({"feature": c, "VIF": np.inf if r2 >= 1 else 1 / (1 - r2)})
    return pd.DataFrame(rows).sort_values("VIF", ascending=False)

vif_table(train.drop(columns=TARGET)).head()

    VIFj = 1/(1 − R²j) where R²j regresses feature j on all the others — being able to say that sentence is the answer, and this five-line implementation proves you mean it without needing statsmodels. The np.inf guard handles a perfectly collinear column, where R² = 1 and the division would blow up.

    Code — cell 72: correlation screen for multicollinearity 
    # Correlation screen for multicollinearity (faster first pass than VIF)
corr = train.select_dtypes(include=np.number).corr(numeric_only=True)
high = (corr.where(np.triu(np.ones(corr.shape), k=1).astype(bool))
            .stack().rename("corr").reset_index()
            .query("abs(corr) > 0.7"))
print("pairs with |corr| > 0.7:", len(high))
corr.round(2).iloc[:5, :5]

    The np.triu(..., k=1) mask keeps the strict upper triangle, so each pair is counted once and the diagonal of 1.0s does not flood the result — that masking line is the part worth memorising.

    Interpretation. Maximum VIF across the eight features is 1.0103 and the correlation screen finds 0 pairs above 0.7 . Both say the same thing — num_* came from make_regression, which draws independent Gaussians — and VIF ≈ 1 is the "no collinearity at all" reading, since VIF = 1/(1 − R²) equals 1 exactly when a feature is unpredictable from the others. But look at the screen as written: its maximum off-diagonal |corr| is 0.6844 , and that pair is num_2 with target , because train.select_dtypes(include=np.number) includes the target column. Among features only, the maximum is 0.0615 . A collinearity screen that includes the target is measuring signal, not collinearity, and on a dataset with one strong predictor it would raise a false alarm every time. Drop the target first.
    Code — cell 73: Welch t-test, chi-square, confidence interval 
    from scipy import stats

a = np.random.normal(100, 15, 200)
b = np.random.normal(104, 15, 200)

t, p = stats.ttest_ind(a, b, equal_var=False)
print(f"Welch t-test: t={t:.3f}, p={p:.4f} -> {'reject H0' if p < .05 else 'fail to reject H0'} at 5%")

tab = pd.crosstab(np.random.choice(["A", "B"], 300), np.random.choice(["yes", "no"], 300))
chi2, p2, dof, _ = stats.chi2_contingency(tab)
print(f"Chi-square: chi2={chi2:.3f}, dof={dof}, p={p2:.4f}")

print("95% CI for mean(a):",
      np.round(stats.t.interval(0.95, len(a) - 1, loc=a.mean(), scale=stats.sem(a)), 3))

    equal_var=False (Welch) should be your default two-sample t-test — it costs nothing when variances are equal and saves you when they are not. stats.sem is the standard error of the mean, s/√n, which is the only fiddly part of a confidence interval.

    An honest re-run that flips the verdict. The kit's saved output reports "reject H0 at 5%". Re-drawing the two samples gives t = −1.947, p = 0.0522 , which fails to reject at 5% . Nothing is broken: the true means differ by 4 with σ = 15 and n = 200 per group, giving a genuine effect that this design detects only about half the time, so p straddles 0.05 across draws. That is a power statement, and it is the right thing to say in an interview — "p = 0.0522 with n = 200 per arm; the study is underpowered for a 4-point difference", not "the means are the same". The chi-square on two independent random columns behaves as it must: χ² = 0.009, dof = 1, p = 0.9233 , and the 95% CI for mean(a) is [98.959, 102.991] , which covers the true 100.

    22.7   Test-day operating procedure

    The two hours, in order.
    1. Read all three questions first (2 min). Note the exact output format each one wants.
    2. Q1 first, Q3 second, Q2 last if time is tight — Q3 carries the pass/fail test-cases, and a half-cleaned dataset still trains a model.
    3. After every transformation, print(df.shape). Silent row loss from an inner join is the most common self-inflicted failure — and §22.1.2's cell-6 landmine is the version of it that loses the whole table.
    4. Write the submission file early with a baseline model, then overwrite it as you improve. You never want zero output at the buzzer.
    5. Docs are allowed: help(pd.merge), pd.DataFrame.groupby?, dir(pd.Series.str) in a cell beats trying to recall an argument name.
    6. Leave 5 minutes to re-run the notebook top-to-bottom (Kernel → Restart & Run All). A notebook that only works out of order is a notebook that fails their test harness.
    Section recap. Three questions, three habits. Q1 is stack → join → derive → aggregate → reshape, and every step is checked by a row count: 1150 in, 1150 after three joins , pivot grand total equal to net_rev.sum() . Q2 is profile → dtypes → categories → duplicates → impossible values → missing → re-profile, and the re-profile is not optional: null rates here more than tripled between the two profiles because domain rules turned junk into honest NaN . Q3 is baseline → bake-off → CV → tune → refit → submit, with the baseline (137.646 ) established before any model and the submission written before any tuning; here the untuned Lasso at 18.1221 was never beaten by anything that followed, and the final test RMSE was 17.897 against a test baseline of 142.881 . And two habits that cut across all three: the datetime block of §22.3 — dtype → to_datetime(coerce) → sort → parts → durations → cyclical → lag/rolling, with the parse rate printed at step two — and, if the question turns out to be a forecast, the time discipline of §22.4: split on dates, cross-validate forward (shuffled 5-fold read 20% low here ), beat the seasonal naive before claiming anything , and remember that a tree predicts a constant above the largest target it has ever seen . Everything in this section rests on one structural rule imported from §21.7: anything that learns from the data lives inside the pipeline, and the pipeline lives inside the cross-validation — the same rule §14 states for SMOTE, §22.2.8 states for imputation, and §22.4.1 states for a rolling window.

    22.8   Practice

    Practice 22.1 — Three tables: 6 orders, a 3-row customer lookup, a 3-row product lookup. Order A6 has cust_id = 4 and prod_id = 99, neither of which is in a lookup. Produce revenue by region, and say what you would have lost with an inner join.

    The data. orders: A1(cust 1, prod 10, 2 units), A2(2, 11, 1), A3(1, 12, 5), A4(3, 10, 3), A5(2, 12, 2), A6(4, 99, 1). cust: 1→North, 2→South, 3→North. prod: 10→100.0, 11→250.0, 12→40.0.

    Step 1 — left join both lookups with an indicator, and read the indicator before anything else.

    j = (orders.merge(cust, on="cust_id", how="left", indicator="m_cust")
           .merge(prod,  on="prod_id", how="left", indicator="m_prod"))
j.loc[j["m_cust"] != "both", "order_id"].tolist()   # -> ['A6']
j.loc[j["m_prod"] != "both", "order_id"].tolist()   # -> ['A6']

    Exactly one order, A6, fails both joins . The left join keeps all 6 rows ; an inner join would return 5 , silently deleting 1 order — one order in six, with no error message. That is the answer to the second half of the question: with an inner join you would never learn that A6 exists, and the row-count check (6 in, 5 out) is the only thing that would have told you.

    Step 2 — derive, then aggregate on the rows that can be attributed.

    j["revenue"] = j["units"] * j["price"]
agg = (j.dropna(subset=["region"])
         .groupby("region", as_index=False)
         .agg(orders=("order_id", "nunique"), units=("units", "sum"), revenue=("revenue", "sum"))
         .sort_values("revenue", ascending=False))
    regionordersunitsrevenue
    North310700.00
    South23330.00

    Check it by hand: North = A1 (2 × 100) + A3 (5 × 40) + A4 (3 × 100) = 200 + 200 + 300 = 700; South = A2 (1 × 250) + A5 (2 × 40) = 250 + 80 = 330. Total attributed revenue 1030.00 , North's share 67.96% .

    Step 3 — the sentence that earns the mark. One row has revenue = NaN because price did not join, and it is excluded from the aggregate by dropna(subset=["region"]). So report: "Revenue is attributed for 5 of 6 orders; order A6 references an unknown customer (4) and an unknown product (99) and is excluded. It should be raised as a data-quality issue rather than silently dropped." Note that groupby would have dropped the NaN region anyway — the explicit dropna is there so that the decision is visible in the code rather than being a default you did not notice (§22.6.7).

    Practice 22.2 — Clean this 8-row frame: id 1–7 with 3 repeated, city in six spellings including "?", amount as text with commas / "N/A" / a negative, signup in three formats plus "not known", and age containing 199 and −3. State every decision.

    The frame. city: "Delhi ", "delhi", "MUMBAI", "?", None, "Mumbai", "Bengaluru", "MUMBAI"; amount: "1,200", " 950 ", "N/A", "3,400", "880", None, "-50", "N/A"; signup: "2023-01-05", "05/02/2023", "not known", "2023-03-11", None, "2023-04-02", "2023-05-20", "not known"; age: 34, 199, 28, -3, 41, 37, NaN, 28.

    Order of operations — dtypes, then domain rules, then duplicates, then fills:

    d2 = dirty.copy()
d2["amount"] = (d2["amount"].astype("string").str.replace(r"[^0-9.\-]", "", regex=True)
                            .replace("", pd.NA).pipe(pd.to_numeric, errors="coerce"))
d2.loc[(d2["amount"] <= 0).fillna(False), "amount"] = pd.NA        # -50 is not an amount
d2["city"] = (d2["city"].astype("string").str.strip().str.lower()
                        .replace({"?": pd.NA, "bengaluru": "bangalore"}))
d2["signup"] = pd.to_datetime(d2["signup"], format="mixed", dayfirst=True, errors="coerce")
d2.loc[~d2["age"].between(0, 100), "age"] = np.nan                  # 199 and -3
d2 = d2.drop_duplicates(subset=["id"], keep="first").reset_index(drop=True)

    What each step did.

    • Duplicates: 2 rows are involved in the id duplication (id = 3 appears twice, and the two copies are identical after cleaning), so 8 rows become 7 . Here id genuinely is a key, unlike §22.2.4's cust_id — say why you believe that before deduping.
    • City: 6 spellings collapse to 3 real levels (delhi, mumbai, bangalore) with 2 nulls : "?" is a missing-value marker, not a city, and Bengaluru/Bangalore is a synonym decision you must state. After fillna("Missing") there are 4 levels .
    • Amount: the regex handles both "1,200" and " 950 "; "N/A" becomes NaN; and -50 is killed by the domain rule, not by the parser — it parses perfectly well, it is just not a legal amount. That leaves 4 parsed values and 3 missing out of 7. Median-fill (median = 1075.00 of 880, 950, 1200, 3400) after setting an amount_was_na flag, because with 3400 in a 4-value sample the mean would be dragged upward — this is exactly the "skewed ⇒ median" row of §22.2.6's table.
    • Signup: 2 NaT remain from "not known" and None. Do not impute a date; leave it missing and flag it. Also note dayfirst=True reads 05/02/2023 as 5 February — state the assumption.
    • Age: 199 and −3 go to NaN, then median-fill at 35.5 .

    Final state: amounts [1200, 950, 1075, 3400, 880, 1075, 1075] , cities [delhi, delhi, mumbai, Missing, Missing, mumbai, bangalore] , ages [34, 35.5, 28, 35.5, 41, 37, 35.5] , and 0 nulls outside signup . Note the shape of the result: 3 of 7 amounts and 3 of 7 ages are now the same imputed constant. On a real dataset that is a warning — the _was_na flags exist so a model can tell the difference between "1075" and "we did not know".

    Practice 22.3 — 12 rows, columns x1, x2, a categorical grp, target y. Train on the first 9, predict the last 3, and beat a test RMSE of 5.0. Which model, and what does the tree do?

    The data (x1 = 1…12; x2 = 2, 5, 4, 9, 6, 13, 8, 17, 10, 21, 12, 25; grp alternating a/b; y = 14.5, 11.0, 25.5, 31.5, 36.0, 43.5, 51.0, 60.5, 62.0, 74.5, 74.5, 92.0). Train = rows 1–9, test = rows 10–12, so the test rows sit beyond the training range of both numeric columns — that is the whole point of the drill.

    Step 1 — baseline first, always. The training mean is 37.2778 , and predicting it for all three test rows gives RMSE 43.8388 . The threshold of 5.0 is therefore asking for an 8.8-fold improvement, which tells you immediately that a real model is required, not a tweak.

    Step 2 — the same nine-line skeleton as §22.6.5.

    pre = ColumnTransformer([
    ("num", Pipeline([("imp", SimpleImputer(strategy="median")), ("sc", StandardScaler())]), ["x1", "x2"]),
    ("cat", OneHotEncoder(handle_unknown="ignore", sparse_output=False), ["grp"])])
lin = Pipeline([("pre", pre), ("model", LinearRegression())]).fit(X_tr, y_tr)
    modeltest RMSEbeats 5.0?
    DummyRegressor (train mean)43.8388no
    DecisionTree(max_depth=3)21.1699no
    Linear, x1+x2 only (no grp)4.1634yes
    Ridge(alpha=1) with grp3.0663yes
    LinearRegression with grp1.4148yes

    Answer: plain linear regression with the categorical one-hot encoded, test RMSE 1.4148 — comfortably under the 5.0 threshold and R² = 0.9706 . Predictions [76.75, 73.95, 92.80] against actuals [74.50, 74.50, 92.00] .

    Step 3 — the two things to say out loud.

    • The tree cannot extrapolate. DecisionTreeRegressor scores 21.1699 and fails the threshold , because its predictions [60.5, 62.0, 60.5] are leaf averages of training rows and can never exceed the largest training y (62.0), while the true values run to 92.0. A tree predicts a constant outside the training hull; a linear model extends the trend. This is the single best answer to "when would you not use a random forest", and it is the generalisation of the §22.5.3 leaderboard's message.
    • Ridge is worse than OLS here (3.0663 vs 1.4148), and that is expected: with 9 training rows and a clean linear signal there is no variance to trade away, so the L2 penalty buys nothing and costs bias — the shrinkage pulls the extrapolated predictions back toward the training mean, which is exactly the wrong direction when the test rows lie outside the training range. Dropping the categorical also costs you: 4.1634 without grp against 1.4148 with it , still a pass but three times the error, because grp carries a genuine ±5.59 shift .

    If the threshold had been 1.0 instead of 5.0, the next moves in order would be: check the residuals for structure (§22.5.5), add the x1 × grp interaction, and only then reach for a different model family. Not the other way round.

    Practice 22.4 — Eight transactions, three customers, timestamps as text. Build the standard datetime feature block: recency against a frozen "today", the gap since the customer's previous transaction, is_weekend, is_night, and a cyclical month encoding. Two of the features come out as zeros — say why.

    The data. cust_id 101 (three transactions), 202 (two), 303 (three); txn_time as strings: 101 → "2025-01-03 09:15:00", "2025-01-19 21:40:00", "2025-02-01 02:05:00"; 202 → "2025-03-08 14:00:00", "2025-03-09 11:30:00"; 303 → "2025-06-14 23:50:00", "2025-06-15 00:20:00", "2025-12-24 18:00:00". Reference date REF = pd.Timestamp("2026-01-01") .

    Step 1 — convert, then sort. In that order, and never skip the sort.

    df["txn_time"] = pd.to_datetime(df["txn_time"], format="%Y-%m-%d %H:%M:%S")
df = df.sort_values(["cust_id", "txn_time"]).reset_index(drop=True)

    An explicit format= costs nothing here and removes the only way this step can go wrong. The sort is what makes diff in step 2 mean anything (§22.3.4).

    Step 2 — the four feature families.

    # (a) gap since this customer's previous transaction  -- groupby -> diff -> total_seconds
df["gap"]            = df.groupby("cust_id")["txn_time"].diff()
df["gap_hours"]      = df["gap"].dt.total_seconds() / 3600
df["gap_days_whole"] = df["gap"].dt.days                       # the trap — see step 4

# (b) tenure: days since this customer's FIRST transaction
df["first_txn"]        = df.groupby("cust_id")["txn_time"].transform("min")
df["days_since_first"] = (df["txn_time"] - df["first_txn"]).dt.days

# (c) calendar flags
df["dow"]        = df["txn_time"].dt.dayofweek
df["is_weekend"] = (df["dow"] >= 5).astype(int)
df["hour"]       = df["txn_time"].dt.hour
df["is_night"]   = ((df["hour"] >= 0) & (df["hour"] < 6)).astype(int)

# (d) cyclical month
df["month"]     = df["txn_time"].dt.month
df["month_sin"] = np.sin(2 * np.pi * df["month"] / 12)
df["month_cos"] = np.cos(2 * np.pi * df["month"] / 12)

# recency: one row per customer, against a FROZEN reference date
recency = (REF - df.groupby("cust_id")["txn_time"].max()).dt.days
    The full feature block, sorted by [cust_id, txn_time]
    cust_idtxn_timegap_hoursgap_days_whole days_since_firstdowis_weekend houris_nightmonth_sinmonth_cos
    1012025-01-03 09:15——040900.50000.8660
    1012025-01-19 21:40396.421616612100.50000.8660
    1012025-02-01 02:05292.42122851210.86600.5000
    2022025-03-08 14:00——0511401.00000.0000
    2022025-03-09 11:3021.5000611101.00000.0000
    3032025-06-14 23:50——0512300.0000−1.0000
    3032025-06-15 00:200.500061010.0000−1.0000
    3032025-12-24 18:004625.6719219220180−0.00001.0000

    Step 3 — recency. Against REF = 2026-01-01, the days since each customer's last transaction are {101: 333, 202: 297, 303: 7} . Customer 303's last transaction was 2025-12-24 18:00, which is 7 days and 6 hours before the reference — .dt.days truncates to 7. Three gap cells are missing , one per customer's first row, and they must stay missing (§22.3.5).

    Step 4 — the two zero columns, which is the actual question.

    • gap_days_whole is 0 for two real gaps. Customer 303's second transaction is 30 minutes after the first , and .dt.days reports 0 ; customer 202's second is 21.5 hours later and also reports 0. .dt.days takes the whole-day component of a duration, so every sub-day gap collapses to zero (§22.3.3). On card-fraud data, where two transactions 30 minutes apart is the entire signal, that column is not merely coarse — it is constant, and a constant feature is dropped by the profiler in §22.2.1 without anyone noticing what was lost. Use total_seconds()/60 whenever the events can be closer together than a day.
    • days_since_first is 0 on customer 202's second row for the same reason (21.5 hours of tenure truncates to 0 days) — and it is correctly 0 on every customer's first row, which is a different kind of zero. Two different meanings in one column is exactly why the gap NaNs should not be filled with 0 either.

    Step 5 — read the flags. Six of eight transactions fall on a weekend and two at night . Notice customer 303's pair straddling midnight: 23:50 is is_night = 0 and 00:20 is is_night = 1, although they are 30 minutes apart. That is the boundary artefact the cyclical encoding of §22.3.6 exists to soften — and the reason to ship hour_sin/hour_cos alongside the hard flag rather than instead of it. The month encoding shows the same property at the year boundary: December is (0.0, 1.0) and January (0.5, 0.866), a distance of 0.5176 instead of the raw 11 .

    Step 6 — the sentence that earns the mark. "Recency is computed against a frozen reference date rather than pd.Timestamp.today(), so the notebook reproduces; gaps are in minutes because the events are sub-daily; first-transaction gaps are left as NaN rather than 0, because 'no previous transaction' and 'an instantaneous repeat' are opposite signals." Mean gaps per customer come out at 344.42, 21.50 and 2313.09 hours , i.e. three completely different behavioural profiles from eight rows — which is the point of the feature.

    Practice 22.5 — A single daily series, 365 observations. Build lag and rolling features, split on time, and beat the seasonal-naive RMSE with XGBoost. Then check what a shuffled 5-fold CV would have told you.

    The data. 365 daily observations from 2024-01-01, generated as 50 + 0.03·t + 5·sin(2π·doy/365.25) + weekday_effect + N(0, 2) with weekday effects [−6, −4, −2, 0, 4, 14, 11] for Monday…Sunday. The noise standard deviation of 2.0 is the RMSE floor: no model can do better, and knowing that number before you start is what stops you tuning for an hour to chase 0.3.

    Step 1 — build the supervised frame, shifting before rolling.

    df["lag_1"]      = df["sales"].shift(1)
df["lag_7"]      = df["sales"].shift(7)
df["roll7_mean"] = df["sales"].shift(1).rolling(7).mean()      # shift FIRST — §22.4.1
df["dow"]        = df["date"].dt.dayofweek
df["is_weekend"] = (df["dow"] >= 5).astype(int)
df["dow_sin"]    = np.sin(2 * np.pi * df["dow"] / 7)
df["dow_cos"]    = np.cos(2 * np.pi * df["dow"] / 7)

FEATS = ["lag_1", "lag_7", "roll7_mean", "dow", "is_weekend", "dow_sin", "dow_cos"]
m = df.dropna(subset=FEATS).reset_index(drop=True)

    The warm-up costs 7 rows , leaving 358 — lag_7 is the binding constraint, and dropping is right: a lag_7 of zero on day 3 would be a lie.

    Step 2 — split on the date, and compute the baselines first.

    cut = m["date"].max() - pd.Timedelta(days=44)     # last 45 days held out
tr, te = m[m["date"] < cut], m[m["date"] >= cut]

rmse(te["sales"], np.full(len(te), tr["sales"].mean()))   # mean baseline
rmse(te["sales"], te["lag_1"])                            # naive
rmse(te["sales"], te["lag_7"])                            # seasonal naive  <- the target

    313 training rows, 45 test rows, cut at 2024-11-16 .

    Step 3 — fit, and read the leaderboard against the floor.

    model = xgb.XGBRegressor(n_estimators=300, learning_rate=0.05, max_depth=3,
                         subsample=0.9, colsample_bytree=0.9,
                         tree_method="hist", random_state=0).fit(tr[FEATS], tr["sales"])
    predictortest RMSE (45 days)vs seasonal naive
    Train mean 8.4165+188.2%
    Naive, yt−1 9.0257+209.1%
    Seasonal naive, yt−7 2.9204—
    XGBoost, 7 features 2.7103−7.2%
    irreducible noise floor2.0000−31.5%

    Answer: 2.7103 against the seasonal-naive 2.9204, a 7.2% improvement , with predictions [69.03, 66.91, 49.35] against actuals [69.45, 68.99, 47.72] on the first three test days .

    Step 4 — the three things to say.

    • The naive baseline is worse than the mean baseline — 9.0257 against 8.4165 — which looks absurd until you see why: the weekday swing spans 20 units, so "yesterday" is systematically the wrong day of the week, and being wrong by a whole weekend is worse than being wrong by the average. Seasonal naive fixes precisely that and drops to 2.9204. Always compute all three; the ordering between them tells you what kind of series you have before you fit anything.
    • The margin over seasonal naive is small, and honestly so. The gap from 2.9204 to the floor of 2.0 is only 0.9204 RMSE of available headroom, and the model takes 0.2101 of it. Importances confirm what it learned: dow 0.518 and lag_7 0.270 — it is essentially reconstructing the seasonal naive and correcting the weekday shape, which is all there is to find. Reporting "7% better than seasonal naive, against a theoretical ceiling of 31%" is a far stronger answer than reporting 2.71 alone.
    • A shuffled 5-fold would have reported 2.4331 — better than the honest held-out 2.7103 by 0.277 , and better than the seasonal-naive baseline by 16.7% instead of 7.2%. The leak is the lag columns: a shuffled fold puts day t in training and day t+1 in validation, and day t+1's lag_1 is day t's target. Use TimeSeriesSplit (§22.4.3).

    If the drill asked you to go further: add lag_14 and a shifted 28-day mean for a better level estimate, and — because this series has a genuine upward trend — check the extrapolation diagnosis of §22.4.7 before trusting the model on a horizon much longer than 45 days.

    A self-contained interactive textbook. All figures and numerical examples are programmatically generated and verified.
